metadata.title: 1D Array (Vector)
metadata.definition: An array whose elements are arranged in a single dimension, often called a vector.

metadata.title: 2-3 Tree
metadata.definition: A type of balanced search tree (B-tree) can contain 2 or 3 keys in each node and have all leaves at the same level, used to maintain efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations.

metadata.title: 2-3-4 Tree
metadata.definition: 2-3-4 plant, a type B plant.

metadata.title: 4th-Generation Environments
metadata.definition: Learn about fourth-generation programming environments and tools, often bundled with high-level query and productivity languages.

metadata.title: A* Algorithm
metadata.definition: A best path finding algorithm prioritizes finding a path from a source vertex to a destination vertex in a graph, using a heuristic function to estimate the lowest cost from the current vertex to the destination. (An example for Handling Exponential Growth)

metadata.title: A* Heuristic
metadata.definition: A best path search algorithm prioritizes the expansion of nodes by estimating the lowest cost from the current node to the destination, commonly used in artificial intelligence and pathfinding.

metadata.title: A* Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the A* search algorithm in real-world problems, including the management of priority queues and related data structures.

metadata.title: A* Search
metadata.definition: Research on widely used informative search algorithms, combining past path costs and heuristic estimation to find optimal paths.

metadata.title: A* Search Algorithm
metadata.definition: understand and apply the A* search algorithm to plan optimal paths for robots.

metadata.title: A* Variants
metadata.definition: Research advanced versions of the A* algorithm such as IDA*, SMA*, and RBFS that are designed to address memory or time constraints.

metadata.title: A*/Beam Search Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement A* search or beam search algorithms to solve a specific problem.

metadata.title: A*/Beam vs. Other Searches
metadata.definition: Compare the performance of the A* or beam search algorithm with other search algorithms based on solution cost, number of nodes expanded, and other criteria.

metadata.title: ABC Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about the architecture and operation of the ABC machine, an abstract machine designed to execute functional programming languages, especially in the context of lazy evaluation and general data structures.

metadata.title: ACID Properties
metadata.definition: Master the four basic properties of transactions in database management systems: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

metadata.title: ACT-R Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture developed at Carnegie Mellon University, focused on modeling human cognition and learning, including memory components and modules.

metadata.title: ADT Operations
metadata.definition: Functions or methods are defined as part of an Abstract Data Type's interface, allowing interaction with the data it represents (e.g. add, delete, search).

metadata.title: AI
metadata.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) studies problems that are difficult or impractical to solve using traditional algorithmic methods.

metadata.title: AI & Data Science Link
metadata.definition: The AI ​​program includes connections to data science through cross-connections with Data Management and other fields, as well as a sample course in Data Science.

metadata.title: AI (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The field of knowledge of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the CS2023 program, is the new name of Intelligent Systems (IS) from CS2013.

metadata.title: AI Action
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that involves AI agents performing actions in their environment.

metadata.title: AI Agent Definition
metadata.definition: understand different definitions of agents in AI and specific examples.

metadata.title: AI Algorithm Advances
metadata.definition: Improvements in AI algorithms have contributed significantly to recent advances, making AI systems more efficient and powerful.

metadata.title: AI Applications
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on practical applications of AI in a variety of fields (e.g., medicine, sustainability, social media).

metadata.title: AI Applications Overview
metadata.definition: Provides an overview of fields and how AI is applied in practice, from healthcare to finance to manufacturing.

metadata.title: AI Approach Suitability
metadata.definition: The skill of determining when an AI approach is appropriate or most effective for solving a particular problem.

metadata.title: AI Apps & Societal Impact
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on the practical applications and social impact of AI. Includes 3 hours of CS Core and 3 hours of KA Core.

metadata.title: AI Architecture
metadata.definition: The organizational structures and design of AI systems.

metadata.title: AI Candidate Assessment
metadata.definition: apply AI to automatically analyze and evaluate job candidates' profiles and skills.

metadata.title: AI Code Generation
metadata.definition: The use of generative artificial intelligence models to automatically generate program code based on high-level descriptions or requirements.

metadata.title: AI Compute Power
metadata.definition: Increasing computing power is a key factor for the development of AI, allowing it to handle complex models and huge amounts of data.

metadata.title: AI Content Curation
metadata.definition: Use AI to personalize and curate news streams and social media content for users.

metadata.title: AI Control Systems
metadata.definition: Systems use AI techniques to manage, regulate and control the operation of devices, machines or processes.

metadata.title: AI Critical Thinking
metadata.definition: The clear goal is to develop critical thinking about AI in every computer science student.

metadata.title: AI Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Issues related to protecting personal information and how data is used in AI training.

metadata.title: AI Ethical Considerations
metadata.definition: Important ethical issues need to be understood and considered when developing and applying AI technology, given its potential for significant impact on society.

metadata.title: AI Ethics
metadata.definition: Ethical principles and ethical issues arise from the development and deployment of AI.

metadata.title: AI Explainability (XAI)
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that AI systems do not create or exacerbate inequality or discrimination.

metadata.title: AI Fundamentals
metadata.definition: The unit introduces the basic concepts of AI. Includes 2 hours of CS Core and 1 hour of KA Core.

metadata.title: AI Growth & Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the rapid growth of AI and its far-reaching effects on the economy, social structures, and ethical issues.

metadata.title: AI Impact (Advanced)
metadata.definition: A more in-depth analysis of the current and potential applications of AI, as well as its complex impacts on economic, social, ethical and security domains.

metadata.title: AI Interaction Regulations
metadata.definition: Legal and regulatory frameworks govern the design, deployment, and use of human-interactive AI systems to ensure safety, security, and fairness.

metadata.title: AI Interdisciplinary Applications
metadata.definition: AI techniques are increasingly widely used in many different fields such as biology, art, architecture and finance to solve specialized problems.

metadata.title: AI, ML, DL Distinction
metadata.definition: understand and clearly distinguish the concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning and Deep Learning.

metadata.title: AI Medical Diagnosis
metadata.definition: Use AI to support diagnosis and early detection of diseases or health conditions based on medical data.

metadata.title: AI Olfaction & Others
metadata.definition: Explore other non-visual or auditory sensory modalities that AI can use, such as sensing smell (olfactory).

metadata.title: AI Performance Evaluation
metadata.definition: Skills to evaluate the effectiveness and accuracy of deployed AI solutions.

metadata.title: AI Philosophical Issues
metadata.definition: Explore deep philosophical questions related to AI, such as consciousness, intelligence, machine ethics, and the nature of intelligence.

metadata.title: AI Planning
metadata.definition: The field of AI is concerned with designing sequences of actions to achieve a specific goal or set of goals.

metadata.title: AI Popularity
metadata.definition: Over the past decade, the term "artificial intelligence" has become popular in business circles, news articles, and everyday conversations.

metadata.title: AI Problem Characteristics
metadata.definition: The problems that AI studies are often reminiscent of those thought to require human intelligence, and AI solution strategies are often capable of generalizing across multiple classes of problems.

metadata.title: AI Problem Evaluation
metadata.definition: Skills to evaluate the effectiveness and feasibility of an AI solution for a specific problem.

metadata.title: AI Problem Formulation
metadata.definition: Skills to identify and build a real-life problem into one that can be solved using artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: AI Problem Overview
metadata.definition: An overview of the types of problems AI tries to solve.

metadata.title: AI Recidivism Prediction
metadata.definition: applying AI to predict the likelihood that an individual will reoffend after being released can influence sentencing decisions.

metadata.title: AI Regulation
metadata.definition: The legal and regulatory frameworks needed to govern the development and deployment of AI.

metadata.title: AI Representation & Reasoning
metadata.definition: Skill in selecting the most appropriate knowledge representation schemes and inference mechanisms for a specific AI problem.

metadata.title: AI Search
metadata.definition: Algorithmic techniques are used to explore the state space in search of a solution or a path from the initial state to the goal state.

metadata.title: AI Social Impact
metadata.definition: Skills to consider and evaluate the broader effects of AI systems on society, beyond technical performance.

metadata.title: AI Social Impact Analysis
metadata.definition: Extensive research on the impact of artificial intelligence on various aspects of society.

metadata.title: AI Social Impact Assessment
metadata.definition: analyze and evaluate the broad impacts of AI applications on society, including ethical, equity, privacy, and sustainability aspects.

metadata.title: AI Societal Impact
metadata.definition: The importance of understanding and evaluating the broader societal impacts and implications of AI methods and applications.

metadata.title: AI Stock Trading
metadata.definition: Use AI technology to analyze the market, predict trends and automate stock trading transactions.

metadata.title: AI Sustainability
metadata.definition: The environmental and social impacts of AI, and how to develop AI responsibly and sustainably.

metadata.title: AI System Deployment
metadata.definition: Skills to build and develop AI solutions based on selected representations and inference mechanisms.

metadata.title: AI Terminology Shift
metadata.definition: Reflects common terminology changes within the AI ​​field and widespread usage outside the field.

metadata.title: AI Trust
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Trustworthiness
metadata.definition: Build user trust in AI systems through reliability, safety, and performance.

metadata.title: AI Ubiquity
metadata.definition: AI techniques are now widespread in computing, powering everyday applications such as email, social networks, photography, and financial markets.

metadata.title: AI in Middleboxes
metadata.definition: Advances in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in intermediate network devices.

metadata.title: AI: Tech Term vs. Marketing
metadata.definition: "Artificial intelligence" is now both a specialized technical term and a marketing keyword used by businesses to promote the added value of their services.

metadata.title: AL Societal, Ethical & Professional (SEP)
metadata.definition: The unit of knowledge ensures that the social, ethical and professional implications of computing are addressed throughout the AL area topics.

metadata.title: AL-Models
metadata.definition: Study of fundamental and theoretical computational models, covering all core topics of CS and KA in the advanced context of computational theory.

metadata.title: AL-SEP: Ethics & Society
metadata.definition: Improve your understanding and ability to analyze the far-reaching impact of algorithm design and use on society, presented at an advanced level in SEP hours.

metadata.title: AMAT Calculation
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate average memory access time based on parameters such as access time of each memory level and hit/miss ratio.

metadata.title: AOP Alternatives
metadata.definition: Alternative or complementary methods to aspect-oriented programming to handle cross-references, such as using annotations or support tools from the IDE.

metadata.title: API
metadata.definition: The concept of interfaces allows software components to interact with each other, such as APIs.

metadata.title: API gateways
metadata.definition: A management tool or service that acts as a single entry point for a group of microservices. They are a pervasive real-world application point for rate limiting, used to protect backend services by enforcing limits at the network edge.

metadata.title: ARIES Recovery System
metadata.definition: Study in detail the ARIES recovery system, including the analyze, REDO and UNDO phases, used to recover the database after a crash.

metadata.title: AST
metadata.definition: The tree data structure represents the abstract syntactic structure of source code, used in compilers and program analyzers.

metadata.title: AUC
metadata.definition: An index that summarizes the overall performance of a classifier across all thresholds, with higher values ​​indicating a better classification model.

metadata.title: AVL Tree
metadata.definition: A self-balancing binary search tree, where the difference in height between the left and right subtrees of any node is at most 1.

metadata.title: Abduction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Deductive method for finding the most likely explanation for a set of observations.

metadata.title: Abstract Base Classes
metadata.definition: Use abstract base classes to define common interfaces that subclasses must implement.

metadata.title: Abstract Computation Models
metadata.definition: understand the basic abstract model of computation that programming languages ​​share.

metadata.title: Abstract Data Type (ADT)
metadata.definition: Defines a data type through its behavior without revealing its internal implementation.

metadata.title: Abstract Data Types (ADTs)
metadata.definition: The concept of a data type is defined by behavior from the user's perspective, not the internal implementation. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
metadata.definition: Definition and usage of abstract syntax trees (ASTs) to represent the grammatical structure of code.

metadata.title: Abstract vs Concrete Syntax
metadata.definition: Contrast abstract syntax – which focuses on the semantic structure – and concrete syntax – which focuses on the precise textual representation of the language.

metadata.title: Abstraction & Program Representation
metadata.definition: Techniques for creating abstractions in programs and ways of representing programs at different levels.

metadata.title: Access Paths
metadata.definition: The different ways the query optimizer can access data (e.g., table scans, using indexes).

metadata.title: Access Points (APs)
metadata.definition: The function of a wireless access point is to allow wireless devices to connect to a wired network.

metadata.title: Accounting Method
metadata.definition: Also known as the banker's method, this amortized analysis technique assigns an amortized cost to each operation, allowing some operations to be 'overcharged' to build up 'credit' for subsequent expensive operations, ensuring the total credit never becomes negative.

metadata.title: Action & Change Reasoning
metadata.definition: Techniques and models for representing and reasoning about how actions change the state of the world.

metadata.title: Activation Record
metadata.definition: A data structure created on the stack for each function call, containing information such as parameters, local variables, return addresses, and frame pointers.

metadata.title: Actor Model
metadata.definition: The parallel programming model is based on Actors, independent computational units that communicate by exchanging messages.

metadata.title: Acyclic Graph
metadata.definition: A graph does not contain any cycles (a path that starts and ends at the same vertex) like a Tree.

metadata.title: Adjacency List
metadata.definition: A method of representing a graph in which each vertex has a list (usually a linked list or array) of its neighbors.

metadata.title: Adjacency Matrix
metadata.definition: A method of representing a graph using a square matrix, whose elements indicate whether there are any edges between two vertices (usually 0 or 1, or an edge weight).

metadata.title: Advanced Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: The basic classifications of algorithmic complexity, considered at a more advanced level, include higher complexity classes such as exponential and factorial. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Advanced Computer Systems
metadata.definition: In-depth overview of the architecture, components, and operations of computer systems.

metadata.title: Advanced Decidability (Arithmetization, Diagonalization)
metadata.definition: Advanced techniques for decidability analysis, including arithmetic and diagonalization, to prove undecidable problems, such as the Stationarity Problem.

metadata.title: Advanced Functional Dependencies
metadata.definition: In-depth study of functional dependencies, including properties and how they are used in database normalization.

metadata.title: Advanced Linear Algebra
metadata.definition: An advanced linear algebra course, which may require calculus or deeper knowledge, is one way to take the KA Core or go beyond.

metadata.title: Advanced Logic Programming
metadata.definition: Introduces advanced areas of logic programming, including higher-order logic programming, constrained logic programming, and inductive logic programming.

metadata.title: Advanced Logic Structures
metadata.definition: Learn advanced programming constructs in programming logic such as difference-lists, how to create custom data structures, and aggregation operators.

metadata.title: Advanced Matrix Operations
metadata.definition: Ability to perform common matrix operations such as addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication, and matrix transposition. Includes recognizing when two matrices can be multiplied together.

metadata.title: Advanced Network Security
metadata.definition: Advanced cyber security concepts, often related to protection in highly distributed and complex environments.

metadata.title: Advanced Normalization Theory
metadata.definition: In-depth study of normalization theory, including higher normal forms and more complex types of dependencies.

metadata.title: Advanced Programming Constructs
metadata.definition: Explore complex and powerful programming language constructs, such as metaprogramming, aspect-oriented programming, or advanced concurrency mechanisms.

metadata.title: Advanced Programming Constructs (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Study advanced programming structures and techniques.

metadata.title: Advanced System Design
metadata.definition: Study the principles and methods of computer system design at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Advanced System Performance
metadata.definition: Advanced techniques and models to optimize the performance of computer systems.

metadata.title: Advanced System Reliability
metadata.definition: Advanced methods and techniques to ensure computer system reliability.

metadata.title: Advanced System Security
metadata.definition: In-depth topics in computer system security, including advanced threats and prevention measures.

metadata.title: Advanced Systems Engineering
metadata.definition: Systems engineering processes and methods at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Adversarial Training
metadata.definition: A technique for training models to become more robust against adversarial disturbances (adversarial examples), helping to improve model robustness and safety.

metadata.title: Advice
metadata.definition: Code is executed at a certain junction by an aspect.

metadata.title: After Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code is executed after a join point completes, including returning, throwing, or finally.

metadata.title: Agent Architectures
metadata.definition: Frameworks, or structural designs for building intelligent agents, dictate how they process information, make decisions, and perform actions.

metadata.title: Agent Autonomy Types
metadata.definition: Learn about the different levels of autonomy in AI systems, from fully automated to requiring human intervention, or a combination of both.

metadata.title: Agent Emotion Modeling
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for AI agents to recognize, express, and react to emotions, to create more natural interactions.

metadata.title: Agent MDP
metadata.definition: Use Markov Decision Processes to model and solve agent decision-making problems in dynamic and uncertain environments.

metadata.title: Agent Nature (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Study in more detail the structure, types and operations of AI agents, accompanied by specific illustrative examples.

metadata.title: Agent Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish problems with only one agent from problems with many interacting agents.

metadata.title: Agent Rationality
metadata.definition: The concept of rational agent behavior, where the agent acts to achieve its goals in the most efficient manner, based on available information.

metadata.title: Agent Teams
metadata.definition: A collection of collaborating actors with assigned roles and responsibilities to perform more complex tasks.

metadata.title: Agent Theory
metadata.definition: Theoretical study of intelligent agents, including mathematical formulas to describe their behavior, goals, and interactions.

metadata.title: Agent-Environment Interaction
metadata.definition: Learn about how AI agents interact with their environment, including influencing and responding to changes, to achieve their goals.

metadata.title: Agent-based Supply Chain
metadata.definition: apply AI agents to automate, optimize and manage supply chain processes.

metadata.title: Agents & Cognitive Systems
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on types of agents and cognitive systems in AI.

metadata.title: Aggregate Method
metadata.definition: A primary method of amortized analysis that calculates the total cost of a sequence of 'n' operations and divides by 'n' to find the amortized cost per operation.

metadata.title: Aggregate Operations
metadata.definition: Skills in defining and using common operations on data sets such as filter, map, reduce, and other operations.

metadata.title: Algorithm
metadata.definition: Structured computational processes that operate on data elements are the foundation of all theoretical calculations and applied programs.

metadata.title: Algorithm Analysis
metadata.definition: The process of estimating the resources (time, memory) required for an algorithm and evaluating its correctness under different circumstances.

metadata.title: Algorithm Capabilities & Limits
metadata.definition: Understanding of what algorithms can and cannot achieve, as well as the factors that influence their performance and applicability.

metadata.title: Algorithm Complexity
metadata.definition: Study of the computational resources (time, space) an algorithm requires to complete a task. Includes asymptotic analysis and basic complexity classes.

metadata.title: Algorithm Correctness
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for proving the correctness of an algorithm, ensuring the algorithm behaves as expected for all valid inputs.

metadata.title: Algorithm Design
metadata.definition: The process of creating new algorithms or adapting existing algorithms to solve specific problems, taking into account efficiency and correctness.

metadata.title: Algorithm Design Choices
metadata.definition: Explain the effects of design choices related to algorithm design.

metadata.title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze the efficiency and complexity of query processing algorithms, often measured by the number of I/O operations.

metadata.title: Algorithm Environmental Impact
metadata.definition: Explain the impact an algorithm can have on the environment when used to solve a real-world problem.

metadata.title: Algorithm Foundations
metadata.definition: Area of ​​knowledge that focuses on the nature of computation, including the concepts and skills needed to design and analyze algorithms to solve real-world computational problems.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigm Characteristics
metadata.definition: Ability to explain the defining characteristics of various algorithmic models and illustrate them with concrete examples, showing how those examples satisfy the model's characteristics.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigm Evaluation
metadata.definition: Ability to evaluate and select appropriate algorithm models for practical problems, and analyze the advantages, disadvantages and trade-offs between selected models and algorithms.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigms
metadata.definition: Generic design methods for building efficient algorithms provide a framework for solving different types of problems.

metadata.title: Algorithm Performance Cases
metadata.definition: Methods for evaluating the performance of an algorithm based on different input scenarios: best, average, and worst.

metadata.title: Algorithm Social Impact
metadata.definition: Explain how an algorithm can affect different social groups in different ways when used in real-world problems.

metadata.title: Algorithm Societal & Environmental Impact
metadata.definition: evaluate the ethical, social, and environmental consequences of algorithm development and implementation in real-world applications.

metadata.title: Algorithm Strategies
metadata.definition: Algorithm design and development methods to solve different types of computational problems, including exhaustion, divide and conquer, greed, etc.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Accountability
metadata.definition: understand accountability regarding algorithmic decisions and outcomes.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Bias
metadata.definition: Different types of bias can appear in AI algorithms.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Fairness
metadata.definition: understand the concept and importance of fairness in algorithm design and implementation.

metadata.title: Algorithmic SEP
metadata.definition: Enhance and refine understanding of the impact of algorithm design and use on society, presented at an intermediate level during SEP hours.

metadata.title: Algorithmic SEP Basic
metadata.definition: Social, ethical, and professional issues related to algorithmic platforms, are presented at a basic level during SEP hours.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Social Solutions
metadata.definition: Develop algorithmic solutions to solve real-world social problems, for example routing ambulances to hospitals.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Sustainability
metadata.definition: evaluate algorithms for sustainability aspects, including long-term environmental and social impacts.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Transparency
metadata.definition: understand the need for transparency in algorithmic operations and decisions.

metadata.title: Alias Analysis
metadata.definition: Program analysis technique to identify pairs of expressions that can be pseudonyms for each other, helping to improve the accuracy of other analyses.

metadata.title: Aliasing Impact on Analysis
metadata.definition: Situation where two or more different expressions in a program refer to the same memory location, causing difficulty and limiting the possibility of reliable program analysis.

metadata.title: All-Pairs Shortest Path (APSP)
metadata.definition: A category of shortest path problems that aims to find the shortest paths between all possible pairs of nodes in a graph.

metadata.title: Alpha Conversion (Lambda Calculus)
metadata.definition: Explain the process of renaming bound variables in Lambda Calculus without changing the meaning of the expression.

metadata.title: Alpha-beta Pruning
metadata.definition: Research optimization techniques for the Minimax algorithm, helping to remove unnecessary branches in the search tree without affecting the final result.

metadata.title: Ambiguous Problems
metadata.definition: Methods of approaching and solving problems that do not have a unique solution, discontinuous solutions that depend on input data, or that do not exist.

metadata.title: Amdahl's Law
metadata.definition: Amdahl's Law describes the limit of a system's acceleration potential when only part of the system is improved, emphasizing that the part that cannot be accelerated limits the overall efficiency.

metadata.title: Amdahl's Law Limitations
metadata.definition: Discuss the limitations and cases where Amdahl's Law may not apply or make inaccurate predictions about system speedup.

metadata.title: Amortized Analysis
metadata.definition: Technique that analyzes the performance of a sequence of operations, where the high cost of some operations is offset by the low cost of other operations, yielding a low average cost per operation.

metadata.title: Amplitude Amplification
metadata.definition: The concept of using amplitude amplification techniques in quantum computing to achieve polynomial (e.g., square root) speedups over classical algorithms, often in search problems.

metadata.title: Analysis Tools & Frameworks
metadata.definition: Software and libraries that support the construction of program analysis tools, including lexer/parser generators, graph processing libraries, and analysis development environments.

metadata.title: Analysis for Optimization
metadata.definition: Using the results of program analysis to transform code, aiming to improve the performance or other characteristics of a program without changing its semantics.

metadata.title: Analysis for Partial Verification
metadata.definition: Using the results of program analysis to verify that a program satisfies certain properties or requirements, even if the entire program cannot be verified.

metadata.title: Analysis for Verification & Debugging
metadata.definition: How program analysis techniques are used to partially test software for correctness or automatically detect potential errors.

metadata.title: Analytical SQL
metadata.definition: Use SQL to perform complex queries, analyze data, and create reports for business purposes.

metadata.title: Angle Between Vectors
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate angle between two vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Anonymity
metadata.definition: understand concepts and techniques that ensure anonymity in data processing and algorithms.

metadata.title: Anonymous Communication Protocol
metadata.definition: Protocols are designed to protect the identities of users or parties participating in network communications.

metadata.title: Answer Set Programming (ASP)
metadata.definition: A form of non-monotonic logic programming, used to solve search and optimization problems by finding 'solution sets'.

metadata.title: Anti-Spoofing Protection
metadata.definition: Techniques and measures to prevent attacks that spoof IP, MAC addresses, or other identifying information.

metadata.title: Antivirus Systems
metadata.definition: understand the functions and importance of anti-virus systems.

metadata.title: App-Level Pipelining
metadata.definition: Parallel processing technique in which different stages of a task are performed simultaneously on different elements of the system, similar to an assembly line.

metadata.title: App-Level Request Parallelism
metadata.definition: Parallel processing methods at the application level, focus on the simultaneous processing of multiple requests, for example in web services, client-server architectures or distributed systems.

metadata.title: App-Level Single-Threaded Processing
metadata.definition: Execution of applications at the application level uses only a single thread, performing tasks sequentially.

metadata.title: Application Layer
metadata.definition: The highest layer in the system architecture, where the programs and services with which users directly interact are executed.

metadata.title: Application Layer Protocols
metadata.definition: Overview of the roles and functions of protocols operating at the application layer in network architecture.

metadata.title: Application-Level Gateways (ALGs)
metadata.definition: Specialized network components or techniques used to address complexities introduced by NAT, particularly for protocols (like FTP, SIP) that embed IP address information within their payloads, by modifying application-level data to ensure compatibility.

metadata.title: Application-OS Interaction
metadata.definition: Master the differences and how applications interact with services provided by the operating system.

metadata.title: Applied Linear Algebra (Non-Calculus)
metadata.definition: An application-focused linear algebra course, with no calculus prerequisite, is one way to take the KA Core section.

metadata.title: Approximation Algorithms
metadata.definition: The algorithms are designed to find an approximate solution to NP-hard optimization problems in polynomial time, when finding an optimal solution is not feasible.

metadata.title: Approximation in Analysis
metadata.definition: The notion that for a non-trivial program analysis to be sound and stopable, it must usually accept a certain level of approximation, sometimes omitting some details for the sake of feasibility.

metadata.title: Arc Consistency
metadata.definition: Determine the extent to which arc consistency can reduce the search space in the constraint satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Architectural Performance Impact
metadata.definition: Ability to explain how different components of the system architecture (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O) interact and contribute to improving overall performance.

metadata.title: Argumentation
metadata.definition: The study of how to construct, analyze and evaluate logical arguments, especially in multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Arithmetic Competency
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and use basic arithmetic concepts effectively.

metadata.title: Arithmetic Fluency
metadata.definition: Ability to perform arithmetic calculations quickly and accurately.

metadata.title: Arithmetic Operations
metadata.definition: Proficient in basic addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

metadata.title: Arithmetic Progression (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply arithmetic progressions in counting problems.

metadata.title: Arithmetization & Diagonalization for Halting Problem
metadata.definition: apply arithmetic and diagonalization techniques to prove that the Stopping Problem for Turing Machines is undecidable.

metadata.title: Armstrong's Axioms Completeness
metadata.definition: Work on proving the completeness of Armstrong's Axioms, a set of inference rules for functional dependencies, ensuring that all functional dependencies can be derived from a given set.

metadata.title: Around Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code wraps and can control the execution of a junction.

metadata.title: Array
metadata.definition: Array data structure and basic operations with arrays.

metadata.title: Array Data Processing
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for storing, querying, and manipulating array data types in databases.

metadata.title: Array Database
metadata.definition: A type of database designed to efficiently store and manage large multi-dimensional array structured data sets, such as satellite images or sensor data.

metadata.title: Arrays
metadata.definition: A set of data elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations, accessible by an index.

metadata.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: An introduction to aspect-oriented programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Aspects
metadata.definition: Definition of aspect in aspect-oriented programming (AOP), representing cross-cutting concerns.

metadata.title: Assertion Evaluation
metadata.definition: Compare assertion evaluation and expression evaluation mechanisms, especially in the context of programming languages.

metadata.title: Assignment
metadata.definition: Concept of value assignment to variables.

metadata.title: Association Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to discover relationships (association rules) between variables in large data sets.

metadata.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms use a pair of keys (public key and private key) for encryption and decryption.

metadata.title: Asymptotic Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Method for analyzing algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity, focusing on upper and lower bounds for the average and worst case.

metadata.title: Async/Await
metadata.definition: The asynchronous programming model uses the `async` and `await` keywords to manage non-blocking operations.

metadata.title: Asynchronous Communication
metadata.definition: A communication model where senders do not wait for a direct response from receivers, allowing for decoupled operations, increased resilience, and parallel task execution in distributed systems.

metadata.title: Atomicity
metadata.definition: The concept of atomicity, ensures that a set of operations is performed completely or not at all.

metadata.title: Attention (Image Generative Models)
metadata.definition: The role and how the attention mechanism works in deep image generation models to focus on important parts of the data.

metadata.title: Attention (LLMs)
metadata.definition: The role and how attention mechanisms work in large language models to process and produce coherent text.

metadata.title: Attention Mechanism
metadata.definition: A technique that allows a neural network to focus on the most important parts of the input data when processing information, especially useful in NLP and vision.

metadata.title: Attribute Closure
metadata.definition: The set of all attributes that can be determined from an initial set of attributes through the given functional dependencies.

metadata.title: Attribute Grammars
metadata.definition: Declarative specification techniques such as attribute grammars, and their applications in limited context-based grammar processing, allow the definition of attributes associated with nodes in the syntax tree and their systematic computation.

metadata.title: Audio Fourier Coefficients
metadata.definition: apply Fourier transform to analyze the frequency spectrum of audio signals, extracting coefficients representing the frequency components of the signal.

metadata.title: Audio Recognition
metadata.definition: The computer process of identifying and classifying different types of sounds (e.g., environmental noise, animal sounds, music).

metadata.title: Augmented Matrix
metadata.definition: Ability to relate extended matrices to a system of linear equations.

metadata.title: Autoencoders
metadata.definition: The neural network is trained to encode the input data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then decode that representation to reconstruct the original input.

metadata.title: Automatic Memory Management
metadata.definition: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of automatic memory management, including mechanisms such as garbage collection.

metadata.title: Automatic Parallelization Analysis
metadata.definition: Source code analysis techniques to automatically identify and convert parts of a program into a parallel form that can run on multiple processors.

metadata.title: Autonomous Agents
metadata.definition: Autonomous agents are AI systems designed to perceive their environment and interact appropriately with it.

metadata.title: Autonomous Robot Liability
metadata.definition: Research legal frameworks and challenges in determining liability when autonomous robots cause damage or accidents.

metadata.title: Autonomous System (AS)
metadata.definition: Concept and role of Autonomous Systems (AS) as independent administrative units participating in the global routing structure of the Internet.

metadata.title: Autonomous Weapons Ethics
metadata.definition: Discusses the ethical and social issues involved in the development and use of fully autonomous weapons systems capable of making killing decisions without human intervention.

metadata.title: Average Memory Access Time
metadata.definition: Formula used to calculate the average time a system takes to access data from memory, taking into account the memory hierarchy (cache, RAM).

metadata.title: Average-case Analysis
metadata.definition: A complexity analysis technique that relies on probabilistic assumptions about input distributions to determine the expected performance of an algorithm, distinct from amortized analysis which provides guarantees over worst-case sequences.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about axiomatic semantics as a method for describing the meaning of a program through preconditions and postconditions.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Assignment
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as assignments using preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Iteration
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as iterations (loops) using preconditions, postconditions, and loop invariants.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Selection
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as options (if-then-else) using preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

metadata.title: Axioms of Probability
metadata.definition: Master the basic axioms of probability.

metadata.title: B+ Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree structure commonly used to create indexes in databases.

metadata.title: B+ Trees
metadata.definition: Research on the structure and operation of B+ trees, a popular type of index in database management systems.

metadata.title: B-Trees & B+ Trees
metadata.definition: B and B+ tree data structures, commonly used in database systems.

metadata.title: B-tree Index
metadata.definition: The B-tree index data structure is used for efficient search, insertion, and deletion of data, applied in the context of semi-structured databases.

metadata.title: BCNF
metadata.definition: A standard form in relational database design, stricter than 3NF, that eliminates functional dependencies where a non-key attribute depends on part of a candidate key.

metadata.title: BDI Model
metadata.definition: The study of cognitive models for representing the beliefs, desires, and intentions of agents, especially in the context of language processing and social reasoning.

metadata.title: BFS
metadata.definition: Presenting the breadth-first search (BFS) method for graphs.

metadata.title: BGP
metadata.definition: The primary inter-domain routing protocol used on the Internet to exchange routing information between autonomous domains.

metadata.title: BGPsec
metadata.definition: Security extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to authenticate routing information and prevent routing attacks.

metadata.title: BNF & Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: Concept of Backus-Naur Grammar (BNF) to describe language syntax and Regular Expressions to describe character patterns.

metadata.title: BNF Grammar Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use BNF to describe the syntax of context-free grammars, which are fundamental to language design and parsing.

metadata.title: BNF/EBNF Syntax Definition
metadata.definition: Use Backus-Naur Grammar (BNF) and Extended Backus-Naur Grammar (EBNF) to specify the syntax of simple programming constructs such as `if-then-else` conditional statements, data type declarations, and looping constructs in popular programming languages ​​such as C++ or Python.

metadata.title: BST Balance Impact
metadata.definition: Explain how the balanced structure of a binary search tree affects the time complexity of operations such as search, insertion, deletion.

metadata.title: Backtrack Search for CSP
metadata.definition: apply backtracking search to solve constraint satisfaction problems.

metadata.title: Backtracking
metadata.definition: A problem-solving technique by trying to construct a solution step by step; When a potential solution is no longer valid or does not lead to a solution, the algorithm backtracks and tries another option.

metadata.title: Backtracking Algorithm
metadata.definition: Learn about the backtracking algorithm, a technique for solving problems by systematically trying each solution.

metadata.title: Backward Chaining
metadata.definition: An inference strategy starts from a goal and looks for rules that can lead to that goal, tracing back to the necessary conditions.

metadata.title: Backward Dataflow Analysis
metadata.definition: A data flow analysis technique that gathers information about a program by going back from the end to the beginning of the control flow.

metadata.title: Bag of Words
metadata.definition: Bag of Words model to represent text as a vector of word frequency counts, ignoring grammar and word order.

metadata.title: Bag-of-Words Model
metadata.definition: Study the bag of words model, a simple representation in NLP and information retrieval, where word order is ignored and only word frequency is considered.

metadata.title: Bagging
metadata.definition: A model ensemble technique that creates multiple versions of a model by resampling the training data (with replacement) and then combining the predictions.

metadata.title: Balanced Binary Trees
metadata.definition: Types of balanced binary trees, e.g. AVL, 2-3-4, Red-Black Trees.

metadata.title: Balanced Tree
metadata.definition: A binary search tree is structured so that the height of the tree is kept to a minimum or approximately balanced, ensuring best performance for search, insert, and delete operations.

metadata.title: Balls and Bins Problem
metadata.definition: A classic probability problem, often used to analyze the performance of random algorithms and data structures such as hash tables and load distribution.

metadata.title: Bandit Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used for explore-exploit problems, where an agent must make repeated choices from a set of options (arm) to maximize the reward.

metadata.title: Bandwidth
metadata.definition: The importance of network bandwidth for the data transfer ability of applications.

metadata.title: Banker's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm for deadlock avoidance that requires processes to declare maximum resource needs in advance and performs a safety check to ensure resource allocation maintains a safe state, with a time complexity of O(m*n^2).

metadata.title: Bard
metadata.definition: An example of another large language model, developed by Google, is capable of performing many language-related tasks.

metadata.title: Basic AI Literacy
metadata.definition: The clear goal is to develop a basic understanding of AI for every computer science student.

metadata.title: Basic Block
metadata.definition: A basic block is a sequence of instructions in program code such that if one instruction is executed then all other instructions in the sequence will also be executed, used as the basic unit in many program analysis.

metadata.title: Basic Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Groups classify algorithms based on the growth rate of the time or space complexity function.

metadata.title: Basic Data Cleaning
metadata.definition: Basic techniques for handling missing data, duplicate data, and other data errors.

metadata.title: Basic Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: Basic techniques for data cleaning and preprocessing.

metadata.title: Basic Derivatives from Limit
metadata.definition: Perform basic derivative calculations based on limit definitions.

metadata.title: Basic Generative Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A basic introduction to generative neural networks, including large language models (LLMs).

metadata.title: Basic Logic Gates
metadata.definition: Describe basic logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, etc.) and their functions in electronic circuit design.

metadata.title: Basic Matrix Operations
metadata.definition: Basic matrix operations such as matrix addition, matrix multiplication with a scalar.

metadata.title: Basic Neural Networks
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of how neural networks work and their training, without going into computational detail.

metadata.title: Basic Quantum Gates (XNOT, CNOT)
metadata.definition: Introduce and explain basic quantum gates such as XNOT gate (Pauli-X) and CNOT gate (Controlled-NOT).

metadata.title: Basic SQL Query
metadata.definition: Students are provided with SQL query code to access the database in introductory courses.

metadata.title: Basic Type Constructors: Invariants
metadata.definition: For basic type constructors, specify the invariants they enforce to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: Basic Type Constructors: Values
metadata.definition: For basic type constructors (e.g., product, sum, function), clearly identify the sets of values ​​they can describe.

metadata.title: Basis & Dimension (Finite Spaces)
metadata.definition: Determine the basis and dimensions of a finite dimensional space.

metadata.title: Basis Existence in Abstract Spaces
metadata.definition: Discuss the existence of a basis for an abstract vector space.

metadata.title: Basis Expansion
metadata.definition: Technique that transforms data into a higher dimensional space by using basis functions (e.g., polynomial functions, spline functions) to model nonlinear relationships.

metadata.title: Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: Definition and application of Bayes' rule to update the probability of an event based on new information.

metadata.title: Bayes' Theorem
metadata.definition: understand and apply Bayes' theorem in calculating conditional probabilities.

metadata.title: Bayesian Inference
metadata.definition: apply Bayesian inference to more complex examples and problems.

metadata.title: Bayesian Inference Complexity
metadata.definition: An analysis of the computational cost and factors affecting the complexity of exact inference algorithms in Bayesian Networks.

metadata.title: Bayesian Learning
metadata.definition: A machine learning approach based on Bayes' theorem, which combines prior knowledge with observational data to create posterior inference.

metadata.title: Bayesian Networks
metadata.definition: The probabilistic graphical model represents a set of variables and the conditionally independent relationships between them.

metadata.title: Bayesian Reasoning
metadata.definition: Knowledge of probability and ability to apply basic Bayesian reasoning to solve problems in AI.

metadata.title: Bayesian vs. Frequentist
metadata.definition: Differences and comparisons between two main approaches in inferential statistics: Bayesian statistics and frequentist statistics.

metadata.title: Beam Search
metadata.definition: Learn a variant of breadth-first search or best-first search, retaining only a limited number of nodes (beam width) at each level to reduce memory overhead.

metadata.title: Beam Search Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the Beam search algorithm in search problems that require memory efficiency.

metadata.title: Before Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code is executed before a join point is made.

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path from a source to all other vertices in a graph with (possibly negative) edge weights and is capable of detecting negative cycles.

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, the Bellman-Ford algorithm for finding the shortest path from a source in a graph has negative edge weights. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Benchmarking: Use & Limits
metadata.definition: Explains how to use benchmarks to measure system performance, and points out their limitations and shortcomings in reflecting actual performance.

metadata.title: Benefits of Large Data Pre-training
metadata.definition: The advantages of using large amounts of data to train underlying models include generalization and high performance.

metadata.title: Bernoulli Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize the Bernoulli distribution.

metadata.title: Bernstein & Bezier Curves
metadata.definition: applying Bernstein polynomials to Bezier curves.

metadata.title: Bernstein Polynomials
metadata.definition: Distinguish between fundamental polynomials and Bernstein polynomials.

metadata.title: Bernstein-Vazirani Algorithm
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithms can find a hidden binary string (or linear binary function) with just one oracle query, while classical algorithms need many more queries.

metadata.title: Beta Reduction (Lambda Calculus)
metadata.definition: Explain the function application process in Lambda Calculus, replacing parameters with arguments.

metadata.title: Beyond Professional Ethics
metadata.definition: understand and act on broader responsibilities beyond those in the professional code of ethics, including global competencies, culture, and an awareness of the importance and impact of local values ​​and practices.

metadata.title: Bezier Curve
metadata.definition: The concept of parametric curves is widely used in computer graphics and computer-aided design.

metadata.title: Bias & Unintended Consequences
metadata.definition: understand bias in data sets, algorithms, evaluations, and their unintended consequences in machine learning.

metadata.title: Bias (ML)
metadata.definition: Systematic errors or biases in data, algorithms, or machine learning decision-making processes, can lead to inaccurate or unfair results.

metadata.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
metadata.definition: understand the trade-off between bias (underfitting) and variance (overfitting) in machine learning.

metadata.title: Biconditional (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators express a 'if and only if' relationship between two clauses.

metadata.title: Bidirectional Search
metadata.definition: Research algorithms that search simultaneously from the starting state and the goal state, hoping to meet in the middle to increase efficiency.

metadata.title: Big Data Analytics
metadata.definition: understand the technologies and methods used to store, process, and analyze extremely large and complex data sets.

metadata.title: Big Data Management Methods
metadata.definition: Techniques and systems used to efficiently store, process, and analyze large data sets.

metadata.title: Big Data in AI
metadata.definition: The widespread availability of large data sets is a key factor driving recent advances in AI, especially in machine learning.

metadata.title: Big O Notation
metadata.definition: A mathematical notation used to describe the worst-case behavior of a function when the argument goes to infinity, often used to classify the performance of an algorithm.

metadata.title: Big-O Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Introducing the method of analyzing algorithm complexity using Big-O notation.

metadata.title: Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta
metadata.definition: Formal mathematical notation used to describe the upper bound (Big-O), lower bound (Big-Omega), and strict bound (Big-Theta) of algorithmic complexity.

metadata.title: Binary Search
metadata.definition: An efficient search algorithm for sorted data works by repeatedly bisecting the search space. Has O(log n) complexity.

metadata.title: Binary Search O(log n)
metadata.definition: Efficient search algorithm in sorted list, has logarithmic running time complexity O(log₂ n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Binary Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which each node has at most two children, often called left children and right children.

metadata.title: Binomial Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize the binomial distribution.

metadata.title: Bitmap (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A data structure used to represent a set of values ​​using a string of bits, where each bit represents the presence or absence of an element.

metadata.title: Bitmap Compression
metadata.definition: Technique that compresses bitmap indexes to save storage space and improve query performance, especially useful for data with many repeating values.

metadata.title: Blockchain
metadata.definition: A distributed ledger technology that records transactions in a secure and immutable way through the use of cryptographically linked blocks. Usually based on a consensus algorithm.

metadata.title: Bloom Filter
metadata.definition: A space-saving probabilistic data structure used to check whether an element is a member of a set, which can be applied to speed up queries on semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Boolean Algebra
metadata.definition: Study of mathematical operations and logic rules used in digital circuit design and set theory.

metadata.title: Boolean Expressions
metadata.definition: understand and work with boolean expressions that describe the operation of logic circuits.

metadata.title: Boolean Logic Minimization
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for simplifying Boolean logic expressions to optimize electronic circuits and minimize resources.

metadata.title: Boolean Minimization
metadata.definition: Techniques for minimizing logic expressions to simplify circuit design and improve performance.

metadata.title: Boosting
metadata.definition: A model ensemble technique that builds a strong classifier by combining multiple weak classifiers, training sequentially to focus on misclassified data samples.

metadata.title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
metadata.definition: One of the higher standards in relational database design, aimed at eliminating update anomalies and ensuring data integrity by eliminating non-trivial functional dependencies in keys.

metadata.title: Boyer-Moore Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient string search algorithm, often the fastest standard string search algorithm, by ignoring parts of the text that are unlikely to contain a pattern. (An example for Efficient String Matching)

metadata.title: Branch-and-Bound
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy for finding optimal solutions to complex optimization problems, by dividing the search space into branches and eliminating unpromising branches using upper/lower bounds.

metadata.title: Breadth-First Search
metadata.definition: The algorithm searches a tree or graph, exploring all nodes at the same level before moving on to the next level. It is a form of non-informational search.

metadata.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
metadata.definition: The tree or graph traversal algorithm starts from the root node and explores all neighboring nodes at the current level before moving on to deeper levels. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Brute-Force
metadata.definition: A simple algorithm design model that examines all possible possibilities directly to find a solution to a problem.

metadata.title: Brute Force (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The strategy of solving problems by trying every possible possibility directly, is often applied to difficult problems such as the delivery man problem or the bag problem. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Brute Force Strategy
metadata.definition: A method of solving problems by systematically trying every possible possibility until the right solution is found, often the simplest but ineffective method.

metadata.title: Brute Force Strategy Basic
metadata.definition: A strategy that solves a problem by trying every possible possibility directly, for example in linear search. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: Bucket Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm divides elements into a finite number of 'buckets', then sorts each bucket separately. Effective with evenly distributed data. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Buffer Management
metadata.definition: Strategies and algorithms for managing data transfer between main memory and secondary memory in a database management system.

metadata.title: Bugs, Faults, Failures
metadata.definition: understand and clearly distinguish three concepts: bug (error in the source code), fault (error in the system that can lead to errors), and failure (system problem that does not work as expected).

metadata.title: Building Data Assets
metadata.definition: Skill in creating cleaned, transformed, and structured data sets to support business analysis and decision making.

metadata.title: Bus
metadata.definition: A system of communication paths used to transmit data between computer components.

metadata.title: Business Analyst
metadata.definition: The role builds and manages data, regularly using Excel spreadsheets, to support business analysis and reporting.

metadata.title: Bytecode
metadata.definition: Learn about bytecode as a common form of intermediate code, used by virtual machines like the JVM.

metadata.title: CDF & PDF
metadata.definition: understand the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and probability density function (PDF) for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: CDF Probability Calculation
metadata.definition: Skills in using the cumulative density function to calculate probabilities for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: CDN
metadata.definition: Concepts, benefits, and basic operations of a Content Delivery Network (CDN) in increasing the speed and efficiency of web content delivery.

metadata.title: CFG
metadata.definition: A control flow graph (CFG) is a graph that represents all possible paths a program can traverse during execution, with nodes being the basic blocks and edges representing the transfer of control between them.

metadata.title: CFG & CYK Parser
metadata.definition: Learn about Context-Free Grammar (CFG) and graph parsing algorithms like CYK, which are used to determine whether a string belongs to a specific grammar.

metadata.title: CIDR
metadata.definition: A more flexible method of IP address allocation and route aggregation to improve routing efficiency and reduce routing table size.

metadata.title: CNN Intuition
metadata.definition: Understanding the basic structure and operation of CNNs, especially in image processing, which uses convolutional layers to automatically learn spatial features, without going into deep mathematical formulas.

metadata.title: CNOT Gate
metadata.definition: Explain the operation of a CNOT (Controlled-NOT) quantum gate on a quantum bit represented by a matrix and column vector.

metadata.title: CPI Equation
metadata.definition: The CPI (Cycles per Instruction) equation is used to analyze and understand the trade-offs in instruction set design, processing pipeline, and memory system organization.

metadata.title: CPU
metadata.definition: The central processing unit, which is the 'brain' of the computer, performs most of the calculations and controls.

metadata.title: CRUD Applications
metadata.definition: The methods and architecture for designing and implementing database systems focus on basic create, Read, Update, and Delete operations.

metadata.title: CS + X
metadata.definition: The concept of the CS+X space, where the principles of computer science are applied or studied in conjunction with other fields.

metadata.title: CS Adaptability
metadata.definition: Ability to continuously adjust and learn to adapt to the constant evolution of computer science.

metadata.title: CS Collaboration
metadata.definition: Skills to work effectively with others on group projects, as most real-world applications are team efforts.

metadata.title: CS Core
metadata.definition: Topics every computer science graduate is required to know, and every computer science curriculum is expected to cover them all.

metadata.title: CS Core Topics
metadata.definition: Required topics that every computer science graduate must master. Every computer science curriculum is expected to cover all core CS topics.

metadata.title: CS Creativity
metadata.definition: Ability to think creatively to develop new solutions and apply existing solutions to new contexts.

metadata.title: CS Curriculum Evolution
metadata.definition: Computer Science is a rapidly evolving industry, bringing both new opportunities and associated challenges. Updating courses and curricula to keep up with the times requires significant resources from computer science educators and should be recognized and supported. CS2023 has highlighted emerging technologies and significantly expanded the rapidly growing sectors to meet this challenge.

metadata.title: CS Education Diversity
metadata.definition: Computer Science education has been facing a long-standing challenge of diversity in participation. The industry benefits from the active participation of all classes and all demographic groups, regardless of demographic identity. CS2023 recommends that programs strive to convey the message that Computer Science belongs to everyone and promote active participation by all populations. The CS2023 guidelines include a practice paper on accessibility in computer science education.

metadata.title: CS Faculty Recruitment & Retention
metadata.definition: Recruiting and retaining faculty is a significant challenge, especially given the high demand for graduates with advanced degrees in Computer Science. A prominent trend over the past decade is the formation of a team of lecturers dedicated to teaching. Educational institutions must find a balance between meeting teaching needs and supporting professional development for lecturers to ensure they keep their knowledge updated and maintain their enthusiasm.

metadata.title: CS Faculty Resource Pressure
metadata.definition: At many educational institutions, explosive growth in student numbers has put significant pressure on faculty resources, as reflected in class sizes and course loads. Managing faculty workloads is critical to ensuring the vitality of faculty, both in terms of the quality of their teaching and their professional development.

metadata.title: CS Lifelong Learning
metadata.definition: Ability to self-learn, self-direct self-development and commitment to lifelong learning to adapt to the rapid development of computer science.

metadata.title: CS Math
metadata.definition: The role of the mathematical component in computer science has been expanded in CS2023, reflecting its increase in importance.

metadata.title: CS Math & Theory Foundation
metadata.definition: Emphasize that theoretical and mathematical foundations are core to what makes computer science a science and are essential for long-term career success. For Operating Systems, this includes understanding algorithms, data structures, and underlying theoretical models.

metadata.title: CS Professional Skills
metadata.definition: Employers are always looking for professional qualities (often called soft skills) such as perseverance, self-direction and adaptability in graduates. CS2023 emphasizes the need to clarify this, which has always been implicit, so that students are aware of the importance of these qualities for future career success and develop them during their studies. In CS2023, the most relevant professional qualities have been identified in each knowledge area.

metadata.title: CS Theory vs. Tools Balance
metadata.definition: Discuss the challenge of finding the right balance between the goals of providing a solid theoretical/mathematical foundation and equipping students with tool/technology skills for immediate employability. This is a challenge common to all areas of knowledge, including Operating Systems, where both theory (e.g., process management) and practice (e.g., using debugging tools) are important.

metadata.title: CS2023 KA Math Requirements
metadata.definition: CS2023 has separately identified mathematics requirements for each knowledge area, including Operating Systems, to provide flexibility in the curriculum to accommodate varying levels of student preparation.

metadata.title: CSP Modeling
metadata.definition: Ability to model logic or Sudoku problems into a constraint satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Cache & Coherency
metadata.definition: understand caches and cache coherency in databases, operating systems, distributed systems, and computer architecture.

metadata.title: Cache & Locality
metadata.definition: understand caches and how spatial locality and temporal locality affect performance in processors and systems.

metadata.title: Cache Memory
metadata.definition: Small, high-speed memory is used to store frequently accessed data to reduce main memory access time.

metadata.title: Calculate Continuous Cond. Exp.
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating conditional expectations for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Continuous Distributions
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating marginal and conditional distributions from a complete distribution for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Discrete Cond. Exp.
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating conditional expectations for discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Discrete Distributions
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating marginal and conditional distributions from a complete distribution for discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Exp. & Variance
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating expected value and variance for common discrete and continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Calculus I (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Standard Calculus I course, corresponding to the requirements of most academic programs. Total 40 hours of study.

metadata.title: Calculus II
metadata.definition: The Calculus II course, which is an additional option (40 hours) for programs seeking to strengthen calculus requirements, is not required.

metadata.title: Calculus in Probability
metadata.definition: Use calculus tools to solve problems related to probability.

metadata.title: Calculus-based Probability
metadata.definition: The probability course requires calculus knowledge, for programs that want a more rigorous and in-depth approach.

metadata.title: Calculus-based Statistics
metadata.definition: The statistics course series requires calculus knowledge, for programs that want a more rigorous and in-depth approach.

metadata.title: Call Semantics
metadata.definition: The rules and manner by which a function (or procedure) is called, including how arguments are passed and return values ​​are processed, as well as how the state of the program changes during the function call.

metadata.title: Call-by-Need
metadata.definition: Master the concept of call-by-need, an argument passing strategy that combines call-by-name and call-by-value, where the argument is evaluated no more than once as needed and the result is cached.

metadata.title: Calling Convention
metadata.definition: The reason why separate compilation requires standardized function calling conventions so that independently compiled modules can interact properly.

metadata.title: Campus Network
metadata.definition: Network structure and management deployed over a limited geographic area such as a university campus or enterprise.

metadata.title: Candidate Key
metadata.definition: An attribute or set of attributes in a table that uniquely identifies each row and contains no child attributes that also uniquely identify the rows.

metadata.title: Canonical Cover
metadata.definition: A minimal set of functional dependencies is equivalent to a given set of functional dependencies, no functional dependencies can be inferred from other functional dependencies in that set.

metadata.title: Cartesian Product
metadata.definition: Cartesian product operation between sets.

metadata.title: Case-based Reasoning
metadata.definition: A method of inference that solves new problems by adapting solutions used in similar cases before.

metadata.title: Central Limit Theorem
metadata.definition: understand the Central Limit Theorem, which describes that the distribution of the sum (or mean) of independent and homogeneous random variables tends to be normally distributed as the number of variables increases.

metadata.title: Centralized Routing
metadata.definition: Routing method in which a single central entity is responsible for calculating and distributing routes.

metadata.title: Chain Rule
metadata.definition: apply the chain rule to calculate the derivative of composite functions.

metadata.title: Chaining
metadata.definition: A method of hash collision resolution in which each location in a hash table contains a linked list or other data structure for all elements hashed to that location.

metadata.title: Challenges of Large Data Pre-training
metadata.definition: Challenges and difficulties encountered when training underlying models on big data, such as cost, bias, and privacy issues.

metadata.title: Change of Representation
metadata.definition: Techniques in the transform and conquer paradigm that change the representation of data or a problem so that solving becomes easier or more efficient (e.g., using heap for heapsort).

metadata.title: Channels
metadata.definition: The communication mechanism allows threads or goroutines to send and receive data securely.

metadata.title: Characteristic Poly for Eigen
metadata.definition: Use characteristic polynomials to calculate eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors.

metadata.title: Characteristic Polynomial
metadata.definition: Find the characteristic polynomial of a matrix.

metadata.title: ChatGPT
metadata.definition: An example of a widely used worm generation model, discussion of operation, uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: Chinese Room Experiment
metadata.definition: A study of the 'Chinese Room' thought experiment and the philosophical debates it raises about the nature of understanding and consciousness in AI.

metadata.title: Chomsky Hierarchy
metadata.definition: The Chomsky Hierarchy classifies formal languages ​​based on their representational capabilities.

metadata.title: Chomsky Hierarchy Relations
metadata.definition: analyze the correspondence relationship between automaton types (FSA, PDA, LBA, Turing Machine), language types (regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursively enumerable) and grammar types in the Chomsky hierarchy.

metadata.title: Choose PL & Paradigm
metadata.definition: Ability to choose the programming model and language best suited to the specific problem.

metadata.title: Church-Turing Thesis
metadata.definition: Explain the Church-Turing Thesis, which asserts that a Turing Machine can compute any function that an algorithm can compute, and what it means for computer science.

metadata.title: Circuit Switching
metadata.definition: Principle and application of circuit switching technique, where a dedicated path is permanently established for a communication session.

metadata.title: Circuit breakers
metadata.definition: A design pattern in distributed systems to protect against cascading failures. They monitor service calls and, if failures reach a certain threshold, 'trip' to prevent further calls to the failing service, distinct from rate limiting which protects healthy services from overload.

metadata.title: Circular Hash Space
metadata.definition: A conceptual space, typically represented as a circular ring (e.g., 0 to 2^32 - 1), onto which both data keys and server nodes are mapped in Consistent Hashing. Key assignment is determined by moving clockwise from the key's position to the first encountered node.

metadata.title: Circular Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which the last node points back to the first node (or another node), forming a continuous loop.

metadata.title: Circular wait
metadata.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, where a set of processes {P0, P1, ..., Pn} exists such that P0 is waiting for a resource held by P1, P1 for P2, and so on, with Pn ultimately waiting for P0.

metadata.title: Class Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define a class, including its properties and methods, in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Class Definition: Fields
metadata.definition: How to define fields (member variables) in a class to store the state of an object.

metadata.title: Class Definition: Methods
metadata.definition: How to define methods (member functions) in a class to define the object's behavior.

metadata.title: Class Design, Implement, Test
metadata.definition: The process of designing, implementing, and testing a class to meet specific behavioral requirements.

metadata.title: Class Hierarchy & Code Reuse
metadata.definition: Build a simple class hierarchy using the subclassing mechanism for efficient code reuse across different subclasses.

metadata.title: Class NP
metadata.definition: The set of decision problems whose solutions can be verified by a non-deterministic polynomial Turing machine.

metadata.title: Class NP-Complete
metadata.definition: The set of problems in NP, to which every other problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time, represents the hardest problems in NP.

metadata.title: Class NSpace
metadata.definition: The set of problems that can be solved by a Turing machine is unknown in a limited amount of space.

metadata.title: Class P
metadata.definition: The set of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic polynomial Turing machine.

metadata.title: Class PSpace
metadata.definition: The set of problems that can be solved by a Turing machine is defined in a polynomial amount of space.

metadata.title: Classification
metadata.definition: Understanding the classification problem in supervised learning.

metadata.title: Classification Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to assign category labels to data points based on features learned from the training data set.

metadata.title: Classification Metrics
