metadata.definition: Metrics used to evaluate the performance of classification models, including error rate, accuracy, coverage, F1-score, etc.

metadata.title: Classification Problem
metadata.definition: A type of supervised learning problem in which the goal is to predict a discrete label or category for an input data point.

metadata.title: Classification Problem Formulation
metadata.definition: The ability to structure a real-world problem so that it can be solved using classification techniques, including determining the input and output characteristics to be predicted.

metadata.title: Classifier Accuracy
metadata.definition: Technique that quantifies the performance of a classifier by calculating the proportion of correct predictions it makes on a test data set.

metadata.title: Classifier Training
metadata.definition: The process of tuning the parameters of a classification model by feeding it labeled training data so that it can learn to map inputs to output classes.

metadata.title: Clausal Form
metadata.definition: A standard form of logic formulas, commonly used in theorem solutions and proofs, consisting of clauses containing only selection operators.

metadata.title: Client-Server Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database architecture where clients send requests to servers that manage and store data.

metadata.title: Client-Server Model
metadata.definition: understand the client/server architecture, in which the client requests a service from the server and the server provides that service.

metadata.title: Clocks
metadata.definition: Component that generates signals that synchronize activities in a computer system.

metadata.title: Closed & Open World Assumption
metadata.definition: Distinguish between closed-world assumptions (what is not known is false) and open-world assumptions (what is not known may be true or false).

metadata.title: Closure Creation at Runtime
metadata.definition: understand how function closures are created at runtime by 'capturing' the environment from its declared scope.

metadata.title: Closure Data Encapsulation
metadata.definition: apply function closure as a mechanism to encapsulate data, where the data is kept private within the closure's environment and can only be accessed and manipulated through that closure function.

metadata.title: Closure Idioms: Iterators
metadata.definition: Use function closures as arguments to iterators or collection traversals to customize the behavior of each element.

metadata.title: Closure Idioms: Reusable Code
metadata.definition: Develop reusable code patterns by passing functions (or closures) as arguments, allowing flexibility in behavior without modifying the main structure.

metadata.title: Closure Runtime Representation
metadata.definition: Study how functions can be passed as parameters or returned from other functions, especially the concept of closure, and how they can be represented at runtime to preserve their definition environment.

metadata.title: Closure Scope & Variables
metadata.definition: Ability to properly analyze and understand how variables and lexical scope operate in programs that use function closures, including accessing variables from the outside environment.

metadata.title: Closures: Callbacks
metadata.definition: apply function closure in common use cases such as call-backs, where a function is passed as an argument to be executed later by another function.

metadata.title: Cloud Computing Model
metadata.definition: The concept of cloud computing, services and architecture related to the provision of computing resources over a network.

metadata.title: Cloud Data Processing Frameworks
metadata.definition: Cloud-based frameworks and platforms are used for large-scale data processing and analysis.

metadata.title: Cloud Database
metadata.definition: Database systems are deployed and managed on cloud computing infrastructure, providing scalability, flexibility and cost efficiency.

metadata.title: Cloud Databases
metadata.definition: Databases are built, deployed, and delivered as a service through a cloud computing platform.

metadata.title: Clustering
metadata.definition: The technique of grouping similar data points into clusters, or groups, based on some similarity measure, is a core task of unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: Clustering Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to group similar data points together into clusters, based on their similarity.

metadata.title: Cobegin-coend
metadata.definition: Language construct for specifying a block of instructions that can be executed in parallel, starting with `cobegin` and ending with `coend`.

metadata.title: Code Generation
metadata.definition: Learn about the stage of translating source code to target code (machine code or intermediate code) in the compilation process.

metadata.title: Code Generation (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Methods for generating machine code from high-level source code.

metadata.title: Code Optimization
metadata.definition: Learn about code optimization techniques to improve the performance, size, or energy consumption of the generated program.

metadata.title: Code Optimization as Analysis
metadata.definition: Realize that code optimization techniques in compilers often rely on program analytics to gather information and make decisions that improve performance.

metadata.title: Coffman conditions
metadata.definition: Four necessary conditions that must simultaneously hold for a deadlock to arise: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

metadata.title: Cognitive Agent
metadata.definition: Agent architectures simulate human cognitive abilities such as reasoning, learning, planning, and knowledge maintenance.

metadata.title: Cognitive Architectures
metadata.definition: Frameworks or theories about the overall structure of a cognitive system, integrating different information processing capabilities.

metadata.title: Cognitive Decision Making
metadata.definition: The process by which the cognitive system chooses between different actions or outcomes, often based on goals, knowledge, and available information.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Acquisition
metadata.definition: Methods and processes for capturing new knowledge from the environment, data, or people and integrating it into cognitive systems.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Maintenance
metadata.definition: Processes and techniques for updating, modifying, and managing the knowledge base of a cognitive system over time.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Organization
metadata.definition: Methods for structuring and organizing knowledge to optimize retrieval and use in cognitive systems.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Refinement
metadata.definition: The process of improving the accuracy, completeness, and efficiency of knowledge in a cognitive system through learning or feedback.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: How knowledge is encoded and stored so that cognitive systems can use it to reason and make decisions.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Utilization
metadata.definition: How the cognitive system applies existing knowledge to solve problems, make decisions, or perform tasks.

metadata.title: Cognitive Perception
metadata.definition: The ability of a cognitive system to collect, interpret, and process information from the environment through sensors or input data.

metadata.title: Cognitive Prediction
metadata.definition: The ability of a cognitive system to estimate future events or states based on current and past information.

metadata.title: Cognitive System Evaluation
metadata.definition: Practical use cases of cognitive systems and methods to evaluate their performance, efficiency, and rationality.

metadata.title: Cognitive Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems are designed to simulate and replicate human cognitive abilities such as learning, reasoning, memory, problem solving, and decision making.

metadata.title: Collaboration
metadata.definition: A necessary professional disposition for team projects, demonstrating a willingness and intention to work together to achieve common goals.

metadata.title: Collaboration Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career orientation, which refers to the willingness and intention to work together to complete tasks, especially important in group projects.

metadata.title: Collaborative Agent
metadata.definition: Agents work together to achieve a common goal or share information to improve each other's performance, applicable in both software agents and multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Collaborative Data Management
metadata.definition: Data stewards and data users must collaborate to ensure accurate data is accessed and used only appropriately.

metadata.title: Collections, Iterators & Libraries
metadata.definition: Learn about data collection classes (e.g., lists, sets, maps), iterators, and other standard library components in programming languages.

metadata.title: Combination Calculation
metadata.definition: Perform combinatorial calculations of a set.

metadata.title: Combinational Logic
metadata.definition: Logic circuits whose output depends only on the current input, with no memory or previous state.

metadata.title: Combinatorial Explosion
metadata.definition: understand the problem where the size of the search space increases exponentially with the number of variables or choices, making it difficult to solve.

metadata.title: Common Continuous Distributions
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and differentiate common continuous distributions such as uniform, normal, and exponential.

metadata.title: Common Discrete Distributions
metadata.definition: Ability to recognize and differentiate common discrete distributions such as uniform, Bernoulli, binomial, and geometric.

metadata.title: Common Subexpression Graph Reduction
metadata.definition: Ability to illustrate in detail the graph reduction process when executing a lambda expression, especially when common subexpressions are present, to understand how to optimize execution in functional languages.

metadata.title: Communication Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, which refers to the willingness and intention to apply effective communication skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Commutativity
metadata.definition: The property of operations that their order of execution does not affect the final result.

metadata.title: Compare ML Algos & Metrics
metadata.definition: Compare two Machine Learning algorithms on a data set, implementing your own data preprocessing steps and evaluation methods (e.g., metrics and how to handle the train/test set split).

metadata.title: Compare ML Paradigms
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish and compare the characteristics, operating principles, and appropriate applications of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Compare ML Techniques
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast several machine learning techniques (e.g., decision trees, logistic regression, Naive Bayes, neural networks, and belief networks), providing examples of where each strategy is superior.

metadata.title: Compare Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: Compare the strengths and weaknesses of different programming models.

metadata.title: Competency Model
metadata.definition: Curriculum patterns in which the knowledge, skills, and career dispositions needed to perform a task are grouped together.

metadata.title: Competitive Agents
metadata.definition: Agents in a multi-agent system have conflicting goals and compete with each other to maximize their own utility or reward.

metadata.title: Compiler Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the compiler's execution model, including the stages of compilation and machine code generation.

metadata.title: Compiler Phases
metadata.definition: Overview of the stages required to automatically convert source code into assembly or other low-level languages, including lexical, syntactic, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, optimization, and final code generation.

metadata.title: Compiler Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the limitations and benefits of compilers in converting source code to machine code.

metadata.title: Compiler Semantic Analysis (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Semantic analysis methods are used in compilers.

metadata.title: Complex Data Type Layout
metadata.definition: How complex data types such as arrays, structures, or objects are arranged and stored in memory.

metadata.title: Complex Relations with Logic Connectives
metadata.definition: Skills in using logical connections (AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN) to build complex relationships from basic relationships.

metadata.title: Complex Type Rules
metadata.definition: List and explain the specific type rules that govern how a given complex type (e.g., array, structure, class) is used.

metadata.title: Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on methods for quantifying the efficiency of algorithms in time and space. (Total hours CS Core: 6, KA Core: 3)

metadata.title: Complexity Analysis Framework
metadata.definition: Systematic structure for evaluating algorithm performance in time and space. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Compose PL Features
metadata.definition: understand how programming language features are put together.

metadata.title: Composite Data Functions
metadata.definition: understand and apply function design principles to complex data, in which large functions are built upon applying smaller functions to each constituent element of the data.

metadata.title: Composite Data Types
metadata.definition: Data types are built from other types using set operations, for example: records/structs, unions, arrays, lists, functions, references.

metadata.title: Composite Type Values
metadata.definition: Describes a collection of values ​​of a complex type (e.g., array, record, class) in a programming language.

metadata.title: Composition vs Inheritance
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast object-oriented design paradigms such as composition and inheritance, analyzing the pros and cons of each and when to use each.

metadata.title: Compositional Type Constructors
metadata.definition: Understanding the fundamentals of type constructors allows building complex types from simpler types.

metadata.title: Compression-Reconstruction Trade-off
metadata.definition: Concept of trade-off between data size reduction (compression) and the ability to recover the original data from the compressed version.

metadata.title: Computability
metadata.definition: The study of which problems can be solved by an algorithm, and which problems cannot, through formal computational models.

metadata.title: Computation as State Transition System
metadata.definition: Describes computational processes as a system characterized by a set of known configurations (states) and transitions from a single configuration (state) to another.

metadata.title: Computational Complexity
metadata.definition: Research on the amount of resources (time, space) needed to solve computational problems, providing a theoretical basis for evaluating algorithm performance.

metadata.title: Computational Models & Formal Languages
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on theoretical models of computation and the formal languages ​​used to describe them. (Total hours CS Core: 9, KA Core: 23)

metadata.title: Computational Persistence
metadata.definition: The ability to persevere through difficulties and challenges in solving computational problems, which is an iterative process.

metadata.title: Computational Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Techniques and approaches for designing and implementing algorithmic solutions to real-world computational problems.

metadata.title: Computational Problems
metadata.definition: Problems can be solved using computer algorithms, often defined in terms of inputs and desired outputs.

metadata.title: Computational Science (Deprecated)
metadata.definition: The Computational Science (CN) knowledge area from CS2013 has been removed from the CS2023 curriculum because there is very little computer science content that does not overlap with other knowledge areas. In CS2013, it is allocated 1 core hour for modeling and simulation.

metadata.title: Compute Gradient
metadata.definition: Practical skills in calculating gradient vectors of specific functions.

metadata.title: Compute Partial Derivatives
metadata.definition: Practical skills in calculating partial derivatives of specific functions of many variables.

metadata.title: Computer Arch: I/O
metadata.definition: Research the mechanisms and operating principles of input/output systems in computer architecture.

metadata.title: Computer Arch: Perf & Power
metadata.definition: analyze the relationship between performance and energy consumption in computer architecture design.

metadata.title: Computer Architecture History
metadata.definition: Master the role and evolution of the basic building blocks of computers in the historical development of computer architecture.

metadata.title: Computer Building Blocks
metadata.definition: Describe the basic components that make up a computer (e.g. CPU, memory, I/O devices) and their functions.

metadata.title: Computer Components
metadata.definition: understand the basic building blocks and components of a computer system, including logic gates, flip-flops, registers, interconnections, datapaths, control units, and memory.

metadata.title: Computer Resource Types
metadata.definition: understand different types of computer resources such as shared processor, memory, disk, and network bandwidth.

metadata.title: Computer System Concepts
metadata.definition: Master the fundamental concepts in the field of computer systems.

metadata.title: Computer System Latency
metadata.definition: understand the concept of latency in general computer systems.

metadata.title: Computer Vision
metadata.definition: The field that studies how computers can 'understand' and process images and videos from the real world, including methods of image acquisition, representation and analysis.

metadata.title: Computer as Instruction FSM
metadata.definition: Describes how a computer operates as a state machine, with the ability to interpret and execute machine instructions, switching between states based on these instructions.

metadata.title: Computer as State Machine
metadata.definition: understand how a computer can be modeled as a state machine, with different states corresponding to current data and instructions.

metadata.title: Conceptual Models
metadata.definition: High-level data models are used to describe the overall data structure and relationships between entities, independent of the specific DBMS.

metadata.title: Conceptual to Relational Mapping
metadata.definition: The process of converting a conceptual data model (for example, an E-R diagram) into a concrete relational data model, including creating tables, columns, and key definitions.

metadata.title: Conceptual to Relational Schema Design
metadata.definition: Ability to build a relational schema from a conceptual schema, including handling 1:1, 1:n, and n:m relationships.

metadata.title: Concurrency & Other Paradigms
metadata.definition: The relationship and integration between concurrency and other programming paradigms, such as functional programming.

metadata.title: Concurrency Bug Detection
metadata.definition: Program analysis methods to identify errors related to concurrency, such as race conditions or deadlocks.

metadata.title: Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: Techniques that ensure data consistency when multiple users or applications access and modify the same data simultaneously.

metadata.title: Concurrency Control: 2PL
metadata.definition: Research 2-phase locking (2PL) mechanism to ensure serialization in concurrent environments (See also: OS-Concurrency).

metadata.title: Concurrency Granularity
metadata.definition: understand the importance of choosing the right granularity for concurrent tasks to optimize performance and exploit resources efficiently.

metadata.title: Concurrency Properties
metadata.definition: Important properties of parallel systems relate to the ordering and consistency of data.

metadata.title: Concurrency Structures Examples
metadata.definition: Illustrate concurrency constructs with simple programming examples, such as reading and writing to a buffer simultaneously or sequentially.

metadata.title: Concurrent Process Interaction
metadata.definition: Knowledge of interactions between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Conditional Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the conditional distribution of a random variable given the value of another random variable.

metadata.title: Conditional Expectation
metadata.definition: Define and understand the conditional expectation of a random variable.

metadata.title: Conditional Independence
metadata.definition: understand the concept of conditional independence of random variables.

metadata.title: Conditional Planning
metadata.definition: A type of planning that creates plans with ramifications, allowing the agent to react to uncertain outcomes of actions.

metadata.title: Conditional Probability
metadata.definition: Define and calculate the probability of one event occurring given that another event has occurred.

metadata.title: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: Skills in calculating conditional probabilities and using Bayes' rule to solve probability problems, along with the ability to explain the principles of this rule.

metadata.title: Confidence Interval
metadata.definition: The concept of an estimated range of values ​​for a population parameter, along with a degree of confidence that the interval contains the true parameter. Includes the ability to calculate confidence intervals as a measure of uncertainty.

metadata.title: Configuration Space & Maps
metadata.definition: Learn about the configuration space (the set of all possible positions and orientations of the robot) and the types of environment maps used to plan the robot's movements.

metadata.title: Confusion Matrix
metadata.definition: A detailed tool to analyze classifier performance, providing insight into the types of errors made, especially useful in complex classification scenarios.

metadata.title: Congestion Control
metadata.definition: Strategies are used to prevent and handle congestion in the network to maintain performance.

metadata.title: Conjunction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if all the component clauses are true (AND).

metadata.title: Conjunction as Product Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship the logical conjunctions (A and B) are mapped to the product type (A x B).

metadata.title: Connected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which there is a path between every pair of vertices, i.e. all vertices are connected.

metadata.title: Consensus
metadata.definition: The concept of consensus in a distributed system, where processes must reach a common agreement on a value or state.

metadata.title: Consensus Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms enable a distributed group of agents to reach agreement on a single data value or system state, even in the presence of errors or malicious behavior.

metadata.title: Consistency Properties
metadata.definition: Attributes that ensure data consistency in a parallel or distributed system.

metadata.title: Consistent Hashing
metadata.definition: A specialized distributed hashing scheme designed to minimize the number of keys that need to be remapped when nodes (servers) are added to or removed from a distributed system. It operates by mapping both data keys and server nodes onto the same conceptual circular hash space, assigning keys to the first node encountered clockwise from the key's position.

metadata.title: Constants
metadata.definition: Concept of constants in programming.

metadata.title: Constrained Optimization
metadata.definition: Solve optimization problems when there are additional constraints.

metadata.title: Constraint Checkers
metadata.definition: Learn about constraint checking tools used to verify constraints imposed on variables or program state.

metadata.title: Constraint Satisfaction (CSP)
metadata.definition: Study of constraint satisfaction problems (CSP), where the goal is to find a set of values ​​for variables such that all constraints are satisfied.

metadata.title: Constructors
metadata.definition: How to define constructors in a class to initialize objects when they are created.

metadata.title: Consumer
metadata.definition: A component or service in a message queue or event-driven system responsible for receiving or subscribing to messages or events from a broker, processing them, and acknowledging their receipt.

metadata.title: Content Delivery
metadata.definition: The methods and systems used to deliver content (e.g., videos, web pages, data) to end users efficiently and quickly.

metadata.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
metadata.definition: The server system distributes web and multimedia content to end users based on geographical location, to increase access speed and reduce load on the origin server.

metadata.title: Content Providers
metadata.definition: understand the role of content providers in creating, storing and distributing information and services on the Internet.

metadata.title: Content Switching / URL Hash (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A Layer 7 (Application Layer) load balancing strategy that inspects the request content, such as URL or HTTP headers, to route requests to specific servers or services. It offers fine-grained control but incurs higher processing overhead compared to Layer 4 strategies.

metadata.title: Context-Aware Computing
metadata.definition: understand systems and algorithms that collect and use contextual information to provide appropriate services or decisions.

metadata.title: Context-Free Language (Type-2)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of context-free languages, corresponding to stack automatons.

metadata.title: Context-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: Source-level static analysis techniques that consider the code's execution context, such as type checking or identifier resolution, to determine their binding locations.

metadata.title: Context-Sensitive Language (Type-1)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of context-sensitive languages, corresponding to linear boundary automatons.

metadata.title: Continuations
metadata.definition: Learn about continuations as a powerful control abstraction mechanism that enables non-local control of the flow of execution.

metadata.title: Continuous Math
metadata.definition: The field of mathematics underpins many recent burgeoning computer science fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science, and quantum computing. It is emphasized that it is necessary along with discrete structures.

metadata.title: Continuous Planning
metadata.definition: Plan in environments where time and actions can occur continuously rather than discretely.

metadata.title: Continuous Random Variable
metadata.definition: Define and understand continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Continuous Uniform Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize uniform continuous distribution.

metadata.title: Contour Shape Representation
metadata.definition: A way to represent the shape of an object by describing its outer boundary (contour).

metadata.title: Contour/Polygon Construction
metadata.definition: Algorithms combine basic visual features (such as line segments or points) to form more complex geometric structures such as contours or polygons of objects.

metadata.title: Control Flow (Code Gen)
metadata.definition: How control structures (e.g., if, loop) in source code are converted into jump and conditional statements in machine code or assembly language.

metadata.title: Control Structure Definition
metadata.definition: understand the principles and techniques for defining control structures in a programming language.

metadata.title: Controlling Model Complexity
metadata.definition: Intuitively understand methods for controlling solution complexity such as regularization and pruning.

metadata.title: Convergence & Divergence
metadata.definition: Explain the concept and criteria for determining convergence and divergence of sequences and series.

metadata.title: Convexity
metadata.definition: understand the concept of convex functions and convex sets in the context of optimization.

metadata.title: Convexity (Optimization)
metadata.definition: The concept of convex functions and convex regions is important in determining the existence and uniqueness of optimal solutions.

metadata.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A detailed study of the structure, layers (convolution, pooling, fully connected) and operation of CNNs, including mathematical aspects and extensive applications in computer vision.

metadata.title: Cook-Levin Theorem
metadata.definition: The fundamental theorem in complexity theory proves that the SAT problem is NP-Complete.

metadata.title: Coordinate Geometry
metadata.definition: Study geometry using the Cartesian coordinate system, linking algebra and geometry.

metadata.title: Copying GC
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm divides heap memory into two regions and moves live objects from the currently used region to the remaining region.

metadata.title: Core Database Concepts (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic database concepts are integrated into the CS Core curriculum, especially in the absence of specialized database courses.

metadata.title: Core System Design Principles
metadata.definition: understand key design principles for computer systems, including performance, reliability, and security.

metadata.title: Corner Detection
metadata.definition: An image processing technique for finding special points in an image where two edges intersect, often used as feature points for tracking or image registration.

metadata.title: Corpus-based Methods
metadata.definition: Learn about using large data sets (corpora) to analyze, model, and develop NLP applications.

metadata.title: Correlated vs. Uncorrelated Subqueries
metadata.definition: Ability to differentiate and understand the difference between correlated and uncorrelated nested SQL queries.

metadata.title: Counting
metadata.definition: Counting techniques in combination and probability, including permutations, combinations, and combinations.

metadata.title: Counting Card Hands
metadata.definition: Determines the number of ways to get certain decks of cards (e.g. full flood).

metadata.title: Counting Methods
metadata.definition: apply counting reasoning methods.

metadata.title: Counting Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm uses the frequency of occurrence of elements to place them in their correct position. Effective when the value range is small. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Counting with Constraints
metadata.definition: Determine the number of ways to arrange people around the table, subject to seating arrangement constraints.

metadata.title: Cross Compiler
metadata.definition: Learn about cross compilers, tools that translate source code for a target platform different from the one on which it is running.

metadata.title: Cross-Cutting Concerns
metadata.definition: Skill in applying critical and cross-cutting aspects of the software development process, including optimizing performance, ensuring system security, and adhering to best software development practices to improve quality and efficiency. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

metadata.title: Cross-Layer Error Signaling
metadata.definition: How errors are reported and propagated from layer to layer in a layered system, allowing higher layers to recognize and react.

metadata.title: Cross-Modal Data Conversion
metadata.definition: Technique that transforms data from one type of sensor (e.g., tactile) into a format that can be processed by another sensory domain (e.g., visual).

metadata.title: Cross-Validation
metadata.definition: More advanced cross-validation techniques, including different variations (e.g., K-fold, leave-one-out) to evaluate model performance and robustly tune parameters.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms and techniques used to secure information and communication, including encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and more.

metadata.title: Cryptography
metadata.definition: understand cryptography as a fundamental tool for system security.

metadata.title: Cumulative Distribution Function
metadata.definition: understand the concept and application of the cumulative distribution function in probability.

metadata.title: Current ML Theory
metadata.definition: Describes the current state of machine learning theory, including its achievements and limitations.

metadata.title: Curriculum Competency Model
metadata.definition: Curriculum patterns in which the knowledge, skills, and professional qualities needed to perform a task are grouped together.

metadata.title: Curse of Dimensionality
metadata.definition: Problems arise when analyzing and organizing data in high-dimensional space, as data becomes more sparse and algorithms become less efficient.

metadata.title: Customer Data Ownership
metadata.definition: understand the concept that data about customers belongs to (or is owned by) those customers.

metadata.title: Cuts, Backtracking, Nondeterminism
metadata.definition: Concept of cuts to control the search process, backtracking mechanism and non-determinism in logic programs.

metadata.title: Cybercrime
metadata.definition: List the types of crimes related to computers and the internet.

metadata.title: Cyclic Graph
metadata.definition: A graph contains at least one cycle (a path that starts and ends at the same vertex).

metadata.title: D2D Communication
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of direct communication between devices without the need for an access point or central server, commonly found in IoT.

metadata.title: D2D Communication Applications
metadata.definition: Describe practical applications of direct communication between devices.

metadata.title: DALL-E
metadata.definition: An example of an outstanding deep image generation model, capable of generating images from text descriptions.

metadata.title: DB Buffer Management
metadata.definition: understand how database management systems manage caches in main memory to optimize data access from disk.

metadata.title: DBMS Core Function Design
metadata.definition: Research and design the basic functions of a database management system, including query mechanisms, transaction management, cache management, and data access methods.

metadata.title: DBMS Internal Structure
metadata.definition: Detailed study of the internal architecture and operating mechanisms of a Database Management System (DBMS), including memory management, data storage, indexing, transaction management, and error recovery.

metadata.title: DBMS Internals
metadata.definition: Research on the components and internal mechanisms of database management systems.

metadata.title: DBMS User Skills
metadata.definition: Skills needed to use a database management system to organize, access, and update data.

metadata.title: DFA vs NFA
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the capabilities of deterministic and non-deterministic automatons in models such as FSA and PDA, including parity in computational power.

metadata.title: DFS
metadata.definition: Presenting the depth-first search (DFS) method for graphs.

metadata.title: DL
metadata.definition: A subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers (deep neural networks) to learn representations of data with multiple levels of abstraction.

metadata.title: DM (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Data Management (DM) knowledge area in the CS2023 program is the new name of Information Management (IM) from CS2013.

metadata.title: DM-Core
metadata.definition: Core Topics in Data Management (3 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Data
metadata.definition: A data-related topic in the Database Systems course (1 hour).

metadata.title: DM-Internals
metadata.definition: Topics on the structure and inner workings of database systems (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Modeling
metadata.definition: Data modeling topics (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-NoSQL
metadata.definition: NoSQL Database Topics (4 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Processing
metadata.definition: Topics on data processing (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Querying
metadata.definition: Topic on data query (6 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Relational
metadata.definition: Relational database topics (4 hours).

metadata.title: DM-SEP
metadata.definition: One topic in the Database Systems course (3 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Security
metadata.definition: Topics on data security (3 hours).

metadata.title: DMZ
metadata.definition: A physical or logical network segment that contains externally exposed services, designed to enhance the security of the internal network.

metadata.title: DNS
metadata.definition: understand the function, structure, and operation of the Domain Name System (DNS) in translating domain names into IP addresses.

metadata.title: DNSSEC
metadata.definition: Security measures are applied to DNS to protect the integrity and authenticity of DNS records.

metadata.title: DS Societal & Ethical Responsibility (SEP)
metadata.definition: Specific ethical and social impacts of data science applications, integrated throughout the course.

metadata.title: DTD
metadata.definition: A markup language used to define the valid structure of an XML or SGML document.

metadata.title: Dangling Pointer
metadata.definition: Explains the causes of hanging pointer problems and the methods programmers can use to avoid or fix them.

metadata.title: Data Abstraction
metadata.definition: Ability to display data at different levels of detail, hiding underlying setting details from the user.

metadata.title: Data Access Methods
metadata.definition: Techniques used to efficiently access and retrieve data from storage structures in a database management system.

metadata.title: Data Analysis
metadata.definition: Introduces basic concepts and techniques in data analysis, including collecting, cleaning, transforming, exploring, and modeling data to extract useful information and support decision making.

metadata.title: Data Anonymization
metadata.definition: Techniques and principles for removing or masking personally identifiable information from data, making individuals unidentifiable.

metadata.title: Data Availability & Quality
metadata.definition: Issues of data availability, scarcity and purity.

metadata.title: Data Availability & Scarcity
metadata.definition: Issues related to data availability to train AI models, including cases where data is abundant or scarce.

metadata.title: Data Bias
metadata.definition: Systematic errors in the data or in the way the data is collected, leading to unfair or inaccurate results or decisions.

metadata.title: Data Bias Mitigation
metadata.definition: Ability to apply methods to compensate for biased data sets and minimize their impact.

metadata.title: Data Center Network
metadata.definition: The special architecture and requirements of the networks used in data centers to connect servers and storage devices.

metadata.title: Data Center Networking
metadata.definition: Network architecture and technology specifically designed for data centers to support high traffic and virtualized applications.

metadata.title: Data Collection
metadata.definition: The process of collecting, filtering, and cleaning data from various sources to prepare it for processing and analysis.

metadata.title: Data Collection Scale
metadata.definition: Consider the scale and volume of data collected, along with its challenges and social/legal implications.

metadata.title: Data Creation
metadata.definition: The first phase of the data lifecycle, which involves collecting and entering new data into the system.

metadata.title: Data Creation Phase
metadata.definition: The first phase of the data lifecycle, focuses on collecting, ingesting or creating new data from different sources.

metadata.title: Data Custodian
metadata.definition: A role responsible for the secure and ethical storage and use of institutional data.

metadata.title: Data Custodian Role
metadata.definition: Responsibility for technical management and data maintenance, ensuring data is stored securely, accessible and in compliance with policies.

metadata.title: Data Definition & Protection
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast mechanisms for defining and protecting data elements in procedural, functional, and object-oriented approaches.

metadata.title: Data Dependence Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze dependencies between read and write data operations to identify parts of the program that can be safely and efficiently executed in parallel.

metadata.title: Data Destruction
metadata.definition: The final stage of the data lifecycle where data is securely and permanently deleted from all storage systems.

metadata.title: Data Discovery Techniques
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for exploring, analyzing, and summarizing key characteristics of data sets.

metadata.title: Data Disposal Phase
metadata.definition: The final stage in the data lifecycle, involves securely and permanently deleting or discarding data when it is no longer needed, in compliance with legal and ethical requirements.

metadata.title: Data Encoding
metadata.definition: Methods of converting data into electrical or optical signals for transmission over a network.

metadata.title: Data Engineer
metadata.definition: The role writes analytical SQL, Python and Scala code to build data assets for business teams.

metadata.title: Data Ethical Issues
metadata.definition: Awareness of the ethical principles that govern the collection, use, storage and sharing of data.

metadata.title: Data Ethics (SEP)
metadata.definition: Examining the role of data from a social, ethical, and professional issues (SEP) perspective could be the content of an in-depth course.

metadata.title: Data Evaluation Phase
metadata.definition: The phase of analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data in reports, charts, or other forms to support decision making and understanding.

metadata.title: Data Exploration
metadata.definition: Master data exploration techniques, including data dynamics, representations, descriptive statistics, and visualization methods to better understand data sets.

metadata.title: Data Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that data collection, use and analysis do not result in discrimination or disadvantage to particular groups of individuals.

metadata.title: Data Flow Graph
metadata.definition: A diagram that describes how data moves and is transformed by mathematical operations in a program.

metadata.title: Data Governance
metadata.definition: A set of policies, standards, roles, and processes to ensure the quality, availability, usability, integrity, and security of data within an organization.

metadata.title: Data Independence
metadata.definition: Ability to change the schema at one level without affecting the schema at higher levels (physical and logical data independence).

metadata.title: Data Inference Attacks
metadata.definition: Learn how to infer sensitive information from non-sensitive data and measures to prevent inference attacks, especially in the context of database systems (See also: SEC-Crypto).

metadata.title: Data Infrastructure Engineer
metadata.definition: The role implements data management systems in various data applications (e.g. OLTP).

metadata.title: Data Integrity Risks
metadata.definition: analyze common risk factors that can affect data integrity and preventative measures to maintain data accuracy and consistency (See also: SEC-Governance).

metadata.title: Data Lakes
metadata.definition: Concepts and applications of data lakes for storing large amounts of raw, unstructured or semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Data Life Cycle
metadata.definition: The different stages that data goes through from creation to destruction.

metadata.title: Data Lifecycle
metadata.definition: The study of the different stages data goes through, from creation to destruction, including Creation, Processing, Evaluation/Reporting, Retention/Retrieval and Destruction.

metadata.title: Data Lineage
metadata.definition: The complete history of the data, including where it originated, how it was transformed, moved and used over time.

metadata.title: Data Management Ethics & Society
metadata.definition: Consider the social, ethical and professional aspects related to data management, including issues of privacy, security, responsibility, social impact of data use and industry ethical standards.

metadata.title: Data Mining Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms and techniques are used to discover patterns, trends, and insights from large data sets.

metadata.title: Data Modeling
metadata.definition: The process of creating an abstract and consistent model of the data used in an information system.

metadata.title: Data Modeling (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces the basic principles and techniques for designing data structures, including the concepts of entities, attributes, and relationships.

metadata.title: Data Modeling (KA Core)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of various data models (e.g., relational model, entity-relationship model), normalization, and advanced database design principles.

metadata.title: Data Normalization
metadata.definition: The process of organizing the columns and tables of a relational database to reduce data duplication and improve data integrity.

metadata.title: Data Normalization/Standardization
metadata.definition: understand data normalization and standardization techniques.

metadata.title: Data Ownership
metadata.definition: Legal rights and control over a particular set of data, including the rights of access, modification, and distribution.

metadata.title: Data Parallelism
metadata.definition: Data parallelism technique, where the same operation is applied simultaneously to different elements of a large data set.

metadata.title: Data Parallelism Support
metadata.definition: Language features and programming constructs that support data parallelism, including examples such as `forall`, loop unrolling techniques, and paradigms such as Map/Reduce.

metadata.title: Data Preparation
metadata.definition: Steps to process raw data to make it suitable and efficient for a machine learning model, including cleaning, transforming, and encoding the data.

metadata.title: Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: understand the importance and pitfalls of data preprocessing choices.

metadata.title: Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Overview of concepts, principles and laws related to protecting personal information from unauthorized access, use or disclosure.

metadata.title: Data Privacy Regulations
metadata.definition: Master key laws and regulations related to data security and privacy, such as GDPR, HIPAA, etc., and their impact on data system design and management (See also: SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy, SEC-Foundations, SEC-Governance).

metadata.title: Data Processing
metadata.definition: The stage in the data lifecycle that involves transforming, organizing, and storing data for effective use.

metadata.title: Data Processing Phase
metadata.definition: The transformation phase, which organizes, cleans, and prepares data for use, includes activities such as normalization, integration, and transformation.

metadata.title: Data Professional Issues
metadata.definition: Understanding of responsibilities and professional standards when working with data in various roles.

metadata.title: Data Protection
metadata.definition: Measures and strategies to ensure the security, integrity and accessibility of data, including methods to protect against loss, corruption, unauthorized access and other threats.

metadata.title: Data Protection Paradigms
metadata.definition: analyze and compare different methods for defining and protecting data (e.g., encapsulation, immutability, scope) in procedural, functional, and object-oriented programming paradigms.

metadata.title: Data Provenance
metadata.definition: A detailed record of the origin of the data and the sequence of operations that have been applied to it since its creation.

metadata.title: Data Quality
metadata.definition: Importance and techniques to ensure high quality data, free of errors or noise, for AI applications.

metadata.title: Data Querying
metadata.definition: Skills in using query languages ​​(e.g., SQL) to retrieve information from databases.

metadata.title: Data Reliability
metadata.definition: The degree to which data is considered accurate, consistent, and reliable for its intended use.

metadata.title: Data Replication
metadata.definition: The process of creating and maintaining multiple copies of data at different locations to increase availability, fault tolerance, and performance.

metadata.title: Data Representation
metadata.definition: How the data is encoded or structured so that it can be used effectively by machine learning algorithms, e.g., feature vector format.

metadata.title: Data Retention & Retrieval
metadata.definition: The stage in the data lifecycle that involves storing data for a certain period of time and the ability to retrieve it when needed.

metadata.title: Data Retention Phase
metadata.definition: Stages secure and organized data storage, as well as the ability to access and retrieve data as needed according to policies and regulations.

metadata.title: Data Retransmission
metadata.definition: Mechanism to retransmit lost or corrupted data packets to ensure reliability.

metadata.title: Data Review & Reporting
metadata.definition: The stage in the data lifecycle where data is analyzed, evaluated, and presented in reports or visualizations.

metadata.title: Data Scale Issues
metadata.definition: Ethical, social, and technical challenges and implications arise from collecting, storing, and processing extremely large data sets, including privacy and security.

metadata.title: Data Science Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used in data science (like Python with Pandas, R libraries) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Data Science Life Cycle
metadata.definition: understand the stages in the data science lifecycle, from business understanding to deployment and user adoption, as a basis for data analytics and machine learning projects (See also: AI-ML).

metadata.title: Data Science Lifecycle
metadata.definition: Understanding of the different stages in the lifecycle of a data science project, from collection to deployment.

metadata.title: Data Security
metadata.definition: Measures and tools to protect data from unauthorized access, modification, destruction or disclosure.

metadata.title: Data Security & Privacy (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of data security, including threats, vulnerabilities, access controls, and principles for protecting user privacy and sensitive data.

metadata.title: Data Security & Privacy (KA Core)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of data security techniques, policies and standards, encryption, intrusion detection and prevention, privacy management, and compliance with relevant laws.

metadata.title: Data Security & Privacy Ethics
metadata.definition: Discuss ethical issues related to data collection, storage, processing, and sharing, especially in the context of security and privacy (See also: SEC-SEP, SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: Data Security Role
metadata.definition: Examining the role of data from a security perspective (Security - SEC), could be the content of an in-depth course.

metadata.title: Data Security States
metadata.definition: understand the importance and different methods to protect data in different states: when data is inactive (at rest), while in transit (in transit) and while being processed (during processing) (See also: SEC-Foundations, SEC-Crypto).

metadata.title: Data Security vs. Privacy
metadata.definition: Clear distinction between data security (protecting data from unauthorized access) and data privacy (managing how personal data is collected, used and shared) (See also: SEC-Foundations).

metadata.title: Data Smoothing
metadata.definition: Techniques that reduce noise or fluctuations in data to highlight trends and patterns.

metadata.title: Data Societal Issues
metadata.definition: Understanding the broad impacts of data on society, including privacy, bias and equality.

metadata.title: Data Splitting
metadata.definition: The process of dividing the overall data set into different subsets (training, validation, testing) to effectively train and evaluate the model.

metadata.title: Data Standardization
metadata.definition: Adjusting data values ​​so they have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, helps machine learning algorithms work more effectively.

metadata.title: Data Storage Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement a simple data storage system.

metadata.title: Data Storage Ethical Aspects
metadata.definition: Consider ethical issues arising from data storage and use, including responsibility for personal data, fairness, transparency and avoidance of bias.

metadata.title: Data Storage Legal Aspects
metadata.definition: Understanding of legal regulations related to data collection, storage, use and sharing, including data protection laws, privacy and industry standards.

metadata.title: Data Storage Privacy Concerns
metadata.definition: Identify and understand issues related to protecting personal information and sensitive data stored in systems, ensuring compliance with privacy principles.

metadata.title: Data Storage Techniques
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and use data management techniques to store data effectively in current systems.

metadata.title: Data Structure & Algorithm Selection
metadata.definition: Prepare a presentation to justify the choice of the appropriate data structure and/or algorithm to solve a given practical problem.

metadata.title: Data Structures
metadata.definition: Ways of organizing data to allow efficient storage and access, are the foundation of all theoretical calculations and applied programs.

metadata.title: Data System Deployment
metadata.definition: Skills to install, configure and deploy data management systems and solutions.

metadata.title: Data Transformation
metadata.definition: Techniques that transform data to improve model performance or make data more consistent with assumptions.

metadata.title: Data Type Binding
metadata.definition: How data types are associated with variables, function arguments, function returns, and fields in data structures.

metadata.title: Data Type Definition
metadata.definition: The concept of a data type is a set of values ​​along with a set of operations that can be performed on those values.

metadata.title: Data Update Query
metadata.definition: Skill in using query languages ​​(e.g., SQL) to modify information that already exists in a database.

metadata.title: Data Visualization
metadata.definition: Ability to display data graphically and interpret various types of graphs, especially histograms.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Applications
metadata.definition: How data visualization techniques are used to explore, present, and communicate findings from data analysis.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Fundamentals
metadata.definition: The fundamentals and theoretical foundations behind designing and creating effective data visualizations.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Libraries
metadata.definition: Knowledge of popular software libraries used to create data visualizations.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for presenting data in graphic or visual form to help users more easily understand and analyze information.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Types
metadata.definition: Understanding of different types of charts and graphs for data visualization.

metadata.title: Data as Resource
metadata.definition: View data as a valuable asset that needs to be managed, similar to other enterprise resources.

metadata.title: Data in Organization
metadata.definition: Understanding of the strategic and operational importance of data to an organization's operations, decisions and goals.

metadata.title: Data/Control Abstraction
metadata.definition: Concepts of data abstraction and control abstraction in language design.

metadata.title: Database Access
metadata.definition: Students use databases to retrieve data in introductory programming courses, instead of using file I/O or interactive data entry. This level usually includes being provided with an access code.

metadata.title: Database Administration
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on database system administration.

metadata.title: Database Architecture
metadata.definition: The overall structure of a database system, including its components and how they interact with each other.

metadata.title: Database Attack Protection
metadata.definition: Learn methods and techniques to protect data and database systems from threats and attacks, including injection attacks such as SQL injection (See also: SEC-Foundations).

metadata.title: Database Auditing & Forensics
metadata.definition: The study of database auditing, including activity logging techniques, and its important role in digital forensics to detect and analyze security breaches (See also: SEC-Forensics).

metadata.title: Database Core Concepts
metadata.definition: Introduces the basic concepts of database systems, including their rationale, advantages, and key components, providing a foundation for deeper understanding.

metadata.title: Database Design
metadata.definition: The process of determining the structure of a database to store and manage data effectively.

metadata.title: Database Design & Modeling
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on data design and modeling.

metadata.title: Database Development
metadata.definition: One of four main perspectives for approaching databases, including implementation algorithms.

metadata.title: Database Implementation Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to implement and operate database systems.

metadata.title: Database Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about database languages ​​like SQL, which are examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Database Normal Forms
metadata.definition: Rules for evaluating the degree of normalization of a relational table, with Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) being one of the higher normal forms, eliminating more data anomalies than previous normal forms.

metadata.title: Database SEP Topics
metadata.definition: Database-related Software Engineering Practice (SEP) topics are integrated into the curriculum using the 'Databases across the curriculum' approach.

metadata.title: Database Security
metadata.definition: Measures to protect databases from threats, unauthorized access and data loss.

metadata.title: Database Systems Advantages
metadata.definition: understand the key benefits of using a database system over traditional data storage methods, such as reduced duplication, improved data sharing, security, and data integrity.

metadata.title: Database Systems Components
metadata.definition: Identify and describe the elements that make up a complete database system, including users, applications, database management system (DBMS), and data.

metadata.title: Database Systems Core Concepts (KA Core)
metadata.definition: A more in-depth study of the core concepts of database systems, delving into their technical and theoretical aspects.

metadata.title: Database Systems Purpose
metadata.definition: understand the primary functions and goals that a database system is designed to serve, such as efficiently managing large amounts of data and ensuring consistency and integrity.

metadata.title: Database Tuning & Performance
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques to tune and improve overall database performance.

metadata.title: Database Usage
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on database usage.

metadata.title: Databases Across Curriculum
metadata.definition: An approach that integrates database concepts across the curriculum, from introductory to advanced courses, to integrate database-related CS Core concepts.

metadata.title: Dataframes
metadata.definition: A table data structure with columns of different types, widely used in data analysis and data science.

metadata.title: Datalink Layer
metadata.definition: Functions and protocols of the data link layer, responsible for transmitting data frames between devices on the same local network (single-hop).

metadata.title: Dataset Bias
metadata.definition: Types of bias possible in the dataset.

metadata.title: De-identification
metadata.definition: The process of removing or modifying personally identifiable information from data to protect privacy.

metadata.title: Dead Letter Queues (DLQs)
metadata.definition: A dedicated queue used in message queue systems to store messages that could not be successfully processed after a certain number of retries or due to other processing failures, facilitating error handling and debugging.

metadata.title: Deadlock
metadata.definition: A state in operating systems where two or more processes are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for a resource held by another process in the same set.

metadata.title: Deadlock Handling Strategies
metadata.definition: Learn methods to detect, prevent, and resolve deadlocks in concurrent database systems.

metadata.title: Deadlock avoidance
metadata.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks that dynamically allocates resources only if doing so leaves the system in a safe state.

metadata.title: Deadlock detection and recovery
metadata.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks where the system allows deadlocks to occur, periodically runs a detection algorithm (e.g., graph traversal for cycles), and then recovers by either terminating processes or preempting resources and rolling back process states.

metadata.title: Deadlock prevention
metadata.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks that ensures at least one of the four necessary Coffman conditions never occurs (e.g., requiring processes to request all resources at once or imposing a total ordering on resource acquisition).

metadata.title: Debugging Tools
metadata.definition: understand and use specialized software tools to detect, analyze and fix errors in program source code.

metadata.title: Decentralized Routing
metadata.definition: Routing method in which each router calculates its own routes based on local information and information exchanged with neighboring routers.

metadata.title: Decidability, Computability, Halting Problem
metadata.definition: The concepts of problem determinism, function computability, and Halting Problem along with their meaning in computational theory.

metadata.title: Decimals
metadata.definition: understand and work with decimals, including operations and conversions between fractions and decimals.

metadata.title: Decision Making Incomplete Info
metadata.definition: Explore how AI agents process and make decisions with only partial information about the world state or available options.

metadata.title: Decision Making Under Uncertainty
metadata.definition: Research methods and algorithms for AI agents to make optimal decisions when information about the environment or the results of actions are not completely clear.

metadata.title: Decision Theory
metadata.definition: The study of the decisions of agents when the consequences of their choices are not known with certainty, including probabilistic and utility inference methods.

metadata.title: Decision Tree
metadata.definition: A nonparametric prediction model uses a decision tree structure in which each internal node represents an attribute, each branch represents an attribute value, and each leaf node represents a class or value.

metadata.title: Decision Trees
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of decision trees as an example of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Decision-Theoretic Agent
metadata.definition: Agents make decisions based on the principles of decision theory, considering the utility and probability of different outcomes.

metadata.title: Declarations
metadata.definition: Concept of declaration in programming, including nested declarations.

metadata.title: Declarative Query Language
metadata.definition: Learn to use query languages ​​in which the user specifies the desired result without specifying how to achieve it, for example, SQL.

metadata.title: Declare Before Use
metadata.definition: The rule requires variables or functions to be defined or declared before being used in a program.

metadata.title: Decomposition Normal Form Identification
metadata.definition: The ability to detect the normal form that a given decomposition achieves (e.g., 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF).

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy that solves a problem by transforming it into a smaller version of the same problem, for example searching a tree by depth or breadth. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer (Advanced)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy that solves a problem by transforming it into a smaller version of the same problem, for example topological sorting. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Constant
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem decreases by a constant (usually 1) at each step, for example in insertion sort.

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Constant Factor
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem decreases by a constant factor (e.g., bisection) at each step, for example in binary search.

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Variable Size
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem is reduced by a variable amount at each step, depending on the input data.

metadata.title: Deduction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Method of inference from general rules to specific conclusions.

metadata.title: Deep Architectures
metadata.definition: Overview of other types of neural network architectures beyond feedforward and convolutional networks, designed for specific types of data and tasks.

metadata.title: Deep Feedforward Networks
metadata.definition: A detailed study of the structure, operation, and mathematical aspects of deep feedforward neural networks (also known as MLPs), including activation functions, backpropagation, and optimization.

metadata.title: Deep Feedforward Networks (Intuitive)
metadata.definition: understand the structure and basic operation of multi-layer feedforward neural networks, in which information only moves in one direction from the input layer to the output layer, without going into deep mathematical formulas.

metadata.title: Deep Generative Models
metadata.definition: Discusses tools that use deep generation models, how they work at a high level, their uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: Deep Image Generative Models
metadata.definition: The operating mechanism of deep learning models capable of creating new images, including structure and principles.

metadata.title: Deep Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers (deep networks) to learn representations of data at different levels of abstraction.

metadata.title: Deep Learning (PR)
metadata.definition: Use deep neural networks, such as convolutional networks (CNN) and recurrent networks (RNN), to automatically learn features and perform high-performance pattern recognition.

metadata.title: Deep Learning Representation
metadata.definition: How data is encoded or transformed by deep networks to create meaningful features, helping the model learn more complex patterns.

metadata.title: Deep Learning for NLP
metadata.definition: Learn advanced deep learning techniques applied in the field of Natural Language Processing.

metadata.title: Deep Nets (Learned Rep.)
metadata.definition: Use deep neural networks as a powerful tool to automatically learn and extract meaningful, hierarchical representations from input data.

metadata.title: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)
metadata.definition: Technique that examines the detailed content of network packets to perform security, traffic management, or analysis functions.

metadata.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)
metadata.definition: The combination of reinforcement learning and deep learning, using deep neural networks to represent value or policy functions, allows learning from complex, high-dimensional input data.

metadata.title: Def-Use Chain
metadata.definition: A definition-use chain is a data structure or analysis in which each definition of a variable is associated with all the places that variable can be used after that definition.

metadata.title: Default Reasoning
metadata.definition: A form of nonmonotonic inference where conclusions are drawn based on default assumptions in the absence of conflicting information.

metadata.title: Define PL Features
metadata.definition: understand how programming language features are defined.

metadata.title: Definite & Indefinite Integral
metadata.definition: Explain the definition and difference between definite and indefinite integrals.

metadata.title: Definite Iteration
metadata.definition: The concept of a definite iteration structure, such as a `for` loop.

metadata.title: Delayed Gratification
metadata.definition: The ability to wait to see practical applications or benefits of mathematical knowledge, especially in the context of information technology.

metadata.title: Deliberative Agents
metadata.definition: A type of agent capable of planning, reasoning, and building models of the world to make decisions.

metadata.title: Demand paging
metadata.definition: A memory management technique, also known as swapping, where pages are loaded into physical memory only when they are referenced (on demand) following a page fault, allowing programs larger than physical RAM to run.

metadata.title: Denormalization (Performance)
metadata.definition: The process of intentionally introducing data redundancy into a normalized database schema to improve query performance, often by reducing the number of joins required.

metadata.title: Denormalization Reasons
metadata.definition: Gives the rationale and context for denormalizing a relationship in the database, often to improve performance.

metadata.title: Denormalization for Performance
metadata.definition: apply denormalization as a tuning technique to improve query performance by reducing the number of joins, although it may increase data redundancy.

metadata.title: Denotational Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about model semantics as a method for describing the meaning of a program by mapping it to abstract mathematical objects.

metadata.title: Dependencies & Preconditions
metadata.definition: Understanding of data dependencies and preconditions in parallel tasks, necessary to ensure correctness and order of execution.

metadata.title: Dependency Preserving Decomposition
metadata.definition: A property of schema decomposition ensures that all original functional dependencies can be tested by testing only the functional dependencies in the decomposed child tables.

metadata.title: Dependent Types
metadata.definition: Learn about dependent types, an advanced concept where data types can depend on data values.

metadata.title: Deployed Deep Generative Models
metadata.definition: An in-depth introduction to deep learning-based generative AI models deployed in practice.

metadata.title: Depth-First Search
metadata.definition: The algorithm searches the tree or graph, exploring as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking and exploring another branch. It is a form of non-informational search.

metadata.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
metadata.definition: The tree or graph traversal algorithm starts at the root node and explores as far each branch as possible before backtracking. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Deque
metadata.definition: Double-ended queue, allowing elements to be added and removed from both ends. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Deques
metadata.definition: A double-ended queue allows elements to be added and removed from both ends of the queue efficiently.

metadata.title: Derivations & Ambiguity
metadata.definition: The concepts of left-most derivation and right-most derivation arise in grammar, and ambiguity may arise.

metadata.title: Derivative Limit Definition
metadata.definition: Explain the definition of the derivative as a limit.

metadata.title: Derivative as Function
metadata.definition: Explain the concept that the derivative of a function is also a function.

metadata.title: Deriving Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: understand how to differentiate and prove the Bayes' Rule formula.

metadata.title: Description Logics (DLs)
metadata.definition: A family of knowledge representation languages ​​used to model concepts and the relationships between them.

metadata.title: Detecting Data Bias & Errors
metadata.definition: Ability to identify biased data sets and other sources of error that can affect machine learning results.

metadata.title: Deterministic & Stochastic Grammar
metadata.definition: understand and distinguish between deterministic grammars (which always produce the same result for the same input) and stochastic grammars (which use probability to choose between options).

metadata.title: Deterministic vs. Stochastic
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the outcome of an action is certain from those where there is an element of chance.

metadata.title: Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm
metadata.definition: One of the earliest quantum algorithms, demonstrating that quantum computers can solve some problems faster than classical computers under certain circumstances.

metadata.title: Device-to-Device (D2D) Communication
metadata.definition: Principles of direct communication between devices, such as communication in IoT.

metadata.title: Dictionary
metadata.definition: The data structure stores key-value pairs, allowing quick access to values ​​via keys.

metadata.title: Dictionary Add
metadata.definition: The operation adds a new key-value pair to the dictionary data structure.

metadata.title: Dictionary Remove
metadata.definition: The operation removes a key-value pair from a dictionary data structure based on its key.

metadata.title: Dictionary Search
metadata.definition: The operation retrieves the value associated with a specific key in a dictionary data structure.

metadata.title: Dictionary/Map
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores key-value pairs, allowing the value to be retrieved by its unique key.

metadata.title: Differential Evolution
metadata.definition: A metaheuristic optimization algorithm belongs to the family of evolutionary algorithms, used to solve continuous optimization problems using mutation, hybridization, and selection operators.

metadata.title: Differential Privacy
metadata.definition: Explain how differential privacy protects personal information in a data set.

metadata.title: Digital & Analog System Examples
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and provide real-life examples of digital and analog systems, clarifying the differences between them.

metadata.title: Digital Circuit Design
metadata.definition: Principles and methods of designing electronic circuits that operate with digital signals.

metadata.title: Digital Logic
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of electronic circuits are based on the binary system, the foundation for computer design.

metadata.title: Digital System Clock
metadata.definition: The role of clock in synchronizing and controlling operations in digital systems.

metadata.title: Digital System Memory
metadata.definition: Devices or systems used to store data in computer and digital systems.

metadata.title: Digital System Sequencing
metadata.definition: How operations and state transitions are arranged in a particular sequence to perform a certain function in a digital system.

metadata.title: Digital System State
metadata.definition: The concept of state is a set of currently stored values ​​of a system, influencing its future behavior.

metadata.title: Digital vs. Analog Systems
metadata.definition: Difference between digital system and analog system.

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights.

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm (Greedy)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of finding a globally optimal solution, such as Dijkstra's algorithm for finding the shortest path. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Dimensionality Reduction
metadata.definition: Techniques for reducing the number of random variables are considered by obtaining a smaller set of key variables. Includes the ability to apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to data dimensionality reduction problems.

metadata.title: Directed Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges are directed, meaning the connection from one vertex to another is not necessarily symmetric.

metadata.title: Disconnected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which at least one pair of vertices has no path between them, i.e. it is made up of many connected components.

metadata.title: Discrete & Continuous System Examples
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and provide practical examples of discrete and continuous systems, clarifying the differences between them.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (CS Core)
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of discrete mathematics, considered a core requirement for all Computer Science (CS) majors. Total 29 hours of study.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (FPL)
metadata.definition: Discrete mathematical principles underpin the field of Programming Language Foundations.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of discrete mathematics complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 11 class hours.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic discrete mathematics concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Boolean Algebra
