metadata.definition: Concepts and rules of Boolean algebra, the foundation for digital logic, electronic circuit design, and programming.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Counting
metadata.definition: Counting techniques and principles in discrete mathematics, including permutations, combinations, and compensation principles.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Digital Logic
metadata.definition: Basic principles of digital logic, used in the design of computer circuits and digital systems.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Finite State Machines
metadata.definition: A mathematical model of computation used to design sequential reaction systems, including states and state transitions.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Functions & Relations
metadata.definition: Concepts of mapping, functions, types of functions (unijective, complete, bijective) and types of relationships between sets.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Graphs & Relations
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of graphs, vertices, edges, types of graphs (directed, undirected) and how to represent relationships graphically.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Various methods and techniques for proving mathematical statements, including direct, indirect, induction, and contradiction proofs.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Recurrence Relations
metadata.definition: Equations define a series of numbers in terms of previous terms in the series, used for algorithmic analysis and problem solving.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Regular Grammars
metadata.definition: A type of formal grammar used to describe formal languages, often involving finite state machines and regular expressions.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Set Operations
metadata.definition: Concepts of sets, elements and basic operations on sets such as union, intersection, difference, complement.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: State & Invariants
metadata.definition: The concepts of a system's state and invariants are always true throughout the system's operation.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Trees
metadata.definition: Tree data structure, types of trees (binary trees, search trees) and their properties in discrete mathematics.

metadata.title: Discrete Mathematics
metadata.definition: Discrete Mathematics requirements.

metadata.title: Discrete Random Variable
metadata.definition: Define and understand discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Discrete Structures
metadata.definition: The mathematics literacy area, covered in the ACM CS2013 report, was the predecessor to the current MSF area. Although still an important part, the range of mathematics required for modern computer science has expanded beyond just discrete structures.

metadata.title: Discrete Structures (CS2013)
metadata.definition: One of the main mathematical components in the CS2013 curriculum, now part of the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) in CS2023.

metadata.title: Discrete Uniform Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize uniform discrete distributions.

metadata.title: Discrete vs Continuous Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems with a finite and countable number of states or actions from those with an infinite or continuously variable space of states or actions.

metadata.title: Discrete vs. Continuous Systems
metadata.definition: Difference between discrete and continuous systems.

metadata.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) Data Structure
metadata.definition: A data structure that manages a collection of disjoint sets, commonly optimized with path compression and union by rank/size to achieve a nearly constant amortized time complexity, often expressed as O(α(N)).

metadata.title: Disjunction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if at least one component clause is true (OR).

metadata.title: Disjunction as Sum Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship, the logical selection (A or B) is mapped to the total type (A + B).

metadata.title: Distance Between Points
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating the distance between two points in the coordinate system.

metadata.title: Distributed Application Models
metadata.definition: Describes the basic architectural models for distributed applications, including how they interact and distribute work across multiple systems.

metadata.title: Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: The concept of distributed computing, where tasks are broken down and performed across multiple computers in a network to achieve a common goal.

metadata.title: Distributed Computing Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to distributed computing, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Distributed DBMS
metadata.definition: Database management systems allow data to be stored and managed on many different physical computers, but still operate as a single logical database.

metadata.title: Distributed Data Management
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and principles of distributed data management, allocated 2 class hours.

metadata.title: Distributed Data Processing
metadata.definition: Distributed data processing concepts and techniques, including frameworks such as MapReduce and cloud frameworks.

metadata.title: Distributed Data Storage
metadata.definition: A method of storing data on multiple networked nodes or servers, allowing for scalability, fault tolerance, and efficient data access.

metadata.title: Distributed Database
metadata.definition: Database systems in which data is stored on multiple interconnected computers, often located in different geographical locations.

metadata.title: Distributed Hashing
metadata.definition: A method used in distributed systems to distribute data or keys across multiple interconnected nodes (servers) using a hashing function, aiming for efficient data distribution and retrieval.

metadata.title: Distributed Query Processing
metadata.definition: Technique for handling queries on data stored across multiple locations in a distributed database system.

metadata.title: Distributed Storage Design
metadata.definition: analyze design principles applied in distributed storage systems.

metadata.title: Distributed Transaction Model
metadata.definition: The model manages transactions involving multiple data sources or resources on different nodes in a distributed system, ensuring consistency and integrity.

metadata.title: Distributed Transactions
metadata.definition: Learn how to manage transactions that span multiple databases or systems, including challenges and solutions for consistency and reliability (See also: PDC-Coordination).

metadata.title: Distributed systems
metadata.definition: Systems where components located on networked computers communicate and coordinate their actions by passing messages. In this context, they are the environment where rate limiting and throttling are applied to control resource access.

metadata.title: Distributed, Concurrent, Parallel Integration
metadata.definition: understand and integrate the concepts of distributed, concurrency, and parallelism with various programming models as a core area in the context of multicore computing, cloud computing, and computer networks.

metadata.title: Distributed/Cloud Databases
metadata.definition: Study the architecture, challenges, and techniques of distributed databases and how they are deployed and managed in cloud computing environments to achieve scalability, high availability, and fault tolerance.

metadata.title: Distribution Types Comparison
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish and explain relationships between simultaneous, marginal, and conditional distributions.

metadata.title: Diverse AI Applications
metadata.definition: Research and apply artificial intelligence in many different fields such as medicine, health, sustainability, social media, economics, education, and robotics.

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy divides the problem into smaller subproblems, solves the subproblems independently, and then combines the solutions. For example: merge sort, quick sort. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer (Advanced)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy divides the problem into smaller subproblems, solves the subproblems independently, and then combines the solutions. For example, Strassen's algorithm for matrix multiplication. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
metadata.definition: A robust algorithmic strategy consists of three steps: dividing the larger problem into smaller subproblems, recursively solving the subproblems, and combining the subsolutions to form the solution of the original problem.

metadata.title: DoS Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to overload systems or network services, making them unable to provide services to legitimate users.

metadata.title: DoS Protection
metadata.definition: Measures and systems designed to detect, mitigate and prevent denial of service attacks.

metadata.title: Domain Hierarchy
metadata.definition: The hierarchical structure of the domain name system (Domain Name System - DNS) and how it organizes the management and resolution of domain names into IP addresses.

metadata.title: Domain-Specific Language (DSL)
metadata.definition: understand the concepts and applications of domain-specific languages, designed for a specific application domain.

metadata.title: Domain-Specific Language Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design a specific programming language (Domain-Specific Language - DSL) according to the requirements of a specific application area or type of problem.

metadata.title: Doubly Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which each node points to both the next and previous node in the chain, allowing two-way traversal.

metadata.title: Duplicate Detection by Sorting
metadata.definition: Technique for finding duplicate elements in a list by first sorting the list, then traversing adjacent elements to detect similar values.

metadata.title: Dynamic Arrays
metadata.definition: A data structure (like Java's ArrayList or C++'s std::vector) that can grow or shrink in size, achieving an amortized O(1) time complexity for appending elements despite occasional O(N) reallocations when the underlying array needs to be resized.

metadata.title: Dynamic Checked Properties
metadata.definition: Defines program properties that are checked at run time (dynamic testing) in a variety of programming languages.

metadata.title: Dynamic Code Evaluation (`eval`)
metadata.definition: understand and use the ability to dynamically evaluate code at runtime, typically via the 'eval' function, and its advantages and associated security risks.

metadata.title: Dynamic Dispatch
metadata.definition: The concept of dynamic dispatching, the mechanism that determines which methods will be called at runtime based on the type of the object.

metadata.title: Dynamic Dispatch & Control Flow
metadata.definition: Predict and verify the flow of control in programs using dynamic dispatch.

metadata.title: Dynamic Graph Construction
metadata.definition: Investigate how to build a state space graph dynamically during the search process, instead of having the entire graph from the beginning.

metadata.title: Dynamic Hash Indexes
metadata.definition: Study dynamic hash indexes and how they self-adjust to handle growth or decrease in the size of data.

metadata.title: Dynamic Memory Management
metadata.definition: Techniques for allocating and freeing memory during program runtime.

metadata.title: Dynamic NAT
metadata.definition: A type of Network Address Translation that maps a private IP address to one of a pool of available public IP addresses, typically assigned on a first-come, first-served basis.

metadata.title: Dynamic Programming
metadata.definition: A mathematical optimization technique and algorithm design method that solves complex problems by dividing them into simpler subproblems and storing their results to avoid recalculation.

metadata.title: Dynamic Recompilation
metadata.definition: A technique of recompiling parts of a program at runtime, often to apply new optimizations based on the program's actual behavior or to adapt to a changing environment.

metadata.title: Dynamic Recompilation Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the advantages, disadvantages, and difficulties of dynamic recompilation.

metadata.title: Dynamic Search Space
metadata.definition: The study of search spaces that change during problem solving, requires adaptive algorithms.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Code Reusability
metadata.definition: Explain how dynamic styling can promote more flexible code reuse, especially in scenarios where the type doesn't need to be known completely in advance.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Deferred Type Decisions
metadata.definition: Explain the benefit of dynamic styling in allowing style decisions to be deferred, facilitating rapid prototyping.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Flexible Code Patterns
metadata.definition: understand how dynamic typing supports flexible models, allowing the convenient use of heterogeneous collections.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Incomplete Program Execution
metadata.definition: Explain how dynamic typing can allow incomplete or incomplete programs to run, useful for iterative development.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Late Error Detection
metadata.definition: Explain the benefit of dynamic typing in allowing errors to occur at runtime or avoiding some errors until execution.

metadata.title: Dynamic vs Static Properties
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate dynamic and static properties in programming languages, including how they are defined and behave at compile time and run time.

metadata.title: E-R Data Model
metadata.definition: An abstract model is used to describe the structure of a database through entities, attributes, and relationships.

metadata.title: E-R Diagram
metadata.definition: A graphical tool for representing entities, attributes, and relationships between them in a conceptual database model.

metadata.title: EBNF Grammar Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use EBNF to describe the syntax of a context-free grammar, which provides a more extensible and readable syntax than BNF.

metadata.title: ECN
metadata.definition: The mechanism allows routers to directly notify the sender of congestion without dropping the packet.

metadata.title: EDA Methods
metadata.definition: Initial techniques for analyzing data sets aim to summarize their main characteristics, often using visual methods.

metadata.title: EDAC Comparison
metadata.definition: Ability to compare different error detection and correction methods based on criteria such as additional data cost, implementation complexity, and relative execution time for the encoding, error detection, and correction processes.

metadata.title: Eager Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the concept of immediate evaluation, where an expression is evaluated immediately.

metadata.title: Early Programmatic DB Access
metadata.definition: Encourage learning and practice of database access through programming early in the curriculum, reflecting industry needs and realities.

metadata.title: Edge Computing
metadata.definition: understand edge computing, where data is processed closer to its source rather than sent to a cloud data center.

metadata.title: Edge Detection
metadata.definition: An image processing technique for identifying points in an image that have abrupt changes in pixel intensity, often representing the boundaries of objects.

metadata.title: Edge-based Segmentation
metadata.definition: Image segmentation techniques are based on detecting boundaries and edges in images, where pixel intensities change suddenly.

metadata.title: Effective Formal Methods Application
metadata.definition: The ability to recognize the situations and contexts in which formal methods can be applied most effectively, as well as how to structure the development process to maximize their value.

metadata.title: Efficient Collections & Iterators
metadata.definition: Effectively use collection classes and iterators to solve a problem.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Access
metadata.definition: Techniques and strategies to ensure data can be quickly, securely, and efficiently retrieved from the database system, minimizing latency and enhancing throughput.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Access Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods to optimize query performance by avoiding direct access and reprocessing of raw data, often including the use of special data structures and aggregation tools.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Storage
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods to optimize storage space utilization and access performance for data in a database system, especially important in OLTP applications.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Structures
metadata.definition: Data structures are specifically designed to optimize data access and processing, especially in big data situations, to improve performance.

metadata.title: Efficient String Matching
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to quickly find occurrences of one or more patterns in a large text string.

metadata.title: Eigenspace Diagonalization
metadata.definition: Use matrix eigenspaces, when possible, to diagonalize a matrix.

metadata.title: Eigenvalue
metadata.definition: The concept of scalar values ​​represents the scaling factor to which the eigenvectors are scaled.

metadata.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
metadata.definition: Find the eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors of a matrix.

metadata.title: Eigenvalues Significance
metadata.definition: Explain the meaning of eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors.

metadata.title: Eigenvector
metadata.definition: The concept of vectors only scales (scales) by a constant when a linear transformation is applied.

metadata.title: Eigenvector Linear Transform
metadata.definition: Use eigenvectors to represent a linear transformation of a particular basis.

metadata.title: Elementary Algebra
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of algebra, including variables, expressions, and equations.

metadata.title: Elementary Row Operations
metadata.definition: Ability to perform basic row operations on matrices.

metadata.title: Embedded Computing Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used in embedded computing (like C, Rust) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Embedded Systems
metadata.definition: Software development for specialized computer systems embedded in larger devices or systems, often with limited resources and real-time requirements. This is an important unit of knowledge in SPD.

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Actuators
metadata.definition: Study the parts of embodied agents that allow them to physically impact the environment (e.g., robotic arms, wheels).

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Dynamics
metadata.definition: Learn about the laws of physics and motion behavior that govern embodied agents and their interactions with the environment.

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Sensors
metadata.definition: Study the types of sensors that embodied agents use to collect information from the physical environment.

metadata.title: Embodied Agents
metadata.definition: Learn about AI agents that have a physical existence in the real or simulated world, capable of physically interacting with the environment.

metadata.title: Emerging Data Roles
metadata.definition: Understanding of new and evolving job positions in the data management field, reflecting technological change.

metadata.title: Emerging Data Tech
metadata.definition: Research into new and advanced data technologies that are supplementing or replacing traditional relational systems.

metadata.title: Emerging Networking Topics (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Emerging technologies and trends in the field of computer networking at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Emerging Networking Topics (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Emerging technologies and trends in the field of computer networking for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Emerging Topics
metadata.definition: Core units of knowledge on cutting-edge and evolving topics in networking and communications, such as network virtualization, quantum networks, and middleboxes. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Empirical & Asymptotic Measurement
metadata.definition: Methods for measuring algorithm performance, including actual measurement and evaluation based on the growth rate of the complexity function.

metadata.title: Empirical Performance Measurement
metadata.definition: The methods realistically measure the runtime and memory consumption of algorithms by running them against specific data sets. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Encapsulation Mechanisms
metadata.definition: understand and use encapsulation mechanisms in programming to manage access and protect data.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Data Hiding
metadata.definition: apply data hiding as an object-oriented idiom for encapsulation, hiding the internal implementation details of an object.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Interfaces
metadata.definition: Use interfaces as an encapsulation idiom, revealing only the method signature without the implementation.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Member Visibility
metadata.definition: Controls the visibility of class members (public, private, protected) as part of encapsulation.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Mixins
metadata.definition: Use mixins as an encapsulation mechanism, allowing classes to combine functionality from multiple sources.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Privacy
metadata.definition: apply privacy as an object-oriented idiom for encapsulation, controlling access to class members.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Traits
metadata.definition: Use traits as an encapsulation mechanism, allowing reuse of behavior across classes without inheritance.

metadata.title: End-to-end principle
metadata.definition: A fundamental networking design principle implying that intelligence should primarily reside in end hosts, which NAT breaks by modifying packet headers mid-transit and complicating certain protocols that rely on transparent end-to-end communication.

metadata.title: Endianness
metadata.definition: Two different byte arrangements in memory for multi-byte values, affecting data compatibility between systems.

metadata.title: English-centric PL Impact
metadata.definition: Discusses the effects, both positive and negative, of predominantly English-based programming languages ​​on the global developer community and inclusivity.

metadata.title: Ensemble Learning
metadata.definition: Research advanced model ensemble methods, including boosting, bagging, and random forest, to improve model performance and robustness.

metadata.title: Entity Integrity
metadata.definition: The rule ensures that each row (record) in a table has a unique primary key and is not empty.

metadata.title: Entity Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques for identifying and merging records referencing the same entity in different data sources.

metadata.title: Environment Variables
metadata.definition: Concepts, how to set, access and use environment variables in shell scripting.

metadata.title: Environment vs Store
metadata.definition: Distinguish between environment (environment - maps variable names to memory addresses or values) and memory (store - maps memory addresses to values), along with their properties.

metadata.title: Equational Logic
metadata.definition: Master the concept of equational logic, a system of logic based on solving equations and the principle of substituting equals, commonly used in functional-logic programming and rewriting theory.

metadata.title: Equivalent Computation Models
metadata.definition: Study of different computational models with power equivalent to Turing Machines, demonstrating that they can simulate each other.

metadata.title: Error Control
metadata.definition: Techniques used to detect and correct errors during data transmission over a network.

metadata.title: Error Correcting Codes
metadata.definition: Describe the importance and how error correcting codes (ECCs) are used to detect and correct data errors in memory, storage devices, and communications networks.

metadata.title: Error Correction
metadata.definition: Data encryption methods so that the original data can be restored even if errors occur during transmission.

metadata.title: Error Detection
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques used to identify and detect errors occurring in system components or layers.

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.definition: Error and exception handling techniques and methods in shell scripts to ensure stable and reliable program operation.

metadata.title: Error Rate
metadata.definition: The proportion of false predictions (including false positives and false negatives) in the total number of predictions of a classification problem.

metadata.title: Error State Reflection
metadata.definition: Technique for communicating error status from lower layers to higher layers in a layered application, allowing the upper layers to react appropriately.

metadata.title: Ethernet
metadata.definition: Popular wired LAN standard, including different versions, frame structures, and operating mechanisms.

metadata.title: Ethical & Safe Algorithms
metadata.definition: understand and evaluate algorithms from a social, ethical, and security perspective.

metadata.title: Ethical AI Interaction
metadata.definition: Ethical concerns arise from AI systems' interactions with humans, including privacy, responsibility, bias, and fairness.

metadata.title: Ethical Data Visualization
metadata.definition: Understanding of ethical issues related to the presentation and interpretation of data through visualization.

metadata.title: Ethical ML Explainability
metadata.definition: The ethical aspect of ensuring that machine learning model decisions and operations can be understood and explained by humans contributes to building trust and accountability. (Related to AI-009 but focusing on ethical aspects).

metadata.title: Euclidean Algorithm
metadata.definition: apply Euclid's algorithm to calculate the greatest common divisor (GCD).

metadata.title: Euler Method
metadata.definition: A simple numerical method to approximate solutions of ordinary differential equations.

metadata.title: Euler for Integration
metadata.definition: Skills in using the Euler method to approximate the value of a definite integral.

metadata.title: Euler for Multivariable ODE
metadata.definition: Skills in using the Euler method to approximately solve a system of ordinary differential equations or ODEs with many variables.

metadata.title: Euler for Single-Variable ODE
metadata.definition: Skills in using the Euler method to find approximate solutions for ODEs with only one dependent variable.

metadata.title: Evaluation Bias
metadata.definition: The presence of bias in the process of evaluating the performance of a machine learning model, can lead to an incorrect assessment of the model's ability to generalize or be fair.

metadata.title: Event
metadata.definition: Define an event as a subset of the sample space.

metadata.title: Event Broker
metadata.definition: A central component in message queue and event-driven systems that manages queues, stores messages or events, and facilitates their reliable delivery from producers to consumers. Examples include Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus, or Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

metadata.title: Event Calculus
metadata.definition: A logic-based knowledge representation method used to reason about time and occurrences.

metadata.title: Event Handlers & Listeners
metadata.definition: Skills in defining and implementing event handlers or listeners in a reactive programming framework.

metadata.title: Event Independence
metadata.definition: The ability to determine whether two events are independent or not.

metadata.title: Event Parameterization
metadata.definition: How to parameterize event dispatchers and the arguments (data) associated with the event to pass information.

metadata.title: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA)
metadata.definition: An architectural paradigm where services communicate by producing and consuming events representing significant state changes, often via an event broker, leading to highly decoupled, scalable, and responsive distributed systems. It offers superior fault tolerance, scalability, and loose coupling compared to synchronous models but introduces complexities like eventual consistency and message ordering.

metadata.title: Event-Driven Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to event-driven programming, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Event-Driven Programming
metadata.definition: The programming model focuses on handling events and reacting to them asynchronously, including the concepts of data flow and events.

metadata.title: Event-Driven State Machines
metadata.definition: Conceptualize event-driven and reactive programs as state transition systems, where events trigger state changes.

metadata.title: Event-Reactive Programming (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of event-driven and reactive programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Event-Reactive Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in event-driven and reactive programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Event-driven & Reactive PL
metadata.definition: A programming model in which the flow of program execution is determined by events and continuously reacts to changes. The number of core hours spent on this topic has increased by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Eventual Consistency
metadata.definition: A characteristic of distributed systems where, after an update, all copies of the data will eventually reflect that update, though there might be a period of temporary inconsistency. Ensuring this across services is identified as a key challenge in Event-Driven Architecture.

metadata.title: Exact Bayesian Inference
metadata.definition: Algorithms to calculate exact probability distributions of variables in a Bayesian Network given observational information.

metadata.title: Excel Data Management
metadata.definition: Skills in using spreadsheet software such as Excel to organize, analyze and present data.

metadata.title: Exception Handling
metadata.definition: Exception handling techniques for robust program management of errors and unusual situations.

metadata.title: Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution after it has been translated, linked, and loaded into memory.

metadata.title: Existential Quant. as Dependent Product
metadata.definition: understand the relationship between existential quantification and dependency products in the context of dependency types.

metadata.title: Existential Quantifier as Dependent Product
metadata.definition: understand how existential quantifiers can be represented as dependent products in a dependent type system.

metadata.title: Expectation & Variance
metadata.definition: Ability to clearly define the concepts of expectation and variance of random variables.

metadata.title: Expectation-Maximization (EM)
metadata.definition: An iterative algorithm for finding maximum likelihood estimates or maximum posterior estimates of parameters in statistical models with unobservable latent variables.

metadata.title: Expected Utility Maximization
metadata.definition: A principle in decision theory according to which a rational agent should choose the action that maximizes the total expected value (utility) of all possible outcomes.

metadata.title: Expected Value
metadata.definition: Defines the expectation (mean value) of a random variable.

metadata.title: Expectimax Search
metadata.definition: Research search algorithms used in games with random elements (chance nodes) or in the process of solving Markov decision making problems (MDP), combining optimization and expectations.

metadata.title: Experiment Design
metadata.definition: create a systematic plan for performing machine learning experiments, including how to collect, prepare data, and evaluate models to ensure reliable results.

metadata.title: Experimental Methodology (ML/DS)
metadata.definition: Methods and processes for designing, performing, and analyzing experiments in machine learning and data science.

metadata.title: Explain Multivariable Optimization
metadata.definition: Ability to demonstrate and explain how multivariate analysis is applied to solve optimization problems.

metadata.title: Explainable AI (XAI)
metadata.definition: The field of research in machine learning aims to create models that are more understandable to humans, providing transparency into how decisions are made and the reasoning behind predictions.

metadata.title: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off
metadata.definition: The balance between trying new actions to explore the potential for greater rewards (exploration) and leveraging existing knowledge to maximize immediate rewards (exploitation) in reinforcement learning problems.

metadata.title: Exponent Notation
metadata.definition: understand and use exponential notation to represent repeated multiplications.

metadata.title: Exponent Rules
metadata.definition: understand and apply rules such as multiplication, division, and powers of exponents.

metadata.title: Exponential & Logarithmic Functions
metadata.definition: General understanding of exponential and logarithmic functions and their graphs.

metadata.title: Exponential Complexity Handling
metadata.definition: Techniques and strategies for solving or approximating problems of exponential algorithmic complexity, in search of more feasible solutions.

metadata.title: Exponential Complexity O(2^n)
metadata.definition: The complexity class represents an exponential growth of computational time or space with input size, often appearing in NP-hard problems with no known polynomial algorithm.

metadata.title: Exponential Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize exponential distributions.

metadata.title: Exponential Growth Handling
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms are used to solve problems whose search space or complexity increases exponentially, often by pruning or estimation.

metadata.title: Exponential Time O(2^n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases exponentially with the input size, often indicating intractable problems. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Expression Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand expression evaluation methods and rules in different programming languages.

metadata.title: Expressions
metadata.definition: Concept of expressions in programming.

metadata.title: Extended Static Checking
metadata.definition: Frameworks and tools enable annotations to be added to source code to support extended static checks, beyond basic syntax and type checks, to enhance software reliability.

metadata.title: External Calls
metadata.definition: Discusses the need to allow external calls and system libraries, as well as the consequences for language implementations.

metadata.title: External Sorting
metadata.definition: Algorithms that sort data that cannot fit completely into main memory are commonly used in query processing.

metadata.title: External fragmentation
metadata.definition: Wasted space outside allocated memory blocks, where total available memory is sufficient, but it is not contiguous enough to satisfy a new allocation request. This is eliminated at the logical level by paging.

metadata.title: External vs. Internal Events
metadata.definition: Distinguish and handle events that arise from outside the system (e.g., user interactions) and events that are generated internally by the program.

metadata.title: FORR Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture designed to model decision making and learning, especially in strategically demanding tasks.

metadata.title: FPL (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area of ​​Foundations of Programming Languages ​​(FPL) in the CS2023 program is the new name of Programming Language (PL) from CS2013.

metadata.title: FSM Problem Description
metadata.definition: Ability to create state machine descriptions to solve simple problems, such as traffic light sequences or pattern recognizers.

metadata.title: FSM Time-Series Behavior
metadata.definition: Infer the time series behavior of a state machine from its state machine representation (for example, a state machine that manages a TCP connection).

metadata.title: Factorial
metadata.definition: Mathematical function that calculates the product of all positive integers less than or equal to a given positive integer. Often used as an example to illustrate the concepts of iteration and recursion.

metadata.title: Factorial Complexity O(n!)
metadata.definition: The complexity class represents very rapid growth of computational time or space, typical for algorithms that iterate over all permutations, as in some brute-force methods.

metadata.title: Factorial Time O(n!)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the factorial of the input size, which often occurs in permutation or all-instance problems. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Factorization
metadata.definition: The skill of decomposing an algebraic expression into its factors.

metadata.title: Fast Fourier Transform
metadata.definition: Efficient algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and inverse Fourier transform of a series, which has wide applications in signal and image processing.

metadata.title: Fast/Slow Paths Analysis
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and analyze components or processing flows in a system that cause slow paths or fast paths.

metadata.title: Fault Management
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish between the stages of error management: detecting errors, handling errors when they occur, and recovering the system after errors, along with the technical methods to implement each stage.

metadata.title: Fault Models
metadata.definition: Models to classify and analyze the types of errors that can occur in parallel and distributed systems, e.g. node failures, network failures.

metadata.title: Fault Tolerance
metadata.definition: The degree to which applications can operate acceptably in the presence of packet loss in the network.

metadata.title: Fault Types
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish different types of errors in computer systems, including program errors, system errors, hardware errors (e.g., corrupted memory), and exceptions (e.g., division by zero).

metadata.title: Feasibility & Intractability
metadata.definition: Classify problems into those that can be solved in polynomial time (feasible) and those that cannot (or are very difficult) to solve in polynomial time (impossible).

metadata.title: Feature Encoding
metadata.definition: Methods for encoding categorical variables and real-valued data for machine learning models.

metadata.title: Feature Extraction Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to extract salient and meaningful features from raw data (e.g., images, sounds) to reduce data dimensionality and improve machine learning performance.

metadata.title: Feature Importance
metadata.definition: The ability to determine how much each input feature contributes to the prediction or decision of a machine learning model, helps to better understand the model's behavior.

metadata.title: Feature Visualization
metadata.definition: Techniques to visualize and understand what the layers of a deep neural network are learning or detecting in the input data, helping to explain the model.

metadata.title: Fifth Normal Form (5NF)
metadata.definition: The highest standard in relational databases, resolving join dependencies to ensure that all dependencies are inferred from candidate keys. (Equivalent to PJNF)

metadata.title: File Abstraction & Ops
metadata.definition: How shell scripts handle and manipulate files is through file abstraction concepts and related operators (e.g. read, write, check for existence).

metadata.title: File I/O
metadata.definition: File import/export method, mentioned as an alternative to database access in introductory courses.

metadata.title: File Structure to Relation Mapping
metadata.definition: Ability to map appropriate file structures to relations and indexes in the database management system.

metadata.title: File Structures
metadata.definition: Learn about the basic file structures used to store data on disk in a database management system.

metadata.title: File Structures & Storage
metadata.definition: The methods and techniques used to organize and store data on physical storage devices, including file formats, indexes, and how the data is organized.

metadata.title: File System Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement a complex file system.

metadata.title: File System Tree
metadata.definition: Use trees to represent the organization of a hierarchical file system.

metadata.title: Finite Resource Management
metadata.definition: Defines how finite computing resources (e.g., shared processor, memory, storage, and network bandwidth) are managed through careful allocation to existing entities.

metadata.title: Finite State Automaton (FSA)
metadata.definition: Concepts, operations, and applications of finite-state automatons, including deterministic and non-deterministic variants.

metadata.title: Finite State Machine
metadata.definition: Mathematical model for systems that can be in one of a finite number of states.

metadata.title: Finite State Machine (FSM)
metadata.definition: Concepts and applications of finite state machines, including types such as non-deterministic finite state machines (NFA) and deterministic finite state machines (DFA).

metadata.title: Firewall
metadata.definition: Devices or software that control the flow of data into and out of a network based on defined security rules.

metadata.title: First & Higher-Order Logic
metadata.definition: Distinguish between First Order Predicate Logic, which only quantifies variables, and Higher Order Logic, which can quantify predicates or functions.

metadata.title: First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: The logic system extends propositional logic by adding predicates, functions, and quantifiers, allowing the representation of more complex sentences.

metadata.title: Fixed Window Counter
metadata.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that maintains a simple counter which resets at fixed time intervals. It offers O(1) time complexity for checks and O(N) space for N clients, but is susceptible to burst traffic occurring at the boundaries of the windows.

metadata.title: Flexible CS Math Requirements
metadata.definition: CS2023 provides flexibility so that students with limited mathematics proficiency can better navigate the curriculum. Instructors may require a prerequisite mathematics course or teach required mathematics as part of a computer science course, applicable to subjects with specific mathematics requirements such as Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Flow Control
metadata.definition: Techniques that regulate the rate at which data is sent between two devices to prevent the recipient from being overloaded.

metadata.title: Flow-Insensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that does not consider the order of execution of instructions, is often faster but less accurate, e.g. type checking.

metadata.title: Flow-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that considers the execution order of instructions and program state at different points in the control flow, for example, forward and backward data flow analysis.

metadata.title: Floyd's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm to find the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph, which can handle negative edge weights (but no negative cycles).

metadata.title: Floyd's Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, Floyd's algorithm to find all shortest paths. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a graph with weight (can be negative, but has no negative cycles). apply dynamic planning.

metadata.title: Fog Computing
metadata.definition: The concept of fog computing, an intermediate layer between edge and cloud computing, extends cloud services closer to the edge of the network.

metadata.title: Ford-Fulkerson Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to calculate maximum flow in flow network. It works by finding paths that increase the flow from the source to the destination until there are no more paths that can be increased.

metadata.title: Formal Automata Models
metadata.definition: An overview of formal automaton models used to describe language recognition and computation processes.

metadata.title: Formal Development Methodologies
metadata.definition: apply formal techniques to design, analyze, and verify software systems to ensure correctness and reliability.

metadata.title: Formal Grammars
metadata.definition: System of rules for creating or analyzing strings in a formal language, often used in formal language theory. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Formal Language Description
metadata.definition: The use of precise mathematical methods to define the syntax and semantics of a programming language, often using tools such as formal grammar and domain theory.

metadata.title: Formal Language, Grammar, Chomsky Hierarchy
metadata.definition: An overview of formal languages, the grammar used to describe them, and the Chomsky hierarchy that classifies language types based on the expressive power of the grammar.

metadata.title: Formal Languages
metadata.definition: A finite set of strings constructed from a set of symbols (alphabet), defined by a formal grammar. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Formal Languages (FPL)
metadata.definition: Formal language principles underpin the field of Programming Language Platforms.

metadata.title: Formal Limit Definition
metadata.definition: Explain the exact mathematical definition of limit.

metadata.title: Formal Logic Proofs for Real Problems
metadata.definition: apply formal logic proofs to real-world problems, such as predicting software behavior.

metadata.title: Formal Methods
metadata.definition: Software development methods rely on rigorous mathematics to describe, design and verify systems, to ensure correctness and safety. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Math-based software development methods to increase reliability and correctness.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (Predicate Logic)
metadata.definition: apply formal methods of symbolic predicate logic.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (Propositional Logic)
metadata.definition: apply formal methods of symbolic propositional logic.

metadata.title: Formal Methods Effectiveness
metadata.definition: Ability to analyze and discuss optimal cases and ways to apply formal methods in the software development process, evaluating their benefits and limitations.

metadata.title: Formal Modeling and Refinement
metadata.definition: The process of creating formal (mathematical) models of software systems and then manually refining or implementing them to meet design requirements.

metadata.title: Formal Modeling for Architecture
metadata.definition: Skills in applying formal modeling techniques to design, analyze and verify the correctness of software system architectures.

metadata.title: Formal Models of Computation
metadata.definition: Abstract mathematical models are used to study computation, including theoretical constructs such as Turing machines, grammars, and languages. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Formal PL Specification
metadata.definition: Ability to specify programming languages ​​formally and concisely.

metadata.title: Formal Program Behavior
metadata.definition: Formal specification of the behavior of a program.

metadata.title: Formal Program Correctness Proofs
metadata.definition: Use formal methods to prove the correctness of a program, an optional advanced topic.

metadata.title: Formal Program Properties Proofs
metadata.definition: Use formal methods to demonstrate other properties of the program, an optional advanced topic.

metadata.title: Formal Recurrence Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques for analyzing the complexity of recursive algorithms using formal mathematical tools such as recursive equations.

metadata.title: Formal Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn to define the semantics of programming languages ​​precisely and without ambiguity using mathematical and logical tools.

metadata.title: Formal Semantics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Methods for describing the semantics of programming languages ​​formally and accurately.

metadata.title: Formal Specification Languages
metadata.definition: The study of languages ​​and methods used to describe the behavior of software systems in a precise, unambiguous, and verifiable manner.

metadata.title: Formal Type System Definition
metadata.definition: Be able to define a formal and compositional type system, including rules for each language construct.

metadata.title: Formulating Data Analysis Problems
metadata.definition: Ability to convert business or research questions into solvable problems using data analysis.

metadata.title: Forward & Inverse Kinematics
metadata.definition: Learn about forward kinematics (determining the final position based on joint angles) and inverse kinematics (determining joint angles to achieve the desired final position) of a robot arm.

metadata.title: Forward Chaining
metadata.definition: An inference strategy starts from known facts and applies rules to infer new facts until the goal is achieved.

metadata.title: Forward Dataflow Analysis
metadata.definition: A data flow analysis technique that gathers information about a program by going from the beginning to the end of the control flow.

metadata.title: Forward Kinematics
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply forward kinematics techniques to determine the position and orientation of robot joints based on joint angles.

metadata.title: Forwarding Match Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to look up the packet's destination address in the forwarding table and determine the appropriate output port.

metadata.title: Forwarding Table
metadata.definition: The data structure that the router uses to store destination and output port information for packets.

metadata.title: Foundational Data Structures & Algorithms
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on fundamental data structures and algorithms, providing an essential foundation for every computer science student. (Total hours CS Core: 11, KA Core: 6)

metadata.title: Foundational Models
metadata.definition: The concept of large models is trained on vast data and can be adapted for a variety of tasks.

metadata.title: Fourth Normal Form (4NF)
metadata.definition: A higher standard form than BCNF, resolving anomalies caused by multivalued dependencies.

metadata.title: Fractions
metadata.definition: understand and work with fractions, including basic operations.

metadata.title: Frame Pointer & Return Address
metadata.definition: Mechanism by which the runtime system uses the frame pointer and return address stored in the activation record to restore the execution state of the calling function after the called function completes.

metadata.title: Frames
metadata.definition: Equally sized units into which physical memory is divided to correspond with pages in a paging system.

metadata.title: Framing
metadata.definition: The process of dividing a data bit stream into separate frames for transmission over a physical channel, including adding a frame header and trailer.

metadata.title: Frequency Table
metadata.definition: Ability to create and interpret frequency tables to summarize the distribution of data.

metadata.title: Function Call
metadata.definition: Mechanism for calling and executing a function in a program.

metadata.title: Function Call Translation
metadata.definition: Explain how to translate function and procedure calls, including parameter passing mechanisms, so that they can be executed on an abstract machine.

metadata.title: Function Closures
metadata.definition: Understanding function closure, a function is 'encapsulated' along with its lexical reference environment, allowing the function to access variables from an external scope even when that scope is no longer active.

metadata.title: Function Graph Interpretation
metadata.definition: Ability to analyze information and draw conclusions from function graphs.

metadata.title: Function Notation
metadata.definition: understand and use the symbol f(x) to represent functions and their values.

metadata.title: Function Return Translation
metadata.definition: Learn how to interpret and handle returns from function or procedure calls, including restoring state and releasing resources.

metadata.title: Function Type Rules
metadata.definition: understand the style rules that apply to functions and how they ensure the correctness of function calls.

metadata.title: Function Types
metadata.definition: understand function types, describe the input and output types of a function.

metadata.title: Functional Dependencies Intro
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of functional dependencies in relational databases, describing binding relationships between attributes.

metadata.title: Functional Dependency Theory
metadata.definition: Describe how functional dependency theory generalizes the concept of locking in databases.

metadata.title: Functional Encapsulation
metadata.definition: apply encapsulation mechanisms in functional programming, including closures to protect internal state and modular interfaces to organize and hide implementation details.

metadata.title: Functional Modular Interface
metadata.definition: Master how to design and use modular interfaces to organize and manage code components in a functional programming context, promoting modularity and reusability.

metadata.title: Functional Programming
metadata.definition: A programming model that constructs programs by applying and combining functions, avoiding changing states. The number of core hours spent on this topic has been reduced by 2 hours.

metadata.title: Functional Programming (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of functional programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Functional Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in functional programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Functional-Logic Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how to integrate the functional and logic programming paradigms through in-depth concepts such as equational logic, narrowing, residuation, and semantic unification.

metadata.title: Functions
metadata.definition: Concept of functions, domain of determination, domain of values ​​and basic types of functions.

metadata.title: Fundamental Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Standard categories for classifying computational problems based on the resources required to solve them, such as O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).

metadata.title: Fundamental KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on basic knowledge representation and inference. Includes 1 hour of CS Core and 2 hours of KA Core. There is an additional hour of CS Core shared with Mathematical Foundations (Probability).

metadata.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
metadata.definition: Discover and apply basic theorems of calculus to calculate integrals.

metadata.title: Futures
metadata.definition: The concept of Futures is an object that represents a value that will be available in the future, usually as a result of an asynchronous calculation.

metadata.title: GA vs. Other Optimizers
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast genetic algorithms with classical search techniques, explaining when to use genetic algorithms to learn a model versus other forms of optimization (e.g., gradient descent).

metadata.title: GANs
metadata.definition: A class of machine learning algorithms in which two neural networks (a generator and a discriminator) compete with each other to generate realistic new data and differentiate real/fake data.

metadata.title: GIS Database
metadata.definition: Database systems are specifically designed to store, manage, analyze and display geospatial data.

metadata.title: GIT
metadata.definition: Knowledge area of ​​Graphics and Interactive Techniques (GIT) in the CS2023 program.

metadata.title: GPU
metadata.definition: Graphics processor, specialized for image and graphics processing, as well as parallel computing tasks.

metadata.title: Game Solved Meaning
metadata.definition: analyze what it means to find a perfect optimal strategy for a game (e.g., checkers), that guarantees never losing if the opponent makes no mistakes.

metadata.title: Game Theory
metadata.definition: The study of strategies and interactions of intelligent and rational agents in competitive or cooperative situations, especially in the context of multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Necessity
metadata.definition: Explain why some data elements cannot be automatically released at the end of a procedure/method call and require a garbage collection mechanism.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the benefits and limitations of garbage collection, including the concept of reachability of objects in memory.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Reachability
metadata.definition: Learn about garbage collection as an automatic memory management technique that focuses on the concept of reachability to identify objects that need to be freed.

metadata.title: Gated Ensembles
metadata.definition: A model ensemble architecture in which a 'gating' network learns to dynamically combine the output of component models based on the characteristics of the input.

metadata.title: Gaussian Elimination
metadata.definition: Ability to perform Gauss elimination to solve systems of linear equations.

metadata.title: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)
metadata.definition: A statistical model that represents data points as originating from a finite mixture of Gaussian (usually Gaussian) distributions, used for clustering and density estimation.

metadata.title: Gaussian Processes
metadata.definition: A non-parametric machine learning method based on multivariate Gaussian distribution, used for regression and classification problems.

metadata.title: General Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Explain general recursive functions, their meaning, and their implementation on a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: Generalization Bounds
metadata.definition: Mathematical bounds dictate how well a model can generalize on new, never-before-seen data, based on its performance on training data and the complexity of the model.

metadata.title: Generative AI
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that involves generating new content, such as narratives, conversations, images, models or recommendations.

metadata.title: Generative AI Architecture
metadata.definition: Research into the necessary evolution in computer architecture aims to better support generative AI technologies, a potential and important area of ​​future research.

metadata.title: Generative AI Content
metadata.definition: apply AI in creating diverse types of content such as essays, poetry from suggestions, artwork from descriptions, and even fake images or videos (deepfakes) of real people.

metadata.title: Generative AI Education Challenges
metadata.definition: Exploiting generative AI to serve the goals of formal education is one of the most important challenges facing the community over the next few years. This also applies to how AI is integrated and used in teaching and learning topics related to Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI Hardware Design
metadata.definition: Research on the impact and application of generative AI technology in the hardware design process.

metadata.title: Generative AI Impact on CS KAs
metadata.definition: CS2023 includes a chapter that lists well-founded speculations about the implications of generative AI for various fields of knowledge. This includes predictions about how generative AI could influence the content and methods of teaching in the field of Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI in CS Education
metadata.definition: Discusses the potential of generative AI to revolutionize computer science education, including impact on course content, pedagogy, and assessment techniques. This is a general principle that applies to the design and teaching of courses in all fields, including Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI in Intro Programming
metadata.definition: CS2023 includes a curriculum practice article on the implications of generative AI for introductory programming. Introductory programming is fundamental to many aspects of computer science, including understanding and developing Operating System components.

metadata.title: Generative Language Models
metadata.definition: Learn about language models that produce new, coherent, and meaningful text.

metadata.title: Generative Models (Bayes)
metadata.definition: The models learn the joint probability distribution of data and labels, allowing the generation of new data samples and the estimation of label probabilities for a given input.

metadata.title: Generative Models (CV)
metadata.definition: Machine learning models are capable of generating new image data similar to training data, which is used in image synthesis, quality enhancement, and style transformation.

metadata.title: Generative Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A type of neural network that is capable of generating new data (e.g., images, text) that is similar to the training data it learned from.

metadata.title: Generative Programming
metadata.definition: understand generative programming, a programming method that automatically generates source code, components, or software systems based on specific descriptions or requirements.

metadata.title: Generic Libraries Usage
metadata.definition: Know how to effectively use generic libraries, such as collection data structures (lists, sets, maps) in languages ​​that support generics.

metadata.title: Generic Parameters & Typing
metadata.definition: understand how global parameters work in styling and how they enable flexible and reusable code.

metadata.title: Generic Types Definition & Use
metadata.definition: Ability to define and use program elements (functions, classes, methods) that apply generic styles to achieve flexibility.

metadata.title: Generics for Collections
metadata.definition: Make effective use of generic types when working with collections (e.g. List<T>, Map<K, V>) to ensure type safety and reusability.

metadata.title: Generics, Subtyping, Overloading Comparison
metadata.definition: Discuss and clearly distinguish the differences between the concepts of generics (parametric polymorphism), subtyping (subtype polymorphism) and overloading (overloading).

metadata.title: Genetic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study of a class of optimization algorithms inspired by natural selection and genetics, used to find approximate solutions to complex problems.

metadata.title: Geographically distributed systems
metadata.definition: Distributed systems where components are deployed across multiple distinct physical locations. This setup introduces specific challenges for managing state consistently, especially for mechanisms like rate limiting.

metadata.title: Geometric Areas
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate the area of ​​basic geometric shapes such as squares, rectangles, triangles, circles.

metadata.title: Geometric Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize geometric distributions.

metadata.title: Geometric Eigenvalues/vectors
metadata.definition: Define eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors from a geometric perspective.

metadata.title: Geometric Progression (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply exponential progression in counting problems.

metadata.title: Geometric Transformations by Matrix
metadata.definition: Relate various matrix transformations (e.g., rotation, scale, translation) to geometric illustrations.

metadata.title: Geospatial Data
metadata.definition: Data describing objects, events or phenomena located on Earth, including spatial and non-spatial attributes.

metadata.title: Gibbs Sampling
metadata.definition: A Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm is used to sample from a multivariate probability distribution that is difficult to sample directly.

metadata.title: Global & Cultural Competence
metadata.definition: Ability to understand, interact and work effectively in multicultural and global environments, with an awareness of differences in values ​​and practices.

metadata.title: Global & Local Minima
metadata.definition: Distinguish and determine global minima versus local minima in optimization problems.

metadata.title: Goal-based Agents
metadata.definition: Learn about AI agents acting to achieve one or more specific goals, often through planning and search.

metadata.title: Good Communication
metadata.definition: A vocational disposition refers to the willingness and intention to apply communication skills to complete tasks effectively.

metadata.title: Good PL Design Criteria
metadata.definition: analyze the criteria for evaluating a good programming language design, including principles such as orthogonality.

metadata.title: Gradient
metadata.definition: The partial derivative vector of a function of many variables indicates the fastest increasing direction of the function.

metadata.title: Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: An iterative optimization algorithm that finds the local minimum (or maximum) of a function by moving against the function's gradient.

metadata.title: Gram-Schmidt Orthonormalization
metadata.definition: Explain the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process.

metadata.title: Grammar Transformation
metadata.definition: Grammar transformation techniques to remove ambiguity or make the grammar more suitable for specific parsing strategies.

metadata.title: Graph
metadata.definition: A nonlinear data structure consists of a set of vertices (nodes) and edges (links) connecting those vertices. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Algorithms
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in the algorithm.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Counting
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in counting problems.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Data Structures
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in data structures.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in proof techniques.

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to solve problems related to graph structure, such as path finding, spanning tree finding, connectivity analysis, etc.

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms (Advanced)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of graph data structures and the complex algorithms used to process them, within the context of a 4-course framework. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Graph Analysis
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for analyzing data represented as graphs in data science.

metadata.title: Graph Data
metadata.definition: Data is represented as nodes (entities) and edges (relationships) between them, commonly used in social networks, recommendation systems.

metadata.title: Graph Data Modeling
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to represent data in graph form and applications in data modeling.

metadata.title: Graph Database (NoSQL)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of graph databases and how they are used in NoSQL systems.

metadata.title: Graph Databases
metadata.definition: Research graph databases, modeling and querying data as nodes and edges, suitable for data with complex relationships.

metadata.title: Graph Matching
metadata.definition: In graph theory, a set of edges with no vertices in common, often used in pairwise assignment or search problems. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Graph Problem Modeling
metadata.definition: Model a variety of real-world computer science problems using appropriate graphs.

metadata.title: Graph Properties
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples some properties of graph types.

metadata.title: Graph Reduction Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about graph reducers, an execution model for functional programming languages, especially those that use deferred evaluation, where expressions are represented as graphs and reduced as needed.

metadata.title: Graph Representation
metadata.definition: Different ways of storing graph structures in computer memory, such as adjacency lists or adjacency matrices, affect the efficiency of graph operations.

metadata.title: Graph Search Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Study a problem-solving method by traversing a graph representing the state space to find the path from the initial state to the goal state.

metadata.title: Graph Search Space Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the amount of memory that graph search algorithms require to operate, according to the number of vertices and edges.

metadata.title: Graph Search Time Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the computational time required by graph search algorithms to find a solution, according to the number of vertices and edges.

metadata.title: Graph Theory
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts of graph theory and their applications.

metadata.title: Graph Theory Basics
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples the basic terms of graph theory.

metadata.title: Graph Traversal
metadata.definition: The process of moving through relationships (edges) in a graph data structure to discover related entities or find paths.

metadata.title: Graph as Search Space
metadata.definition: understand how to represent the problem space as a graph, where vertices are states and edges are operators.

metadata.title: GraphQL
metadata.definition: A server-side runtime and query language for executing queries using a data type system defined by the provider.

metadata.title: Graphical Models
metadata.definition: Introduction to graphical models such as Naive Bayes and Bayesian networks for knowledge representation and inference.

metadata.title: Graphing Functions
metadata.definition: Skills in geometric representation of functions on the coordinate plane.

metadata.title: Graphs
metadata.definition: A non-linear data structure consisting of nodes/vertices and edges connecting them, used to model complex relationships.

metadata.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
metadata.definition: Explain the concept of greatest common divisor (GCD).

metadata.title: Greedy Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope that this sequence of choices will lead to a globally optimal solution.

metadata.title: Greedy Best-First Search
metadata.definition: Learning search algorithms use heuristics to always expand the node believed to be closest to the target.

metadata.title: Greedy Method
metadata.definition: Concept of the greedy method in algorithm design, including how it works and the conditions to ensure an optimal solution.

metadata.title: Greedy Optimality
metadata.definition: evaluate when a greedy algorithm can provide an optimal solution to a problem and when it cannot.

metadata.title: Greedy Strategy
metadata.definition: An algorithm design method in which a locally optimal choice is made at each step in the hope that it will lead to a globally optimal solution.

metadata.title: Green Computing
metadata.definition: Principles for designing and using computer systems, software, and programming languages ​​in a way that saves energy and minimizes environmental impact.

metadata.title: Grid Search
metadata.definition: A systematic method for fine-tuning hyper-parameters by trying all possible combinations of parameter values ​​within a predetermined grid, often combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Grover's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithm for searching in unstructured or unsorted databases, providing quadratic speed-up compared to classical search.

metadata.title: Growing CS Math Demand
metadata.definition: Recognizes the growing need for mathematics in computer science (e.g., in machine learning) and the frequent inadequate mathematical preparation of students entering programs. This is an important consideration for curriculum design, including for Operating Systems courses that involve optimization or performance analysis.

metadata.title: Growth Mindset
metadata.definition: The belief that the ability to learn and develop mathematics does not depend on innate talent but through effort and study.

metadata.title: Guards
metadata.definition: Guards are used to control the execution of sections of code based on the state of the system in a concurrent environment.

metadata.title: HAI Communication Methods
metadata.definition: The ways in which humans and AI agents exchange information, including both verbal and nonverbal communication.

metadata.title: HAI Nonverbal Communication
metadata.definition: Research on how AI agents can use or interpret non-verbal signals such as gestures, facial expressions, and tone of voice to interact with humans.

metadata.title: HAI Practical Issues
metadata.definition: Practical challenges and considerations in designing, implementing, and maintaining AI human-agent interaction systems.

metadata.title: HAI Verbal Communication
metadata.definition: The techniques and challenges of using spoken or written language for AI agents to interact with humans.

metadata.title: HCI
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus is the study of the design and use of computer systems that interact well with humans.

metadata.title: HRI Collaboration & Communication
metadata.definition: Learn diverse forms of human-robot communication and cooperation, from explicit commands to nonverbal signals, to achieve common goals.

metadata.title: HRI Intent Prediction
metadata.definition: Research methods for robots to predict human actions, tasks or goals to improve coordination in HRI.

metadata.title: HTTP
metadata.definition: Details about the HTTP protocol, how it works in exchanging data on the World Wide Web.

metadata.title: Hadoop System Design
metadata.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Hadoop system.

metadata.title: Halting Problem Undecidability
metadata.definition: The theorem proves that no algorithm can determine in general terms whether an arbitrary computer program stops (terminates) or runs forever. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Handcrafted Features
metadata.definition: Data features are designed by humans based on domain knowledge and experience, which often requires a high level of expertise and can be time-consuming.

metadata.title: Handle Ill-posed Problems
metadata.definition: The way to solve problems is not clearly defined or is misplaced.

metadata.title: Handling Exponential Growth
metadata.definition: Techniques and approaches for managing and solving problems of exponentially growing time complexity, often by finding approximate solutions or using heuristics.

metadata.title: Hardware Interface Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used to communicate with hardware (e.g. VHDL, Verilog) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Hardware Layer
metadata.definition: The physical layer of a computer system, including the CPU, memory, and peripherals, where the most basic operations are performed.

metadata.title: Hardware as Computation Model
metadata.definition: The concept of hardware as a fundamental model for computation, including basic logic building blocks, logic expressions, minimization, and sum of product forms.

metadata.title: Hash Collision Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the performance of hash collision resolution methods, typically with respect to the time required to find, add, or delete elements when there is a collision.

metadata.title: Hash Collision Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques used to handle the situation when two different keys hash to the same index in the hash table, such as probing or chaining.

metadata.title: Hash Files
metadata.definition: Learn about hash files and how they use hash functions to organize and access data quickly based on hash keys.

metadata.title: Hash Functions & Tables
metadata.definition: Hash functions, and hash tables, are desired data structures in data management.

metadata.title: Hash Indices
metadata.definition: A type of index that uses hash functions to map data keys to their storage locations.

metadata.title: Hash Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the hash join algorithm, which uses hash functions to group and connect records.

metadata.title: Hash Map & Collision Strategies
metadata.definition: A data structure that maps keys to values ​​using a hash function, including methods for dealing with two keys hashing into the same location. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Hash Table
metadata.definition: The data structure uses a hash function to map keys to values, allowing searches, insertions, and deletions with constant average time.

metadata.title: Hash Table/Map
metadata.definition: A data structure that maps keys to values ​​using a hash function to calculate an index or 'hash' into an array of buckets or slots.

metadata.title: Hash Tables
metadata.definition: A data structure (like Java's HashMap or Python's dict) that uses a hash function to map keys to values, offering amortized O(1) for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, assuming a good hash function and occasional rehashing.

metadata.title: Hashing
metadata.definition: Technique of mapping input data of arbitrary size to a fixed-sized value (hash value), commonly used for fast searches, data integrity checking, and in hash tables for storage.

metadata.title: Health Checks
metadata.definition: Mechanisms used by load balancers to periodically monitor the status and responsiveness of backend servers, ensuring traffic is only directed to healthy and operational servers.

metadata.title: Heap (Data Structure)
