metadata.definition: A complete binary tree organized to satisfy the heap property (e.g. max-heap: largest element at the root; min-heap: smallest element at the root), commonly used to implement priority queues.

metadata.title: Heap Files
metadata.definition: Learn about heap files, a way of storing data in no particular order where records are added wherever there is free space.

metadata.title: Heap Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: heap-based allocation.

metadata.title: Heap Object Allocation
metadata.definition: The process of allocating memory for objects on the heap at runtime, typically performed by the language's runtime environment or operating system.

metadata.title: Heap Priority Queue
metadata.definition: A priority queue is implemented using a heap data structure, where elements are retrieved based on their priority instead of order of arrival.

metadata.title: Heap Sort O(n log n)
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on a heap data structure, which has a runtime complexity of O(n log n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Heapsort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the binary heap data structure. It sorts by building a max-heap and continuously extracting the largest element. Has complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Heapsort Algorithm
metadata.definition: A sorting algorithm based on the heap data structure, where the sorting problem is transformed into building and maintaining a heap.

metadata.title: Held-out Data Performance
metadata.definition: Method for estimating model performance on held-out data.

metadata.title: Heterogeneous Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database solutions where nodes can use different database management systems or data schemas.

metadata.title: Heuristic Design & Admissibility
metadata.definition: Learn how to design effective heuristic functions and understand the concept of heuristic feasibility to ensure algorithm optimization.

metadata.title: Heuristic Graph Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search algorithms that use heuristic functions to estimate the distance to the target, helping to increase search efficiency.

metadata.title: Heuristic Search Applicability
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the applicability of different heuristic search techniques to a specific problem.

metadata.title: Heuristic Search Types
metadata.definition: understand and differentiate between different heuristic search techniques.

metadata.title: Hidden Markov Models (HMM)
metadata.definition: A statistical model in which the system being modeled is assumed to be a Markov process with hidden states that are not directly observable, but can only be inferred from available observations.

metadata.title: Hierarchical Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method that divides a large problem into smaller, more abstract sub-problems and solves them in a hierarchical structure.

metadata.title: High Availability
metadata.definition: A system property ensuring that an application or service remains continuously operational and accessible to users, even in the event of component failures, often achieved through redundancy and failover mechanisms.

metadata.title: High-Availability Configurations
metadata.definition: Architectural setups, such as active-passive or active-active pairs, designed to ensure continuous system operation and minimize downtime by providing redundancy and automatic failover for critical components like load balancers.

metadata.title: High-Level Data Structures
metadata.definition: Learn low-level memory allocation and data access for high-level data structures such as basic data types, n-dimensional arrays, vectors, records, and objects.

metadata.title: High-Level IR Manipulation
metadata.definition: How to define, traversing, and modifying high-level program representations, typically ASTs or other intermediate representations, during semantic analysis.

metadata.title: High-Level Perception Fusion
metadata.definition: The process of synthesizing low-level features (e.g., edges, corners) into more complex perceptual concepts (e.g., contours, objects, phonemes).

metadata.title: High-Perf Web Server Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and deploy a high-performance web server.

metadata.title: High-Performance Parallel Computing
metadata.definition: Study the paradigms and languages ​​used for massively parallel high-performance computing, such as CUDA, OpenMP, MPI.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Aggregate Operations
metadata.definition: apply operations on collections (e.g. map, filter, reduce) that themselves take other functions as arguments, allowing flexible customization of data processing behavior.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Functions
metadata.definition: Master the concept and use of higher-order functions – functions that can take other functions as arguments, return a function, or store functions – to write flexible and abstract code.

metadata.title: Hill-climbing Algorithm
metadata.definition: Study a simple local search algorithm that always moves to a better neighboring state, with the goal of reaching the peak (maximum).

metadata.title: History of AI
metadata.definition: Overview of important milestones, key figures and development of the field of artificial intelligence over time.

metadata.title: Hold and wait
metadata.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, where a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes.

metadata.title: Holding locks for excessively long durations
metadata.definition: A common pitfall that increases the likelihood of deadlocks by increasing the time window during which other processes might contend for the locked resources, contributing to 'hold and wait'.

metadata.title: Homogeneous Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database solutions where all nodes use the same database software and data schema.

metadata.title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
metadata.definition: Ability to relate a matrix to a system of homogeneous linear equations.

metadata.title: Honeypots
metadata.definition: Systems or networks designed to attract and monitor attacker activity, gathering information about attack techniques.

metadata.title: Horizon Effect
metadata.definition: Study the horizon effect in games, where the Minimax algorithm can ignore bad results that are outside the specified search depth.

metadata.title: Horizontal Scalability
metadata.definition: The ability of a system to increase its capacity by adding more machines or nodes to a distributed system, allowing for seamless growth and increased performance without requiring fundamental architectural changes or massive data migrations.

metadata.title: Horn Clauses, Facts, Goals
metadata.definition: understand the definitions and roles of Horn clauses, facts, goals and subgoals in logic programming.

metadata.title: Hosts
metadata.definition: The role of terminal devices such as computers, servers, smartphones, etc., in computer networks.

metadata.title: How LLMs Work
metadata.definition: The underlying mechanism and architecture of large language models capable of understanding and generating natural text.

metadata.title: Hubs
metadata.definition: The function and limitations of a concentrator are as a basic networking device, operating at the physical layer.

metadata.title: Human Autonomy in AI
metadata.definition: The relationship between AI systems and human decision-making and control capabilities.

metadata.title: Human Supervision Robotics
metadata.definition: Research the importance and methods to ensure humans can still effectively monitor and control autonomous robotic systems.

metadata.title: Human-Agent Interaction
metadata.definition: The study of how humans and AI agents interact, including interface design, communication, and trust.

metadata.title: Human-Computer Interaction
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
metadata.definition: Explore the research field of how humans and robots can interact naturally and effectively.

metadata.title: Human-Robot Teaming & Physical HRI
metadata.definition: Research on how humans and robots can form teams to complete tasks, including direct physical interaction between the two.

metadata.title: Human-like Reasoning/Behavior
metadata.definition: Distinguish and understand behaviors or reasoning processes that simulate how humans think and act, often not necessarily optimally.

metadata.title: HyperLogLog
metadata.definition: An algorithm that estimates the number of unique elements in a large data set with little error and low memory consumption.

metadata.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
metadata.definition: The process of finding optimal values ​​for the hyperparameters of a machine learning model to achieve the best performance, usually through grid search or random search combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Space
metadata.definition: The set of all functions or models that a machine learning algorithm can choose from to solve a particular problem.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Space & Complexity
metadata.definition: Understanding hypothesis spaces and their complexity in machine learning.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Testing
metadata.definition: Statistical hypothesis testing methods for evaluating claims about a data set or population.

metadata.title: IAS (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Information Assurance and Security (IAS) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Security (SEC) in CS2023.

metadata.title: ICARUS Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture focuses on high-level cognitive modeling, conceptual learning, and goal-based planning.

metadata.title: IDA* Search
metadata.definition: Informed Iterative Depth First Search, a variant of A* that minimizes memory requirements.

metadata.title: IDS
metadata.definition: Systems monitor network and system activity to detect signs of attacks or policy violations.

metadata.title: IDS & Firewalls
metadata.definition: understand the role and operation of intrusion detection systems (IDS) and firewalls in system security.

metadata.title: IM (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Information Management (IM) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Data Management (DM) in CS2023.

metadata.title: IP Hash (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A load balancing strategy that uses a hash of the client’s source IP address to determine the destination server, ensuring session persistence for a given client. It offers O(1) decision time but can lead to uneven distribution or session loss if a server fails.

metadata.title: IP Scalability Issues
metadata.definition: Research into Internet Protocol (IP) and scalability challenges as the Internet evolves, along with applicable solutions.

metadata.title: IP Versions
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between versions of the Internet Protocol, mainly IPv4 and IPv6, in terms of addressing structure, features, and extensibility.

metadata.title: IP address
metadata.definition: A unique numerical label used in networking for identifying devices, which NAT modifies in packet headers to facilitate communication between private and public networks.

metadata.title: IPv4
metadata.definition: Details about the structure, packet format, and working mechanism of IPv4, the most popular version of IP.

metadata.title: IPv4 address space conservation
metadata.definition: The primary benefit and reason for NAT's existence, allowing the reuse of limited IPv4 address ranges by enabling many private devices to share a single public IP, thereby conserving the available global IPv4 addresses.

metadata.title: IPv6
metadata.definition: Details of the structure, packet format and operating mechanism of IPv6, designed to replace IPv4 and solve the problem of address exhaustion.

metadata.title: IS (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The knowledge field of Intelligent Systems (IS) in the CS2013 program, was renamed Artificial Intelligence (AI) in CS2023.

metadata.title: ISP
metadata.definition: Learn about the functions, roles and types of Internet Service Providers (ISPs) in providing network connectivity.

metadata.title: Idempotency
metadata.definition: The property of an operation or a consumer service such that performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once, which is required in event-driven architectures for safely handling potential duplicate messages.

metadata.title: Identifier Resolution
metadata.definition: The process of determining which variable or function is referenced by a particular identifier in the source code, and the locations in the program where an identifier is declared and associated with a value or object.

metadata.title: Identifying Subspaces
metadata.definition: Determines whether specific subsets of a vector space are subspaces or not.

metadata.title: Ill-defined Problems
metadata.definition: Approach and solve problems where requirements or constraints are not clearly defined.

metadata.title: Image Acquisition
metadata.definition: Methods and technologies for collecting image data from sensor devices such as cameras.

metadata.title: Image Processing
metadata.definition: Techniques for transforming, enhancing, or extracting information from digital images, including filtering, transforming, and restoring images.

metadata.title: Image Properties
metadata.definition: Image characteristics and properties such as brightness, contrast, color, texture, and shape.

metadata.title: Image Representation
metadata.definition: Ways to store and structure image data for computer processing, such as pixel matrices, histograms, or feature-based descriptions.

metadata.title: Image Segmentation
metadata.definition: Technique of dividing a digital image into segments (sets of pixels) to simplify or change the image representation, making analysis easier.

metadata.title: Immutable State Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in designing and implementing basic algorithms that comply with the principle of immutability in functional programming, avoiding directly changing the state of variable variables to minimize errors and increase predictability.

metadata.title: Immutable Variables & Data Copying
metadata.definition: Study the concept of immutable variables and compare data copying and reduction in functional programming.

metadata.title: Imperative Integration
metadata.definition: Study how functional programming concepts and techniques can be integrated or interacted with the traditional imperative programming paradigm, creating hybrid programming approaches.

metadata.title: Imperative Programming
metadata.definition: A programming model focuses on describing the steps (commands) that a program must perform to change its state. Often integrated with other paradigms such as object oriented.

metadata.title: Imperative as OOP Subset
metadata.definition: understand imperative programming not as a separate paradigm but as a subset of object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Imperative vs OOP
metadata.definition: List and explain the basic differences between the imperative programming model and the object-oriented programming model.

metadata.title: Implement Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Ability to code and configure statistical learning algorithms to build models from data, often using specialized libraries and frameworks.

metadata.title: Implication (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators express an 'if... then...' relationship between two clauses.

metadata.title: Implication as Function Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship, the logical implication (A => B) is mapped to the functional type (A -> B).

metadata.title: Implicit Congestion Notification
metadata.definition: Detect congestion through indirect signs such as packet loss or increased latency.

metadata.title: Implicit Upcasting
metadata.definition: understand how implicit casting (safely converting a subtype to its parent type) works in typed languages.

metadata.title: Improper lock ordering
metadata.definition: A common pitfall leading to deadlocks where locks are acquired in different sequences by different processes, creating conditions for circular wait.

metadata.title: In-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in in-order.

metadata.title: Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
metadata.definition: apply the inclusion-exclusion principle.

metadata.title: Inclusive PL Design
metadata.definition: The ability to consciously design programming languages ​​so that they are friendly, accessible, and free of potentially offensive terms or constructs promotes an inclusive programming environment.

metadata.title: Indefinite Iteration
metadata.definition: The concept of an indefinite iteration structure, such as a `while` loop.

metadata.title: Index Performance Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the impact of using indexes on query speed, update costs, and storage capacity.

metadata.title: Index Selection
metadata.definition: The process of choosing the most suitable index to use for a particular query to optimize performance.

metadata.title: Index Structures
metadata.definition: understand the different types of index structures and their importance in speeding up database queries.

metadata.title: Index-Only Plans
metadata.definition: Query plans can be executed entirely using indexes without accessing the original data table.

metadata.title: Indexed Data Elements
metadata.definition: Data structures whose elements are accessed via an index, such as arrays and vectors.

metadata.title: Indexes for Query Performance
metadata.definition: Understanding how indexes are used to speed up data retrieval and improve the performance of queries, especially in large and complex database systems.

metadata.title: Indicator Random Variable
metadata.definition: Definition and understanding of indicator random variables.

metadata.title: Indices
metadata.definition: Data structures are used to improve the speed of retrieving data from the database.

metadata.title: Indirection for Isolation
metadata.definition: Describe how the concept of indirection (e.g., through virtual memory, virtual machines) is used to create the illusion that each program or environment has a separate computer and resources, even when they are actually shared.

metadata.title: Induction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Method of inference from specific cases to a general law.

metadata.title: Inductive Proofs for Typed Languages
metadata.definition: The ability to use mathematical induction to prove the properties of all programs in a language that are precisely typed according to a formally defined type system.

metadata.title: Inefficient Algorithm Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the economic and other impacts of using ineffective algorithms.

metadata.title: Inference Rules (Predicate Logic)
metadata.definition: Use inference rules to construct proofs in predicate logic.

metadata.title: Inference Rules (Propositional Logic)
metadata.definition: Use rules of inference to construct proofs in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Infinite Set vs Sequence
metadata.definition: Explain the basic difference between the concepts of infinite sets and sequences in mathematics.

metadata.title: Infinite Streams
metadata.definition: Working with infinite data streams, often combined with deferred evaluation.

metadata.title: Info Retrieval Agent
metadata.definition: Agents specialize in searching, retrieving, and filtering information from different sources for users.

metadata.title: Informal Logic for Real Problems
metadata.definition: apply informal but rigorous logical reasoning to real-world problems, such as solving puzzles.

metadata.title: Information Extraction
metadata.definition: Learn about techniques for automatically extracting structured information from unstructured text.

metadata.title: Information Gathering Agent
metadata.definition: Agents are designed to automatically collect and synthesize information from their environment.

metadata.title: Information Hiding
metadata.definition: The principle of abstraction, where complex details of lower layers are hidden from higher layers, simplifies system design and use.

metadata.title: Information Retrieval
metadata.definition: Learn about methods and systems for searching and retrieving relevant information from a document collection.

metadata.title: Information Systems Mgmt
metadata.definition: The field of managing information systems to support organizational operations and decision making.

metadata.title: Inheritance
metadata.definition: The concept of inheritance, allows subclasses to inherit properties and methods from the superclass, including cases of multiple inheritance.

metadata.title: Inheritance vs Composition Costs
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the benefits and costs/impacts of using inheritance (subclassing) and composition (especially how to build components based on higher-order functions).

metadata.title: Input Size & Basic Operations
metadata.definition: Basic factors to analyze algorithm complexity: input data size and number of primitive operations performed.

metadata.title: Insertion Sort
metadata.definition: A simple sorting algorithm constructs the final sorted array or list element by element by inserting each unsorted element into its correct position. Has O(n^2) complexity.

metadata.title: Instance Simplification
metadata.definition: Techniques in the transform and conquer paradigm that transform a complex representation of a problem into a simpler representation that is easier to solve, often by preprocessing the data.

metadata.title: Instruction Scheduling
metadata.definition: The stage in the code generation process where the execution order of instructions is optimized to improve performance, often by exploiting the processor's pipeline architecture.

metadata.title: Instruction Selection
metadata.definition: The stage in code generation where operations in the program's intermediate representation are mapped to specific instructions of the target instruction set.

metadata.title: Instruction Set
metadata.definition: The set of all instructions that a processor can understand and execute, is the goal of code generation.

metadata.title: Integral Applications
metadata.definition: apply integration to solve real-life problems.

metadata.title: Integrate Socio-Ethical Issues
metadata.definition: Emphasize that a computer solution is not just technical but must also incorporate social, ethical, and professional considerations. This is a fundamental principle that applies to the design and implementation of systems, including Operating Systems, where design decisions can have far-reaching impacts.

metadata.title: Integrating Ethics in Technical CS
metadata.definition: Identify the challenge of integrating social, ethical, and professional issues into the technical coverage of the curriculum so that they become inevitable. This is the responsibility of every educator, which applies to the teaching of technical subjects such as Operating Systems, where issues of privacy, security, and equity may arise.

metadata.title: Integration Rules
metadata.definition: apply the rules of integration to examples with important functions.

metadata.title: Intelligent Behavior
metadata.definition: Discuss the criteria and definitions of behavior considered intelligent.

metadata.title: Intelligent Behavior Simulation
metadata.definition: Ways in which computers can simulate aspects of intelligent behavior.

metadata.title: Intended Data Use
metadata.definition: understand the intended and intended uses of collected data.

metadata.title: Intent-Based Networking (IBN)
metadata.definition: The concept and principles of intent-based networking enable network management through business objectives rather than specific device configurations.

metadata.title: Inter-Domain Routing
metadata.definition: Routing protocols and techniques are used to exchange routing information between different autonomous domains.

metadata.title: Inter-Unit Communication
metadata.definition: Mechanisms for exchanging information between program units such as procedures, functions and modules, including non-local variables, global variables, parameter-passing and import-export mechanisms between modules.

metadata.title: Interactive Input
metadata.definition: Direct data entry, via an interactive interface, is mentioned as an alternative to database access in introductory courses.

metadata.title: Interactive Program Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement a simple interactive program.

metadata.title: Interactive SQL Execution
metadata.definition: Ability to execute SQL queries interactively via command line interface or GUI tool.

metadata.title: Intermediate Code
metadata.definition: Research the role and usage of intermediate code in the language translation process to increase portability and optimization.

metadata.title: Intermediate Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Basic classifications of algorithm complexity, advanced above the foundation level, include logarithmic, linear logarithmic, and quadratic classes. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Intermediate SQL Query
metadata.definition: Students write their own SQL queries at the intermediate level.

metadata.title: Internal fragmentation
metadata.definition: Wasted space within a memory block (specifically, within pages in a paging system) where the allocated memory is larger than the actual requested memory.

metadata.title: Internet Hourglass Model
metadata.definition: Describes the hourglass model of the Internet protocol suite, highlighting the IP layer as the common core, supporting many technologies on the lower layer and many applications on the upper layer.

metadata.title: Internet Organization
metadata.definition: Describes the overall structure and organization of the Internet, including its major components and their relationships.

metadata.title: Internet Users
metadata.definition: understand the role of end users in the Internet ecosystem and how they interact with network services and resources.

metadata.title: Interop Data Representation
metadata.definition: How data types and data structures are represented in memory to allow different languages ​​to share and understand data.

metadata.title: Interop Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: Methods for passing arguments between functions written in different programming languages, often involve standardized calling conventions and data formats.

metadata.title: Interpretable Models
metadata.definition: Machine learning models are designed to make it easier to understand how they operate or make decisions, with ways of representing data or knowledge that enhance interpretation.

metadata.title: Interpreter Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the interpreter's execution model, where source code is read and executed line by line.

metadata.title: Interpreter Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the limitations and benefits of interpreters in executing source code.

metadata.title: Interrupt
metadata.definition: Signal sent to the CPU to pause the current job and handle an emergency event.

metadata.title: Interrupt-driven Programming
metadata.definition: Programming method in which tasks are triggered and processed when an interrupt event occurs.

metadata.title: Intra-Domain Routing
metadata.definition: Routing protocols and techniques are used within a single Autonomous System (AS) domain.

metadata.title: Intractability
metadata.definition: The concept of problems for which there are no known polynomial time algorithms to solve them, often requiring exponential or factorial time. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Invariants
metadata.definition: Properties of a system or program that do not change throughout its operation.

metadata.title: Invariants (Loop, Recursion)
metadata.definition: Use invariants (e.g. loop invariants) to prove the correctness of algorithms in iterative, recursive, or tree search structures.

metadata.title: Inverse Kinematics
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply inverse kinematics techniques to determine the joint angle required for a desired end position and orientation.

metadata.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL)
metadata.definition: A technique for inferring the hidden reward function that an agent is trying to optimize, based on observations of that agent's behavior.

metadata.title: Inverted Index
metadata.definition: An index structure maps content values ​​to their location in the database, commonly used for full-text search in semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Inverted page tables
metadata.definition: A type of page table that stores one entry per physical frame, rather than one per virtual page, aiming to reduce the physical memory overhead, particularly for systems with many processes.

metadata.title: IoT
metadata.definition: The concept of a network of physical devices, vehicles, appliances, and other objects embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies to connect and exchange data.

metadata.title: Iteration Constructs
metadata.definition: Control structures allow a program to repeat a block of instructions multiple times, for example: for, while, do-while.

metadata.title: Iteration Strategy Basic
metadata.definition: Technique that solves a problem by repeating a set of instructions until a certain condition is achieved, a typical example is linear search. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: Iteration and Recursion
metadata.definition: Two basic methods for repeating a block of code or a process. Iteration uses loops (for, while), while recursion uses functions that call themselves.

metadata.title: Iteration vs Recursion
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between two basic programming techniques for solving problems, including for example factorials or tree searches. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Iterative Algorithms
metadata.definition: Concepts and examples of algorithms that use iterative structures to solve problems.

metadata.title: Iterative Deepening DFS (IDDFS)
metadata.definition: DFS variant research combines the benefits of BFS (optimality) with the benefits of DFS (memory efficiency).

metadata.title: Iterative Improvement
metadata.definition: Algorithms start with a feasible solution and then continuously improve it by taking small steps until a stopping criterion is reached (e.g., no further improvement is possible).

metadata.title: Iterator & Aggregate Idioms
metadata.definition: Select and use the most natural and effective idioms in different programming languages ​​for working with iterators and set operations, optimizing readability and performance.

metadata.title: Iterators
metadata.definition: Concept of iterators to traverse data structures.

metadata.title: Iterators & Collection Operations
metadata.definition: Define and use iterators and other operations on aggregates, including operations that take functions as arguments, in a variety of programming languages, choosing the most natural expressions for each language.

metadata.title: Iterators Definition & Usage
metadata.definition: Skill in defining and using iterators to efficiently and flexibly traverse data sets, often in a functional programming context.

metadata.title: JIT Compilation
metadata.definition: A method of compiling code during a program's runtime, often used in virtual machines to convert bytecode to native machine code to improve performance.

metadata.title: JIT Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the Just-In-Time (JIT) execution model and how it works in language translation and execution.

metadata.title: JIT Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the advantages, disadvantages, and difficulties of Just-in-time (JIT) compilation and dynamic recompilation.

metadata.title: JSON (NoSQL)
metadata.definition: Open, lightweight, easy-to-read text data format widely used in NoSQL databases to store structured data.

metadata.title: JSON Schema
metadata.definition: A JSON-based standard for describing the structure and format of JSON data.

metadata.title: Johnson's algorithm
metadata.definition: An all-pairs shortest path (APSP) algorithm that can handle graphs with negative edge weights by first re-weighting edges (typically using Bellman-Ford) and then running Dijkstra's algorithm V times. It is particularly efficient for sparse graphs.

metadata.title: Join Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a common column or related condition.

metadata.title: Join Dependency (JD)
metadata.definition: A constraint in a relational database ensures that a table can be decomposed into smaller tables and then rejoined without losing or adding information.

metadata.title: Join Points
metadata.definition: Points in a program's execution flow where an aspect can be inserted (e.g., method invocation, field access).

metadata.title: Joint Control & Dynamics
metadata.definition: Study how to control each individual joint of the robot and understand how the dynamics (force, torque) affect the robot's movements.

metadata.title: Joint Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the simultaneous distribution of multiple random variables.

metadata.title: Journaling
metadata.definition: Additional techniques and methods to enhance system reliability, beyond redundancy techniques, such as journaling in the file system.

metadata.title: K-means Clustering
metadata.definition: An iterative clustering algorithm divides the data into k clusters, where each data point belongs to the cluster with the closest center.

metadata.title: KA Core
metadata.definition: Topics are recommended for more in-depth study in a specific area of ​​knowledge, with additional conceptual nuances.

metadata.title: KA Core Topics
metadata.definition: Recommended topics for more in-depth study in a specific Area of ​​Knowledge. They complement the core CS topics.

metadata.title: KA Definition (CS2023)
metadata.definition: In the CS2023 syllabus, a Knowledge Area is expanded to include Learning Units and Career Trends. Formula: Knowledge Area = {Knowledge Units} + {Career Trends}.

metadata.title: KMP Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient string search algorithm that avoids rechecking previously checked text characters. (An example for Efficient String Matching)

metadata.title: KRR
metadata.definition: Knowledge of knowledge representation methods and inference techniques in Artificial Intelligence.

metadata.title: Kernel Functions (SVM)
metadata.definition: Functions are used in SVM to transform data into a higher dimensional space, allowing the search for nonlinear separating hyperplanes.

metadata.title: Key-Value & Document Models
metadata.definition: Research the characteristics and applications of Key-Value and Document data models in NoSQL systems.

metadata.title: Key-Value Store
metadata.definition: A type of NoSQL database that stores data as key-value pairs, providing quick access by key.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which the goal is to select items with different weights and values ​​to maximize the total value while not exceeding the bag's weight limit, another example of a problem that can be solved by brute force or dynamic programming.

metadata.title: Knowledge Area
metadata.definition: In CS2023, a knowledge area is expanded to include knowledge units and career trends.

metadata.title: Knowledge Area Definition
metadata.definition: In CS2023, a knowledge area is defined as a collection of knowledge units and professional characteristics.

metadata.title: Knowledge Area Structure
metadata.definition: In CS2023, a Knowledge Area is defined as the combination of Knowledge Units and associated Professional Qualities.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Methods and structures for encoding information and knowledge in a way that can be stored, accessed, and manipulated by AI systems.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation Issues
metadata.definition: Discuss the challenges and difficulties in representing knowledge effectively so that computers can process and reason.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation Types
metadata.definition: understand different types of knowledge representation in AI.

metadata.title: Knowledge Unit
metadata.definition: Specific knowledge blocks make up a Knowledge Area in the CS2023 curriculum.

metadata.title: Knowledge-based AI
metadata.definition: Knowledge-based methods are retained in the AI ​​program to ensure broad education and unique capabilities.

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Greedy algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree for a weighted undirected graph, by continuously adding edges with the least weight without forming cycles.

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm (Greedy)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of finding a globally optimal solution, for example the Kruskal algorithm for finding a minimum spanning tree. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: L'Hopital's Rule
metadata.definition: apply L'Hospital's rule and other methods to solve indeterminate limit types.

metadata.title: L-values and R-values
metadata.definition: Concept of L-values ​​(representing assignable memory locations) and R-values ​​(representing the value of an expression); how to map mutable variable names to L-values ​​and immutable variable names to R-values.

metadata.title: L1 Normalization
metadata.definition: A form of normalization that adds the absolute value of the weights to the objective function (also called Lasso Regression), which tends to bring some weights to zero, helping with feature selection.

metadata.title: L2 Regularization
metadata.definition: A form of normalization that adds the square of the weight magnitude to the objective function (also called Ridge Regression or weight decay), which helps reduce large weights and avoid overfitting.

metadata.title: LAN Topologies
metadata.definition: Different physical and logical layouts of local area networks, affect performance and reliability.

metadata.title: LIME
metadata.definition: An agnostic model explanation technique provides local explanations for the predictions of any classifier or regressor, by approximating the model's behavior around a particular example.

metadata.title: LLMs
metadata.definition: High-level overview of major language models (e.g. ChatGPT, Bard), their uses, and limitations/difficulties.

metadata.title: LLN & CLT Relation
metadata.definition: Ability to explain the importance and application of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem in probability calculations and statistical analysis.

metadata.title: Lagrange Multipliers
metadata.definition: apply the Lagrange multiplier method to solve constrained optimization problems.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus
metadata.definition: Study Lambda Calculus as a formal system for expressing computation based on functional abstraction and application.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus Computation
metadata.definition: Explains how calculations are performed in Lambda Calculus, including concepts such as Alpha transformation and Beta reduction.

metadata.title: Lambda Common Subexpressions
metadata.definition: understand the concept and impact of common subexpressions in lambda expressions, and how they can be leveraged to improve performance through techniques such as graph reduction.

metadata.title: Lambda Expressions & Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand lambda expressions (anonymous functions) and how they are evaluated in functional programming.

metadata.title: Lambda Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: understand the mechanics of passing parameters when using lambda expressions.

metadata.title: Lambda SECD Machine
metadata.definition: Able to explain in detail how a simple lambda expression is deployed and executed on an abstract virtual machine such as a SECD machine, illustrating the process of storing and reclaiming the environment.

metadata.title: Lambda Variable Binding & Scope
metadata.definition: Master the variable binding and scope rules that apply to lambda expressions.

metadata.title: Language Assertions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking assertions to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: Language Components
metadata.definition: Defines the basic components of a programming language, including alphabets, delimiters, sentences, syntax, and semantics.

metadata.title: Language Core Abstractions
metadata.definition: Explain how core language constructs such as data abstraction and control abstraction are implemented in a system.

metadata.title: Language Design: Completeness
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles that provide enough functionality and expressiveness to solve a wide range of problems or tasks.

metadata.title: Language Design: Efficient Object Code
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles to create object code that runs efficiently in terms of time and resources, optimizing application performance.

metadata.title: Language Design: Fast Translation
metadata.definition: Principle of designing programming languages ​​to be compiled or interpreted quickly, optimizing development and response time.

metadata.title: Language Design: Implementation Strategy
metadata.definition: The methods and techniques considered when designing a language, influence how the compiler, interpreter, or runtime environment is built for that language.

metadata.title: Language Design: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: Programming language design principle in which independent features can be freely combined without causing unwanted side effects, increasing flexibility and reducing complexity.

metadata.title: Language Design: Readability
metadata.definition: Principles of programming language design so that the source code is easy to understand, read, and maintain by humans.

metadata.title: Language Design: Security
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles to minimize potential security vulnerabilities and prevent unsafe behavior.

metadata.title: Language Design: Simplicity
metadata.definition: Principle of designing a programming language so that its syntax, semantics, and features are easy to learn, use, and understand.

metadata.title: Language Interoperability
metadata.definition: Challenges and techniques that enable components written in different programming languages ​​to communicate and operate together, including mechanisms for parameter passing and data representation.

metadata.title: Language Invariants
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking invariants of objects or data structures.

metadata.title: Language Portability
metadata.definition: The ability of a programming language and programs written in that language to run on different hardware platforms and operating systems without significant modification.

metadata.title: Language Post-conditions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking post-conditions of functions or methods.

metadata.title: Language Pragmatics
metadata.definition: The study of practical and contextual factors that influence the design, use, and effectiveness of programming languages, including technical, economic, and psychological considerations.

metadata.title: Language Pragmatics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: The study of how programming languages ​​are used and influence their design and use.

metadata.title: Language Pre-conditions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking pre-conditions of functions or methods.

metadata.title: Language Semantics
metadata.definition: understand the importance of semantic definitions to clarify the meaning of linguistic structures.

metadata.title: Language Semantics Induction Proof
metadata.definition: Use induction to prove the properties of all programs in a language, based on the definition of its formal semantics.

metadata.title: Language Syntax
metadata.definition: understand how a programming language is described and parsed.

metadata.title: Language Translation
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of the programming language translation process.

metadata.title: Language Translation & Execution (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Advanced techniques in language translation, including code optimization, code generation, and runtime architectures.

metadata.title: Language Translation & Execution (Intro)
metadata.definition: The basic stages of translating a programming language into machine or intermediate code, and executing the program.

metadata.title: Language Translation Execution (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Fundamentals of how programming languages ​​are translated and executed, required for all students.

metadata.title: Language Translation Execution (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in language translation and implementation, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Language Translation Process
metadata.definition: Study the entire language translation process, from parsing to execution, including the main stages.

metadata.title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
metadata.definition: New techniques became popular and were added to the curriculum.

metadata.title: Large Software Modularity
metadata.definition: Discuss the importance and principles of massive software modularization to improve structure and maintainability.

metadata.title: Latency
metadata.definition: The delay between the request for an activity and the start or completion of that activity.

metadata.title: Law of Large Numbers
metadata.definition: understand the Law of Large Numbers, which describes the behavior of the sample mean as the number of samples increases.

metadata.title: Layer 4 (Transport Layer)
metadata.definition: A layer of the OSI model responsible for end-to-end communication, typically inspecting IP addresses and ports for routing decisions in load balancing.

metadata.title: Layer 7 (Application Layer)
metadata.definition: The highest layer of the OSI model, where application-level protocols and data inspection (e.g., HTTP headers, URLs) occur, enabling content-aware load balancing.

metadata.title: Layered Agent
metadata.definition: Agent architectures include multiple layers to handle behaviors at different levels of abstraction, combining reaction and planning.

metadata.title: Layered Program Debugging
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and correct errors in programs built on a layered architecture, using specialized debugging tools.

metadata.title: Layered Program Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement a simple program (e.g., TCP client/server application) by applying layering principles.

metadata.title: Layered System Architecture
metadata.definition: understand how computer systems are built in a layered architecture, based on the principle of separation of concerns, with clearly defined interfaces that hide the details of lower layers from higher layers.

metadata.title: Layered System Error Handling
metadata.definition: Strategies and mechanisms to handle detected and signaled errors, ensuring system stability and resilience across layers.

metadata.title: Layered System Performance Experiment
metadata.definition: Ability to design a performance experiment on a layered system to study and determine how a specific system parameter affects the overall performance of the system.

metadata.title: Layered Systems Performance
metadata.definition: Deep understanding of layered system architecture, different types of workloads and platforms, how they affect performance, and the challenges that arise when evaluating performance in these complex environments.

metadata.title: Layering Principles
metadata.definition: understand the fundamental principles behind layered architecture in networks, including the benefits of abstraction and separation of functions.

metadata.title: Lazy Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand delayed evaluation, an evaluation strategy in which execution of an expression is postponed until its value is actually needed, which optimizes performance and allows processing of an infinite stream of data.

metadata.title: Lazy Evaluation Implementation
metadata.definition: Learn and implement techniques for implementing deferred evaluation mechanisms in systems or programming languages.

metadata.title: Lazy vs Eager Evaluation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast two expression evaluation strategies: lazy evaluation and eager evaluation.

metadata.title: Leaky Bucket algorithm
metadata.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that smooths out request bursts by processing requests from an internal queue at a steady rate. Requests are dropped if the bucket (queue) overflows. It also offers O(1) time and O(N) space plus queue overhead.

metadata.title: Learned Feature Representations
metadata.definition: Understanding feature representations learned through machine learning models.

metadata.title: Learned Representation
metadata.definition: Data features are automatically discovered and extracted from raw data by the model (e.g., by a deep neural network), which is often more efficient and flexible than manual representation.

metadata.title: Learned Representations
metadata.definition: The trend in AI is a shift from knowledge representations manually designed by engineers to representations learned automatically through optimization on large data sets.

metadata.title: Learned Subsymbolic KR
metadata.definition: Understanding learned symbolic sub-representations.

metadata.title: Learning Agent
metadata.definition: Agents have the ability to improve their performance over time by learning from experience or data.

metadata.title: Learning Curve
metadata.definition: Histograms show model performance (e.g., accuracy, error) as a function of the amount of training data or number of training iterations, used to diagnose overfitting or underfitting.

metadata.title: Learning Theory
metadata.definition: An overview of the mathematical research on machine learning, focusing on understanding why machine learning algorithms work and their generalizability.

metadata.title: Learning Theory Overview
metadata.definition: Explain the fundamentals behind the ability of machine learning algorithms to learn and generalize from limited data, including the concepts of training error and generalization error.

metadata.title: Learning from Demonstration (LfD)
metadata.definition: A method in machine learning that allows a system to learn a behavior by observing examples of that behavior performed by an agent (usually a human).

metadata.title: Learning-based Agents
metadata.definition: Research AI agents capable of improving their performance through experience, using machine learning algorithms.

metadata.title: Least Common Multiple
metadata.definition: Mathematical concept, the smallest positive integer that is divisible by both (or more) given integers. Usually calculated by reducing to the greatest common divisor.

metadata.title: Least Connection (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A load balancing strategy that routes new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, requiring the load balancer to maintain connection state and potentially involving O(N) server scans or O(log N) with optimized data structures like a min-heap to find the minimum.

metadata.title: Least Response Time / Fastest Response Time (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A dynamic load balancing strategy that directs traffic to the server which has demonstrated the quickest response time in recent health checks or actual request processing, requiring active monitoring.

metadata.title: Least Squares (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: Method to find approximate solutions for inconsistent linear equations by minimizing the sum of squares of the residuals.

metadata.title: Legal Data Collection
metadata.definition: understand regulations, laws and policies related to data collection, storage and use.

metadata.title: Levels of Indirection
metadata.definition: Describe the concept of levels of indirection in a computer system, with the specific example of virtual memory used to effectively manage physical memory resources.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis
metadata.definition: Learn about the lexical analysis stage in the language translation process, turning character strings into tokens.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis & Parsing
metadata.definition: The concept of lexical analysis/scanning and parsing is based on given language specifications.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis with Regex
metadata.definition: Lexical analysis or scanning uses regular expressions to identify tokens.

metadata.title: Library Usage
metadata.definition: understand how to use software libraries to reuse code and build applications more efficiently.

metadata.title: Light Speed & Performance
metadata.definition: understand the relationship between the speed of light (one foot per nanosecond) and computer clock speed (one GHz).

metadata.title: Limit Calculation Methods
metadata.definition: apply different methods (in addition to L'Hospital) to deal with indeterminate limit types.

metadata.title: Limits
metadata.definition: understand basic concepts of limits of functions and sequences in calculus, including the definition and calculation of limits.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra
metadata.definition: An important area of ​​mathematics, proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 89% in importance for careers in industry and graduate study, with particular importance for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of linear algebra complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 35 hours of study.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic linear algebra concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra Basics (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces basic definitions in linear algebra, including becoming familiar with terms such as vectors. Total 5 class hours.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra in Computer Graphics
metadata.definition: Explore applications of linear algebra in computer graphics, such as geometric transformations and projections.

metadata.title: Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA)
metadata.definition: Concepts, operations and applications of linear edge automatons, computational models involving context-sensitive languages.

metadata.title: Linear Independence
metadata.definition: The concept of vector sets cannot be represented as a linear combination of other vectors in the same set.

metadata.title: Linear Independence for Vectors in Rn
metadata.definition: Discuss linear independence for vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Linear Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list has a clear start (head) and end (tail) point, where the nodes are arranged in a linear sequence.

metadata.title: Linear Probing
metadata.definition: A hash collision resolution method in which alternative locations are searched sequentially or according to a specific pattern (e.g., squared) in a hash table.

metadata.title: Linear Programming
metadata.definition: Mathematical technique for optimizing (maximizing or minimizing) a linear objective function, subject to linear constraints. There are many applications in resource optimization.

metadata.title: Linear Regression
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of linear regression as an example of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Linear Regression: Curve Fitting
metadata.definition: Ability to apply linear regression to fit curves to data. Includes geometric interpretation of linear regression solution (maximum likelihood).

metadata.title: Linear Search
metadata.definition: The simplest search algorithm, examines each element in the list in order until the target is found or the list is exhausted. Has O(n) complexity.

metadata.title: Linear Search Algorithm
metadata.definition: A search algorithm iterates through each element in a list sequentially until the desired element is found or the list is exhausted. (Example for exhaust and repeat)

metadata.title: Linear Search O(n)
metadata.definition: Linear search algorithm with O(n) time complexity.

metadata.title: Linear Systems
metadata.definition: Ability to formulate, solve, apply and interpret properties of systems of linear equations. Includes solving systems of linear equations using matrix language and converting word problems into linear equations.

metadata.title: Linearithmic Time O(n log n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm increases as n multiplied by the logarithm of n, for example merge sort. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Linked List
metadata.definition: A linear data structure consists of a sequence of 'nodes', where each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Linked Lists
metadata.definition: A linear data structure where elements are not stored in contiguous memory locations but are linked by pointers or references.

metadata.title: Linking
metadata.definition: The process of combining separate compilation-generated object files and necessary libraries into a single executable program.

metadata.title: Linux System Design
metadata.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Linux operating system.

metadata.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
metadata.definition: understand the principle of behavioral substitution, where a subtype can replace a parent type without changing the correctness of the program (Liskov principle).

metadata.title: Little-o, Little-Omega, Little-Theta
metadata.definition: Additional mathematical notations to more strictly describe the asymptotic bounds of the complexity function (e.g., Little-o for a non-tight upper bound).

metadata.title: Load Balancing
metadata.definition: The function of distributing network traffic among multiple servers or resources to optimize usage and avoid overload, performed by intermediate network devices.

metadata.title: Load Leveling
metadata.definition: A technique used in distributed systems, often implemented with message queues, to smooth out transient spikes in processing demand by buffering tasks. This ensures a more consistent workload for consumers and prevents system overload, contributing to overall system resilience.

metadata.title: Loading
metadata.definition: Learn about the process of loading a linked program into memory to prepare it for execution.

metadata.title: Local Minima & Search Landscape
metadata.definition: understand the concept of local minima in search spaces and how they affect local search algorithms such as hill climbing.

metadata.title: Local Search
metadata.definition: Study of search algorithms that start from one solution and continuously move to better neighboring solutions, often used for optimization problems.

metadata.title: Local Values Impact
metadata.definition: understand the importance and impact of local values, priorities and practices around the world on work and professional responsibilities.

metadata.title: Local vs Global Solutions
metadata.definition: Distinguish between solutions that are optimal only in a local region of the search space and solutions that are optimal over the entire space.

metadata.title: Locality & Performance
metadata.definition: Explain why the principle of locality (locality of reference - space and time) plays an important role in optimizing and determining the performance of a computer system, especially in cache usage.

metadata.title: Locking
metadata.definition: A concurrency control technique in a DBMS that prevents conflicting transactions from accessing the same data by placing locks.

metadata.title: Logarithmic Time O(log n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the logarithm of the input size, for example binary search. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Logic (FPL)
metadata.definition: Logical principles underpin the field of Programming Language Platforms.

metadata.title: Logic Circuit Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design simple logic circuits using basic logic gates to solve specific problems, such as adders.

metadata.title: Logic Expressions
metadata.definition: understand and create logical expressions to describe the behavior of number systems, using Boolean operators.

metadata.title: Logic Formula Validity
metadata.definition: Calculate the validity of formulas in propositional and predicate logic.

metadata.title: Logic Fundamentals
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of logic and applications in computer science.

metadata.title: Logic Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use formal logic to represent and reason on knowledge from natural language.

metadata.title: Logic Normal Forms
metadata.definition: Calculate normal forms of logical expressions.

metadata.title: Logic Prog. Integration
metadata.definition: Methods and challenges when integrating logic programming with other popular programming paradigms, such as object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Logic Programming
metadata.definition: A style of programming based on formal logic, in which programs are written as logical statements and execution is a process of proving theorems.

metadata.title: Logic Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Concepts and applications of logic programming, recommendations for specialized students.

metadata.title: Logic Programming Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how functional programming concepts and techniques can be integrated or interacted with the logic programming model to create hybrid programming languages ​​and systems.

metadata.title: Logic Puzzles
metadata.definition: Use logic to solve puzzles.

metadata.title: Logic: Abductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: Logical reasoning method for finding the simplest and most feasible explanation for a set of observations, commonly used in diagnostics and artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: Logic: Deductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: The method of logical deduction from one or more general premises believed to be true to reach a specific logical conclusion, ensuring correctness.

metadata.title: Logic: First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: A logical system represents statements about objects, their properties, and the relationships between them, including universal and existential quantifiers.

metadata.title: Logic: Inductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: Method of logical deduction from specific observations or cases to reach a general conclusion, often used in mathematics and computer science.

metadata.title: Logic: Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Study of propositions and basic logical operations such as negation, union, selection, entailment, equivalence, along with truth tables.

metadata.title: Logical KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge about logic-based representation and reasoning.

metadata.title: Logical Reasoning
metadata.definition: Deductive methods for reaching conclusions from given premises.

metadata.title: Logistic Regression
metadata.definition: A classification algorithm uses the sigmoid function to model the probability of a class, often used for binary classification problems.

metadata.title: Long-term Software Maintenance
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to improve long-term software maintainability through understanding language features and implementations.

metadata.title: Longest Common Subsequence
metadata.definition: The ability to find the longest common substring between two or more given strings, a fundamental problem in dynamic programming and computational biology.

metadata.title: Lookahead Tables
metadata.definition: The concept of lookahead tables and how they are applied in the parsing process.

metadata.title: Loop Invariant
metadata.definition: Using loop invariants to prove the correctness of iterative constructs in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Loop Structure Definition
metadata.definition: understand the principles and techniques for defining repeating constructs in a programming language.

metadata.title: Loop Variable Copy Cost
metadata.definition: analyze the memory overhead incurred by variable copying in iterative programs, especially in the context of logic programming.

metadata.title: Loose Coupling
metadata.definition: A design principle in which components of a system have little or no direct knowledge of each other's implementation, allowing them to operate and evolve independently. This enhances flexibility, resilience, and scalability, as achieved by message queues and EDA where producers do not need to know about or wait for consumers.

metadata.title: Lossless & Dependency Preserving Decomposition
metadata.definition: The ability to define and protect a given decomposition as lossless and/or dependency-preserving.

metadata.title: Lossless Join Decomposition
metadata.definition: A property of schema decomposition ensures that when child tables are reconnected, no information is lost or spurious information is created.

metadata.title: Low-Level Function Call
metadata.definition: Explains in detail the low-level code required to make function or method calls in modern languages, including setting up stack frames, passing parameters, saving state, and restoring state.

metadata.title: Low-Level Instructions
metadata.definition: Low-level forms of command representation such as virtual machine commands, assembly language, and binary representation.

metadata.title: MAC
metadata.definition: Protocols and rules govern how devices share the same communication medium to avoid conflicts.

metadata.title: MAS Auctions
metadata.definition: Application of auction mechanisms to allocate resources or tasks among competing agents in a multi-agent system.

metadata.title: MAS Learning
metadata.definition: The field that studies how agents in a multiagent system learn and adapt in their interacting environments.

metadata.title: MAS Voting
metadata.definition: Voting methods and algorithms for aggregating the preferences or decisions of multiple agents into a common choice.

metadata.title: MDP-based Planning
metadata.definition: Planning in uncertain environments using a Markov Decision Process framework to find optimal action policies.

metadata.title: MITM Attack
metadata.definition: A type of attack in which an attacker intercepts and can modify communication between two parties without either party knowing.

metadata.title: ML
metadata.definition: A subset of artificial intelligence that enables systems to learn from data, identify patterns, and make decisions with minimal human intervention.

metadata.title: ML Algorithm Selection
metadata.definition: Ability to select the most suitable machine learning algorithm for a specific problem.

metadata.title: ML Applications
metadata.definition: Practical domains and problems that machine learning algorithms can be applied to solve.

metadata.title: ML Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: Specific data preprocessing techniques are needed to prepare data for machine learning models in data science.

metadata.title: ML Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Issues related to protecting personal and sensitive information used in training and deploying machine learning models, ensuring compliance with regulations and individual rights. (Refer also to SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: ML Error Sources
metadata.definition: understand sources of error and undecidability limits in machine learning systems.

metadata.title: ML Ethical Issues
metadata.definition: Describe ethical issues related to data selection, preprocessing steps, algorithm selection, and visualization/presentation of results in a practical Machine Learning application.

metadata.title: ML Ethics
metadata.definition: The study of ethical, social, and legal issues arising from the development and deployment of machine learning systems, including issues of bias, fairness, privacy, and accountability.

metadata.title: ML Ethics Case Studies
metadata.definition: analyze specific cases where ethical issues in machine learning have arisen and how they were or could be resolved.

metadata.title: ML Ethics: Real Scenarios
metadata.definition: Emphasizes the importance of considering the ethical implications of machine learning in real-life situations and with real data.

metadata.title: ML Evaluation Techniques
metadata.definition: Ability to apply appropriate evaluation techniques to measure machine learning model performance.

metadata.title: ML Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that machine learning systems make decisions or predictions that do not discriminate or disadvantage specific individuals or groups, regardless of their sensitive attributes.

metadata.title: ML Fundamentals
metadata.definition: understand and apply simple machine learning methods to solve problems in Artificial Intelligence.

metadata.title: ML Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: apply gradient descent algorithm in machine learning problems.

metadata.title: ML Hardware
metadata.definition: The physical components of computers and systems are designed or optimized to accelerate the complex and resource-intensive calculations of machine learning algorithms.

metadata.title: ML Input Features
metadata.definition: Attributes or independent variables of data are used as input to a machine learning model to make predictions or decisions.

metadata.title: ML Intellectual Property
metadata.definition: Legal and ethical issues related to ownership of data, models, algorithms, and other intellectual products in the field of machine learning.

metadata.title: ML KRR
metadata.definition: Knowledge of knowledge representation and inference methods in the context of Machine Learning applications.

metadata.title: ML Learning Types
metadata.definition: Ability to understand, develop, and apply mechanisms for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: ML Model Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals of machine learning model evaluation.

metadata.title: ML Model Interpretability
metadata.definition: Ability to explain trained machine learning models, including understanding their strengths and limitations.

metadata.title: ML Output Prediction
metadata.definition: The value or label that a machine learning model is trained to produce based on input features.

metadata.title: ML Paradigm Selection
metadata.definition: The ability to determine which machine learning style (supervised, reinforcement, unsupervised) is most appropriate to solve a specific problem based on the nature of the data and the goal.

metadata.title: ML Performance Evaluation
metadata.definition: Explain proper evaluation procedures in Machine Learning, including the difference between performance on training and test sets, as well as problems that can occur during evaluation that lead to inaccurate performance reporting.

metadata.title: ML Privacy
metadata.definition: Challenges and solutions related to protecting personal information when using data to train and deploy machine learning models.

metadata.title: ML Tasks
metadata.definition: understand definitions and diverse examples of machine learning tasks.

metadata.title: ML Trust
metadata.definition: The level of confidence a user or stakeholder has in a machine learning system's ability to operate reliably, securely, and fairly, especially in mission-critical applications.

metadata.title: ML as Optimization
metadata.definition: understand that training a machine learning model often involves minimizing a loss function or maximizing an objective function by adjusting model parameters through optimization algorithms.

metadata.title: ML as Search
metadata.definition: The concept of machine learning involves searching the space of models or parameters to find the model that best fits the given data and goals.

metadata.title: ML in Computer Vision
metadata.definition: Examples of the use of machine learning in computer vision, such as object recognition, face detection, and image analysis.

metadata.title: ML in Data Mining
metadata.definition: applying machine learning techniques to discover valuable patterns, trends, and insights from large data sets. (Refer also to DM/Data Analytics).

metadata.title: ML in Economics
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are for market forecasting, consumer behavior analysis, and financial optimization.

metadata.title: ML in Education
metadata.definition: The use of machine learning to improve the teaching and learning process, including intelligent tutoring systems, personalizing learning pathways, predicting student performance and analyzing educational data.

metadata.title: ML in Gaming
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are to develop gaming AI, create intelligent opponents, and optimize playing strategies.

metadata.title: ML in Healthcare
metadata.definition: Examples include the use of machine learning for disease diagnosis, drug development, medical image analysis, and treatment personalization.

metadata.title: ML in NLP
metadata.definition: Examples of the use of machine learning in natural language processing (NLP), such as machine translation, sentiment analysis, and text generation.

metadata.title: ML in Robotics
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are for robot control, environmental perception, and motion planning.

metadata.title: ML/DS Ethics
metadata.definition: Ethical issues related to the development, deployment, and use of machine learning and data science systems.

metadata.title: MSF
metadata.definition: The foundational knowledge area of ​​mathematics and statistics is the mainstay of modern computer science education. MSF inherits the 'Discrete Structures' area of ​​ACM CS2013 and covers mathematical and statistical topics essential to growing fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: MSF (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) knowledge area in CS2023, expands from CS2013's Discrete Structures to include probability, statistics, and linear algebra.

metadata.title: MVC Architecture
metadata.definition: Ability to describe an interactive system using a Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture, clearly distinguishing data model (Model), user interface (View), and control logic (Controller) components.

metadata.title: MVC Separation
metadata.definition: understand and apply the principle of separation of Model, View, and Controller components in event-driven application design.

metadata.title: Machine Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of artificial intelligence that allows systems to learn from data without being explicitly programmed, which can be used in all aspects of AI.

metadata.title: Machine Learning (ML)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on machine learning methods. Includes 4 hours of CS Core and 6 hours of KA Core.

metadata.title: Machine Learning Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms allow systems to learn from data, recognize patterns, and make decisions without being explicitly programmed.

metadata.title: Machine Learning for Data Science
metadata.definition: Machine learning techniques are applied in data science, including data preprocessing, missing data filling, supervised/semi-supervised/unsupervised learning, text analysis, graph analysis, PageRank, empirical methodology, evaluation, and ethics.

metadata.title: Machine Learning in Robotics
metadata.definition: Selected machine learning topics are well integrated with robotics, e.g. neural networks for object recognition.

metadata.title: Machine Translation
metadata.definition: Research methods and models to automatically translate text from one language to another.

metadata.title: Macros
metadata.definition: Use macros as a form of metaprogramming to generate code automatically during compilation or runtime.

metadata.title: Magnitude Estimation
metadata.definition: The ability to quickly estimate the approximate value or range of a number or calculation result.

metadata.title: Malloc/Free
metadata.definition: Standard library functions to allocate (malloc) and free (free) memory dynamically as required by the program.

metadata.title: Manual Heap Memory Management
metadata.definition: Study manual memory management techniques, including how to allocate, free, and reuse memory on the heap.

metadata.title: Map-Reduce Models
metadata.definition: Learn big data processing paradigms like Map-Reduce, Multi-stage Map-Reduce, and Incremental Map-Reduce in a NoSQL context (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: MapReduce
metadata.definition: MapReduce programming model and framework for processing and generating large data sets with distributed algorithms.

metadata.title: MapReduce (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduction to the MapReduce programming model for processing and analyzing large data sets in a distributed and parallel manner, commonly used in Big Data systems.

metadata.title: MapReduce Model
metadata.definition: A programming model and software framework for processing large data sets using distributed algorithms across a computer cluster.

metadata.title: MapReduce Usage
metadata.definition: A programming model for processing large data sets with a parallel and distributed algorithm on a computer cluster.

metadata.title: Mapping
metadata.definition: The concept of correspondence between elements of two sets.

metadata.title: Mapping Real-world to Counting
metadata.definition: Mapping real-world applications to appropriate formal counting methods.

metadata.title: Marginal Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the marginal distribution, as derived from the concurrent distribution.

metadata.title: Mark-Sweep GC
metadata.definition: A two-phase garbage collection algorithm: the mark phase identifies all accessible objects, and the sweep phase reclaims memory from unmarked objects.

metadata.title: Markov Blankets
metadata.definition: The set of nodes in a Bayesian Network such that, knowing their value, a node becomes independent of all other nodes in the network.

metadata.title: Markov Chains
metadata.definition: Introduction to Markov chains and their basic properties.

metadata.title: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs)
