metadata.definition: A mathematical framework for modeling decision making in situations where outcomes are partly random and partly under the control of the decision maker. This is the basis of many reinforcement learning algorithms.

metadata.title: Markov Models
metadata.definition: An introduction to Markov models, including basic applications.

metadata.title: Markov Networks
metadata.definition: The undirected probability graph model represents dependency relationships between variables through potential functions on subgroups of variables.

metadata.title: Master Theorem
metadata.definition: Theorems used to solve recursive equations have a certain form, often appearing when analyzing the complexity of divide-and-conquer algorithms.

metadata.title: Materialized Views
metadata.definition: Database views whose results are physically stored in the database, allowing faster queries for complex or frequent queries.

metadata.title: Math & Statistics Foundations
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Matrix Definition
metadata.definition: Basic definition of matrices.

metadata.title: Matrix Diagonalization
metadata.definition: Perform diagonalization of matrices.

metadata.title: Matrix Geometric Interpretation
metadata.definition: Interpret matrices and their operations in geometric space.

metadata.title: Matrix Operations
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of matrices and mathematical operations such as addition, subtraction, and matrix multiplication.

metadata.title: Matrix-Vector Equation
metadata.definition: understand and work with equations involving matrices and vectors.

metadata.title: Max-Cut Problem
metadata.definition: Optimization problem on graph: find a partition of vertices into two sets such that the number of edges going between the two sets is maximum. It is an NP-hard problem.

metadata.title: Maximize Computing Benefits
metadata.definition: Strive to ensure that computer technology provides maximum benefit to society at large.

metadata.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate maximum posterior estimates and establish relationships with the regularized least squares method.

metadata.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
metadata.definition: A method of parameter estimation by finding parameter values ​​that maximize the probability of observing the given data.

metadata.title: Mean (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic concept of mean value in statistics, a term that students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: Meaning of Ax=b
metadata.definition: understand the matrix equation Ax=b as a system of linear equations and how it is represented.

metadata.title: Measures of Central Tendency
metadata.definition: The concept of values ​​representing the center of a data set. Includes the ability to recognize, describe and calculate averages, medians and quantiles to locate data.

metadata.title: Media Bandwidth
metadata.definition: The concept of bandwidth is the maximum capacity of a channel to transmit data on a communication environment.

metadata.title: Memory Arenas
metadata.definition: A memory management technique in which related objects are allocated from a single large memory region, increasing allocation efficiency and freeing the entire region at once.

metadata.title: Memory Consistency Effects
metadata.definition: Understanding of how memory-consistency models affect programming language semantics and correct code generation in multiprocessor systems.

metadata.title: Memory Fragmentation
metadata.definition: The state of memory being divided into many small, non-consecutive blocks, leading to wasted space even though the total capacity is free.

metadata.title: Memory Hierarchy Trade-offs
metadata.definition: Describe the trade-off relationships between the capacity of memory levels, hit/miss rates, and access times to optimize the overall performance of the memory hierarchy.

metadata.title: Memory Leak
metadata.definition: Explains the causes of memory leaks and the methods programmers can use to avoid or fix them.

metadata.title: Memory Management (Code Gen)
metadata.definition: Techniques and strategies that compilers use to allocate and free memory for variables, data structures, and other program elements during code generation.

metadata.title: Memory Management (PL)
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of memory management in a programming language environment.

metadata.title: Memory Management Unit (MMU)
metadata.definition: A hardware component that translates virtual addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses using a page table.

metadata.title: Memory Organization
metadata.definition: Explain how programming language implementations typically organize memory into global data, program code, heap, and stack sections.

metadata.title: Memory management
metadata.definition: The operating system's crucial function of allocating and deallocating memory resources to running processes, ensuring efficient utilization, protection, and isolation.

metadata.title: Memory overcommitment
metadata.definition: A technique enabled by virtual memory that allows the operating system to run programs whose total memory requirements exceed the available physical RAM.

metadata.title: Memory protection
metadata.definition: A benefit of virtual memory that ensures processes are isolated from each other, preventing one process from accessing or corrupting the memory of another.

metadata.title: Memory sharing
metadata.definition: A benefit of virtual memory that allows multiple processes to efficiently share the same physical memory regions, often used for shared libraries or inter-process communication.

metadata.title: Memory, Disk, Network Latency
metadata.definition: Compare latency between memory, disk, and network-accessed memory.

metadata.title: Merge Sort O(n log n)
metadata.definition: A sorting algorithm based on the divide-and-conquer principle, with running time complexity O(n log n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Mergesort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the divide-and-conquer method, which divides the list into smaller sublists, sorts them recursively, and then merges them. Has complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Message Integrity Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to modify or corrupt data during transmission to change the content or invalidate the message.

metadata.title: Message Passing
metadata.definition: Models communication between processes or threads through message exchange instead of memory sharing.

metadata.title: Message Passing (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of message passing mechanisms for communication between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Message Passing Overhead
metadata.definition: analyze the performance costs (such as latency, bandwidth) associated with message passing mechanisms in distributed systems.

metadata.title: Message Queues
metadata.definition: A fundamental component in asynchronous inter-service communication, acting as a buffer that decouples senders (producers) from receivers (consumers) by storing messages reliably until they can be processed, typically involving a broker to manage delivery.

metadata.title: Metadata Management
metadata.definition: The process of managing information about data (metadata) to help organize, access, and understand data more effectively.

metadata.title: Metaprogramming
metadata.definition: Learn about metaprogramming, a programming technique in which a program has the ability to manipulate (analyze, modify, create) other programs or itself during runtime or compilation.

metadata.title: Metaprogramming & Reflection
metadata.definition: The study of metaprogramming, which allows a program to manipulate itself, and reflection, the ability to examine and modify a program's structure and behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Method Dispatch (OOP)
metadata.definition: The way methods in object-oriented programming languages ​​are looked up and dispatched to their correct implementation at run time, often using hash tables or similar data structures.

metadata.title: Method Overriding
metadata.definition: The concept of method overriding, allows a child class to provide its own implementation of a method already defined in the parent class.

metadata.title: Methods (Programming)
metadata.definition: Functions or procedures associated with an object or class in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Meticulousness
metadata.definition: A professional quality that demonstrates care and attention to detail, required for fields requiring a mathematical background.

metadata.title: Meticulousness Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating care and attention to detail, especially needed when working with mathematical foundations.

metadata.title: Microbenchmark Pitfalls
metadata.definition: Identify and understand the limitations and potential pitfalls of using microbenchmarks to measure performance, especially that they may not accurately reflect performance in real-world environments.

metadata.title: Middleboxes
metadata.definition: Intermediate network devices perform additional functions beyond basic routing, including advances in the use of AI, intent-based networking, filtering, deep packet inspection, load balancing, NAT, and CDN.

metadata.title: Midjourney
metadata.definition: Example of another deep image generation model, known for its ability to generate high-quality artistic images.

metadata.title: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) Communication
metadata.definition: Wireless communication technology uses the millimeter wave band, often used in 5G.

metadata.title: Minimax Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the Minimax search algorithm in fighting game applications.

metadata.title: Minimax Search
metadata.definition: understand and apply the Minimax search algorithm to solve two-player fighting games.

metadata.title: Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithms
metadata.definition: Set of algorithms used to find a subtree of a weighted undirected graph, including all vertices, with the smallest possible total edge weights.

metadata.title: Missing Data Imputation
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for handling and filling in missing data values ​​in a data set.

metadata.title: Missing Value Handling
metadata.definition: Missing value handling techniques such as imputing or marking as missing, along with their consequences.

metadata.title: Mixing incompatible synchronization primitives
metadata.definition: A common pitfall that can lead to deadlocks or other concurrency issues due to inconsistent behavior or subtle interactions between different mechanisms not designed to work seamlessly together.

metadata.title: Mixins
metadata.definition: Learn about mixins as a way to reuse code and add functionality to classes without traditional multiple inheritance.

metadata.title: Mobile Code Sandboxing
metadata.definition: Discusses the use of sandboxing (isolated environments) in mobile code to enhance security.

metadata.title: Mobile Communication Principles
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of mobile communication, including technologies such as 4G and 5G.

metadata.title: Mobile Communication Registration
metadata.definition: Describe aspects of the registration process in mobile communication.

metadata.title: Mobile Systems & Apps
metadata.definition: Develop software and applications for mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets, including elements such as touchscreens, device sensors, power management and cross-platform compatibility. This is an example of a specialized platform.

metadata.title: Mobility Support
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the concepts and technologies that support mobility in networks, including device-to-device communication and multi-hop wireless networks. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Model Checking
metadata.definition: A technique for verifying the correctness of a hardware or software system design by automatically checking whether an abstract model of the system satisfies certain specifications.

metadata.title: Model Evaluation
metadata.definition: Methods and metrics are used to measure how well a machine learning model performs its task on unseen data.

metadata.title: Model Understanding & Limitations
metadata.definition: Master how a model works, its limitations and pitfalls, and the implications of the decisions the model makes.

metadata.title: Model-Based Development
metadata.definition: Learn about model-based development (MBD), where models are used as the primary means to design, deploy, and test systems.

metadata.title: Model-based Reasoning
metadata.definition: An inference method uses a qualitative or quantitative model of a system to predict or explain its behavior.

metadata.title: Modeling & Simulation
metadata.definition: A core topic is allocated 1 hour of study in the Computational Science (CN) area of ​​CS2013.

metadata.title: Modeling Application
metadata.definition: Modeling applications are considered a cross-cutting topic in computer science.

metadata.title: Modeling Research
metadata.definition: Modeling research as it stands is seen as more relevant in the CS+X (Computer Science combined with other fields) space, rather than as a core area of ​​knowledge.

metadata.title: Modeling with Symbolic Logic
metadata.definition: Describe how symbolic logic can be used to model real-life situations or applications.

metadata.title: Modern Robotic Systems & Sensors
metadata.definition: Explore the most advanced robotic systems, the types of sensors they use, and how sensor data is processed for decision making.

metadata.title: Modular Arithmetic
metadata.definition: Principles and operations in modulo arithmetic.

metadata.title: Modular Arithmetic Operations
metadata.definition: Perform calculations involving modulo arithmetic.

metadata.title: Modular Recognition
metadata.definition: Design identity systems into independent, exchangeable or reusable components, to improve flexibility and maintainability.

metadata.title: Modulation
metadata.definition: The process of transforming one or more properties of a carrier wave (for example, amplitude, frequency, phase) according to an information signal to transmit data over a transmission channel.

metadata.title: Modulation Intro
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of modulation, the process of transforming information signals for transmission through physical media.

metadata.title: Modules
metadata.definition: Concept of modules to organize and reuse code.

metadata.title: Monads
metadata.definition: Learn about monads as a control abstraction and code organization mechanism, especially in functional programming.

metadata.title: MongoDB Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how MongoDB, a document-based NoSQL database, stores and processes semi-structured data (especially BSON, similar to JSON).

metadata.title: Monitor
metadata.definition: A high-level synchronization mechanism allows threads to securely access shared resources through protected methods.

metadata.title: Monomorphic vs. Polymorphic Types
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare between monomorphic (works with only one specific type) and polymorphic (can work with many types).

metadata.title: Monotonic Inference
metadata.definition: A type of inference in which conclusions drawn are never revoked when new information becomes available.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Integration
metadata.definition: understand and apply the Monte Carlo integration method.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Sampling
metadata.definition: Simulation techniques rely on random sampling to estimate quantities in complex probability models.

metadata.title: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
metadata.definition: Learn a heuristic search algorithm to make decisions in complex problems, especially in games, by randomly sampling from the search space.

metadata.title: Motion Analysis (CV)
metadata.definition: Techniques for detecting, tracking, and estimating object or camera motion in an image or video sequence.

metadata.title: Motion Planning & Trajectory Opt.
metadata.definition: Research algorithms to find safe and effective paths for robots to move in environments with obstacles, as well as optimize trajectories according to criteria such as time or energy.

metadata.title: Mu-Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Introduction to Recursive Functions Mu as another formal computational model, equivalent to a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: Multi-Agent Systems
metadata.definition: Systems consist of multiple agents that interact with each other and with the environment to achieve their own goals or common goals.

metadata.title: Multi-Device UX
metadata.definition: The ability to design and deploy applications that provide a seamless and consistent user experience regardless of the device, screen size, or operating system the user is using. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot Coordination
metadata.definition: Research methods for multiple robots to work together effectively to complete a common task, including task assignment and communication.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot Sensor Fusion
metadata.definition: Methods for robots to share and integrate sensor data from multiple sources to gain a more comprehensive view of the environment and support common missions.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot vs. HRI
metadata.definition: analyze the differences in goals, methods, and challenges between collaborative autonomous robotic systems and robotic systems that work alongside humans.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot vs. HRI Contexts
metadata.definition: Study how requirements, constraints, and characteristics of the task environment shape different approaches to multi-robot coordination and human-robot collaboration.

metadata.title: Multi-Thread Multi-Server
metadata.definition: The parallel processing model is more complex, where multiple threads are used across multiple servers to enhance concurrency.

metadata.title: Multi-agent Planning
metadata.definition: Plan for systems that include multiple interacting agents, where each agent may have its own goals and need to coordinate actions.

metadata.title: Multi-agent System
metadata.definition: AI systems consist of multiple agents that interact with each other and the environment to achieve common or individual goals.

metadata.title: Multi-dimensional Array (Matrix)
metadata.definition: An array whose elements are arranged in multiple dimensions, often used to represent matrices or grids.

metadata.title: Multi-hop Network Applications
metadata.definition: Describe practical applications of multihop wireless networks, such as ad hoc networks.

metadata.title: Multi-hop Wireless
metadata.definition: The concept of a wireless network where data is transmitted through multiple intermediate nodes (multi-hop) before reaching the final destination, typically in ad-hoc or sensor networks.

metadata.title: Multi-hop Wireless Networks
metadata.definition: The principles and architecture of wireless networks where data is transmitted over multiple hops, including ad hoc networks, opportunistic networks, and delay-tolerant networks.

metadata.title: Multi-level page tables
metadata.definition: A hierarchical organization of page tables used by modern operating systems to reduce the physical memory overhead associated with very large virtual address spaces.

metadata.title: Multidimensional Arrays
metadata.definition: Array data structures have more than one index to access elements, such as matrices. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
metadata.definition: A type of feedforward neural network consisting of at least three layers of nodes (input layer, one or more hidden layers, and output layer), capable of learning nonlinear relationships.

metadata.title: Multilingual App Support (UTF)
metadata.definition: Methods to make applications more accessible to users globally through support for multiple languages, often using Unicode (UTF) character encoding.

metadata.title: Multimethods
metadata.definition: Learn about multimethods (or generic functions) where the choice of method depends on the type of multiple arguments.

metadata.title: Multimodal Embeddings
metadata.definition: Study how to represent data from multiple modalities (e.g., text, images) into a common vector space to understand multimodal context.

metadata.title: Multimodal I/O
metadata.definition: Ability to process and produce information through a variety of media (e.g., text, images, sound).

metadata.title: Multiple Inheritance
metadata.definition: understand the concept of multiple inheritance in object-oriented programming, its advantages and disadvantages.

metadata.title: Multivalued Dependency (MVD)
metadata.definition: A type of dependency in a relational database that describes a constraint in which one set of attributes defines a different set of values ​​for another attribute, independent of the other attributes.

metadata.title: Multivariable Algebra
metadata.definition: Ability to simplify, expand, and rearrange algebraic expressions involving multiple variables.

metadata.title: Multivariable Calculus
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts of multivariate analysis.

metadata.title: Multivariable Calculus Optimization
metadata.definition: Use partial derivatives and gradients to find extrema of multivariable functions in optimization problems.

metadata.title: Multivariable Chain Rule
metadata.definition: Rules for calculating the derivative of composite functions in the case of functions of many variables.

metadata.title: Multivariate Correlation
metadata.definition: Concept of statistical relationships between multiple variables. Includes the ability to formalize and understand the concept of data correlation (e.g., in 2D).

metadata.title: Multivariate Data
metadata.definition: The concept of data having multiple variables or attributes for each observation.

metadata.title: Multivariate Estimation
metadata.definition: Parameter estimation for multivariate data. Includes the ability to formulate the multivariate maximum likelihood estimation problem as a least squares problem and to interpret the geometric properties of maximum likelihood estimation.

metadata.title: Multivariate Regression
metadata.definition: Regression techniques for multivariate data. Includes the ability to infer and calculate the maximum likelihood solution for linear regression, infer and calculate the maximum posterior estimate for linear regression, and perform both types of estimation in the context of a polynomial regression problem.

metadata.title: Mutable vs Immutable
metadata.definition: Compare mutable and immutable variables, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of reusing existing memory locations versus copying and keeping old values; storing intermediate calculations vs. recalculating.

metadata.title: Mutex
metadata.definition: Mutual exclusion locking mechanism (mutex) to protect shared resources from concurrent access.

metadata.title: Mutual exclusion
metadata.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, meaning at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode.

metadata.title: MySQL Deployment
metadata.definition: Ability to deploy and evaluate typically complex systems such as MySQL based on documentation.

metadata.title: N-ary Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which each node can have at most N children, extended from the concept of a binary tree.

metadata.title: N-gram & HMM
metadata.definition: Study statistical models such as N-grams (sequences of words) and Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to predict and analyze sequences in natural language.

metadata.title: NAT
metadata.definition: The mechanism allows multiple devices in a private network to share a single public IP address, helping to solve the problem of IPv4 address exhaustion.

metadata.title: NLP
metadata.definition: The field of AI focuses on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate natural human language.

metadata.title: NLP to KR
metadata.definition: The ability to create a symbolic or logical representation from a problem statement in natural language.

metadata.title: NLU
metadata.definition: The ability of a computer to understand the meaning of text or speech in natural human language.

metadata.title: NN Learned Representations
metadata.definition: The abstract data features and structures that a neural network automatically learns from input data through its hidden layers, help the model understand and process information effectively.

metadata.title: NN Training Process
metadata.definition: The steps and techniques involved in adjusting the weights and biases of the neural network to minimize prediction error on the training data, often through backpropagation algorithms and gradient optimization methods.

metadata.title: NP-Complete & Reduction Proofs
metadata.definition: Prove that a problem is NP-Complete by attributing a known canonical NP-Complete problem (e.g., 3SAT and Clique) to it.

metadata.title: NP-Complete Problems
metadata.definition: Problems in the NP-Complete class, have the characteristic that if a polynomial time algorithm is found for one problem, all other problems in the NP class can be solved in polynomial time (e.g. SAT, Knapsack, TSP).

metadata.title: NP-Hard, NP, NP-Complete Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between the complexity classes NP, NP-Hard, and NP-Complete, where NP-Hard is the set of problems at least as difficult as the NP-Complete problem, and NP is the set of problems that are verifiable in polynomial time.

metadata.title: NSpace & PSpace Classes
metadata.definition: Space complexity classes are defined by Turing machines: NSpace (non-deterministic polynomial space) and PSpace (deterministic polynomial space).

metadata.title: Naive Bayes
metadata.definition: A classification algorithm based on Bayes' theorem with the assumption of strong independence between features, commonly used in text classification.

metadata.title: Naive Bayes & Linear Models
metadata.definition: Study how Naive Bayes, although based on probability, can be understood and related to linear classification models.

metadata.title: Naive Code Optimization
metadata.definition: Optimization opportunities arise from direct or simple translation, and methods for achieving optimization after the initial translation is performed.

metadata.title: Name Type Equivalence
metadata.definition: understand name equivalence, where two types are considered equivalent if they are defined using the same type name.

metadata.title: Naming & Addressing Schemes
metadata.definition: Describes the principles and techniques used to name and address network resources, including systems such as DNS and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs).

metadata.title: Narrowing
metadata.definition: Learn about narrowing, a powerful combination of evaluation and unification used in functional logic programming to find solutions.

metadata.title: Narrowing, Residuation, Semantic Unification Examples
metadata.definition: Ability to give and explain simple examples to illustrate complex concepts such as narrowing, residuation, and semantic unification, clarifying how they work in functional-logic programming.

metadata.title: Native Code Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution as the processor's native machine code, delivering peak performance.

metadata.title: Natural Join Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study the algorithms used to perform natural joins between tables.

metadata.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on natural language processing.

metadata.title: Natural Language to Predicate Logic
metadata.definition: Converts logic statements from ordinary language to predicate logic expressions.

metadata.title: Natural Language to Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Converts logic statements from ordinary language to propositional logic expressions.

metadata.title: Nature of Agents
metadata.definition: Delve deeper into the properties, architecture, and functionality of AI agents.

metadata.title: Nature of Computation
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals and underlying theories that govern how computing works, independent of language or hardware.

metadata.title: Nearest Neighbor Classification
metadata.definition: A non-parametric classification algorithm assigns a new data point to the class of the closest data point(s) in the training set.

metadata.title: Nearest Neighbor Regression
metadata.definition: A non-parametric regression algorithm uses the values ​​of the closest data points in the training set to predict the value for a new data point.

metadata.title: Negating Logic Statements
metadata.definition: Negation of a logical statement.

metadata.title: Negation (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if the original statement is false and vice versa.

metadata.title: Negative cycles
metadata.definition: A cycle in a graph where the sum of the weights of its edges is negative. Such cycles imply an infinitely short path, leading to undefined shortest paths, and can be detected by algorithms like Bellman-Ford.

metadata.title: Negative edge weights
metadata.definition: A property of a graph edge where the weight (cost) associated with traversing it is a negative value. These can cause issues for some shortest path algorithms, notably Dijkstra's.

metadata.title: Nested Data Compression
metadata.definition: Methods for reducing the storage size of nested data types in semi-structured databases.

metadata.title: Nested Data Encoding
metadata.definition: Techniques for representing hierarchical or nested data types (as in JSON) into a format that can be stored and processed efficiently.

metadata.title: Nested Lambda & Reduction Order
metadata.definition: analyze nested lambda expressions and their reduction order.

metadata.title: Nested Lambda ABC Machine
metadata.definition: Ability to illustrate the execution of a simple nested lambda expression on an abstract machine like the ABC machine, understanding how levels of nesting are handled.

metadata.title: Nested Loop Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the nested loop join algorithm, one of the basic connection algorithms, traversing each pair of records.

metadata.title: Network Access Control
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and policies to restrict access to network resources (e.g. servers, data, services) to authorized users or devices.

metadata.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
metadata.definition: A fundamental networking technique that modifies IP address and port information in packet headers while they traverse a routing device, enabling multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address. It functions by maintaining a translation table.

metadata.title: Network Addressing
metadata.definition: Protocols and techniques used to assign and manage addresses (e.g., IP addresses, MAC addresses) to network devices, allowing routing and forwarding of data.

metadata.title: Network App Requirements
metadata.definition: analyze the various requirements that network applications place on the network, including quality of service (QoS) factors.

metadata.title: Network Applications
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge about network applications, how they work, and the impact of network structures and protocols on the behavior of distributed applications. This is a CS Core unit with 3.5 hours of study.

metadata.title: Network Applications (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The types of applications that operate on the network and how they interact with network protocols at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Applications (Introductory)
metadata.definition: The types of applications that operate on networks and how they interact with network protocols for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Components
metadata.definition: Identify and differentiate the basic types of devices and components that make up a computer network.

metadata.title: Network Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Describes specific network-based countermeasures deployed to combat security threats.

metadata.title: Network Cryptography
metadata.definition: Application of cryptography to protect confidentiality, integrity and authentication in network communications.

metadata.title: Network Encapsulation
metadata.definition: Data encapsulation principle, where data from a higher layer is encapsulated with the current layer's header (and footer) when transmitted to lower layers.

metadata.title: Network Encoding
metadata.definition: The process of converting data into a signal form suitable for transmission over a physical communication channel, including transmission encoding schemes.

metadata.title: Network Forensics
metadata.definition: Techniques and tools used to identify the origin of attacks or malicious traffic in a network.

metadata.title: Network Forwarding Methods
metadata.definition: The techniques and mechanisms that routers use to forward packets from the input port to the appropriate output port.

metadata.title: Network Framing
metadata.definition: The process of packaging data bits into frames at the data link layer, including adding control and address bits for transmission over a specific physical link.

metadata.title: Network Importance
metadata.definition: understand the central role networks play in modern computing systems and their contributions to everyday life, as well as the transformation they bring.

metadata.title: Network Isolation
metadata.definition: Technique that separates parts of the network to limit the spread of attacks or unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Network Layer
metadata.definition: Network layer functions and protocols, responsible for routing packets across the network from source to final destination.

metadata.title: Network Layers
metadata.definition: understand the network's layered architecture (for example, TCP/IP or OSI model) and the specific roles and functions of each layer.

metadata.title: Network Mobility (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to supporting users and mobile devices in the network at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Mobility (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to supporting users and mobile devices in networks for introductory courses.

metadata.title: Network Monitoring
metadata.definition: The process of monitoring and analyzing network traffic, performance, and events to detect unusual activity or threats.

metadata.title: Network Naming
metadata.definition: Systems and methods used to name and identify resources or devices in a network, allowing them to be easily addressed and accessed.

metadata.title: Network Protocol as State Machine
metadata.definition: understand how network protocols can be modeled as a state machine, with states corresponding to different stages of the communication process.

metadata.title: Network Queueing
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts of queuing in networks and how they affect network performance.

metadata.title: Network Reliability
metadata.definition: Principles and mechanisms that ensure that data is transmitted over a network accurately, completely, and in order, despite errors or interruptions.

metadata.title: Network Reliability (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and principles to ensure reliability in network communications at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Reliability (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and principles for ensuring reliability in network communications for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Reliability Principles
metadata.definition: The fundamentals for achieving reliability in network communications, including ensuring data is not lost, is not duplicated, and arrives in the correct order.

metadata.title: Network Security
metadata.definition: Overview of principles, technologies, and practices for protecting computer networks and data from threats, attacks, and unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Network Security (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Principles, techniques, and mechanisms to protect networks from advanced threats and attacks.

metadata.title: Network Security (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles, techniques, and mechanisms for protecting networks from threats and attacks for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Security Case Studies
metadata.definition: analyze different aspects of cyber security through real-life case studies.

metadata.title: Network Security Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Collection of techniques, tools, and policies used to protect networks from threats and attacks.

metadata.title: Network Storage
metadata.definition: Data storage solutions and technologies are accessed and managed over the network, allowing resources and data to be shared.

metadata.title: Network Switching
metadata.definition: Operating mechanism of switching devices (switches) to forward data frames in the local network.

metadata.title: Network Threats & Attacks
metadata.definition: analyze unique types of attacks and threats to network systems, how they operate, and their impact.

metadata.title: Network Topology Representation
metadata.definition: Use graphs or trees to represent network topology.

metadata.title: Network Virtualization
metadata.definition: Concepts and principles of network virtualization, including technologies such as SDN and data center networks.

metadata.title: Networking Basics
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the fundamentals of networking and communications, including the importance of networking, Internet architecture, switching techniques, layering, network components, and queuing concepts. This is a CS Core unit with 2.5 class hours.

metadata.title: Networking Basics (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Foundational concepts and fundamentals of computer networks at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Networking Basics (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Foundational concepts and fundamentals of computer networking for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Networking Challenges
metadata.definition: understand current and future challenges in designing, deploying, managing, and securing large-scale and complex network systems.

metadata.title: Networking SEP Context
metadata.definition: Social, ethical and professional issues related to the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Neural Net Focus
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on neural networks to reflect recent advances in the field of AI.

metadata.title: Neural Net Training
metadata.definition: Study the fundamentals and challenges of training neural networks, including weight initialization, optimization, learning rates, and normalization techniques.

metadata.title: Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A machine learning model inspired by the structure and function of the human brain, consisting of interconnected layers of artificial neurons.

metadata.title: Neural Tangent Kernel
metadata.definition: A theoretical concept that helps understand the behavior of large neural networks (with an infinite number of neurons) during training, linking them to kernel models.

metadata.title: Neurodiversity in Programming
metadata.definition: Discuss how programming languages ​​and development environments can be designed to accommodate people with neurological differences, encouraging inclusion in the industry.

metadata.title: Neurosymbolic AI
metadata.definition: The methods integrate both learned and symbolic representations.

metadata.title: New SQL Features
metadata.definition: Explore new features and enhancements introduced in recent versions of the SQL language, which expand query and data management capabilities.

metadata.title: No Free Lunch Theorem
metadata.definition: understand the 'There is no free lunch' theorem and its implications in machine learning.

metadata.title: No preemption
metadata.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, implying resources cannot be forcibly removed from a process holding them.

metadata.title: NoSQL Approaches (CS Core)
metadata.definition: An introduction to the different approaches and types of non-relational (NoSQL) databases (e.g. Key-Value, Document, Column-Family, Graph), as well as their appropriate use cases.

metadata.title: NoSQL Case Studies
metadata.definition: Study real-life cases of cloud storage systems (e.g., S3), graph databases, and analyze situations where NoSQL is not suitable (See also: SPD-Web).

metadata.title: NoSQL Consistency Models
metadata.definition: understand the different consistency models in NoSQL, including update and read consistency, Quorum consistency, and the CAP (Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance) theorem (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: NoSQL Data Consistency
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to data consistency in NoSQL database environments.

metadata.title: NoSQL Database Systems
metadata.definition: Non-relational database systems, designed to handle unstructured and semi-structured data, are commonly used in large-scale web applications and big data.

metadata.title: NoSQL Databases
metadata.definition: Non-relational database systems provide more flexible data storage and retrieval mechanisms, designed for the specific use cases of big data.

metadata.title: NoSQL Storage Systems
metadata.definition: Explore the types of storage systems used in NoSQL environments, including Key-Value systems and Data Lakes.

metadata.title: NoSQL Systems (KA Core)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of specific NoSQL database systems, architectures, data models, query languages, and implementation techniques for applications requiring high scalability and flexibility.

metadata.title: Non-Calculus Probability
metadata.definition: Probability versions do not require calculus knowledge, an option for programs.

metadata.title: Non-Calculus Statistics
metadata.definition: Statistics course versions do not require calculus knowledge, an option for programs.

metadata.title: Non-core Topics
metadata.definition: Elective topics have been renamed in CS2023, which are not mandatory but can be selected by students for more in-depth study according to their interests.

metadata.title: Non-Local Variable Allocation
metadata.definition: Memory allocation and access methods for non-local variables (i.e. variables declared in enclosing scopes but not the current scope), typically use static binding to keep track of nested environments.

metadata.title: Non-Numeric Array
metadata.definition: Arrays contain data elements with non-numeric values ​​(for example, characters, strings, objects).

metadata.title: Non-Procedural Query Invocation
metadata.definition: Various methods for calling non-procedural queries (like SQL) from within common programming languages.

metadata.title: Non-Traditional HW Dev
metadata.definition: The core concept of SPD, which refers to creating software specifically designed for types of hardware other than traditional desktops or servers, requires unique considerations during development.

metadata.title: Non-classical Logics
metadata.definition: Logic systems extend or modify the principles of classical logic to handle problems such as inconsistency, uncertainty, or nonmonotonicity.

metadata.title: Non-monotonic Inference
metadata.definition: A type of inference in which conclusions may change or be revoked as new information is added, as opposed to monotonic inference.

metadata.title: Non-monotonic Reasoning
metadata.definition: Type of inference in which conclusions can be revoked when new information is added.

metadata.title: Normal Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize normal distribution (Gaussian distribution).

metadata.title: Normalization Theory
metadata.definition: Deep dive into relational database normalization principles and techniques to eliminate data redundancy and improve data integrity, based on functional dependencies.

metadata.title: Nothing-Shared Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where each processor has its own memory and disk, not shared directly with other processors.

metadata.title: Number Concept
metadata.definition: Understanding numbers and their role in mathematics and life.

metadata.title: Number Types
metadata.definition: Distinguish between types of numbers such as natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real numbers.

metadata.title: Numeric Array
metadata.definition: Arrays contain data elements with numeric values ​​(e.g. integers, floats).

metadata.title: O(1) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class whose execution time is constant, independent of input size (e.g. array access).

metadata.title: O(1) Constant Time
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm does not vary with input size. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: O(2^n) Complexity
metadata.definition: The class of complexity whose execution time increases exponentially with the input size, typically hard problems (e.g. Knapsack, SAT, TSP).

metadata.title: O(log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: A representation of logarithmic time complexity, which indicates that an algorithm's execution time increases significantly more slowly than the input size, typically involves bisecting the search space.

metadata.title: O(log_b n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Logarithmic time complexity with base b, typically applied to search algorithms on tree or hierarchical data structures (e.g., binary trees, B-trees).

metadata.title: O(n log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: The time complexity is common for efficient sorting algorithms, representing a trade-off between linear and logarithmic performance.

metadata.title: O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Linear time complexity representation, which states that the execution time of the algorithm increases proportionally to the input size (n).

metadata.title: O(n) Linear Time
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm increases proportionally to the input size. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: O(n^2) Complexity
metadata.definition: Represents the squared time complexity, which indicates that the execution time of the algorithm increases with the square of the input size (n).

metadata.title: O(n^c) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class where execution time increases as a power of the input size (e.g. O(n^3) Gauss elimination).

metadata.title: ODE Definition
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of ordinary differential equations, including variables, functions, and their derivatives.

metadata.title: ODE Simulation
metadata.definition: How to use ordinary differential equations to model and simulate dynamic systems.

metadata.title: OLTP Applications
metadata.definition: Database systems are designed to handle large numbers of small, rapid, frequent, and concurrent transactions.

metadata.title: OLTP Implementation
metadata.definition: Techniques and challenges in designing and implementing online transaction processing systems, placing a high priority on transaction performance, data consistency, and concurrency.

metadata.title: OOP
metadata.definition: A programming model based on the concept of 'objects' that can contain data and code. The number of core hours spent on this topic has decreased by 4 hours.

metadata.title: OOP (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Overview of object-oriented programming, including core concepts required for all students.

metadata.title: OOP (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Additional aspects of object-oriented programming, recommended for specialized students.

metadata.title: OOP Design: Class Hierarchy
metadata.definition: Object-oriented design technique, focusing on building class hierarchies to model relationships and structures within a system.

metadata.title: OOP Design: State & Behavior
metadata.definition: Object-oriented design techniques, focusing on decomposing the system into objects with state (data) and behavior (methods).

metadata.title: OOP Encapsulation Mechanisms
metadata.definition: Use object-oriented encapsulation mechanisms such as interfaces and private members.

metadata.title: OOP Inheritance & Subtyping Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between object-oriented inheritance (code sharing and overriding) and subtype polymorphism (the idea of ​​a subtype being usable in a context that expects the parent type).

metadata.title: OOP Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how functional programming concepts can be integrated or interacted with the object-oriented programming paradigm, for example in API design or software architecture.

metadata.title: OOP Runtime Behavior
metadata.definition: How concepts like inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation affect how object-oriented programs operate and manage resources at runtime.

metadata.title: OS Interaction
metadata.definition: How shell scripts interact with and control operating system functions through commands and system calls.

metadata.title: OS Layer
metadata.definition: The software layer provides the interface between hardware and applications, manages system resources, and provides basic services.

metadata.title: OS Principles
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals behind the design and operation of operating systems.

metadata.title: OS Program Initialization
metadata.definition: The interaction points between the program and the operating system during program initialization, including code loading, stack and heap setup, and initial transfer of control.

metadata.title: OS Purpose
metadata.definition: understand the purpose, function and role of the operating system in resource management and service provision.

metadata.title: OS Scheduling
metadata.definition: The operating system function to manage and distribute CPU resources to processes or threads.

metadata.title: Object
metadata.definition: An entity in object-oriented programming that combines data and methods that operate on that data. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Object & AR Data Layout
metadata.definition: How the data of objects (data fields, vtable pointers) and activation records (local variables, parameters, return addresses) are arranged in memory.

metadata.title: Object (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: In object-oriented programming, an instance of a class, including both data (properties) and methods (behavior) that operate on that data.

metadata.title: Object Creation
metadata.definition: The process of creating an instance of a class in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Object Recognition
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and classifying specific objects in an image or video.

metadata.title: Object Recognition NNs
metadata.definition: applying neural networks to object recognition tasks in robotics applications.

metadata.title: Object Runtime Representation
metadata.definition: Study how objects are represented at runtime, including the structure of method tables to manage polymorphism and dynamic method invocation.

metadata.title: Object-Oriented Model
metadata.definition: Data models are based on the concept of objects, inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism, often used in object databases or object-relational mappings.

metadata.title: Objective Function
metadata.definition: Function that an optimization algorithm seeks to minimize (cost/loss function) or maximize (profit function) to achieve the machine learning goal.

metadata.title: Observable Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the agent can observe the entire state of the environment from problems where only a part can be observed.

metadata.title: Offensive PL Terms
metadata.definition: Study the origins and historical meanings of terms like “class,” “master,” and “slave” in the context of programming languages, and discuss their social and ethical implications.

metadata.title: One Thread Per Server
metadata.definition: Parallel processing model in which each server processes requests using a single thread.

metadata.title: One-hot Encoding
metadata.definition: The technique converts categorical variables into a numeric format (binary vector) that can be used by a machine learning model, avoiding erroneous ordering of categories.

metadata.title: Ontology Engineering
metadata.definition: The process of building and developing ontologies, i.e. models that formalize concepts and relationships in a knowledge domain.

metadata.title: Opening/Endgame Books
metadata.definition: Learn about using pre-planned strategies for the opening and late game stages of fighting games to improve AI performance.

metadata.title: Operation Independence
metadata.definition: The property of operations is not dependent on each other and can be performed in parallel without affecting each other.

metadata.title: Operational Databases
metadata.definition: Types of databases used for daily business operations, including both relational and non-relational systems.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics
metadata.definition: Learning about semantics works as a method to describe the meaning of a program by identifying its computational steps.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Assignment
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as assignment, environment usage, and memory.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Environment
metadata.definition: understand the role of the environment in operational semantics for tracking variable bindings.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Expressions
metadata.definition: Operational semantic analysis of expression evaluation, environment and memory usage.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Iteration
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as iteration, environment and memory usage.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Selection
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as selection, environment usage, and memory.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Store
metadata.definition: understand the role of memory (store) in operational semantics for monitoring memory status.

metadata.title: Operator Associativity
metadata.definition: understand the associativity of operators (left to right or right to left) and how they determine the order of evaluation when there are multiple operators with the same precedence.

metadata.title: Operator Precedence
metadata.definition: understand the precedence of operators in expressions and how they affect the evaluation results.

metadata.title: Operator-based Planning
metadata.definition: The planning method uses operator (action) definitions to transition world states.

metadata.title: Optimal Reasoning/Behavior
metadata.definition: Distinguish and understand the behaviors or reasoning processes that achieve the best possible results based on established criteria.

metadata.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: Study optimistic concurrency control methods where transactions are assumed to be conflict-free and conflict checking is performed at the commit stage.

metadata.title: Optimization
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals and applications of optimization.

metadata.title: Optional Type Checking
metadata.definition: Learn about the type checking phase of the language translation process, which can be required or optional depending on the language, to detect type errors.

metadata.title: Oracle-based Quantum Algorithms
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithms use an 'oracle' (black box) to evaluate a function, often with significantly fewer queries than classical computers.

metadata.title: Order Notation
metadata.definition: Introduction to order notation (Big O, Big Omega, Big Theta) used to describe algorithm performance.

metadata.title: Order of Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the rules for the order of evaluation of expressions and arguments in various programming languages.

metadata.title: Order-Based Properties
metadata.definition: Properties related to the execution order of operations in a parallel environment.

metadata.title: Ordered Tree
metadata.definition: A tree data structure whose child nodes are arranged in a certain order (e.g., binary search tree). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
metadata.definition: A linear regression method optimizes by minimizing the sum of squares of residuals between predicted and actual values.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Basis
metadata.definition: Concept of a basis whose vectors are all orthogonal to each other.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Complement Definition
metadata.definition: Define orthogonal complements.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Projection Calculation
metadata.definition: Computes the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace, with a basis for that subspace.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Projection Definition
metadata.definition: Define orthogonal projections.

metadata.title: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: The concept of vectors or subspaces being perpendicular to each other.

metadata.title: Orthogonality for Polynomials
metadata.definition: Describe orthogonality for polynomials.

metadata.title: Ostrich Algorithm
metadata.definition: An ignorance strategy for handling deadlocks, where the system ignores the problem, relying on deadlocks being rare and the overhead of prevention or avoidance being substantial.

metadata.title: Other Query Languages (XPATH, SPARQL)
metadata.definition: An introduction to important query languages ​​other than SQL, such as XPATH (for XML documents) and SPARQL (for RDF data).

metadata.title: Overfitting
metadata.definition: The phenomenon of a model overlearning the training data, including noise, leads to poor performance when faced with new, never-before-seen data.

metadata.title: Overfitting Solutions
metadata.definition: Techniques used to minimize overfitting include regularization, data augmentation, choosing a simpler model, or using early stopping techniques.

metadata.title: Overlapping Processing Stages
metadata.definition: The concept of executing different stages of a task or multiple tasks in parallel, is often applied in pipeline architecture.

metadata.title: Overloading
metadata.definition: Master the concept of overloading, which allows multiple functions or operators to have the same name but differ in type or number of parameters.

metadata.title: P and NP Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Explain the definition and meaning of the P (polynomial time) and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complexity classes, including the relationship between them and their significance in computational theory.

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-C, EXP (Turing)
metadata.definition: The complexity classes P, NP, NP-Complete and EXP are defined based on the execution time of a Turing machine.

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-Complete
metadata.definition: Computational complexity theory models use Turing Machines to define and classify the P, NP, and NP-Complete problem classes, which are central to the Theory of Computation.

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-Complete Classes
metadata.definition: Important problem classes in computational complexity theory: P (solvable in polynomial time), NP (verifiable in polynomial time) and NP-Complete (is NP and the most difficult of NP).

metadata.title: P-space & EXP Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the P-space (polynomial space) complexity class and its relationship to the EXP (exponential time) class.

metadata.title: P2P Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the P2P model, where nodes in the network can act as both clients and servers.

metadata.title: PBD (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Platform Based Development (PBD) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed to Specialized Platform Development (SPD) in CS2023.

metadata.title: PCA & Eigenproblems
metadata.definition: Relate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to solving eigenvector problems.

metadata.title: PCA & Least Squares
metadata.definition: Relate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to solving least-squares problems.

metadata.title: PCA Dimension Reduction
metadata.definition: Relating Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to data dimensionality reduction.

metadata.title: PCA Geometry
metadata.definition: Explain the geometric properties of Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

metadata.title: PCA Multidimensional Data
metadata.definition: apply Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of a multidimensional data set (e.g., images).

metadata.title: PCFG & Weighted CYK
metadata.definition: Research on Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) and how the CYK algorithm can be extended to handle probabilities in grammars.

metadata.title: PDDL
metadata.definition: A standardized language used to describe planning domains and problems in AI, allowing different planners to work on the same problem definition.

metadata.title: PII
metadata.definition: Understanding Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and the importance of protecting it.

metadata.title: PII Protection
metadata.definition: Master the concept of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and strategies to protect it from misuse or unauthorized disclosure (See also: SEC-Foundations, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: PL (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Programming Languages ​​(PL) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Programming Languages ​​Foundation (FPL) in CS2023.

metadata.title: PL Abstractions
metadata.definition: Master common abstractions used in programming languages.

metadata.title: PL Creativity & Responsibility
metadata.definition: Ability to demonstrate innovative approaches in solving programming problems and constructing formal proofs, while taking responsibility for one's choices and results.

metadata.title: PL Culturalization
metadata.definition: How programming languages ​​and applications can support culturally different formats and conventions (e.g. currency, decimal numbers, dates), ensuring globalization.

metadata.title: PL Design Evaluation
metadata.definition: The ability to understand the elements that make up a good programming language design and apply that knowledge to analyze and evaluate the pros and cons of an actual programming language.

metadata.title: PL Design: Good Defaults
metadata.definition: Discuss the role of well-chosen defaults in language design and how they affect the programmer's experience.

metadata.title: PL Design: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: Learn about language design principles like orthogonality, where language features can be used independently and combined consistently.

metadata.title: PL Features
metadata.definition: understand the features and structures of programming languages.

metadata.title: PL Human Factors
metadata.definition: Study of how programming language features affect user experience, productivity, comfort, and programmer perception.

metadata.title: PL Implementation
metadata.definition: Explain how programming languages ​​are implemented.

metadata.title: PL Principles
metadata.definition: Presents the basic principles that govern programming languages.

metadata.title: PL Professionalism
metadata.definition: Attitude and skills that demonstrate the highest standards when using programming languages ​​and formal methods to build systems that are secure and fit for purpose.

metadata.title: PL Semantics
metadata.definition: Types of programming language semantics: operational semantics, axiomatic semantics, denotational semantics, and behavioral semantics.

metadata.title: PL Structures
metadata.definition: understand the structures and features of programming languages.

metadata.title: PL-Hardware Interface
metadata.definition: Describe how programming languages ​​communicate with hardware.

metadata.title: PL-OS Interface
metadata.definition: Describe how programming languages ​​communicate with operating systems.

metadata.title: POS Tagging & Morphology
metadata.definition: Study practical applications of NLP such as word-class tagging (assigning word-class labels to each word) and morphology (studying word structure).

metadata.title: Packet Filtering
metadata.definition: Packet filtering is performed by intermediate network devices for traffic control or security.

metadata.title: Packet Forwarding
metadata.definition: The act of moving a data packet from an input port of a router or switch to an appropriate output port, based on routing information.

metadata.title: Packet Switching
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of packet switching technology, where data is divided into small packets and transmitted independently over the network.

metadata.title: Page Structures
metadata.definition: understand the structure and organization of data pages in a database management system and how they are stored on disk.

metadata.title: Page fault
metadata.definition: An event that occurs when a process attempts to access a virtual page that is not currently resident in physical memory, triggering the operating system to load the page from secondary storage.

metadata.title: Page replacement algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms (e.g., LRU, FIFO, Clock) used by the operating system to decide which page to evict from physical memory when a new page needs to be loaded and all frames are occupied.

metadata.title: Page table
metadata.definition: A data structure maintained by the operating system that maps virtual pages to physical frames, used by the MMU for address translation.

metadata.title: Page table walk
metadata.definition: The process of traversing the page table (which can be O(L) for an L-level page table) to find a virtual-to-physical address mapping when a TLB miss occurs.

metadata.title: PageRank Algorithm
metadata.definition: understand and apply the PageRank algorithm to rank nodes in a graph, especially web pages.

metadata.title: Pages
metadata.definition: Fixed-size units into which the virtual address space is divided in a paging system.

metadata.title: Paging
metadata.definition: A mechanism within virtual memory where the virtual address space is divided into fixed-size units called pages, and the physical memory into equally sized frames, used for translating virtual addresses to physical addresses.

metadata.title: Paradigm Problem Solving
metadata.definition: analyze and compare how different programming paradigms (procedural, functional, object-oriented) approach, structure, and solve the same computational problem, including the advantages and disadvantages of each.

metadata.title: Parallel & Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: Research how to split and execute tasks simultaneously across multiple processors or computers to increase performance. This unit is renamed from 'Concurrency and Parallelism' and has core hours increased by 3 hours.

metadata.title: Parallel Aggregation
metadata.definition: Technique for performing aggregate operations (e.g., SUM, COUNT, AVG) in parallel on data partitions.

metadata.title: Parallel Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to perform calculations simultaneously on multiple processors or threads, to speed up execution of large problems.

metadata.title: Parallel Communication
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for parallel components to communicate and work together.

metadata.title: Parallel Computing Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to parallel computing, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Parallel DBMS
metadata.definition: A database management system uses multiple processors and/or disks at the same time to execute database operations to improve performance.

metadata.title: Parallel DBMS Architecture
metadata.definition: Different architectural models for parallel DBMSs, including shared memory, shared disk, and shared nothing.

metadata.title: Parallel Data Processing
metadata.definition: Concepts and techniques for parallel data processing in data management systems.

metadata.title: Parallel Distributed Computing (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of parallel and distributed computing, required for all students.

metadata.title: Parallel Distributed Computing (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in parallel and distributed computing, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Parallel Execution Control
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and techniques to control the execution flow of parallel tasks.

metadata.title: Parallel Execution Timeline
metadata.definition: Describe on the execution timeline how parallel events and activities can occur simultaneously. Explain how work can be done in less time if parallelism is possible.

metadata.title: Parallel Join
metadata.definition: Technique for performing parallel connections between tables to speed up processing.

metadata.title: Parallel Performance & Speedup
metadata.definition: evaluate the performance of simple sequential and parallel versions of a program with different problem sizes and describe the speedup achieved.

metadata.title: Parallel Processing
metadata.definition: The concept of executing multiple tasks or instructions at the same time, often by using multiple processors or processing cores.

metadata.title: Parallel Programming Models
metadata.definition: Different methods and frameworks for designing and implementing parallel and distributed programs.

metadata.title: Parallel Query Processing
metadata.definition: Learn about parallel query processing to speed up query execution by dividing work across multiple processors or nodes.

metadata.title: Parallel Scan
metadata.definition: Parallel data scanning technique across multiple devices or streams to speed up retrieval.

metadata.title: Parallel Termination
metadata.definition: The concept of termination of parallel programs or tasks, ensuring that all components have completed their work and the system has reached its final state.

metadata.title: Parameter Estimation
metadata.definition: The process of using sample data to estimate the unknown parameters of a probability distribution or statistical model.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: Different methods for passing arguments to functions, including pass by value (copy by value), pass by reference (pass address), pass by result-value (copy in and out), pass by name (text replacement), and pass by need (lazy evaluation), along with their variations and comparisons.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing Mechanisms
metadata.definition: Study different parameter passing mechanisms (e.g., pass by value, pass by reference) and how they are implemented on an abstract machine during language translation.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing Memory
metadata.definition: How memory is allocated and used when information is exchanged between functions or procedures through various parameter passing mechanisms.

metadata.title: Parametric Curves
metadata.definition: apply parametric representations to important curves.

metadata.title: Parametric Polymorphism
metadata.definition: Master the concept of parametric polymorphism, where a function or data type can be written generically to operate on different types without modification.

metadata.title: Parametricity
metadata.definition: Learn about parametricity as a property of the polymorphic type system, which implies behavioral properties of generic functions.

metadata.title: Parametricity for Code Behavior
metadata.definition: The ability to use parametricity to infer or establish the behavior of code based solely on information about its type, independent of the specific implementation.

metadata.title: Parse Tree Generation
metadata.definition: Learn how to build a parse tree for simple statements such as arithmetic expressions or if-then-else statements to represent their syntactic structure.

metadata.title: Parse Tree Illustration
metadata.definition: Illustrates how to construct and interpret a parse tree for a simple arithmetic statement or expression.

metadata.title: Parser Error Recovery
metadata.definition: Error recovery mechanisms are used in the parser to handle syntax errors and continue analysis.

metadata.title: Parsing
metadata.definition: Learn about the grammar analysis stage to build a syntax tree structure (parse tree or abstract syntax tree) from tokens.

metadata.title: Parsing Algorithms
metadata.definition: Research methods and algorithms to analyze the syntactic structure of a sentence in natural language.

metadata.title: Parsing Ambiguity & Precedence
metadata.definition: Illustrate ambiguity in parsing using examples such as nested `if-then-else` statements or arithmetic expressions, and show how this ambiguity can be resolved by applying precedence order.

metadata.title: Parsing Strategies
metadata.definition: Parsing strategies include top-down (e.g., recursive descent, LL) and bottom-up (e.g., LR, GLR) methods.

metadata.title: Partial Computation & Search Pruning
metadata.definition: Programming techniques and structures allow storing intermediate computational results and pruning unnecessary branches in the search tree to optimize performance.

metadata.title: Partial Derivative
metadata.definition: Concept and method of calculating the derivative of a multivariable function with respect to each independent variable.

metadata.title: Partial Derivatives
metadata.definition: Calculate and understand the meaning of partial derivatives.

metadata.title: Partial Order Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method in which only the necessary ordering constraints between actions are specified, allowing unrelated actions to be performed in parallel or in any order.

metadata.title: Path-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that examines specific execution paths through code, allowing the detection of errors or properties that appear only on certain paths, e.g., software model checking and software verification.

metadata.title: Pattern Matching
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms for finding similar patterns, subsequences, or structures in data, commonly used in text processing and biology.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition Methods
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms for finding and identifying patterns in data, often used for classification or clustering.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognizer FSM
metadata.definition: apply finite state machines to design and describe pattern recognition systems.

metadata.title: Pauli-X Gate
metadata.definition: Explain the operation of a quantum XNOT gate (also called Pauli-X) on a quantum bit represented by a matrix and column vector.

metadata.title: Peephole Optimization
metadata.definition: A technique that locally optimizes code by looking at a small 'window' of instructions and replacing inefficient sequences of instructions with more efficient sequences of instructions.

metadata.title: Perception
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that deals with the collection, processing, and interpretation of information from the environment.

metadata.title: Perception & Computer Vision
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge in cognition and computer vision.

metadata.title: Perception in AI
metadata.definition: analyze the role of the ability to acquire and interpret information from the environment (cognition) in the effective operation of AI agents.

metadata.title: Performance Bottleneck
metadata.definition: A point in a system where the capacity is limited, causing a slowdown or constraint on the overall system's performance.

metadata.title: Performance Data Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for collecting performance data and analyzing performance indicators of a system.

metadata.title: Performance Estimation
metadata.definition: The ability to use frontier studies or simple calculations to provide order-of-magnitude estimates of a specific performance metric in a given context.

metadata.title: Performance Evaluation
metadata.definition: Advanced methods and metrics are used to measure and compare the performance of machine learning models, including ROC and AUC curves.

metadata.title: Performance Evaluation (Core)
metadata.definition: More advanced units on system performance evaluation, including complex quantitative methods and models, for advanced students.

metadata.title: Performance Experiment Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and conduct performance-focused experiments for common systems such as operating systems or big data processing systems (e.g., Spark).

metadata.title: Performance Metric Utility
metadata.definition: The ability to explain when and under what conditions a particular system performance metric (e.g., throughput, latency) becomes useful or appropriate for evaluation.

metadata.title: Performance Metrics
metadata.definition: Specific quantities or indices used to measure and evaluate the performance of a computer system.

metadata.title: Performance vs. Problem Size
metadata.definition: analyze the relationship between a system's performance and the size of the problem it is solving, especially in the context of scaling.

metadata.title: Permutation Calculation
metadata.definition: Perform permutation calculations of a set.

metadata.title: Permutation/Combination Interpretation
metadata.definition: Interpret the meaning of permutation and combination in the context of a specific application.

metadata.title: Permutations, Combinations, Counting
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and techniques in counting, including permutations, combinations, and applications of the pigeonhole principle.

metadata.title: Perseverance
metadata.definition: The ability to maintain effort and not give up when faced with difficult mathematical problems.

metadata.title: Persistence
metadata.definition: An important career orientation at the introductory level for students, encouraging persistence in study and work.

metadata.title: Persistence Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating perseverance and persistence in work. Especially considered an essential element at the introductory level for students.

metadata.title: Persistent Data Store Design
metadata.definition: Principles and methods for designing data storage systems capable of persisting data across sessions and application restarts, taking into account legal and ethical aspects.

metadata.title: Persistent Data Structures
metadata.definition: Learn about immutable data structures, where every modification creates a new version of the structure without changing the original version, ensuring persistence and easy state management.

metadata.title: Personal AI Assistant
metadata.definition: Software agents are designed to assist users in daily tasks, providing information and automating activities.

metadata.title: Phoneme Hypothesis
metadata.definition: The process of analyzing audio signals to make predictions about the phonemes (the smallest meaningful units of sound) present in speech.
