metadata.title: Physical Database Design
metadata.definition: The process of designing the actual data storage structures on disk, including the selection of file structures, indexing methods, and data organization to optimize performance.

metadata.title: Physical Layer
metadata.definition: The function of the physical layer, responsible for transmitting raw data bits over a physical transmission medium (e.g., cable, radio waves).

metadata.title: Physical address
metadata.definition: An actual address in the physical RAM, which results from the translation of a virtual address by the Memory Management Unit (MMU).

metadata.title: Pigeonhole Principle
metadata.definition: apply the pigeonhole principle in the context of a formal proof.

metadata.title: Pipeline Concept
metadata.definition: understand pipeline architecture, a technique for improving performance by processing multiple commands or tasks at the same time in overlapping stages.

metadata.title: Piping
metadata.definition: Concept and usage of pipes to connect the output of one command to the input of another command in the shell.

metadata.title: Plan Graphs & GraphPlan
metadata.definition: Techniques for representing planning problems in graph form to find effective solutions, such as the GraphPlan algorithm.

metadata.title: Planning (AI)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on planning techniques in AI.

metadata.title: Planning Languages & Representation
metadata.definition: Standard languages ​​and methods for describing planning problems, including states, goals, and operators.

metadata.title: Planning Operators & State Representation
metadata.definition: How to identify possible actions (operators) and how to describe states of the world in AI planning problems.

metadata.title: Planning Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems are capable of generating a sequence of actions to achieve a specific goal from an initial state.

metadata.title: Planning as Search
metadata.definition: View planning as a search problem in state space or plan space.

metadata.title: Planning, Execution & Replanning
metadata.definition: The study of how plans are created, implemented, and continuously adjusted in changing or uncertain environments.

metadata.title: Platform-Specific Development
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Ply Cutoff
metadata.definition: understand the concept of limiting the depth of a search tree in Minimax and Alpha-beta pruning algorithms to manage computational resources.

metadata.title: PoW vs PoS Trade-offs
metadata.definition: Explain the trade-offs involved when comparing Proof-of-Work and Proof-of-Stake algorithms.

metadata.title: Point Estimation
metadata.definition: The concept of using sample data to calculate a single value (point) to estimate a population parameter. Includes the ability to formulate maximum likelihood estimation in the linear-Gaussian setting as a least squares problem and calculate maximum likelihood estimates.

metadata.title: Pointcut Designators
metadata.definition: Keywords or syntax are used in `pointcut` to specify different types of junction points (e.g. `call`, `execution`).

metadata.title: Pointcuts
metadata.definition: Expression defining the set of junctions at which an `advice` will be applied.

metadata.title: Pointer-based DS
metadata.definition: Data structures use pointers to link elements, allowing for more flexible organization of data in memory.

metadata.title: Polar Coordinates
metadata.definition: apply polar coordinate representations.

metadata.title: Policy Gradient Methods
metadata.definition: A class of reinforcement learning algorithms optimizes parametric policies directly by estimating the gradient of the objective function (usually the total reward) over the policy parameters.

metadata.title: Polymorphism Comparison
metadata.definition: analyze and compare the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of parametric polymorphism, ad-hoc polymorphism (overloading) and subtype polymorphism.

metadata.title: Polymorphism Definition & Benefits
metadata.definition: understand the definition and general advantages of polymorphism in programming languages.

metadata.title: Polymorphism Implementation Models
metadata.definition: understand different paradigms for implementing polymorphism in programming languages, such as monomorphization or erasure.

metadata.title: Polynomial Basis Linear Combination
metadata.definition: Explain linear combinations of basic polynomials.

metadata.title: Polynomial Linear Combination
metadata.definition: Concept of creating a new polynomial by taking a weighted sum of other polynomials.

metadata.title: Polynomials as General Vectors
metadata.definition: Define polynomials as general vectors.

metadata.title: Population (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic definition of the complete set of objects or events of interest in statistics.

metadata.title: Port Address Translation (PAT)
metadata.definition: Also known as NAT Overload, this is the most common form of NAT, allowing multiple private IP addresses to share a single public IP address by uniquely assigning different port numbers to each connection.

metadata.title: Port space exhaustion
metadata.definition: A common operational pitfall in NAT, particularly with Port Address Translation (PAT), where the NAT device runs out of available port numbers to assign for new connections, leading to connection failures and service disruptions.

metadata.title: Post-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in post-order.

metadata.title: Postconditions (Axiomatic Semantics)
metadata.definition: Use postconditions to specify the state that must be true after a piece of code is executed in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Posterior Probability
metadata.definition: The probability of an event or parameter, after considering new data, is calculated by combining the prior probability and the data through Bayes' theorem.

metadata.title: Postgres JSON Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how PostgreSQL supports and manages JSON data, including the functionality and performance when working with this semi-structured data type.

metadata.title: Potential Function
metadata.definition: A function defined for the state of a data structure, used in the potential method of amortized analysis to account for the cost of future operations by capturing the 'potential energy' stored in the data structure.

metadata.title: Potential Method
metadata.definition: Also known as the physicist's method, this amortized analysis technique defines a potential function for the data structure's state, where the amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change in the potential function.

metadata.title: Practice Mindset
metadata.definition: understand that math learning and problem solving are best achieved through continuous practice with exercises.

metadata.title: Pre-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in pre-order.

metadata.title: Precalculus
metadata.definition: Mathematical concepts prepare for studying calculus, including functions and coordinate geometry.

metadata.title: Precision
metadata.definition: Index that evaluates the accuracy of positive predictions, used in advanced classification performance analytics.

metadata.title: Precision & Recall
metadata.definition: Study important performance metrics such as precision and recall in information retrieval and classification tasks.

metadata.title: Preconditions (Axiomatic Semantics)
metadata.definition: Use preconditions to specify a state that must be true before a piece of code is executed in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Pred. Logic Proof Validity
metadata.definition: Explain what it means for a proof in predicate logic to be valid.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic
metadata.definition: Review the basic concepts of predicate logic, including predicates, variables, quantifiers, and inference rules.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic Advantages
metadata.definition: Describe the advantages of predicate logic.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic Limitations
metadata.definition: Describe the limitations of predicate logic.

metadata.title: Predict New Data
metadata.definition: Use a trained machine learning model to create predictions or classifications on never-before-seen data points.

metadata.title: Predicting Software Behavior (Logic)
metadata.definition: Use logic to predict software behavior.

metadata.title: Predictive / Dynamic Strategies (Load Balancing)
metadata.definition: Load balancing strategies that leverage machine learning and real-time metrics (e.g., CPU usage, memory, I/O) to proactively distribute load based on anticipated server capacity and current conditions.

metadata.title: Preferences and Utility Functions
metadata.definition: Concepts in decision theory for quantifying the degree of desirability or value that an agent assigns to various outcomes or states.

metadata.title: Prescriptive vs. Descriptive Polymorphism
metadata.definition: understand the difference between prescriptive polymorphism (where types must conform to a specific interface or rule) and descriptive polymorphism (where behavior is inferred from structure).

metadata.title: Prevent Computing Harm
metadata.definition: Act to protect individuals from negative or harmful effects that may arise from the use or development of computer technology.

metadata.title: Prim's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Greedy algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree for a weighted undirected graph, starting from a vertex and expanding the tree by adding the least weighted edge connecting the new vertex to the existing tree.

metadata.title: Primitive Data Types
metadata.definition: Basic data types are built into programming languages, such as integers, floats, and booleans.

metadata.title: Primitive Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Explain primitive recursive functions, their meaning, and their implementation on a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: Primitive Type Values
metadata.definition: Describes a set of values ​​of a primitive type (e.g., integer, boolean, character) in a programming language.

metadata.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
metadata.definition: Data dimensionality reduction technique. Includes the ability to formulate and reason about PCA as a least squares problem, interpret PCA geometry, and describe when PCA works well (relating to correlated data).

metadata.title: Prior Probability
metadata.definition: The initial belief about the probability of an event or parameter before any new data is observed.

metadata.title: Privacy (SEP)
metadata.definition: Issues related to privacy in the context of technology and networks, from a social, ethical and professional perspective (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Privacy by Design
metadata.definition: Approach integrating privacy into the design and operation of database systems from an early stage.

metadata.title: Privacy by Design Compliance
metadata.definition: An approach that integrates privacy protection requirements into the system, product or service design and development process from the beginning.

metadata.title: Private network
metadata.definition: A local area network that uses specific IP address ranges (e.g., 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) that are not directly routable on the public internet, typically residing behind a NAT device.

metadata.title: Proactive Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Ability to proactively anticipate and resolve potential issues related to usability, security, ethics, etc., before they arise.

metadata.title: Proactive Programming
metadata.definition: It is the programmer's responsibility to anticipate all forms of user input and system behavior, then design solutions that proactively address each case.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in applying probabilistic processes and models to design or analyze stochastic algorithms.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Independence
metadata.definition: understand the concept of independence of random variables in probability.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Inference
metadata.definition: Ability to perform probabilistic inference to draw conclusions based on data and models.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Inference Overview
metadata.definition: Overview of the fundamentals of probabilistic inference.

metadata.title: Probabilistic KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on representation and inference based on probability.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Methods for representing knowledge in probabilistic models, including how to represent uncertainty and stochastic relationships.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Planning
metadata.definition: Planning in environments where the outcomes of actions are uncertain and described by probability distributions.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Process Formalization
metadata.definition: The ability to convert a verbal description of a probabilistic process into formal concepts such as the sample space, the probability of outcomes, and the events involved.

metadata.title: Probability
metadata.definition: An important area of ​​mathematics, proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 98% for importance for careers in industry and graduate study, especially essential for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Probability & Statistics
metadata.definition: Probability and Statistics requirements for those specializing in DM-Analytics.

metadata.title: Probability (CS Core)
metadata.definition: The basics of probability reflect a strong consensus in the academic community about its importance. Total 11 class hours.

metadata.title: Probability (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of probability complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 29 hours of study.

metadata.title: Probability (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: Probability (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic probability concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Probability Density Function
metadata.definition: understand the concept and application of probability density functions for continuous variables.

metadata.title: Probability Integration
metadata.definition: apply integration techniques to solve problems involving probability.

metadata.title: Probability in AI
metadata.definition: Part of the Fundamental Knowledge Representation and Reasoning unit, shared with Mathematical Foundations.

metadata.title: Probability vs. Statistics
metadata.definition: understand the fundamental differences in goals, methods, and approaches between probability theory and statistics.

metadata.title: Probability: Hash Tables
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in hash table performance analysis.

metadata.title: Probability: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in quantum computing.

metadata.title: Probability: Security Apps
metadata.definition: Skills in applying probabilistic processes and models in security applications.

metadata.title: Probability: Text Prediction
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in text prediction systems.

metadata.title: Problem Characteristics
metadata.definition: Understanding the different characteristics of a problem can influence the AI ​​approach.

metadata.title: Problem Characterization Practice
metadata.definition: Practice skills in analyzing and characterizing an AI problem in specific situations, including environment, state, and goals.

metadata.title: Problem Domains & PL Models
metadata.definition: understand the relationships between different problem domains and the appropriate programming models to solve them.

metadata.title: Problem Reduction
metadata.definition: Engineering in the transform and conquer model transforms a problem into another problem that already has an algorithm to solve, then applies that algorithm.

metadata.title: Problem Solving
metadata.definition: The methods and strategies used by AI systems to find solutions to problems, often including search and inference.

metadata.title: Procedural vs Functional vs OOP
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast how computational solutions to a problem differ in procedural, functional, and object-oriented approaches.

metadata.title: Procedural vs. Reactive
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between traditional procedural programming paradigms and reactive programming paradigms in a parallel context.

metadata.title: Procedure Call
metadata.definition: Mechanism to call and execute a procedure (function that does not return a value) in a program.

metadata.title: Procedure Call & Dispatch
metadata.definition: How procedure (or function) calls are compiled and how methods (in object-oriented programming) are dispatched to their correct implementation at run time.

metadata.title: Procedures
metadata.definition: The concept of procedure in programming.

metadata.title: Processor Memory Hierarchy
metadata.definition: Introduction to the processor memory hierarchy.

metadata.title: Producer
metadata.definition: A component or service in a message queue or event-driven system responsible for sending or publishing messages or events to a broker.

metadata.title: Product Feature Engineer
metadata.definition: A role that uses both SQL and NoSQL operational databases to build and improve product features.

metadata.title: Product Rule (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply the multiplication rule in counting problems.

metadata.title: Product Type Rules
metadata.definition: Master the styling rules that apply to product types (also called records or structures) and how they handle the components of product types.

metadata.title: Product Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of product types, which represent collections of values ​​of different types (e.g. records, structures).

metadata.title: Professional Characteristics
metadata.definition: Values, beliefs, and attitudes are malleable, helping to demonstrate consistent desired workplace behaviors. Includes willingness and intention to apply skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Professional Dispositions
metadata.definition: A set of essential attitudes, values ​​and personal characteristics that help a professional not only succeed at work but also thrive in the long term.

metadata.title: Professional Propensities
metadata.definition: Values, beliefs, and attitudes can change, helping to shape desirable workplace behaviors (e.g., persistence, self-direction). They are essential factors for success at work and are sought after by employers.

metadata.title: Professional Propensity
metadata.definition: Values, beliefs and attitudes can change, allowing for consistent desirable workplace behaviors; When indistinguishable from skills, they refer to the willingness and intention to apply skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Professional Trait: Collaborative
metadata.definition: An essential professional trait for team projects, demonstrating a willingness and intention to work together.

metadata.title: Professional Trait: Communicative
metadata.definition: A professional trait that demonstrates the willingness and intention to apply communication skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Professional Trait: Meticulous
metadata.definition: An essential career trait for mathematical foundations, requiring care and attention to detail.

metadata.title: Professional Trait: Persistence
metadata.definition: A career trait is considered essential at the introductory level of students.

metadata.title: Professional Trait: Self-Direction
metadata.definition: A career trait expected at advanced levels of student research.

metadata.title: Professional Trends
metadata.definition: These are values, beliefs and attitudes that can be changed, helping to form consistent and desirable behaviors in the work environment. They are sought after by employers and essential to career success.

metadata.title: Program
metadata.definition: understand that a program is a set of meaningful, unambiguous statements, written according to the rules of a language.

metadata.title: Program Abstraction & Representation
metadata.definition: Methods of representing the structure and meaning of a computer program at different levels of abstraction. This unit is renamed from 'Program Representation' and has core hours reduced by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Program Abstraction Representation (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Program abstraction and representation methods, recommendations for specialized students.

metadata.title: Program Analysis
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of program analysis techniques.

metadata.title: Program Analysis & Tools
metadata.definition: The study of automatically examining a program's source or object code to detect errors, optimize, or understand program behavior. This unit was renamed from 'Static Analysis'.

metadata.title: Program Analysis Tools (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Techniques and tools for analyzing programs to determine properties and behavior.

metadata.title: Program Development Model
metadata.definition: understand the basic model of program development.

metadata.title: Program Error Recovery
metadata.definition: Methods to handle and recover from program errors that occur during execution, to maintain stable operation.

metadata.title: Program Flow Monitoring
metadata.definition: Technique of monitoring and recording the execution flow of a program to understand its behavior and determine the cause of errors.

metadata.title: Program Isolation & Protection
metadata.definition: Explain why it is necessary to isolate and protect the execution of individual programs and environments when they share the same underlying hardware or software resources.

metadata.title: Program Processing Programs
metadata.definition: Types of programs that receive input from other programs, such as interpreters, compilers, type-checkers, and documentation generators.

metadata.title: Program Profiling Tools
metadata.definition: Ability to use specialized software tools to analyze program activity (profiling) and measure its performance indicators.

metadata.title: Program Runtime Behavior
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of program behavior during execution.

metadata.title: Program/Network Protocol FSM
metadata.definition: Explain how a program or network protocol can be represented as a state machine and that alternative representations can exist for the same computation.

metadata.title: Programmatic DB Access
metadata.definition: Skills and knowledge to connect and interact with existing databases through programming code, using APIs, drivers (JDBC, ODBC) or ORM.

metadata.title: Programmatic SQL Data Iteration
metadata.definition: Ability to process and iterate through data result sets programmatically retrieved from an SQL query.

metadata.title: Programmatic SQL Execution
metadata.definition: Ability to execute SQL queries through program code, for example using APIs or database drivers.

metadata.title: Programming Abstraction
metadata.definition: Learn about abstractions used in programming to manage system complexity, such as functions, classes, modules.

metadata.title: Programming Accessibility
metadata.definition: Methods and considerations for making programming languages, tools, and development environments more accessible to people with disabilities, including assistive technology support.

metadata.title: Programming Concepts
metadata.definition: Presents the basic concepts that make up programming languages.

metadata.title: Programming Language Basics
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and principles that underlie understanding and analyzing various programming languages. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design
metadata.definition: Requires deeper familiarity with the fundamentals for designing new languages.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Study the principles and philosophies behind the design of programming languages.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design Principles
metadata.definition: Basic principles guide the design of programming languages ​​that are efficient, easy to use, and highly applicable.

metadata.title: Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: A basic programming style or approach that guides the organization and structure of a program. Modern languages ​​often integrate multiple paradigms.

metadata.title: Programming Persistence
metadata.definition: Ability to demonstrate perseverance and persistence in finding solutions to complex programming problems, even when the correct approach is not always obvious and requires process refinement.

metadata.title: Programming Rigour
metadata.definition: Careful attention to detail is necessary when using programming languages ​​and applying formal methods to avoid errors and ensure correctness.

metadata.title: Programs & Processes
metadata.definition: Concept of programs and processes in the operating system environment, and how shell scripts manage or interact with them.

metadata.title: Project Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm used to select columns (attributes) from a table, removing duplicate columns.

metadata.title: Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF)
metadata.definition: A higher normal form than 4NF, resolving anomalies caused by connection dependencies. (Equivalent to 5NF)

metadata.title: Projection & Least Squares Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between orthogonal projections and least square approximations.

metadata.title: Projection (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: Concept of projecting a vector onto a subspace or another vector.

metadata.title: Projection Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to perform projection (column selection) operations, including handling the removal of duplicate records.

metadata.title: Prolog
metadata.definition: A popular logic programming language, commonly used in AI applications involving knowledge representation and inference.

metadata.title: Promises
metadata.definition: Concept of Promises as an object that represents the final result of an asynchronous operation.

metadata.title: Proof Discharge Verified Software
metadata.definition: Engineering specifies software requirements and uses automated or semi-automated tools to complete proof discharges of the correctness of fully verified software systems, using preconditions/postconditions, refinement types, etc.

metadata.title: Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods to prove the correctness of mathematical propositions, including direct proof, contradiction, and induction.

metadata.title: Proof of Stake (PoS)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism in distributed systems where validators are chosen based on the amount of cryptocurrency they own and 'stake', to secure the network.

metadata.title: Proof of Uncomputability by Reduction
metadata.definition: Explain an example of proving a problem to be non-computable by reducing it to a known non-computable problem.

metadata.title: Proof of Work (PoW)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism used in distributed systems (e.g., Bitcoin) to prevent service abuse and validate transactions, requires a certain amount of computational work.

metadata.title: Proof-Assisted Programming
metadata.definition: Skills in using programming languages ​​that integrate proof assistant tools to build software components that are completely formally specified and verified.

metadata.title: Proof-of-Stake Algorithm
metadata.definition: Explain Proof-of-Stake algorithms, especially the trade-offs associated with them.

metadata.title: Proof-of-Work Algorithm
metadata.definition: Explain Proof-of-Work algorithms, especially the trade-offs associated with them.

metadata.title: Prop. Logic Proof Validity
metadata.definition: Explain what it means for a proof in propositional logic to be valid.

metadata.title: Propositional & First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: Review the fundamentals of propositional and first-order logic, used as the foundation for knowledge representation and reasoning in AI.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Basic logic is the study of propositions and how they are connected by logical operators.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic Advantages
metadata.definition: Describe the advantages of propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic Limitations
metadata.definition: Describe the limitations of propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositional Planning
metadata.definition: A type of planning that uses propositional logic to represent states and goals, often involving conversion to a Boolean satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Propositional Resolution
metadata.definition: Deductive technique for proving the unsatisfactoriness of a set of propositions in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositional Theorem Proving
metadata.definition: Use deductive methods, such as solution, to prove the correctness of a theorem in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositions as Types
metadata.definition: Explore the Curry-Howard relationship, where logical statements correspond to types in the type system, and proofs correspond to programs.

metadata.title: Proprietary Networks
metadata.definition: The existence and role of large networks owned and operated by specific companies or organizations, often used for distributed computing, storage, and private content distribution.

metadata.title: Proprioception
metadata.definition: The ability of a robot or AI system to sense the position, orientation, and movement of its own body parts.

metadata.title: Pseudo-Linear Complexity O(n)
metadata.definition: Sorting algorithms have near-linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions, such as counting sort. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Pseudo-linear O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Algorithms that have nearly linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions (e.g., limited range of input values), typically do not rely on comparison.

metadata.title: Public AI Access
metadata.definition: For the first time in history, the public has access to sophisticated AI-driven tools.

metadata.title: Public IP address
metadata.definition: A globally unique IP address used on the internet, which a NAT device uses to represent multiple devices from a private network when communicating with public servers.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma Proofs
metadata.definition: apply Pumping Lemma to prove that a language does not belong to a certain class of formal languages.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma for CFL
metadata.definition: Use Pumping Lemma to demonstrate the limits of stack automaton and context-free languages, i.e. prove a language is not context-free.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
metadata.definition: Use Pumping Lemma to prove the limits of finite-state automatons and regular languages, i.e. prove that a language is not regular.

metadata.title: Pure Functions & Compositional Reasoning
metadata.definition: Understanding that function calls have no side effects facilitates compositional reasoning.

metadata.title: Pushdown Automaton (PDA)
metadata.definition: Concept, operation and applications of stack automaton, a computational model more powerful than FSA, capable of processing context-free language.

metadata.title: Python for Data Assets
metadata.definition: Use the Python programming language to develop, manage, and process data, creating data assets for analysis.

metadata.title: QFT Superpolynomial Speedup
metadata.definition: The concept of using quantum Fourier transform to achieve a significant (better than polynomial) speedup in algorithm runtime compared to classical algorithms.

metadata.title: QoS Routing
metadata.definition: Routing is based on quality of service requirements such as bandwidth, latency, and packet loss.

metadata.title: Quadratic Time O(n²)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the square of the input size, for example in select sort. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Quantified Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of quantified type, allowing type variables to be introduced and used within a specific scope (e.g. Forall in polymorphism).

metadata.title: Quantitative Analysis Tools
metadata.definition: Analytical tools and techniques are used to perform performance assessments quantitatively, providing numerical data for decision making.

metadata.title: Quantum Algorithms
metadata.definition: The algorithms are designed to run on quantum computers, exploiting quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to solve complex problems.

metadata.title: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: An overview of the field of quantum computing, its basic principles and potential.

metadata.title: Quantum Internet
metadata.definition: The concept and potential of an Internet based on quantum principles.

metadata.title: Quantum Measurement (Probabilistic Outcome)
metadata.definition: Explain the probabilistic measurement results of a quantum state.

metadata.title: Quantum Mechanics Postulates
metadata.definition: Study the basic postulates of quantum mechanics that underlie quantum computing.

metadata.title: Quantum Network Security
metadata.definition: Security issues and solutions related to quantum networks.

metadata.title: Quantum Networking
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of quantum networks, using quantum mechanical principles for secure communication (e.g., quantum key distribution), and developing new applications in computing.

metadata.title: Quantum Networks
metadata.definition: An introduction to the field of quantum networks, including concepts such as quantum teleportation, quantum security, and the quantum Internet.

metadata.title: Quantum Operation Matrix Representation
metadata.definition: The way to represent quantum operations (quantum gates) uses matrices to influence the qubit state.

metadata.title: Quantum State Composition
metadata.definition: How the states of multiple qubits combine to form the states of a larger quantum system.

metadata.title: Quantum State Composition (Tensor Product)
metadata.definition: Explain how to combine the states of multiple quantum systems through the use of tensor products.

metadata.title: Quantum State Evolution
metadata.definition: Rules and how quantum states change over time or due to the effects of quantum operations.

metadata.title: Quantum State Evolution (Unitary Operators)
metadata.definition: Explain the state evolution of a quantum system through the use of unitary operators.

metadata.title: Quantum State Measurement
metadata.definition: The process of measuring quantum states and the associated wave function collapse.

metadata.title: Quantum State Space
metadata.definition: Explain the state space of a quantum system, represented as a unit vector in Hilbert space.

metadata.title: Quantum Teleportation
metadata.definition: The concept of quantum teleportation in the context of quantum networks.

metadata.title: Qubit Column Vector Representation
metadata.definition: How to represent the state of qubits (quantum bits) using column vectors in linear algebra.

metadata.title: Qubit Representation (Matrix/Vector)
metadata.definition: Explain how a quantum bit is represented as a matrix and column vector in quantum computing.

metadata.title: Query Building
metadata.definition: Skills in building effective and accurate queries to extract desired information from data.

metadata.title: Query Building (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Learn to write basic queries in a standard query language (e.g., SQL) to retrieve, insert, update, and delete data in a database.

metadata.title: Query Building (KA Core)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of building complex queries, optimizing query performance, using advanced functions, triggers, stored procedures and other complex data query techniques.

metadata.title: Query By Example (QBE)
metadata.definition: Introduction to QBE, a visual query language for relational databases.

metadata.title: Query Construction
metadata.definition: The process of creating statements or expressions to retrieve, modify, or manipulate data in a database.

metadata.title: Query Mechanisms
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques used to process and execute data queries in a database management system.

metadata.title: Query Operator Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study the basic algorithms used to implement query operators such as select, projection, and join.

metadata.title: Query Optimization
metadata.definition: The process of finding the most efficient execution plan for a query to reduce time and resources.

metadata.title: Query Plan Construction
metadata.definition: The process of building a detailed execution plan for a query, including the order of operations and access methods.

metadata.title: Query Processing
metadata.definition: The process of executing a query on a database, including parsing, optimization, and execution steps.

metadata.title: Query Transformations
metadata.definition: Techniques that change the structure of a query without changing its semantics, in search of a more efficient execution plan.

metadata.title: Queue
metadata.definition: The FIFO (First In First Out) data structure allows elements to be added at the end and deleted from the beginning.

metadata.title: Queueing & Congestion
metadata.definition: understand how overqueuing and buffer overflow lead to network congestion and performance degradation.

metadata.title: Queueing & Latency
metadata.definition: analyze how wait times in the queues of network devices (e.g., routers) contribute to the overall latency of data transmission.

metadata.title: Queueing & QoS
metadata.definition: Explore how priority and queue management policies can affect the level of service (QoS) provided to different types of network traffic.

metadata.title: Queueing Theory
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of queuing models and related formulas.

metadata.title: Queueing Theory Basics
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of queuing theory, used to analyze network performance.

metadata.title: Queues
metadata.definition: An abstract data structure that operates on the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle, with the main operations being insert (enqueue) and remove (dequeue).

metadata.title: Quicksort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the divide and conquer method, selecting a pivot element and partitioning the array around it. Has average complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Quorum Consistency Models
metadata.definition: Explore quorum-based data consistency models, used to ensure reliability and availability in distributed systems.

metadata.title: RAM
metadata.definition: Random access memory is the computer's main memory used to store running programs and data.

metadata.title: RBFS Search
metadata.definition: Recursive first-best search, a memory-friendly variant of A* uses recursion to perform a heuristic deepening search.

metadata.title: REST APIs
metadata.definition: Architecture and principles of Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interfaces (REST APIs) for communication between distributed systems.

metadata.title: ROC Curve
metadata.definition: A graph showing the model's classification performance at all possible classification thresholds, commonly used to evaluate binary classification models.

metadata.title: RPKI
metadata.definition: A public key-based system for authenticating ownership information of Internet resources (IP addresses and AS numbers), to enhance routing security.

metadata.title: Race Conditions
metadata.definition: Definition and examples of race conditions in parallel programs, where multiple threads access and change shared data without proper synchronization.

metadata.title: Radix Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is not based on comparison, sorting elements by grouping them by individual digits or characters. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Random Access MAC
metadata.definition: Media access methods allow devices to transfer data at any time, handling collisions if they occur (e.g. CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).

metadata.title: Random Forest
metadata.definition: An ensemble learning algorithm uses multiple decision trees, each trained on a randomly sampled subset of data and a random feature subset, and then the predictions are aggregated.

metadata.title: Random Processes
metadata.definition: understand the concepts and classifications of stochastic processes.

metadata.title: Random Search
metadata.definition: An effective method for fine-tuning hyperparameters is by randomly sampling parameter combinations from a defined space, often combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Random Variable Definition
metadata.definition: Ability to define random variables and indicator random variables.

metadata.title: Random Variable Independence
metadata.definition: The skill of determining whether two random variables are independent of each other or not.

metadata.title: Random Variables
metadata.definition: understand the concept and properties of random variables in probability and statistics.

metadata.title: Random Variables & Distributions
metadata.definition: understand random variables and types of probability distributions.

metadata.title: Randomized Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms use randomness as part of their logic, often to find efficient solutions to problems that the algorithm determines are difficult to solve, or to achieve good average performance.

metadata.title: Ransomware
metadata.definition: Learn about ransomware attacks and effective strategies to prevent data loss, data destruction, and ensure recovery from such attacks (See also: SEC-Coding, SEC-Forensics).

metadata.title: Rate limiting
metadata.definition: A critical mechanism in distributed systems that strictly enforces a maximum request count within a time window, leading to request rejection once the limit is hit. Its primary purposes are to prevent abuse, ensure fair resource allocation, maintain system stability, and manage operational costs.

metadata.title: Rational vs. Non-rational Reasoning
metadata.definition: The difference between making decisions based on optimal logic and data versus other forms of reasoning.

metadata.title: Reactive Agent Architectures
metadata.definition: Simple agent architectures respond directly to environmental stimuli without the need to plan or maintain internal models.

metadata.title: Reactive Agents
metadata.definition: A type of agent that only reacts directly to the current environment without the ability to plan or complex reasoning.

metadata.title: Reactive Components
metadata.definition: understand the components that make up a reactive programming system, including event sources, signals, listeners, dispatchers, event objects, adapters, and event handlers.

metadata.title: Reactive Programming Advantages
metadata.definition: Compare procedural and reactive programming paradigms, emphasizing the advantages of reactive programming in handling and responding to events.

metadata.title: Reactive Programming Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to reactive programming, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Reactive Use Cases
metadata.definition: Identify common and typical applications of event-driven and reactive programming in areas such as graphical user interfaces (GUIs), mobile devices, robotics, and servers.

metadata.title: Real-world Data ML
metadata.definition: The importance of using real data instead of textbook examples in machine learning.

metadata.title: Real-world ML Ethics
metadata.definition: Focuses on analyzing real-life situations and concrete examples to better understand the ethical implications of real-world machine learning systems and methods to address them. (Refer to SEP-Context).

metadata.title: Recall
metadata.definition: The metric evaluates the model's ability to find all actual positives, used in advanced classification performance analyses.

metadata.title: Recent AI Successes
metadata.definition: Examples of how AI has been successfully applied in practice.

metadata.title: Recommendation Systems
metadata.definition: Software systems that provide recommendations of items (products, movies, articles, etc.) to users, based on their interests, past behavior, and/or the behavior of similar users.

metadata.title: Record/Struct/Tuple
metadata.definition: Aggregate data structures allow fields or attributes of different data types to be grouped into a single unit.

metadata.title: Records
metadata.definition: The data structure allows data fields of different types to be grouped under a single name.

metadata.title: Records, Structs, Tuples
metadata.definition: Composite data types allow data items of different types to be grouped under a single name. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Recovery & Buffer Manager
metadata.definition: understand the relationship and interaction between the recovery manager and the cache manager in a database management system.

metadata.title: Recurrence Relations
metadata.definition: Equations define a series of numbers based on previous values, often used in algorithm analysis.

metadata.title: Recurrence Relations for Time Complexity
metadata.definition: The technique uses recursive equations to model and solve the time complexity of recursively defined algorithms.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
metadata.definition: Neural networks are specifically designed to process sequential data (e.g. time series, text), capable of maintaining an internal 'memory' state.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
metadata.definition: Research Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), a type of neural network suitable for processing sequence data such as text.

metadata.title: Recursion Memory Mapping
metadata.definition: Describe how features such as recursion and memory management are mapped into the memory organization model of a programming language.

metadata.title: Recursion vs Loops vs Map/Reduce
metadata.definition: Compare and apply recursion, loops, and pipelining techniques such as map/reduce to solve problems.

metadata.title: Recursive Algorithms
metadata.definition: Concepts and examples of algorithms that use recursive (calling itself) structures to solve problems.

metadata.title: Recursive Definitions
metadata.definition: apply recursive definitions to sequences and structures (e.g., Fibonacci numbers, linked lists, parse trees, fractals), solve basic recursive relationships, and prove by induction the recursive definitions. Contact recursive/iterative code, describe and prove closed form for recursive relationships.

metadata.title: Recursive Function Components
metadata.definition: Explain the basic components that make up recursive functions: zero function, successor, selection, primitive recursion, composition, and the Mu operator.

metadata.title: Recursive Functions on Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Explain how primitive and general recursive functions can be implemented or simulated on a Turing Machine model.

metadata.title: Recursive Types
metadata.definition: understand recursive types, types defined by themselves, commonly used for data structures such as linked lists and trees.

metadata.title: Recursively Enumerable Language (Type-0)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of recursive enumeration languages, corresponding to Turing Machines.

metadata.title: Red-Black Tree
metadata.definition: A self-balancing binary search tree, uses a 'color' attribute (red or black) for each node along with strict rules to maintain balance after modification operations.

metadata.title: Reducibility
metadata.definition: The concept of reducibility between problems and different types of reducibility is used to classify the difficulty of problems.

metadata.title: Reduction
metadata.definition: The technique of converting one problem into another problem, often used to prove the NP-hardness or NP-completeness of a problem.

metadata.title: Redundancy Encoding
metadata.definition: Encoding techniques add redundant information to data to detect and correct errors, including error correction codes, CRC, FEC, and RAID.

metadata.title: Reference Counting GC
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm keeps track of the number of references to each object and releases memory when the reference count reaches zero.

metadata.title: Referential Integrity
metadata.definition: The rule ensures that foreign key values ​​in one table refer to existing primary key values ​​in another table or are null.

metadata.title: Reflection
metadata.definition: Master the concept of reflection, the ability of a program to inspect, introspect, and modify its own structure and behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Reflex Agents
metadata.definition: Research on AI agents that operate based on simple reflex rules, responding directly to environmental signals without the need for complex planning.

metadata.title: Regex Matching
metadata.definition: The process of searching and matching strings according to patterns defined by regular expressions, widely used in text processing.

metadata.title: Regex Pattern Matching
metadata.definition: Perform string manipulation using pattern matching, specifically through regular expressions to search, replace, and parse text.

metadata.title: Regex vs Type-3 Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: Explain the difference between regular expressions used in programming languages ​​(which often have extended features beyond Type-3 regular languages) and formal regular expressions that correspond to Type-3 acceptors.

metadata.title: Region Shape Representation
metadata.definition: A way of representing the shape of an object by describing the properties of the region it occupies (e.g. area, center, moment).

metadata.title: Region-based Segmentation
metadata.definition: Image segmentation methods group neighboring pixels with similar properties (e.g., color, texture) into larger regions.

metadata.title: Register
metadata.definition: Small, high-speed storage elements in a CPU or digital circuit, used to hold data or addresses temporarily.

metadata.title: Register Allocation
metadata.definition: The process of assigning program variables to processor registers to optimize data access and minimize main memory usage.

metadata.title: Regression
metadata.definition: Understanding the regression problem in supervised learning.

metadata.title: Regression Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to predict a continuous variable (dependent variable) based on one or more independent variables.

metadata.title: Regression Metrics
metadata.definition: Metrics used to evaluate the performance of regression models, such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), R-squared, etc.

metadata.title: Regular Expression (Regex)
metadata.definition: Syntax, semantics, and applications of regular expressions for describing and matching patterns in regular languages.

metadata.title: Regular Expression Matching
metadata.definition: Ability to use and understand regular expressions to search, match, and manipulate text based on specific patterns.

metadata.title: Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: understand and use regular expressions to search, match, and manipulate text in shell scripts.

metadata.title: Regular Grammar
metadata.definition: A type of formal grammar used to define formal languages, often used in formal language theory.

metadata.title: Regular Language (Type-3)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties and representations of formal languages, corresponding to finite state automatons.

metadata.title: Regular vs Context-Free Grammars
metadata.definition: Compare and distinguish between regular grammars and context-free grammars, two basic types of grammar in formal language theory.

metadata.title: Regularization (Math)
metadata.definition: Deep dive into the mathematical formulas and calculations of normalization techniques, including L1 and L2, to control model complexity.

metadata.title: Regularization Formulas
metadata.definition: The mathematical representation of the normalization terms (e.g., L1, L2) is added to the objective function to control the complexity of the model.

metadata.title: Regularization for Overfitting
metadata.definition: Techniques that add constraints or penalties to the model to reduce complexity, help the model generalize better on new data, and avoid overfitting to the training data.

metadata.title: Rehashing
metadata.definition: A technique used to resolve hash collisions or when the load factor becomes too high, in which the hash table is rebuilt with a larger size and a new hash function.

metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of machine learning that focuses on how intelligent agents should perform actions in an environment to maximize the concept of cumulative rewards over time.

metadata.title: Relational Algebra
metadata.definition: understand and use relational algebra operators (selection, projection, connect, union, intersection, difference) as the theoretical foundation for SQL.

metadata.title: Relational Data Model
metadata.definition: A data model organizes data into tables (relations) with rows and columns, based on mathematical predicate logic.

metadata.title: Relational Database
metadata.definition: The study of database systems based on the relational model, which is the foundation of traditional data management.

metadata.title: Relational Database (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces the basic concepts of relational databases, including tables, rows, columns, primary keys, and foreign keys, as the foundation for querying and data management.

metadata.title: Relational Database (KA Core)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of relational database theory, relational algebra, relational analysis, and data normalization principles to design efficient and non-redundant databases.

metadata.title: Relational Database Design
metadata.definition: The process of creating an efficient and consistent relational database structure that adheres to the principles of normalization and data integrity.

metadata.title: Relational Model
metadata.definition: A data model organizes data into tables (relations) with rows and columns, based on predicate logic.

metadata.title: Relational Probabilistic Models
metadata.definition: Probabilistic models extend probabilistic graph theory to represent relationships between entities, allowing inference and learning in complex domains.

metadata.title: Relations
metadata.definition: Study of relationships between elements in sets, including equivalence relationships and ordering relationships.

metadata.title: Relations & Functions Mixing
metadata.definition: How to use a combination of relations and functions in logic programming to represent more complex problems.

metadata.title: Reliability
metadata.definition: A system property referring to its ability to perform its required functions under stated conditions for a specified period of time, consistently and without failure.

metadata.title: Reliability Support
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the mechanisms and principles that ensure reliability in network communications, including error control, flow control, and congestion control. This is a KA Core unit with 5.75 hours of study.

metadata.title: Reliability via Redundancy
metadata.definition: Concept of achieving system reliability using redundant components or information.

metadata.title: Reliability vs. Availability
metadata.definition: Distinguish between reliability (the ability to function properly over a period of time) and availability (the proportion of time the system is available) of a system.

metadata.title: Reliability: Check & Retry
metadata.definition: Method of increasing reliability by checking for errors and retrying operations when errors are detected.

metadata.title: Remote Procedure Call (RPC)
metadata.definition: The concept of the RPC mechanism, allows a program to call a procedure (or function) in another address space (usually on another computer) as if it were a local procedure.

metadata.title: Replication
metadata.definition: Method of increasing reliability by creating copies (duplication, mirroring, replicas) of data or system components.

metadata.title: Representation (General)
metadata.definition: The study of how data is structured, encoded, or transformed into suitable formats so that machine learning algorithms can process and learn effectively.

metadata.title: Representation Learning
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on representation learning to reflect recent advances in the field of AI.

metadata.title: Representation Theory (Database)
metadata.definition: Study of how information and knowledge are represented in various database models, including the theories underlying data and relational representation.

metadata.title: Residuation
metadata.definition: understand the concept of residuation, a mechanism in functional-logic programming that allows calculations to be delayed until enough information is available to perform them without looking up.

metadata.title: Resilience / Fault Tolerance
metadata.definition: The inherent ability of a system to continue operating and providing its services effectively even when components fail. This is a key benefit of message queues and event-driven architectures, often achieved through redundancy, robust error handling, and reliable message storage.

metadata.title: Resource & Problem Scale Impact
metadata.definition: evaluate how the performance of a system or application changes based on the scale of the problem being solved and the scale of allocated resources.

metadata.title: Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)
metadata.definition: A graphical model used to analyze deadlocks, where nodes represent processes and resource types, and directed edges indicate resource requests or assignments; a cycle in a RAG with single-instance resource types signifies a deadlock.

metadata.title: Resource Constraint Management
metadata.definition: Ability to cope with and optimize the use of limited resources such as computing power, memory capacity, storage space, and network/communication bandwidth. Effective management of these limits is critical in development for specialized platforms. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

metadata.title: Resource Management
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on the principles and mechanisms of resource management in computer systems. Includes resource allocation and scheduling.

metadata.title: Resource Management (Core)
metadata.definition: More advanced unit of knowledge on the principles and mechanisms of resource management in computer systems, intended for advanced students.

metadata.title: Resource Scheduling Algorithms
metadata.definition: understand popular resource allocation/scheduling algorithms such as FCFS (first-come-first-serve), priority-based scheduling, fair scheduling, and priority scheduling.

metadata.title: Responsible Algorithms
metadata.definition: understand the principles of designing and implementing algorithms responsibly, considering social and ethical impact.

metadata.title: Responsible Data Custodian
metadata.definition: Concepts and responsibilities of those who play a role in protecting and managing data in a safe, ethical and legal manner.

metadata.title: Responsive Data Management
metadata.definition: The data stored and accessed must always meet the needs/requirements of the organization.

metadata.title: Rice's Theorem
metadata.definition: Explain Rice's Theorem, an important result in the theory of computation about the undecidability of non-trivial properties of computable functions.

metadata.title: Robot Control Architectures
metadata.definition: Study different ways to design robot control systems, including proactive (planning) and reactive (sensor-based) architectures, along with the Braitenberg vehicle concept.

metadata.title: Robot Economic Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the economic impacts of robotics, including productivity, production costs, and resource distribution.

metadata.title: Robot Ethics
metadata.definition: analyze ethical issues related to robot design, deployment, and use, such as privacy, responsibility, and fairness.

metadata.title: Robot Labor Impact
metadata.definition: Research the broader impacts of robotics on society, the economy and the labor market, including right-to-work issues.

metadata.title: Robot Localization
metadata.definition: The ability to locate the robot in the environment based on features and maps.

metadata.title: Robot Navigation Analysis
metadata.definition: evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of different robot navigation strategies, considering their effectiveness, reliability, and applicability in specific situations.

metadata.title: Robot Navigation Strategies
metadata.definition: Study different methods and algorithms for robots to move in environments with complete or incomplete information, including path planning, obstacle avoidance, and positioning.

metadata.title: Robot Privacy Ethics
metadata.definition: analyze ethical and privacy issues arising from the use of robots, especially robots capable of collecting sensitive data or interacting with humans.

metadata.title: Robot Sensor Perception
metadata.definition: Ability to use robotic techniques to collect and process information from sensors to perceive the environment.

metadata.title: Robot Social Impact
metadata.definition: analyzes the impacts of robotics on society, including employment, social interaction, and cultural change.

metadata.title: Robot-Human Trust
metadata.definition: Research the importance of trust and factors that influence the building, maintenance or loss of trust between humans and robots.

metadata.title: Robotics
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge about robotics.

metadata.title: Robotics Actuators
metadata.definition: Learn about the types of actuators that robots use to move, manipulate, or physically interact, such as wheels, robotic arms, and grippers.

metadata.title: Robotics Computer Vision Basics
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply simple computer vision techniques in robotics applications.

metadata.title: Robotics Constraints
metadata.definition: Knowledge of important constraints and considerations in robot design, operation and programming.

metadata.title: Robotics Coordinate Systems
metadata.definition: Study how to represent the position and orientation of a robot and its components using coordinate systems, translations and rotations in 2D and 3D space.

metadata.title: Robotics Ethics
metadata.definition: Focus on social impact and specific, integrated robotics applications throughout the robotics course.

metadata.title: Robotics Fundamentals
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and use robotics techniques to perceive the world using sensors, position the robot, plan paths, and navigate in simple robotics applications.

metadata.title: Robotics Hardware
metadata.definition: Knowledge focuses on the robot's hardware, including components and structures.

metadata.title: Robotics Impact
metadata.definition: Explore the diverse applications of robotics and analyze the social, economic, and ethical impacts associated with their deployment.

metadata.title: Robotics Manipulation & Grasping
metadata.definition: Learn about techniques and strategies for robots to manipulate and grasp various objects in physical environments.

metadata.title: Robotics Motion Planning
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply motion planning techniques for robots.

metadata.title: Robotics Navigation & Control
metadata.definition: Study of algorithms and strategies that allow robots to move through their environment autonomously and perform the necessary control actions.

metadata.title: Robotics Overview
metadata.definition: Overview of current challenges, unsolved problems, and significant advances in the field of robotics.

metadata.title: Robotics Pathfinding
metadata.definition: Ability to plan paths and navigate robots in simple environments.

metadata.title: Robotics Platforms
metadata.definition: Develop software and applications for robotic systems, including unique considerations and challenges related to robotic hardware, sensors, actuators, and interactions with the physical environment. This is an important unit of knowledge in SPD.

metadata.title: Robotics Search Techniques
metadata.definition: Selected search topics are well integrated with robotics, e.g. A* algorithm and path search.

metadata.title: Robotics Sensors
metadata.definition: Study specific types of sensors used in robotics, including LIDAR, sonar, vision systems, depth sensors, stereoscopic, event cameras, microphones, and tactile sensors.

metadata.title: Robotics Sensors & Actuators
metadata.definition: Learn about the input devices (sensors) and output devices (actuators) that robots use to interact with the physical world.

metadata.title: Robotics Software Architecture
metadata.definition: Knowledge of software architectures used to develop and control robots.

metadata.title: Robotics Uncertainty
metadata.definition: Explores the nature of uncertainties in sensor data and in the implementation of robot control actions, as well as methods for managing them.

metadata.title: Robotics World Models
metadata.definition: Learn how robots build and maintain internal representations of their surroundings (world models) to plan and navigate.

metadata.title: Role of Data
metadata.definition: Study of the importance, value, and fundamental applications of data in information systems and the broader context of computer science and society.

metadata.title: Round Robin (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A load balancing strategy that sequentially directs requests to each server in turn, offering O(1) decision time but not accounting for individual server load or capacity.

metadata.title: Router
metadata.definition: The function and operating principle of a router is to connect subnets and forward packets between them.

metadata.title: Routing
metadata.definition: The process of determining the best path for data packets from source to destination across a network linking different networks, using routing protocols.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the principles and techniques of routing (determining paths) and forwarding (moving packets) in networks. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The principles, algorithms, and protocols used to route and forward packets in networks at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles, algorithms, and protocols used to route and forward packets in networks for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Routing Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to manipulate routing information in the network to redirect traffic or cause congestion.

metadata.title: Routing Models & Hierarchy
metadata.definition: Overview of the methods and hierarchies used to route packets in computer networks.

metadata.title: Rule-based Expert Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems simulate human decision-making using a set of 'IF-THEN' rules.

metadata.title: Run-time Systems
metadata.definition: Learn about the components and mechanisms that support program execution at runtime, including memory management, garbage collection, and scheduling.

metadata.title: Runtime Behavior & Systems
metadata.definition: The study of how a program behaves during execution, including memory management, garbage collection, and services provided by the runtime environment. This unit was renamed from 'Runtime Systems'.

metadata.title: Runtime Behavior Systems (KA Core)
metadata.definition: understand program behavior during execution and runtime support systems.

metadata.title: Runtime Metadata
metadata.definition: Explain the use of metadata in object representation and run-time activation records, such as class pointers, array lengths, return addresses, and frame pointers.

metadata.title: Runtime System Services
metadata.definition: Identify the services provided by the runtime systems of modern programming languages.

metadata.title: SDF
metadata.definition: One of the key knowledge areas identified in the CS2023 curriculum.

metadata.title: SDN
metadata.definition: The concept of SDN, where the network control plane is decoupled from the data plane, enables flexible network configuration and management through centralized software.

metadata.title: SE
metadata.definition: An area of ​​knowledge in the CS2023 curriculum.

metadata.title: SEC
metadata.definition: One of the key knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum, focusing on concepts and practices related to information security and privacy.

metadata.title: SEC (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Security (SEC) knowledge area in the CS2023 program, is the new name of Information Assurance and Security (IAS) from CS2013.

metadata.title: SECD Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about the architecture and operation of the SECD (Stack, Environment, Control, Dump) machine, a classic abstract virtual machine used to execute lambda expressions and functional programming languages.

metadata.title: SEP
metadata.definition: One of the key Knowledge Areas (KAs) in the CS2023 syllabus, focusing on ethical issues, social responsibility, and professional aspects of the computer science profession.

metadata.title: SEP (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area of ​​Society, Ethics, and the Profession (SEP) in the CS2023 program is the new name of Social Issues and Professional Practice (SP) from CS2013.

metadata.title: SEP in Data Management
metadata.definition: Emphasis on consideration of Social, Ethical, and Professional aspects when studying and practicing Data Management, including in both CS and KA core courses, to develop responsible professionals.

metadata.title: SF
metadata.definition: An area of ​​knowledge in the CS2023 curriculum.

metadata.title: SHA-256
metadata.definition: Cryptographic hash functions belong to the SHA-2 family, which produces a unique 256-bit (32-byte) hash value from input data. Widely used in information security and blockchain.

metadata.title: SLAM in Robotics
metadata.definition: Learn about the Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) problem, where a robot builds a map of its environment while simultaneously tracking its own position within that map.

metadata.title: SMA* Search
metadata.definition: A* search simplifies memory, a variant of A* that can handle larger search spaces by eliminating the least promising nodes when memory runs out.

metadata.title: SOAR Architecture
metadata.definition: An artificial intelligence synthesis and cognitive architecture designed to solve problems by searching the state space and using 'chunking' to learn.

metadata.title: SP (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area Social Issues and Professional Practice (SP) in the CS2013 program, was renamed Society, Ethics and Professional Practice (SEP) in CS2023.

metadata.title: SPD
metadata.definition: An area of ​​knowledge in the CS2023 syllabus, related to the development of applications or systems on specialized technology platforms.

metadata.title: SPD (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Specialized Platform Development (SPD) knowledge area in the CS2023 program, is the new name for Platform-based Development (PBD) from CS2013.

metadata.title: SQL
metadata.definition: Standard language for managing and manipulating data in relational database systems.

metadata.title: SQL Data Definition Language (DDL)
metadata.definition: Use SQL to define relational schemas, including table creation, integrity constraints, and other specifications.

metadata.title: SQL Data Manipulation Language (DML)
metadata.definition: Use the SQL update language subsection (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) to add, modify, or delete data in the database.

metadata.title: SQL EXCEPT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the SET DIFFERENCE (subtract) operator to find row differences between result sets.

metadata.title: SQL INTERSECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the INTERSECTION operator to find common rows between result sets.

metadata.title: SQL Index Creation
metadata.definition: How to use SQL commands to create and manage different types of indexes on database tables.

metadata.title: SQL Integrity Constraints
metadata.definition: understand and define data integrity constraints (e.g. primary key, foreign key, NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE) in SQL.

metadata.title: SQL JOIN Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using JOIN clauses to join data from multiple tables.

metadata.title: SQL PROJECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries to project (select specific columns) data.

metadata.title: SQL Queries
metadata.definition: Skills in writing and executing Structured Query Language (SQL) statements to manipulate and retrieve data from relational databases.

metadata.title: SQL Query Formulation
metadata.definition: understand and implement the steps to build an effective SQL query.

metadata.title: SQL SELECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using SELECT clauses to select data.

metadata.title: SQL SET DIVISION Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using the SET DIVISION operator to resolve 'all' or 'every' queries.

metadata.title: SQL Schema Definition with Constraints & Triggers
metadata.definition: Ability to define entire relational schema in SQL, including all integrity constraints and delete/update triggers.

metadata.title: SQL System Design
metadata.definition: analyze the design principles applied in SQL database systems.

metadata.title: SQL UNION Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the UNION operator to combine result sets.

metadata.title: SSA
metadata.definition: Static single assignment (SSA) is an intermediate representation of program code in which each variable is assigned a value only once, simplifying data flow analysis.

metadata.title: SSL
metadata.definition: The security protocol was once used to establish secure communication channels over networks, a predecessor to TLS.

metadata.title: STP
metadata.definition: The protocol is used to prevent loops in an Ethernet switched network by creating a single spanning tree.

metadata.title: SVD Applications
metadata.definition: apply Separate Value Decomposition (SVD) to a concrete example (e.g., movie ratings).

metadata.title: SVD vs PCA Geometry
metadata.definition: Explain the geometric differences between Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

metadata.title: Safe state
metadata.definition: A state in a system from which all processes can complete without deadlocking, typically in the context of deadlock avoidance.

metadata.title: Safety & Liveness
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of safety and liveness in parallel and distributed computing, ensuring programs execute correctly and can progress.

metadata.title: Sample (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic definition of a subset of a population selected for statistical analysis.

metadata.title: Sample Space
metadata.definition: Definition of sample space in probability theory, the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

metadata.title: Sample Sufficiency
metadata.definition: The concept of evaluating whether the size and quality of a sample is sufficient to draw reliable conclusions about a population.

metadata.title: Sampling
metadata.definition: Concepts and techniques of selecting a subset from a population for analysis.

metadata.title: Sampling Bias
metadata.definition: The concept of systematic bias in the sampling process, leading to inaccurate estimates.

metadata.title: Sandboxing
metadata.definition: A security technique in which a program or part of a program is run in a restricted environment, isolated from critical system resources to prevent potential negative effects.

metadata.title: Satellite Communication
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of satellite communication.

metadata.title: Satellite Networks
metadata.definition: The technology and applications of the network use satellites to provide connectivity, especially to areas that are remote or difficult to reach through traditional infrastructure.

metadata.title: Savitch's Theorem
metadata.definition: An important theorem in space complexity theory, which states that any problem that can be solved by a non-deterministic Turing machine in space S(n) can also be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in space S(n)^2.

metadata.title: Scala for Data Assets
metadata.definition: Use Scala programming language to develop large-scale data solutions, especially in Big Data environments.

metadata.title: Scalability
metadata.definition: A system property referring to its ability to handle an increasing amount of work or its potential to be enlarged to accommodate that growth, often by adding resources (e.g., servers).

metadata.title: Scalable Pointer Alias Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques that analyze the relationship between pointers and determine when two different expressions may refer to the same memory location (alias), designed to work efficiently on large programs.

metadata.title: Scaling Concepts
metadata.definition: understand system scalability, which is the ability to handle increased workloads effectively.

metadata.title: Scanner/Parser Generation
metadata.definition: Method for automatically generating scanners and parsers from the declarative specifications of the language.

metadata.title: Scheduled Access MAC
metadata.definition: Media access methods in which devices are authorized to transmit data according to a specific schedule, avoiding conflicts.

metadata.title: Scheduling Algorithm Development
metadata.definition: Develop popular scheduling algorithms and evaluate their performance.

metadata.title: Scheduling Algorithm Mechanics
metadata.definition: Describe how common resource allocation/scheduling algorithms work.

metadata.title: Scheduling Algorithm Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the advantages and disadvantages of popular scheduling algorithms.

metadata.title: Scheduling Priority
metadata.definition: Technique of assigning priorities to processes or threads so that the operating system decides the order of execution.
