metadata.title: Scheduling Pros & Cons (Core)
metadata.definition: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of common scheduling algorithms.

metadata.title: Schema Decomposition
metadata.definition: The process of dividing a large relational schema into smaller schemas to achieve higher normal forms.

metadata.title: Scope & Binding Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques for resolving the scope resolution of identifiers and binding resolution of names to corresponding objects in the program.

metadata.title: Scope Rules
metadata.definition: Scope rules of variables, including static scoping and dynamic scoping; visibility of variables and the concept of side-effects.

metadata.title: Search (AI)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on search methods in AI. Includes 2 hours of CS Core and 6 hours of KA Core. There are 3 additional CS Core hours shared with Algorithm Foundations (Search no information).

metadata.title: Search Algorithms
metadata.definition: Methods used to locate a specific item or set of items in a data structure.

metadata.title: Search Bias
metadata.definition: Bias in the way an algorithm searches or explores the solution space, can cause optimal solutions or important regions of the space to be overlooked.

metadata.title: Search Space
metadata.definition: In-depth study of the structure and characteristics of the search space, including how it affects the effectiveness of algorithms.

metadata.title: Search Space Topology
metadata.definition: Study the shape and characteristics of the search space 'landscape', including local minima, peaks, saddles, etc., and their impact on search.

metadata.title: Search Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which values ​​are stored in a particular order (e.g., smaller keys are in the left subtree, larger keys in the right subtree) to allow efficient searches, insertions, and deletions.

metadata.title: Search Tree Construction
metadata.definition: Learn the techniques and challenges of building search trees to represent state space efficiently.

metadata.title: Secondary Memory
metadata.definition: Long-term and non-volatile data storage devices, such as hard drives, SSDs.

metadata.title: Secure Channel
metadata.definition: Communication channels are protected by encryption and other measures to ensure data security and integrity.

metadata.title: Secure Compiler Development
metadata.definition: Learn the principles and techniques for developing secure compilers to prevent security vulnerabilities in the generated code and ensure the integrity of the compilation process.

metadata.title: Secure Ethical Data Storage
metadata.definition: Responsibility for ensuring the organization's data is stored securely and in accordance with ethical principles.

metadata.title: Secure Ethical Data Use
metadata.definition: Responsibility for ensuring the organization's data is used securely and in accordance with ethical principles.

metadata.title: Secure Network Architecture
metadata.definition: Architectural designs and models are used to build and deploy highly secure networks.

metadata.title: Secure Routing Protocol
metadata.definition: Routing protocols are designed with security mechanisms to protect against routing attacks.

metadata.title: Security
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Security (SEP)
metadata.definition: Security aspects from a social, ethical and professional perspective, in relation to technology and networks (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Security Architecture
metadata.definition: understand security architecture in system design to prevent security issues.

metadata.title: Security Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Strategies, tools, and techniques used to minimize risk and protect networks from threats (e.g., firewalls, encryption, VPNs, intrusion detection/prevention systems).

metadata.title: Security Systems
metadata.definition: Describe typical countermeasure systems to protect the system.

metadata.title: Security Threats
metadata.definition: Identify and classify common types of threats to cybersecurity, e.g., denial of service (DoS) attacks, malware, intrusions, phishing.

metadata.title: Security in Data Management
metadata.definition: Emphasis is placed on considering Security aspects when studying and practicing Data Management, including in both CS and KA core courses, to ensure data systems are securely protected.

metadata.title: Select Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm is used to select rows (tuples) from a table that satisfy a certain condition.

metadata.title: Selected NLP Topics
metadata.definition: Selected topics in Natural Language Processing, including TF-IDF, bag of words, and text classification.

metadata.title: Selection Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to perform selection (row filtering) operators during query processing.

metadata.title: Selection Constructs
metadata.definition: Control structures allow a program to execute different blocks of statements based on a condition, e.g. if-else, switch.

metadata.title: Selection Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is simple, iteratively finding the smallest (or largest) element from the unsorted section and placing it at the beginning of the sorted section. Has O(n^2) complexity.

metadata.title: Selection Sort O(n²)
metadata.definition: An in-place sorting algorithm compares the elements in the list to find the smallest (or largest) element and swaps it with the element in the first unsorted position. Runtime complexity is O(n²). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Selection Statements
metadata.definition: Concept of selection structure or conditional statement.

metadata.title: Selectivity Estimation
metadata.definition: Methods that estimate the number of records that will be returned by a query operator, important for optimization.

metadata.title: Self-Direction
metadata.definition: A career orientation is expected at advanced levels of study, demonstrating the ability to self-manage and lead oneself in study and work.

metadata.title: Self-Direction Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating the ability to self-manage and orient work independently. Expected at advanced levels of study and research.

metadata.title: Self-Driving Cars
metadata.definition: An application of autonomous agents, where vehicles are capable of operating on their own without human intervention.

metadata.title: Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs)
metadata.definition: A type of artificial neural network belonging to the family of self-organizing neural networks, used to reduce data dimensionality and visualize complex relationships in data.

metadata.title: Semantic Analysis (AG)
metadata.definition: The way attribute grammar is used to describe and perform semantic analysis, checking the validity and meaning of a program goes beyond syntax.

metadata.title: Semantic Analysis (Compiler)
metadata.definition: Techniques for checking the meaning and validity of a program after parsing, including type checking, symbol table management, and intermediate code generation.

metadata.title: Semantic Networks
metadata.definition: A method of representing knowledge as a graph, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships between them.

metadata.title: Semantic Representation
metadata.definition: Explore methods for representing the semantic meaning of natural language, a core task in Natural Language Processing.

metadata.title: Semantic Roles
metadata.definition: Study how entities in a sentence play different roles (e.g., agent, object, tool) in an event or action.

metadata.title: Semantic Unification
metadata.definition: Understanding semantic unification, an extension of traditional unification, considers the meaning or semantics of expressions in addition to their syntactic structure.

metadata.title: Semantic Web
metadata.definition: An extension of the World Wide Web where data is given semantic meaning, allowing computers to understand and process information more effectively.

metadata.title: Semi-Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: Learning methods use both labeled and unlabeled data to train the model.

metadata.title: Semi-structured CRUD Trade-offs
metadata.definition: analyze the performance and complexity trade-offs when performing CRUD (create, read, update, delete) operations on semi-structured databases, due to their flexible nature.

metadata.title: Semi-structured DB Indexing
metadata.definition: Indexing techniques to speed up queries on semi-structured data, taking into account their flexible and nested structure.

metadata.title: Semi-structured DB Storage
metadata.definition: Methods and systems are used to store semi-structured data efficiently, balancing flexibility and performance.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Data
metadata.definition: The data does not follow the fixed schema model of a relational database but contains tags or delimiters to separate semantic elements, e.g. XML, JSON.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Data Model
metadata.definition: The data models used to represent data do not have a strict fixed structure as in relational databases, but have some organization through tags or tree structures, e.g. XML, JSON.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Database
metadata.definition: Databases store data that does not follow the fixed structural model of a relational database, but contains tags or delimiters to separate semantic elements. JSON is a common example.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Query Processing
metadata.definition: Methods and strategies for executing queries in semi-structured databases, supporting both online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) use cases.

metadata.title: Semi-structured/Unstructured Databases
metadata.definition: Study how to store, manage, and query data types that do not fit neatly into the traditional relational model, including XML, JSON, free text, and multimedia objects.

metadata.title: Separate Compilation
metadata.definition: The technique of compiling different parts of a program independently, then linking them together to form the final program.

metadata.title: Separate Compilation Limits Optimization
metadata.definition: Discussion of separate compilation limits the compiler's ability to optimize because the full impact of function calls outside the current module cannot be known in advance.

metadata.title: Separation of Concerns (SoC)
metadata.definition: Design principle in which a system is divided into parts with as little functional overlap as possible, each responsible for a separate concern.

metadata.title: Sequence & Series Limits
metadata.definition: apply methods to find and prove limits for specific examples of sequences and strings.

metadata.title: Sequences
metadata.definition: understand basic concepts of series in calculus, including definitions and types of series.

metadata.title: Sequential & Parallel Programs
metadata.definition: Write a simple sequential problem and a simple parallel version of the same program.

metadata.title: Sequential Logic
metadata.definition: Logic circuits whose output depends on both the current input and the previous state (with a memory element).

metadata.title: Sequential Processing
metadata.definition: The concept of performing tasks or commands in a step-by-step sequence, each step completed before the next step begins.

metadata.title: Serializability
metadata.definition: understand the principles and methods of ensuring that the result of the simultaneous execution of multiple transactions is equivalent to several sequential executions of the same transactions.

metadata.title: Series
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts of series in calculus, including definition, convergence, and divergence.

metadata.title: Session Persistence (Sticky Sessions)
metadata.definition: A mechanism that ensures all subsequent requests from a particular client are routed to the same backend server that handled the client's initial request, crucial for stateful applications.

metadata.title: Set
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores a unique set of values, in no particular order. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Set Difference
metadata.definition: Subtraction (difference) operation between sets.

metadata.title: Set Intersection
metadata.definition: Intersection operation between sets.

metadata.title: Set Operations
metadata.definition: Union, intersection, difference, complement and other operations on sets.

metadata.title: Set Theory
metadata.definition: Set theory, including basic operations.

metadata.title: Set Theory, Relations, Functions
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of sets, relations, functions, and the calculation of sets, including operations, sum/product rules, the inclusion-exclusion principle, and distinguishing between finite, countable, and uncountable sets.

metadata.title: Set Union
metadata.definition: Union operation between sets.

metadata.title: Sets
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores unique, unordered elements and supports operations such as union, intersection, and difference.

metadata.title: Sets & Relations
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of sets, operations on sets and relationships between elements.

metadata.title: Shape Representation
metadata.definition: Methods for describing and encoding the shape of an object in an image, such as by contour, region, or geometric feature.

metadata.title: Shapley Values
metadata.definition: A method from game theory to allocate 'value' or equitable contribution to each feature in making predictions of a machine learning model.

metadata.title: Sharding & Replication
metadata.definition: Learn data distribution techniques such as Sharding and Replication in NoSQL systems to increase scalability and availability (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: Shared Memory
metadata.definition: Communication model where processes or threads access and modify the same memory region.

metadata.title: Shared Memory (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of shared memory mechanisms for communication between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Shared Workspace HRI
metadata.definition: Learn about scenarios and designs where humans and robots share a physical space to perform tasks.

metadata.title: Shared-Disk Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where all processors have access to the same set of disks.

metadata.title: Shared-Memory Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where all processors share a common memory address space.

metadata.title: Shell Data Structures
metadata.definition: Use basic data structures such as arrays and lists in shell scripting to organize and manage data.

metadata.title: Shell Scripting
metadata.definition: Write scripts using a command line interface (shell) to automate system tasks or file management. This is a new unit added to the program with 2 core hours.

metadata.title: Shell Scripting (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of shell script programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Shor's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The famous quantum algorithm for factoring large integers and calculating discrete logarithms, has the potential to break many existing public cryptosystems.

metadata.title: Shortest Path Algorithms
metadata.definition: A set of algorithms used to find the path with the least weighted sum between two vertices or between a vertex and all other vertices in the graph.

metadata.title: Shortest Path Problem
metadata.definition: The problem of finding a path between two nodes (or all pairs of nodes) in a graph such that the sum of the weights of its constituent edges is minimized.

metadata.title: Side Effects
metadata.definition: Side-effects can occur due to the use of non-local variables, global variables and aliased variables.

metadata.title: Side-Effect Free Programming
metadata.definition: The concept of side-effect free programming, where functions depend only on their inputs and do not cause changes in external state.

metadata.title: Simon's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The quantum algorithm searches for a hidden 'cycle' of a function, demonstrating a superpolynomial speed-up compared to the best classical algorithm.

metadata.title: Simple Error Correction
metadata.definition: Ability to apply basic algorithms that use redundant information (e.g., parity bits) to detect and correct simple errors in data.

metadata.title: Simple Event Probability
metadata.definition: Skills in calculating probabilities for basic events, using probability definitions and formulas.

metadata.title: Simple Feature Expansion
metadata.definition: Basic feature expansion techniques are simple, such as squaring univariate features.

metadata.title: Simple Neural Networks
metadata.definition: Neural network models, with few layers and basic structure, are often used as an introductory step before learning more complex architectures.

metadata.title: Simple Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Basic machine learning algorithms are based on statistical principles, used to solve classification or regression problems, such as logistic regression, k-NN, or simple decision trees.

metadata.title: Simple Statistical Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: Understanding how statistical supervised learning models work is simple enough to properly use existing implementations.

metadata.title: Simplex Algorithm
metadata.definition: A popular algorithm for solving linear programming problems, finding the optimal solution by moving between vertices of a polyhedral feasible region.

metadata.title: Simulated Annealing
metadata.definition: Learn a metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by metallurgy, capable of escaping local minima.

metadata.title: Single Point of Failure
metadata.definition: A part of a system that, if it fails, will stop the entire system from working. It represents a critical vulnerability in system design.

metadata.title: Single-Hop Communication
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the fundamentals of direct communication between two devices within a single network link. This is a KA Core unit with 3 class hours.

metadata.title: Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP)
metadata.definition: A category of shortest path problems that aims to find the shortest paths from a single designated source node to all other nodes in a graph.

metadata.title: Single-agent System
metadata.definition: AI systems in which a single agent operates and interacts with its environment.

metadata.title: Single-hop Communication (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The principles and mechanisms of direct communication between devices without requiring multiple hops at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Single-hop Communication (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles and mechanisms of direct, multi-hop device-to-device communication for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Single-variable Derivative Apps
metadata.definition: apply derivatives of one variable to solve real-life problems.

metadata.title: Singly Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which each node points to the next node in the chain, but there is no link back.

metadata.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
metadata.definition: The concept of a strong matrix decomposition has many applications in computer science.

metadata.title: Situation Calculus
metadata.definition: A first-order predicate logic language is used to represent knowledge about actions and their effects.

metadata.title: Skepticism & Inquiry
metadata.definition: Thinking does not passively accept formulas but has curiosity about how they are formulated and the theoretical basis.

metadata.title: Skip Index
metadata.definition: A type of index that allows queries to 'jump' over parts of unrelated data, speeding up searches in semi-structured data structures.

metadata.title: Sliding Window Counter
metadata.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that offers a more efficient approximation than the Sliding Window Log by combining counts from current and previous fixed windows. It achieves O(1) time and O(N) space.

metadata.title: Sliding Window Log
metadata.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that stores timestamps of all requests. It checks for requests within the current time window, providing high accuracy. However, it incurs O(K) time complexity per check (where K is the maximum requests in the window) and O(K) space per client.

metadata.title: Smoothing & Backoff
metadata.definition: Learn smoothing and redundancy techniques for handling invisible events (sparse data) in statistical language models.

metadata.title: Sniffing Attack
metadata.definition: Technique for gathering information by intercepting and analyzing network traffic passing through a point in the network.

metadata.title: Snowflake JSON Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how Snowflake, a cloud-based data warehouse, processes and analyzes JSON data, leveraging its special features for semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Social Data Collection
metadata.definition: Understanding the impact of data collection on individuals and society, including issues of ethics and public acceptance.

metadata.title: Social Network Graph
metadata.definition: Use graphs to represent social networks.

metadata.title: Social, Ethical & Professional Issues
metadata.definition: Ethical issues, social responsibility, and professional implications of programming language development and use.

metadata.title: Social, Ethical, Professional
metadata.definition: New units have been added, covering topics on social responsibility, professional ethics, and issues related to practicing in the field of computer science. Class hours are included in total SEP hours.

metadata.title: Socially Assistive Robots
metadata.definition: Learn about robots designed to assist humans in social, educational or healthcare activities.

metadata.title: Society, Ethics & Profession
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Society, Ethics, Professionalism
metadata.definition: Social, ethical, and professional aspects related to the field of computer science and software development. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Society, Ethics, Professionalism (SEP)
metadata.definition: Social, ethical and professional issues related to the field of programming languages ​​are integrated into Social, Ethical and Professional Knowledge (SEP) classes.

metadata.title: Socket API
metadata.definition: How to use Socket APIs for network programming, creating applications that communicate over the network.

metadata.title: Software & Systems Development
metadata.definition: Foundational knowledge of how to develop software, computer systems (including operating systems) and applications, is the minimum requirement for all Computer Science graduates according to CS Core standards of CS2023.

metadata.title: Software Agent
metadata.definition: Computer programs perform autonomous tasks on behalf of users or other programs in a digital environment.

metadata.title: Software Development Basics
metadata.definition: Core concepts and skills required for software development, often taught in introductory courses. This is another area of ​​knowledge that FPL can build on or overlap.

metadata.title: Software Development Fundamentals
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Software Engineering
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Software Execution Efficiency
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to improve software execution efficiency through understanding language features and implementations.

metadata.title: Software Intellectual Property
metadata.definition: understand intellectual property rights related to software and computer systems.

metadata.title: Software Licenses
metadata.definition: Lists and compares common software licenses.

metadata.title: Software Model Checking
metadata.definition: An automatic verification technique that explores all possible states of a program to verify specified properties.

metadata.title: Software Requirements on PL Design
metadata.definition: Discuss how software requirements shape the development and evolution of programming languages.

metadata.title: Software Verification
metadata.definition: The process of ensuring that software meets given requirements or specifications, often through formal or semi-formal methods.

metadata.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
metadata.definition: The network architecture separates the control plane from the data plane, allowing flexible network management and configuration through software.

metadata.title: Solution Diligence
metadata.definition: Care and attention to detail ensure the correctness and completeness of solutions.

metadata.title: Solution Lifecycle Responsibility
metadata.definition: Demonstrate responsibility in all aspects of a technology solution, including the design, implementation and maintenance phases.

metadata.title: Solve Single-Variable Linear Eq.
metadata.definition: Ability to find solutions to linear equations with one unknown variable.

metadata.title: Solve Single-Variable Quadratic Eq.
metadata.definition: Ability to find solutions (or roots) to quadratic equations with one unknown variable.

metadata.title: Solve Two-Variable Linear Eq.
metadata.definition: Ability to find solutions to systems of linear equations with two unknown variables.

metadata.title: Solve Two-Variable Quadratic Eq.
metadata.definition: The ability to find solutions to quadratic equations involving two variables, often through a system of equations or in analytic geometry (e.g., conics).

metadata.title: Sort-Merge Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the sort-merge join algorithm, which requires tables to be sorted before merging.

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms
metadata.definition: Systematic methods are used to arrange a set of items in a specific order (e.g., numbers, letters).

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Algorithms designed to sort the elements of a list in a certain order, including more efficient algorithms and algorithms with pseudo-linear complexity. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms Intermediate
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to arrange the elements of a list in a certain order. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Sound Type System Invariants
metadata.definition: Describes precisely the invariants that a sound type system ensures are preserved during program execution.

metadata.title: Soundness
metadata.definition: The property of a program analyzer that ensures that it never misses any errors or unexpected properties (e.g., if it says there are no errors, there really are no errors).

metadata.title: Source Code Representation
metadata.definition: Data structures are used to represent source code for execution, translation, or transport purposes.

metadata.title: Source Routing
metadata.definition: A routing technique in which the sender specifies all or part of the path that the packet will take.

metadata.title: Space Complexity
metadata.definition: The study of the amount of memory or storage space an algorithm requires to run, often expressed in asymptotic notation.

metadata.title: Space Complexity (Pspace, Savitch's Theorem)
metadata.definition: Concept of space complexity (amount of memory required), space complexity classes such as Pspace and Savitch's Theorem.

metadata.title: Space-Time Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Concept in algorithm design where memory resources are used to reduce execution time, or vice versa, a typical example is hashing. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Space-filling Curve Indexing
metadata.definition: The indexing technique uses space-filling curves to map multidimensional geographic data into a one-dimensional order, optimizing the storage and querying of semi-structured geographic data.

metadata.title: Span
metadata.definition: The concept of the set of all possible linear combinations of a set of vectors.

metadata.title: Spanning Sets for Vectors in Rn
metadata.definition: Discuss the generating systems (spanning sets) for vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Spark Deployment
metadata.definition: Ability to deploy and evaluate typically complex systems such as Spark based on documentation.

metadata.title: Spark System Design
metadata.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Spark system at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Spatial Reasoning
metadata.definition: Infer spatial relationships between objects, including location, shape, and orientation.

metadata.title: Speaker Recognition
metadata.definition: The technology determines a speaker's identity from their voice, as opposed to recognizing speech content.

metadata.title: Special Function Derivatives
metadata.definition: Work with examples of derivatives of important functions (e.g., exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric).

metadata.title: Special Function Integrals
metadata.definition: Calculate integrals of important functions (e.g. exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric).

metadata.title: Special Graph Cases
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples special cases of various types of graphs, including trees.

metadata.title: Specialized Platform API Dev
metadata.definition: Skills to create application programming interfaces (APIs) to enable software components to interact with each other and with hardware, supporting the specific and unique functions of each specialized platform. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

metadata.title: Specialized Platform Dev (SPD)
metadata.definition: The Specialized Platform Development (SPD) knowledge area deals with properties that include the creation of software targeting non-traditional hardware platforms. Social and industrial demands have created a high demand for developers on specialized platforms. This is an area where there has been an increase in required hours of study in CS Core compared to CS2013, reflecting the increasing deployment of specialized hardware platforms.

metadata.title: Specialized Platform Development (SPD)
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus, involves the development of applications and solutions on specialized technology platforms.

metadata.title: Specific AI Applications
metadata.definition: At least one application of AI to a specific problem and domain (e.g. medicine, health, sustainability, social networks, economics, education, robotics).

metadata.title: Speech Recognition
metadata.definition: The ability of a computer to convert speech into text or other understandable formats.

metadata.title: Speedup & Scale-up
metadata.definition: Parallel system performance measurement concepts: speedup is reducing execution time with fixed data and more resources; Scaling is maintaining execution time as data and resources increase.

metadata.title: Spoofing Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks in which an attacker impersonates a legitimate entity for fraud or unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Spreadsheet Model
metadata.definition: Use spreadsheets to organize, store, and analyze data, often for simple applications or personal data analysis.

metadata.title: Stable Diffusion
metadata.definition: An example of an open source deep image generation model that allows the generation of images from text or other images.

metadata.title: Stable Sort
metadata.definition: A property of a sorting algorithm that ensures that the relative order of elements with equal keys is maintained in the sorted output.

metadata.title: Stack
metadata.definition: The LIFO (Last In First Out) data structure allows adding and removing elements from one end.

metadata.title: Stack & Heap Allocation
metadata.definition: How processes use stack and heap data structures to allocate and deallocate activation records and dynamic memory.

metadata.title: Stack Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: stack-based allocation.

metadata.title: Stack Memory Deallocation
metadata.definition: understand how memory for local variables on the stack is automatically released when a function or procedure terminates and returns.

metadata.title: Stacks
metadata.definition: An abstract data structure that operates on the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle, with the main operations being push and pop.

metadata.title: Standard Deviation (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic concept of standard deviation in statistics, a term students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: State
metadata.definition: The concept of the state of a system or an object over time.

metadata.title: State & State Transitions
metadata.definition: The concept of the state of a system and how it transitions from one state to another, including the starting state, final state, and lifecycle of states.

metadata.title: State Decomposition
metadata.definition: Learn to break down complex states into simpler representations or hypothesis spaces for more efficient searches.

metadata.title: State Space Representation
metadata.definition: Learn to describe a search problem as a state space, where each state represents a configuration of the problem.

metadata.title: Stateful Execution
metadata.definition: understand the stateful execution model, where functions or components can maintain and modify internal state between calls, affecting output.

metadata.title: Stateful Systems
metadata.definition: Describes systems whose output depends on both the current input and a previous state (with memory/history), storing information about past transactions or events.

metadata.title: Stateful vs Stateless Execution
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare the differences between stateful and stateless execution models, especially emphasizing the advantages and disadvantages of each model in functional programming and system architectures.

metadata.title: Stateless Execution
metadata.definition: Understanding the stateless execution model, where functions or components do not store any internal state and always return the same output for the same input, makes it easy to test and parallelize.

metadata.title: Stateless Systems
metadata.definition: Describes systems whose output depends only on the current input, without storing any information about previous transactions.

metadata.title: Stateless vs. State-Transition
metadata.definition: Distinguish between stateless and state-transition programming models.

metadata.title: Statements
metadata.definition: Concept of command in programming.

metadata.title: States, Goals, Operators
metadata.definition: Learn how to clearly define possible states, desired goal states, and possible actions (operators) to transition between states.

metadata.title: Static & Dynamic Typing Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Learn about the goals and limitations of both static and dynamic typing systems, especially in detecting and eliminating errors as early as possible in software development.

metadata.title: Static Analysis for Optimization
metadata.definition: Static analysis is used to gather information about a program without executing it, which is then used to make more effective code optimization decisions.

metadata.title: Static Checked Properties
metadata.definition: Defines program properties that are checked at compile time (static checking) in various programming languages.

metadata.title: Static Hash Indexes
metadata.definition: Study static hash indexes and how they provide fast access to data based on fixed hash values.

metadata.title: Static Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: static allocation.

metadata.title: Static NAT
metadata.definition: A specific type of Network Address Translation that establishes a fixed, one-to-one mapping between a single private IP address and a single public IP address.

metadata.title: Static Overloading
metadata.definition: understand static overloading, where the choice of function or method to be overloaded is determined at compile time based on parameter type.

metadata.title: Static Overloading & Dynamic Behavior
metadata.definition: Explain how static overloading and related resolution algorithms affect a program's dynamic behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Static Semantics
metadata.definition: Concept of static semantics, the rules of the language can be checked at compile time.

metadata.title: Static Type Violations
metadata.definition: Describes the types of operations that are prohibited by the static type system at compile time, such as passing an argument of the wrong type to a function.

metadata.title: Static Typing Benefits
metadata.definition: Explain the various benefits of static typing during the software development, maintenance, and debugging phases.

metadata.title: Static Typing Limitations
metadata.definition: Explain how the limitations of static typing, including potential rigidity and the need for explicit type declarations, affect writing, maintenance, and debugging.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Code Misuse
metadata.definition: Understanding static typing helps prevent abuse or misuse of code, improving program safety.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Early Error Detection
metadata.definition: Explain the benefits of static typing in detecting program errors at the early compilation stage.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Incomplete Program Detection
metadata.definition: Understanding static typing can help detect parts of programs that are incomplete or style-inconsistent.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Invariant Enforcement
metadata.definition: Understanding how static typing helps enforce program invariants, improves reliability during code development and maintenance.

metadata.title: Static vs. Dynamic Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the environment does not change during solution from problems where the environment changes independently of the agent.

metadata.title: Statistical Analysis
metadata.definition: Statistical analysis techniques to understand data, draw conclusions, and support decisions.

metadata.title: Statistical Experimental Design
metadata.definition: Principles and methods for designing experiments to collect statistically significant data and control extraneous variables.

metadata.title: Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Machine learning methods are grounded in statistical theory, using statistical models and principles to analyze data and make predictions.

metadata.title: Statistical Models & Algorithms
metadata.definition: Knowledge of statistical models and related algorithms for data analysis and prediction.

metadata.title: Statistical Pattern Recognition
metadata.definition: apply statistical methods such as Bayesian analysis and support vector machines (SVM) to build pattern recognition models.

metadata.title: Statistics
metadata.definition: An important field of statistics, it is proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 98% for importance for careers in industry and graduate study, especially essential for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Statistics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of statistics complements CS Core to create a standard 40-hour course. Total 30 hours of study.

metadata.title: Statistics (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: Statistics (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic statistical concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Statistics Basics (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces basic definitions in statistics, including becoming familiar with terms such as mean and standard deviation. Total 10 hours of study.

metadata.title: Step-by-Step Debugging
metadata.definition: Debugging techniques allow the programmer to execute a program one instruction at a time, observing the state of variables and the flow of control.

metadata.title: Stochastic Processes
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of random processes and their applications.

metadata.title: Stochastic Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search methods that use random elements to explore the solution space, especially useful for complex optimization problems.

metadata.title: Stop and Wait Flow Control
metadata.definition: A simple flow control method in which the sender waits for acknowledgment from the receiver after each data packet.

metadata.title: Stored Procedures
metadata.definition: Learn about stored procedures, SQL scripts stored in a database to perform repetitive or complex tasks.

metadata.title: Strassen Algorithm
metadata.definition: A more efficient matrix multiplication algorithm than the standard algorithm, using a divide-and-conquer strategy to reduce the number of multiplications needed, especially useful for large matrices.

metadata.title: Strassen's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm for multiplying two n x n matrices that is faster than the standard matrix multiplication algorithm, using the principle of divide and conquer. (An example for Divide-and-Conquer)

metadata.title: Stratified Splitting
metadata.definition: Data partitioning technique to ensure that the scale distribution of important classes or attributes is preserved in all data subsets (training, validation, testing).

metadata.title: String
metadata.definition: Character string data structure and basic operations with strings.

metadata.title: String as Array
metadata.definition: A sequence of characters is represented as an array, where each character occupies a position in the array and is accessed by index.

metadata.title: Strong Induction Applications
metadata.definition: Give an example of how to use strong induction appropriately.

metadata.title: Strong Scaling
metadata.definition: The concept of strong scaling, describes how the time to solve a fixed-sized problem changes as the number of processing resources increases.

metadata.title: Structural Induction
metadata.definition: The concept of structural induction and its relationship to recursion and recursively defined structures.

metadata.title: Structural Type Equivalence
metadata.definition: understand structural equivalence, where two types are considered equivalent if they have the same underlying structure.

metadata.title: Structured Data
metadata.definition: Data is organized in a fixed format, such as in relational database tables, with predefined fields and data types.

metadata.title: Structured Data Processing (FP)
metadata.definition: Master how to handle complex data structures like trees by defining functions with appropriate cases for each variant or node of data, a fundamental technique in functional programming.

metadata.title: Structured/Streaming Data Systems
metadata.definition: Study database systems and technologies designed to manage and process both structured static data and continuously stream data.

metadata.title: Subclass
metadata.definition: Concept of subclass, a class that inherits from another class for extension or specialization.

metadata.title: Subclass Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define a subclass that inherits from a superclass, in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Subspace & Vector Space Properties
metadata.definition: Recognize and use the basic properties of subspaces and vector spaces.

metadata.title: Subspace Examples
metadata.definition: List examples of subspaces of a vector space.

metadata.title: Subsymbolic AI
metadata.definition: One of the traditional approaches in AI, includes distributed processing models such as neural networks, where knowledge is not explicitly represented symbolically.

metadata.title: Subsymbolic Methods
metadata.definition: Enhance understanding of parasymbolic methods.

metadata.title: Subtype Polymorphism
metadata.definition: Further understanding subtype polymorphism, a form of polymorphism that allows a function or method to operate on objects of different types as long as they are subtypes of a specified type.

metadata.title: Subtyping
metadata.definition: understand the basic concept of subtyping, where one data type can safely be substituted for another.

metadata.title: Subtyping & Implicit Upcasting
metadata.definition: Learn about subtype polymorphism and automatic implicit upcasts in programming languages ​​with type checking.

metadata.title: Subtyping & Inheritance
metadata.definition: analyze the close but distinct relationship between subtyping and inheritance in object-oriented programming languages.

metadata.title: Subtyping & Inheritance Relation
metadata.definition: analyze the complex relationship between the concept of subtyping and inheritance in object-oriented design.

metadata.title: Subtyping Polymorphism
metadata.definition: understand subtype polymorphism, where an object can be considered to be of its own type or any of its parent types.

metadata.title: Sum Rule (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply addition rules in counting problems.

metadata.title: Sum Type Rules
metadata.definition: Master the styling rules that apply to aggregate types (also called unions or variants) and how they handle different cases.

metadata.title: Sum Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of aggregate types, which represent a value that can be of one of many different types (e.g. union, variant).

metadata.title: Sum of Products (SOP)
metadata.definition: understand the standard form of logic expressions, widely used in digital circuit design.

metadata.title: Sum, Product, Quotient Rule
metadata.definition: apply the rules of sum, product, and quotient to calculate the derivative of a function.

metadata.title: Superkey
metadata.definition: An attribute or set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row in a table. A candidate key is a minimal superkey.

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning in which an algorithm is trained on a labeled data set, learning to map inputs to desired outputs.

metadata.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
metadata.definition: A supervised learning algorithm is used for both classification and regression, which works by finding the best dividing hyperplane between data classes.

metadata.title: Sustainability (SEP)
metadata.definition: Sustainability issues related to technology and networks, from a social, ethical and professional perspective (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Swap space
metadata.definition: A designated area on secondary storage (disk) used by the operating system to store virtual pages that are not currently held in physical memory, used during demand paging.

metadata.title: Swarm Intelligence
metadata.definition: Multi-agent systems simulate the collective behavior of populations of organisms (such as ants, birds) to solve problems.

metadata.title: Switches
metadata.definition: The function and operating principle of a switch in connecting devices on the same local area network (LAN) effectively.

metadata.title: Switching Techniques
metadata.definition: Overview of the basic methods for transferring data over a network, including circuit switching and packet switching.

metadata.title: Symbolic AI
metadata.definition: One of the traditional approaches in AI, focuses on representing knowledge through symbols, logic and rules.

metadata.title: Symbolic Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about symbolic execution as a program analysis technique that allows program execution with symbolic rather than concrete input values.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Algorithms
metadata.definition: Describe the application of symbolic logic in algorithms.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Database Queries
metadata.definition: Describe the application of symbolic logic in database queries.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Software Analysis
metadata.definition: Describe applications of symbolic logic in software analysis, such as proving the correctness of a program.

metadata.title: Symbolic Methods
metadata.definition: Lighten the emphasis but retain symbolic methods in the AI ​​program due to its unique capabilities, practical applications, ensuring broad education and support for neurosymbolic methods.

metadata.title: Symbolic Testing, Fuzzing
metadata.definition: Automated software testing techniques include symbolic testing to explore execution paths and fuzzing to find errors by providing invalid or unexpected input.

metadata.title: Symbolic Validation Integration
metadata.definition: Skill in incorporating symbolic validation tools into daily software development processes to improve code quality and reliability.

metadata.title: Symbolic/Logic KR
metadata.definition: Master the concept of symbolic and logical knowledge representation.

metadata.title: Symmetric Cryptography
metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms use the same key for both encryption and decryption.

metadata.title: Synchronization (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of synchronization mechanisms to coordinate concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Synchronous Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about synchronous languages ​​(e.g. Esterel, Luster) used for programming real-time and reactive systems.

metadata.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous
metadata.definition: understand the differences and applications of synchronous and asynchronous programming models in managing parallel tasks.

metadata.title: Syntax Accessibility
metadata.definition: The influence of the syntactic structure of a programming language on its ease of use and accessibility for different user groups, including those with special needs.

metadata.title: Syntax Analysis (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Parsing techniques in compilers and interpreters.

metadata.title: Syntax Diagram to BNF/EBNF
metadata.definition: Illustrates the process of converting syntax diagrams into BNF or EBNF rules for simple constructs such as `if-then-else`, type declarations, and looping structures.

metadata.title: Syntax vs. Semantics
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare syntax (form of the language) and semantics (meaning of the language) in the context of programming languages.

metadata.title: Syntax, Parsing, Semantics
metadata.definition: The ability to clearly distinguish between aspects of syntax (the formal structure of the language) and parsing (the process of checking syntax) and semantics (the meaning of language structures) and evaluation (the process of executing a program).

metadata.title: System Memory Model
metadata.definition: The study of how operating systems and hardware execute programs, manage and allocate memory, and how programs interact with memory. This is a new unit added to the program with 3 core hours.

metadata.title: System Case Studies
metadata.definition: Describe and analyze the design of typical systems such as Apache, Spark and Linux web servers.

metadata.title: System Commands
metadata.definition: Knowledge of basic system commands and their use in shell scripts.

metadata.title: System Design
metadata.definition: The new unit focuses on the basic principles and methods of computer systems design.

metadata.title: System Design (Core)
metadata.definition: More advanced units on systems design, including methodologies, design patterns, and architectural considerations, for advanced students.

metadata.title: System Design Fundamentals
metadata.definition: understand the basic principles and concepts in computer systems design.

metadata.title: System Design Principles
metadata.definition: Describe important criteria when designing a system, including liveness, safety, robustness, scalability and security.

metadata.title: System Engineering Process
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of the systems engineering process.

metadata.title: System Evaluation
metadata.definition: Methods and criteria for system evaluation.

metadata.title: System Events & Performance
metadata.definition: Understanding of system events such as instruction stalls, cache misses, and page faults and how they negatively impact overall performance.

metadata.title: System Fundamentals
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on the fundamental concepts underlying computer systems. Includes concepts of states, state transitions, and finite state machines.

metadata.title: System Latency Analysis
metadata.definition: Ability to describe and analyze the components that cause overall latency in a computer system, including latency from memory access, disk storage, and network communications.

metadata.title: System Libraries
metadata.definition: Discuss the role and integration of system libraries into programming languages.

metadata.title: System Memory Model (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Concepts of how systems execute programs and manage memory, recommended for specialized students.

metadata.title: System Overview
metadata.definition: Overview of the basic concepts and principles of computer systems.

metadata.title: System Performance
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on system performance aspects, including the topics of proximity, virtualization, and isolation.

metadata.title: System Performance (Core)
metadata.definition: More advanced units on system performance, including deeper topics on approximation, virtualization, and isolation, for advanced students.

metadata.title: System Reliability
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on principles and techniques for ensuring computer system reliability, including the concept of redundancy.

metadata.title: System Reliability (Core)
metadata.definition: A more advanced unit on system reliability, including advanced techniques and models for designing fault-tolerant systems, for advanced students.

metadata.title: System Resources
metadata.definition: Research on resource management and use in computer systems.

metadata.title: System Security
metadata.definition: The new unit focuses on fundamentals and security measures for computer systems.

metadata.title: System Security (Core)
metadata.definition: More advanced units on system security, including in-depth topics on vulnerabilities, attacks and defenses, for advanced students.

metadata.title: System Security Basics
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts and principles of security in computer systems.

metadata.title: System Security Threats
metadata.definition: Describes common system security issues such as viruses, denial of service (DoS) attacks, and eavesdropping.

metadata.title: Systems Fundamentals
metadata.definition: One of the knowledge areas in the CS2023 curriculum standard.

metadata.title: Systems Fundamentals (SF)
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus, focusing on the fundamental principles and concepts of how computer systems are structured and operate.

metadata.title: TCP
metadata.definition: TCP's role as a reliable, connection-oriented transport protocol.

metadata.title: TCP CUBIC
metadata.definition: Modern TCP congestion control algorithm, designed to operate efficiently on high bandwidth and high latency networks.

metadata.title: TCP Client/Server Programming
metadata.definition: Skills to develop basic network applications using TCP protocol, with client-server model.

metadata.title: TCP Performance Issues
metadata.definition: Study the challenges and ways to optimize TCP protocol performance in different network environments.

metadata.title: TCP Reno
metadata.definition: Upgraded version of TCP Tahoe, improving fast recovery after small packet loss.

metadata.title: TCP Tahoe
metadata.definition: One of the first versions of the TCP congestion control algorithm, including slow start, congestion avoidance, and fast recovery phases.

metadata.title: TCP Vegas
metadata.definition: The TCP congestion control algorithm uses queuing delay to detect congestion early, instead of waiting for packet loss.

metadata.title: TCP, UDP, Socket API Interaction
metadata.definition: understand how network applications use transport layer protocols (TCP, UDP) and application programming interfaces (Socket APIs) to send and receive data.

metadata.title: TCP/IP Stack Design
metadata.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the TCP/IP network protocol stack.

metadata.title: TF-IDF
metadata.definition: Learn about the TF (Term Frequency) and IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) statistics used to evaluate the importance of a word in a document and in a collection of documents.

metadata.title: TF-IDF Ngram Vectorization
metadata.definition: A technique that converts text into numeric vectors, using term-frequency index-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and word groups (ngrams) to capture context.

metadata.title: TLB hit
metadata.definition: An event where a required virtual-to-physical address mapping is found in the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), allowing for fast address translation.

metadata.title: TLB miss
metadata.definition: An event where a required virtual-to-physical address mapping is not found in the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), necessitating a slower page table walk.

metadata.title: TLS
metadata.definition: Cryptographic protocols are used to provide communication security over computer networks, protecting the integrity and confidentiality of data.

metadata.title: TPU
metadata.definition: Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) were specifically developed by Google to accelerate neural network calculations, especially tensor operations in deep learning.

metadata.title: Tabu Search
metadata.definition: Learn a metaheuristic local search algorithm that uses memory (tabu lists) to avoid repeating explored solutions and escape local minima.

metadata.title: Tactile Sensing
metadata.definition: Research on how AI systems process and interpret information from tactile sensors to physically interact with the environment.

metadata.title: Task Automation
metadata.definition: The use of technology to perform routine or repetitive tasks without human intervention.

metadata.title: Taylor Series
metadata.definition: Construct Taylor series for some important functions.

metadata.title: Taylor Series Approximation
metadata.definition: applying Taylor series to function approximation problems.

metadata.title: Technology Influence on PL Design
metadata.definition: Discuss how technological needs drive the development and evolution of programming languages.

metadata.title: Temporal Reasoning
metadata.definition: Reason about temporal relationships between events and states, including concepts such as before, after, and concurrent.

metadata.title: Temporal Representation
metadata.definition: Explore methods for representing and reasoning about temporal information extracted from text.

metadata.title: Termination
metadata.definition: The property of a program analysis that ensures that it will always finish in a finite amount of time, never run indefinitely.

metadata.title: Test Set
metadata.definition: A completely independent portion of the data is used to evaluate the final performance of the trained model, providing an unbiased estimate of generalization ability.

metadata.title: Text Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques for analyzing and extracting meaningful information from text data in data science.

metadata.title: Text Classification
metadata.definition: Techniques for classifying text into defined categories.

metadata.title: Text Classification & Clustering
metadata.definition: Learn about methods for assigning predefined labels or categories to text.

metadata.title: Theorem Provers, Proof Assistants
metadata.definition: Software tools (such as theorem provers, proof assistants) and formal logic platforms are used to support the construction and verification of mathematical and logical proofs.

metadata.title: Theory of Computation
metadata.definition: The study of mathematical models of computation and problems that can be solved using algorithms.

metadata.title: Thrashing
metadata.definition: A performance degradation state in a virtual memory system where the system spends an excessive amount of time paging data between RAM and disk due to insufficient physical memory, leading to drastically reduced throughput.

metadata.title: Thread-based Programming
metadata.definition: Programming method that uses multiple threads to execute different parts of a program simultaneously.

metadata.title: Threads
metadata.definition: Use a thread as a unit of execution for communication and coordination purposes in a parallel program.

metadata.title: Thresholding Segmentation
metadata.definition: A simple image segmentation method based on choosing a threshold value to separate pixels into two or more groups (e.g., foreground and background).

metadata.title: Throttling
metadata.definition: A mechanism in distributed systems that implies a more nuanced control over request rates, potentially delaying or reducing the processing priority of requests rather than outright dropping them. It's often used to manage overall resource consumption rather than just request volume.

metadata.title: Thundering herd problem
metadata.definition: A common pitfall in distributed systems where many processes or threads, upon being notified of an event (e.g., a service recovery), all attempt to perform an action simultaneously, often due to 'synchronized retries', leading to system overload.

metadata.title: Time Complexity
metadata.definition: A measure of the amount of time taken by an algorithm to run, expressed as a function of the input size (e.g., O(1) for simple distribution or O(log S) to O(S) for state-aware strategies, where S is the number of backend servers).

metadata.title: Time Complexity (Turing Machine)
metadata.definition: Algorithm time complexity analysis based on the Turing Machine model, including asymptotic notations and classification of time complexity classes.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data
metadata.definition: Data collected or recorded in chronological order, often used to track changes in a metric over time.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data Aggregation
metadata.definition: Aggregation techniques (e.g., averaging, summing, counting) on ​​time series data to extract meaningful information from different time periods.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data Joining
metadata.definition: Methods for combining different time series data sets based on time points or related attributes.

metadata.title: Time-Space Efficiency
metadata.definition: There are two main aspects of algorithm performance: the amount of time and the amount of memory space the algorithm requires.

metadata.title: Time-Space Trade-off
metadata.definition: Algorithm design principle where reducing time requirements can increase space requirements and vice versa.

metadata.title: Time-Space Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Algorithm design considerations regarding optimization between execution time and amount of memory space required. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Timestamp Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: Learn how to use timestamps to control the execution order of concurrent transactions and ensure serialization.

metadata.title: Timsort
metadata.definition: The hybrid sort algorithm, which combines insertion sort and merge sort, is designed to work efficiently on many types of real-world data and is the default sorting algorithm in Python and Java.

metadata.title: Token Bucket algorithm
metadata.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that allows for a certain degree of burstiness. It refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity, with each request consuming a token. It offers O(1) time and O(N) space.

metadata.title: Tokens
metadata.definition: Concept of tokens (lexical symbols) and their role in the parsing process.

metadata.title: Topological Sort
metadata.definition: Linearize the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before vertex v in the sort order. (An example for Decrease-and-Conquer)

metadata.title: Total Order Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method in which all actions in the plan are arranged in a specific linear order.

metadata.title: Tractability
metadata.definition: The likelihood that a problem can be solved by an algorithm in a reasonable amount of time (usually polynomial time). (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Traditional Data Roles
metadata.definition: Understanding of traditional job positions in the data management field.

metadata.title: Traditional Modulo Hashing
metadata.definition: A simple hashing method where a key is assigned to a node by calculating `hash(key) % N_nodes`. This approach necessitates remapping nearly all keys when the number of nodes (`N_nodes`) in a system changes.

metadata.title: Traffic Analysis Attack
metadata.definition: Technique that monitors and analyzes network traffic patterns to deduce sensitive information without decrypting the content.

metadata.title: Traffic Light FSM
metadata.definition: apply finite state machines to design and describe the operating sequence of traffic lights.

metadata.title: Traffic Redirection Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to redirect network traffic to an unwanted destination, often to intercept or modify data.

metadata.title: Train-Validation-Test Split
metadata.definition: understand the importance of dividing data into training, validation, and test sets.

metadata.title: Training Set
metadata.definition: The data portion is used to train the machine learning model, where the model learns patterns and relationships from the data.

metadata.title: Traits
metadata.definition: Learn about traits as a mechanism for grouping methods that can be reused in multiple classes.

metadata.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
metadata.definition: Learn about different isolation levels for database transactions (e.g., Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) and their impact on consistency and performance.

metadata.title: Transaction Management
metadata.definition: The system ensures transactions are executed in an atomic, consistent, isolated, and persistent (ACID) manner.

metadata.title: Transactional Agents
metadata.definition: AI agents are designed to carry out buying, selling, auctioning or negotiating activities in financial markets or e-commerce.

metadata.title: Transfer Learning
metadata.definition: Technique of using a model that has been trained on a large task or data set (e.g., pre-trained models) to improve performance on a new task or smaller data set.

metadata.title: Transform-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy involves transforming a given problem into another (usually simpler or already solved) instance, solving the transformed instance, and then transforming the solution back.

metadata.title: Transform-and-Conquer: Heapsort
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy solves a problem by transforming it into a version that a known algorithm can solve, such as heap sorting. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Transformer Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the Transformer architecture, an advanced model based on self-attention, revolutionizing NLP tasks.

metadata.title: Transitive Closure
metadata.definition: In graph theory, transitive closure of a directed graph is a new graph that contains an edge from vertex u to vertex v if there is a path from u to v in the original graph.

metadata.title: Transitive Closure (Warshall)
metadata.definition: An algorithm that calculates all pairs of vertices (u,v) such that there is a path from u to v in a directed graph, such as Warshall's algorithm. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Transitive closure of a graph
metadata.definition: A graph operation that results in a new graph where an edge (u,v) exists if and only if there is a path from u to v in the original graph. Floyd-Warshall algorithm can be used for this application.

metadata.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
metadata.definition: A small, fast hardware cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address mappings to accelerate address translation, offering O(1) average access time on a hit.

metadata.title: Translation table
metadata.definition: A data structure maintained by a NAT device that stores mappings between private IP addresses and ports and unique public IP addresses and ports, crucial for correctly routing packets.

metadata.title: Transmission Media
metadata.definition: Different types of physical media are used to transmit network signals, for example copper cables, fiber optic cables, radio waves.

metadata.title: Transpiler
metadata.definition: Learn about transpiler, a tool that translates source code from one programming language to another programming language of equivalent level of abstraction.

metadata.title: Transport Layer
metadata.definition: Transport layer functions and protocols, responsible for reliable or unreliable data transfer between processes on different hosts.

metadata.title: Traveling Salesperson Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which a salesperson must visit a set of cities and return to the starting point, finding the shortest possible route that passes through each city exactly once. (An example of Brute Force)

metadata.title: Tree
metadata.definition: The hierarchical data structure consists of nodes and edges, with a root node and child branches.

metadata.title: Tree Problem Modeling
metadata.definition: Model a variety of real-world computer science problems using suitable trees.

metadata.title: Tree Search
metadata.definition: General concept of algorithms that explore nodes and branches of a tree data structure to search for a specific node or gather information.

metadata.title: Tree Search O(log b n)
metadata.definition: A search algorithm on a tree data structure with logarithmic runtime complexity, often used for balanced trees or search trees. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Tree Traversal Exploration
metadata.definition: Learn tree traversal techniques to explore the search space, considering it a subtree of a graph.

metadata.title: Trees
metadata.definition: A non-linear, hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes and edges without cycles, with a single root node.

metadata.title: Trees (Discrete Math)
metadata.definition: Tree structures in discrete mathematics, including binary search trees and spanning trees.

metadata.title: Trigonometry
metadata.definition: Understanding of basic trigonometric functions and the unit circle.

metadata.title: Triple Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Explain the three-factor trade-off between hypothesis space size, training set size, and performance accuracy.

metadata.title: Trustworthy Agent
metadata.definition: Agents are designed to exhibit human-like characteristics or emotions to enhance user trust and engagement.

metadata.title: Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Basic concept, structure, and operation of a Turing Machine, a universal computational model that represents any algorithm.

metadata.title: Turing Machine Complexity Models
metadata.definition: Theoretical models for defining and analyzing computational complexity are based on the concept of Turing machines.

metadata.title: Turing Machine Variants
metadata.definition: Study the standard Turing Machine and its variants such as the multiband Turing Machine, the Deterministic Turing Machine, and demonstrate their equivalence in computational power.

metadata.title: Turing Space Complexity
metadata.definition: Define space complexity in the context of the Turing machine model.

metadata.title: Turing Test
metadata.definition: understand the Turing test, a famous test proposed to evaluate the ability of a machine to exhibit intellectual behavior equivalent to or indistinguishable from humans.

metadata.title: Turing Test Limitations
metadata.definition: understand the weaknesses and criticisms of the Turing test as a measure of intelligence.

metadata.title: Turing Time Complexity
metadata.definition: Define time complexity in the context of the Turing machine model.

metadata.title: Two-Player Games
metadata.definition: Research theories and algorithms for solving games involving two players with opposing goals.

metadata.title: Type Check False Positive
metadata.definition: Describe a program example that does not pass type checking in a particular language but will still run without errors (an example of a type system false positive).

metadata.title: Type Checker
metadata.definition: The tool or component of the compiler is responsible for checking the correctness of using data types in the program according to the rules of the language.

metadata.title: Type Checking
metadata.definition: understand type checking, where a system checks the data types of expressions in a program to ensure consistency and safety.

metadata.title: Type Coercion
metadata.definition: understand forced conversion, the automatic or implicit process of converting values ​​from one data type to another.

metadata.title: Type Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define new data types or declare types for variables in programming languages.

metadata.title: Type Errors
metadata.definition: Errors arise when values ​​are used inconsistently with the intended data type, and the role of type safety in preventing them.

metadata.title: Type Errors: Debugging & Coding
metadata.definition: apply knowledge of types and the ability to interpret type error messages to write code accurately and debug programs effectively.

metadata.title: Type Inference
metadata.definition: understand the concept of type inference, the ability of a compiler or interpreter to automatically determine the type of expressions without the need for an explicit type declaration.

metadata.title: Type Rules: Valid Operations
metadata.definition: Explain how style rules in a programming language define the set of valid operations that can be performed on a particular data type.

metadata.title: Type Safety
metadata.definition: The concept of type safety as an important element of program correctness, prevents errors caused by using values ​​inconsistent with the intended type.

metadata.title: Type Safety (Preservation & Progress)
metadata.definition: Understanding the formal definition of type safety, including the concepts of preservation and progress, ensures that the program never encounters type errors.

metadata.title: Type Safety Proof (Preservation & Progress)
metadata.definition: Be able to prove type safety for a simple language using preservation and progress theorems.

metadata.title: Type System Decidability
metadata.definition: Grasp the concept of determinism in relation to type systems, especially the ability to determine the type correctness of a program automatically.

metadata.title: Type System Error Detection
metadata.definition: Give specific examples of program errors that a type system is capable of detecting (e.g., trying to add a string to an integer).

metadata.title: Type System Proofs
metadata.definition: Build proofs of the correctness of the type system, such as type consistency.

metadata.title: Type Systems
metadata.definition: A set of rules that assign a 'type' to programming language constructs to detect errors and increase reliability. The topics 'Basic Type Systems' and 'Type Systems' have been merged into this unit, with the core hours reduced by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Type Systems (Advanced)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of the design, analysis, and implementation of complex type systems, including type theories, type inference, and advanced type systems.

metadata.title: Type Systems (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of type systems in programming languages, required for all students.

metadata.title: Type Systems (Intro)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of type systems in programming languages, including type checking, type safety, and basic data types.

metadata.title: Type Systems (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in type systems, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Type-Based Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about type-based semantics as a method for analyzing and ensuring program correctness through the type system.

metadata.title: Typing & Static Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze the relationship between the type system and other static analysis techniques to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: UDP
metadata.definition: UDP's role as an unreliable, connection-oriented transport protocol.

metadata.title: UML Data Modeling
metadata.definition: Use Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagrams, especially class diagrams, to describe data structures and relationships.

metadata.title: URIs
metadata.definition: Learn about the concept, syntax, and purpose of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) in identifying resources on a network.

metadata.title: Uncertain Sensor Data Interpretation
metadata.definition: Study methods and algorithms for processing and interpreting data from robotic sensors, which often contain uncertainty and noise.

metadata.title: Undecidability & Conservative Approximation
metadata.definition: Explain why nondeterminism in determining program properties requires type systems to conservatively approximate program behavior.

metadata.title: Undecidability in Analysis
metadata.definition: Concept of problems that cannot be solved algorithmically (e.g., stopping problems) and the limitations they impose on the ability to perform accurate and complete program analyses.

metadata.title: Undirected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges are undirected, meaning the connection between two vertices is symmetric (if A goes to B, then B goes to A).

metadata.title: Unification
metadata.definition: Compare expression merging, validation, and evaluation mechanisms, especially in logic programming languages.

metadata.title: Unification & Algorithm
metadata.definition: The concept of unification and its algorithm, along with the distinction between unification, assertion, and expression evaluation in the context of logic programming.

metadata.title: Unification-based Type Inference
metadata.definition: It is possible to implement a type inference algorithm based on unification for a simple programming language.

metadata.title: Uniform Cost Search (UCS)
metadata.definition: Learn an optimal search algorithm for weighted graphs, always expanding the node with the smallest total path cost from the root.

metadata.title: Uninformed Graph Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search algorithms that traverse the graph without using any additional information about the distance to the target (heuristics).

metadata.title: Uninformed Search
metadata.definition: Part of the Search unit, shared with Algorithm Foundations.

metadata.title: Unintended Data Use
