metadata.definition: Be aware of uses of data that may arise beyond the original purpose, which may raise ethical or legal issues.

metadata.title: Univariate Data
metadata.definition: The concept of data having only one variable or one attribute.

metadata.title: Universal & Existential Quantifiers
metadata.definition: Compare and distinguish between universal quantifiers and existential quantifiers in predicate logic.

metadata.title: Universal Quant. as Dependent Function
metadata.definition: understand the relationship between universal quantifiers and dependency functions in the context of dependency types.

metadata.title: Universal Quantifier as Dependent Function
metadata.definition: understand how universal quantifiers can be represented as dependent functions in a dependent type system.

metadata.title: Universal Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Explain the concept of a Universal Turing Machine, its ability to simulate any other Turing Machine, and its operation as a model of a programmable computer.

metadata.title: Unreliable Delivery
metadata.definition: The concept of transmitting data without mechanisms to ensure arrival, order, or non-duplication, is commonly found in protocols such as UDP.

metadata.title: Unstable Sort
metadata.definition: A property of sorting algorithms, which does not guarantee that the relative order of elements with equal keys is maintained in the sorted output.

metadata.title: Unstructured Data
metadata.definition: The data has no predefined structure or organizational pattern, e.g. text, images, video, audio.

metadata.title: Unstructured Data Vectorization
metadata.definition: The process of converting unstructured data (text, video, audio) into digital representations (vectors) that can be processed by computer algorithms.

metadata.title: Unstructured Data in DBMS
metadata.definition: Ability to take an unorganized set of data, apply data modeling principles to organize it using a DBMS.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
metadata.definition: understand and apply the basic mechanisms and principles of unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: Unweighted Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges have no value (weight) associated with them, representing only the existence of a connection.

metadata.title: User-Defined Control Abstractions
metadata.definition: Illustrates the use of deferred evaluation to create user-defined control abstractions.

metadata.title: Using Foundational Models
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for applying and customizing platform models for specific applications.

metadata.title: Utility & Decision Making
metadata.definition: understand the concept of value and how to make decisions under conditions of uncertainty.

metadata.title: Utility-based Agents
metadata.definition: The study of AI agents choosing actions to maximize their utility function, weighing desired and likely outcomes.

metadata.title: VC Dimension
metadata.definition: A measure of the capacity or complexity of a class of functions (e.g. a machine learning model), indicating the maximum number of data points that the model can 'sort' in every possible way.

metadata.title: VLAN
metadata.definition: Concept of dividing a physical network into multiple logical networks (VLANs) to enhance security, performance, and management.

metadata.title: VM Class Loading
metadata.definition: The process of loading classes or modules into a virtual machine's memory when they are required, often involving code verification and dynamic linking.

metadata.title: VM Environment Management
metadata.definition: understand the technical mechanisms for storing and managing (including revoking) execution environments in the context of virtual machines, especially with regard to closures and lexical scoping.

metadata.title: VM Performance Isolation
metadata.definition: Ability to evaluate the performance of applications running on separate virtual machines and determine the extent to which performance isolation mechanisms prevent interference with each other.

metadata.title: VM Security Checks
metadata.definition: Security mechanisms are implemented in virtual machines to limit access and prevent malicious behavior, ensuring program and system safety.

metadata.title: VM Threads
metadata.definition: How virtual machines manage and support the concurrent execution of multiple threads within a program.

metadata.title: VPN
metadata.definition: Technology that allows a secure connection to be made over a public network (such as the Internet) to access private network resources.

metadata.title: Validation Set
metadata.definition: The independent data section is used to fine-tune the model's hyper-parameters and to select the best model, avoiding overfitting during training.

metadata.title: Value & Policy Iteration
metadata.definition: Two basic algorithms in reinforcement learning to find optimal policies in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Value iteration finds the optimal value function, while policy iteration finds the optimal policy directly.

metadata.title: Value Equality Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in designing and implementing algorithms that focus on value equality rather than reference equality are especially important in functional programming and with immutable data.

metadata.title: Variable Binding
metadata.definition: The concept of variable binding in formal systems and programming languages.

metadata.title: Variable Renaming
metadata.definition: The concept of variable renaming, often used to avoid name conflicts.

metadata.title: Variable Scope Rules
metadata.definition: The rules define the area in which a variable can be accessed in the program.

metadata.title: Variable Scopes
metadata.definition: Types of variables in programming: static variables, local variables, non-local variables and global variables; needs and problems that arise when using non-local and global variables.

metadata.title: Variable Types
metadata.definition: Classify variables based on the type of data they store.

metadata.title: Variables
metadata.definition: Concept of variables in programming.

metadata.title: Variance
metadata.definition: Define the variance of a random variable.

metadata.title: Variance & Interquartile Range
metadata.definition: Concept of a measure of dispersion of a data set. Includes the ability to identify, describe and calculate variances and interquartile ranges to determine data dispersion.

metadata.title: Vector Coordinates (Given Basis)
metadata.definition: Describes the coordinates of a vector relative to a given basis.

metadata.title: Vector Definition & Representation
metadata.definition: Describe the algebraic and geometric representations of vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Vector Function & Gradient
metadata.definition: Practice solving problems involving vector-value functions and using gradient notation in specific examples.

metadata.title: Vector Geometric Interpretation
metadata.definition: understand the geometric meaning of vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Vector Operations
metadata.definition: Vector operations include vector addition, vector multiplication by a scalar, and dot product.

metadata.title: Vector Properties in Rn
metadata.definition: List and understand the basic properties of vectors in n-dimensional space.

metadata.title: Vector Space Basis
metadata.definition: The concept of a set of linearly independent vectors forming a subspace.

metadata.title: Vector Space Dimension Definition
metadata.definition: Defines the number of dimensions of a vector space.

metadata.title: Vector Space Model
metadata.definition: Study the vector space model, where documents and queries are represented as vectors to calculate similarity.

metadata.title: Vector Storage
metadata.definition: Systems or techniques designed to store and retrieve vector representations of unstructured data efficiently.

metadata.title: Vector Subspace
metadata.definition: Define and understand the properties of a subspace in a vector space.

metadata.title: Vector-Valued Function
metadata.definition: Function whose output value is a vector.

metadata.title: Vector-valued Functions
metadata.definition: understand and work with vector-valued functions.

metadata.title: Vectors
metadata.definition: Dynamic arrays can change size during program execution.

metadata.title: Vectors (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: The basics of vectors in linear algebra, a term students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: Verification in Programming Languages
metadata.definition: Skill in leveraging verifiers and specification support available in programming languages ​​to formally test and validate desired system properties.

metadata.title: Virtual Assistants
metadata.definition: AI systems assist users by understanding and executing requests, e.g. Siri, Alexa.

metadata.title: Virtual Circuit
metadata.definition: The concept of a pre-established logical path through the network for a data flow, ensuring some level of quality of service.

metadata.title: Virtual Machine (VM)
metadata.definition: The abstraction layer allows running multiple independent operating system environments on the same physical hardware, or an emulated environment.

metadata.title: Virtual Machine Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution in a virtual machine environment, which provides portability and a layer of abstraction from hardware.

metadata.title: Virtual Method Implementation
metadata.definition: Techniques for implementing virtual concepts in object-oriented programming, allowing polymorphism and dynamic binding, including how virtual methods are called.

metadata.title: Virtual Nodes (vnodes)
metadata.definition: Multiple points on a conceptual circular hash ring, where each point represents a single physical server. They are introduced in Consistent Hashing to improve load balancing by distributing the load more evenly and smoothing the impact of node failures or additions.

metadata.title: Virtual address
metadata.definition: An address generated by the CPU that refers to a location within a process's virtual address space, requiring translation by the MMU to a physical address.

metadata.title: Virtual memory
metadata.definition: An abstraction layer over physical RAM that presents each process with a large, contiguous, and private address space, independent of actual physical memory layout or size, achieved primarily through paging.

metadata.title: Virtualization & Isolation Benefits
metadata.definition: Explain why virtualization and isolation mechanisms are important in computer systems, especially to ensure safety (protection) and stable, predictable performance between virtual environments.

metadata.title: Virtualization Implementation Methods
metadata.definition: Different techniques and methods are used to realize virtual memory and virtual machines in computer systems.

metadata.title: Visible Light Communication (VLC)
metadata.definition: Communication technology that uses visible light to transmit data wirelessly.

metadata.title: Vision-based Robot Control
metadata.definition: Learn about robot control systems that use data from visual sensors (cameras) to guide movement and interaction.

metadata.title: Visualize NN Training
metadata.definition: Visualize the training progress of a neural network through learning curves in a popular tool (e.g., TensorBoard) and visualize the features the network has learned.

metadata.title: Vtable
metadata.definition: Data structures are used in object-oriented programming to implement polymorphism through virtual methods, allowing the runtime system to find the right method to call based on the actual type of the object.

metadata.title: Warshall's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to find transitive closure of a directed graph, indicating which pairs of vertices have a path between them.

metadata.title: Warshall's Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, Warshall's algorithm for finding transitive closure. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Weak Consistency Models
metadata.definition: The models ensure that data will eventually be consistent across all replicas, but allow that different replicas may be temporarily out of sync.

metadata.title: Weak Induction Applications
metadata.definition: Give an example of how to use weak induction appropriately.

metadata.title: Weak Scaling
metadata.definition: The concept of weak scaling, describes how the time it takes to solve a problem when both the problem size and the number of processing resources increase proportionally.

metadata.title: Weak vs. Strong Induction
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between weak induction and strong induction.

metadata.title: Weaving (Static & Dynamic)
metadata.definition: The process of integrating aspects into the code base, including static weaving (at compile or load time) and dynamic weaving (at run time).

metadata.title: Web Server Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and deploy a simple web server.

metadata.title: Web Systems & Platforms
metadata.definition: Develop web-based applications and services, including client-server architecture, web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), scalability and security. This is an example of a specialized platform.

metadata.title: Weighted Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which each edge has a numerical value (weight) associated with it, typically representing cost, distance, or strength of the relationship.

metadata.title: Weighted Least Connection (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: A load balancing strategy that combines the Least Connection method with server weights, considering both the number of active connections and the server's assigned processing capacity.

metadata.title: Weighted Majority Vote
metadata.definition: The method combines output from component models by assigning weights to each model, especially useful in model ensembles.

metadata.title: Weighted Majority Vote Ensemble
metadata.definition: A method of combining output from component models in an ensemble by assigning weights to each model and taking a weighted majority decision.

metadata.title: Weighted Round Robin (Load Balancing Strategy)
metadata.definition: An extension of Round Robin where servers are assigned a weight based on their processing capacity, receiving a proportional number of requests. It also has an O(1) decision time for selection.

metadata.title: Well-defined Interfaces
metadata.definition: The concept of clearly designed interfaces between components or classes of a system, helping them to communicate effectively without knowing internal implementation details.

metadata.title: Why NoSQL?
metadata.definition: understand the reasons and use cases when NoSQL systems are preferred over traditional RDBMS (e.g. impedance mismatch between Application [CRUD] and RDBMS).

metadata.title: WiFi
metadata.definition: Wireless LAN standard (IEEE 802.11), including different operating modes, security, and versions.

metadata.title: Window-Based Flow Control
metadata.definition: The flow control method allows multiple data packets to be sent at the same time before receiving an acknowledgment, using the sliding window concept.

metadata.title: Wireless LAN Principles (802.11)
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of wireless local area networks, primarily focusing on the 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standard, including how to support mobile users.

metadata.title: Word2Vec
metadata.definition: A word embedding technique to create vector representations of words, where words with similar meanings have vector representations close to each other in the vector space.

metadata.title: Workflow Automation
metadata.definition: Design and automate task sequences or workflows using shell scripts.

metadata.title: Workloads & Benchmarks
metadata.definition: Concept of workloads and how to use representative benchmarks to test and evaluate system performance.

metadata.title: Worst-case Analysis
metadata.definition: A complexity analysis technique that focuses solely on the maximum possible cost of a single operation, without considering the sequence of operations or typical input distributions.

metadata.title: Write-Ahead Logging
metadata.definition: Learn Write-Ahead logging (WAL) techniques to ensure transaction persistence during database recovery.

metadata.title: XML
metadata.definition: A markup language used to encode documents in a format that can be read by both humans and machines.

metadata.title: XML (NoSQL)
metadata.definition: A markup language used to encode documents in a human-readable and machine-readable format, sometimes used in NoSQL databases.

metadata.title: ZTNA
metadata.definition: A network security model based on the 'never trust, always verify' principle, requiring strict authentication and authorization for every access request.

metadata.title: d-separation
metadata.definition: A graphical criterion for determining conditional independence between sets of variables in Bayesian Networks.

metadata.title: evaluate AI Social Impact
metadata.definition: Assess the social impacts of implementing AI applications.

metadata.title: evaluate Simple ML System
metadata.definition: Evaluating the performance of a simple machine learning system on a real-world dataset.

metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence Definition
metadata.definition: The science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs. It is related to the similar task of using computers to understand human intelligence, but AI does not have to confine itself to methods that are biologically observable.

metadata.title: AI Winter
metadata.definition: A period of reduced funding and interest in artificial intelligence research, following a boom in interest and investment. These periods are often characterized by exaggerated expectations followed by disillusionment when those expectations are not met.

metadata.title: Rational Agent
metadata.definition: An agent that acts to achieve the best possible outcome or, when there is uncertainty, the best expected outcome, given its percepts and its knowledge. Its actions are chosen to maximize its performance measure.

metadata.title: Intelligent Agent
metadata.definition: An entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through effectors. It is autonomous, meaning it can operate without constant human intervention, and strives to achieve its goals.

metadata.title: Problem Solving Agent
metadata.definition: A type of intelligent agent that decides what to do by searching for a sequence of actions that leads to a desired goal state. It typically operates in environments that are static, discrete, observable, and deterministic.

metadata.title: Goal-based Agent
metadata.definition: An agent that explicitly uses a goal to determine its actions, considering the consequences of actions before executing them. It may require search and planning to find a sequence of actions that achieves its goal.

metadata.title: Utility-based Agent
metadata.definition: A more general type of goal-based agent that aims to maximize its utility function, which is an internal mapping from states to real numbers indicating the agent's preference for that state. It chooses actions to achieve the highest expected utility, especially in environments with uncertainty.

metadata.title: State Space Search
metadata.definition: A process of searching through a graph where nodes represent possible states of a problem and edges represent actions that transition between states. The goal is to find a path from an initial state to a goal state.

metadata.title: Informed Search
metadata.definition: Search strategies that use problem-specific knowledge beyond the definition of the problem itself, typically in the form of a heuristic function, to guide the search. This knowledge helps to estimate the cost or distance from a given state to the goal state.

metadata.title: Uniform Cost Search
metadata.definition: A search algorithm that expands the node with the lowest cumulative cost from the start state, effectively finding the least-cost path to a goal. It is complete and optimal if edge costs are non-negative.

metadata.title: Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search
metadata.definition: A search strategy that combines the benefits of Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS) by performing a series of depth-limited DFS searches with increasing depth limits. It is complete, optimal for uniform step costs, and has space complexity of O(bd) and time complexity of O(b^d).

metadata.title: IDA* Search Algorithm
metadata.definition: An informed search algorithm that performs a series of depth-limited Depth-First Searches, similar to Iterative Deepening DFS, but uses a heuristic function to set the depth limit. The limit for each iteration is the smallest f-cost (g+h) of any node that exceeded the previous limit.

metadata.title: Heuristic Function
metadata.definition: A function that estimates the cost or distance from a given state to a goal state in a search problem. It provides an educated guess to guide the search towards promising areas of the state space, often sacrificing optimality for computational efficiency.

metadata.title: Admissible Heuristic
metadata.definition: A heuristic function `h(n)` is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to reach the goal from state `n`. That is, `h(n) <= h*(n)` for all states `n`, where `h*(n)` is the true cost.

metadata.title: Consistent Heuristic
metadata.definition: A heuristic function `h(n)` is consistent (or satisfies the triangle inequality) if for every node `n` and every successor `n'` of `n` with step cost `c(n, n')`, the following holds: `h(n) <= c(n, n') + h(n')`. Every consistent heuristic is admissible.

metadata.title: Hill Climbing
metadata.definition: A local search algorithm that iteratively moves from the current state to an adjacent state with a better value, typically based on an objective function. It stops when it reaches a "peak" where no neighbor has a higher value, which might be a local optimum rather than a global optimum.

metadata.title: Minimax Algorithm
metadata.definition: A decision rule used in game theory, for minimizing the possible loss for a worst-case (maximum loss) scenario. It is often applied in turn-based, two-player zero-sum games to find the optimal move for a player, assuming the opponent plays optimally.

metadata.title: Game Tree
metadata.definition: A directed graph whose nodes are positions (states) in a game and whose edges are moves (actions). The complete game tree for a game is the full plan of all possible games from the initial state to all terminal states.

metadata.title: Constraint Satisfaction Problem
metadata.definition: A problem defined by a set of variables, each with a domain of possible values, and a set of constraints that restrict the values that variables can take simultaneously. The goal is to find an assignment of values to variables that satisfies all constraints.

metadata.title: Backtracking Search (CSP)
metadata.definition: A general algorithm for finding all (or some) solutions to computational problems, notably constraint satisfaction problems, that incrementally builds candidates to the solutions and prunes branches that fail to satisfy constraints. It recursively tries to extend a partial solution by assigning values to variables one by one.

metadata.title: Expert System
metadata.definition: A computer system that emulates the decision-making ability of a human expert, typically composed of a knowledge base and an inference engine. It aims to solve complex problems or provide advice in a specific domain using reasoning capabilities.

metadata.title: Knowledge Base
metadata.definition: A centralized repository for information and knowledge, typically represented in a structured format such as rules, facts, frames, or semantic networks. It contains domain-specific data and heuristics used by an AI system, especially expert systems, to perform reasoning.

metadata.title: Inference Engine
metadata.definition: The component of an expert system or other knowledge-based system responsible for deriving new knowledge or making decisions from existing knowledge in the knowledge base. It applies reasoning mechanisms, such as forward or backward chaining, to facts and rules.

metadata.title: Rule-based System
metadata.definition: An AI system that uses IF-THEN rules to represent knowledge and make decisions, often employed in expert systems. It processes a set of facts against a collection of production rules to infer new facts or trigger actions.

metadata.title: Resolution Principle
metadata.definition: A powerful inference rule used in automated theorem proving, particularly for systems based on first-order logic. It operates on clauses in conjunctive normal form to deduce new clauses, often employed to prove unsatisfiability by deriving a contradiction (the empty clause).

metadata.title: Ontology (AI/KR)
metadata.definition: A formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualization of a domain, defining the types, properties, and interrelationships of entities within that domain. In AI, ontologies provide a structured vocabulary for knowledge representation, enabling more sophisticated reasoning and data integration.

metadata.title: Semantic Network
metadata.definition: A knowledge representation technique where concepts and relationships between them are represented as a graph, with nodes typically representing concepts (objects, ideas, events) and links (edges) representing semantic relationships (e.g., 'is-a', 'has-part', 'causes'). It facilitates inheritance and associative reasoning.

metadata.title: Frame Representation
metadata.definition: A knowledge representation technique in AI that organizes knowledge into frame-like data structures, representing stereotypical situations or objects. Each frame has a collection of 'slots' that contain attributes, values, default values, and procedures (demons) for handling information about a concept.

metadata.title: Cognitive Architecture
metadata.definition: A broad, domain-general computational framework that aims to model the structure and processes of the human mind, often serving as a foundation for building intelligent agents. It typically integrates perception, memory, learning, reasoning, and action mechanisms to produce intelligent behavior.

metadata.title: Blackboard System
metadata.definition: A flexible, opportunistic AI architecture where multiple independent knowledge sources (specialized modules) cooperate to solve a complex problem by asynchronously writing and reading information on a shared global data structure called the 'blackboard.' A control component manages the execution of knowledge sources.

metadata.title: STRIPS Planner
metadata.definition: A classical AI planning system that operates on a set of states, defined by propositions, and a set of actions, each with preconditions and effects (add/delete lists). It searches for a sequence of actions that transforms an initial state into a desired goal state.

metadata.title: Dynamic Programming (AI)
metadata.definition: An optimization technique used to solve complex problems by breaking them down into simpler overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem only once, and storing their solutions to avoid redundant computations. In AI, it's often applied to reinforcement learning and search problems.

metadata.title: Machine Learning Definition
metadata.definition: A subfield of Artificial Intelligence focused on enabling systems to learn from data without being explicitly programmed. It involves designing algorithms that can identify patterns, make predictions, or take actions based on learned experiences, improving performance over time with more data.

metadata.title: Self-Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: A paradigm of machine learning where the model learns from data by generating its own supervisory signals from the data itself, rather than relying on explicit human-provided labels. It often involves solving a 'pretext task' where part of the input is predicted from another part of the input.

metadata.title: Active Learning
metadata.definition: A machine learning paradigm where the learning algorithm can interactively query a user or other information source to obtain the desired output for new data points. It is particularly useful when unlabeled data is abundant but labeling is expensive, aiming to achieve high accuracy with fewer labels.

metadata.title: Online Learning
metadata.definition: A machine learning method where the model is continuously updated as new data becomes available, one data point or a small batch at a time. This approach is suitable for scenarios with streaming data, evolving patterns (concept drift), or when data cannot be stored entirely.

metadata.title: Feature Engineering
metadata.definition: The process of creating new features or transforming existing ones from raw data to improve the performance of machine learning models. It involves domain expertise and creativity to extract salient information that helps the model learn patterns more effectively.

metadata.title: Feature Selection
metadata.definition: The process of choosing a subset of relevant features (variables, predictors) from the original set of features to be used in model construction. The goal is to reduce dimensionality, improve model accuracy, reduce overfitting, and enhance interpretability by removing irrelevant or redundant features.

metadata.title: Feature Extraction
metadata.definition: The process of transforming raw data into a set of features that are more informative and easier for a machine learning model to process, often reducing the dimensionality of the data. Unlike feature selection, it creates new features by combining or projecting original ones.

metadata.title: Underfitting
metadata.definition: A scenario in machine learning where a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns or relationships in the training data, resulting in poor performance on both the training data and unseen test data. It indicates high bias, suggesting the model has not learned enough from the data.

metadata.title: K-Fold Cross-Validation
metadata.definition: A resampling procedure used to evaluate machine learning models on a limited data sample. The dataset is split into `k` equally sized folds, where `k-1` folds are used for training and the remaining fold for validation, repeating `k` times with each fold serving as the validation set exactly once. The average of the `k` evaluation scores provides a more robust estimate of model performance and reduces variance.

metadata.title: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation
metadata.definition: An extreme case of K-Fold Cross-Validation where the number of folds `k` is equal to the number of samples `n` in the dataset. For each iteration, a single data point is used as the validation set, and the remaining `n-1` points are used for training. This method provides an almost unbiased estimate of the generalization error, but is computationally expensive, especially for large datasets.

metadata.title: Bayesian Optimization (Hyperparameters)
metadata.definition: A sequential design strategy for finding the global optimum of expensive black-box functions, often used for hyperparameter tuning in machine learning. It builds a probabilistic model (surrogate model) of the objective function and uses an acquisition function to determine the next most promising hyperparameter combination to evaluate. This approach efficiently explores the search space by balancing exploration and exploitation, typically outperforming grid or random search.

metadata.title: Regularization
metadata.definition: A set of techniques used in machine learning to prevent overfitting by adding a penalty term to the loss function during model training. This penalty discourages overly complex models or excessively large parameter values, thereby improving the model's ability to generalize to unseen data. Common types include L1 and L2 regularization.

metadata.title: L1 Regularization (Lasso)
metadata.definition: A type of regularization that adds the absolute value of the magnitude of the model's coefficients as a penalty term to the loss function. This penalty encourages sparsity in the model, effectively performing feature selection by driving some coefficients to exactly zero. It's often referred to as Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) regression.

metadata.title: L2 Regularization (Ridge)
metadata.definition: A type of regularization that adds the squared magnitude of the model's coefficients as a penalty term to the loss function. This penalty discourages large coefficient values, spreading the error among all features and shrinking them towards zero without forcing them to be exactly zero. It's commonly known as Ridge regression and helps to prevent multicollinearity and improve model stability.

metadata.title: Early Stopping
metadata.definition: A regularization technique used during iterative training processes, primarily with neural networks or gradient boosting models, to prevent overfitting. It involves monitoring the model's performance on a separate validation set and halting training when the performance on this set starts to degrade (e.g., validation loss stops decreasing or starts increasing), even if the training loss continues to decrease. This captures the model at its optimal generalization point.

metadata.title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
metadata.definition: A dimensionality reduction technique primarily used as a pre-processing step in pattern classification. LDA aims to find a linear combination of features that best separates two or more classes by maximizing the ratio of between-class variance to within-class variance. It projects data onto a lower-dimensional space while preserving as much class separability as possible, making it supervised.

metadata.title: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)
metadata.definition: A non-linear dimensionality reduction technique well-suited for visualizing high-dimensional datasets by mapping them to a lower-dimensional space, typically 2 or 3 dimensions. t-SNE aims to preserve the local structure of the data, meaning that points that are close together in the high-dimensional space remain close in the low-dimensional map. It is particularly effective at revealing clusters and manifold structures, but can be slow for very large datasets.

metadata.title: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)
metadata.definition: A general-purpose manifold learning and dimensionality reduction algorithm that is often used for visualization, similar to t-SNE, but is generally faster and preserves more of the global structure of the data. UMAP constructs a high-dimensional graph representing the data's topological structure and then optimizes a low-dimensional graph to be as structurally similar as possible. It is suitable for both visualization and as a pre-processing step for machine learning.

metadata.title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
metadata.definition: A powerful supervised machine learning model used for classification and regression tasks. SVM works by finding an optimal hyperplane that best separates data points into different classes, maximizing the margin between the hyperplane and the nearest data points (support vectors) from each class. It can effectively handle both linearly separable and non-linearly separable data using the kernel trick.

metadata.title: Kernel Trick
metadata.definition: A method used in machine learning, particularly with Support Vector Machines, to implicitly map data into a higher-dimensional feature space without explicitly calculating the coordinates in that space. It allows algorithms to operate in a high-dimensional feature space using only dot products of feature vectors in the original space, making it possible to find non-linear decision boundaries efficiently. Common kernels include polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), and sigmoid.

metadata.title: Polynomial Regression
metadata.definition: A form of regression analysis in which the relationship between the independent variable `x` and the dependent variable `y` is modeled as an `n`-th degree polynomial. It extends linear regression by allowing for non-linear relationships between variables, transforming the original features into polynomial features and then fitting a linear model to these transformed features. This provides greater flexibility in modeling complex data patterns.

metadata.title: Naive Bayes Classifier
metadata.definition: A family of probabilistic classifiers based on applying Bayes' theorem with a 'naive' assumption of conditional independence between every pair of features given the class variable. Despite this strong independence assumption, Naive Bayes classifiers are often very efficient and perform surprisingly well in many real-world scenarios, particularly for text classification and spam detection, due to their simplicity and speed.

metadata.title: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
metadata.definition: A non-parametric, lazy learning algorithm used for both classification and regression. In KNN, the classification of a new data point is determined by the majority class among its `k` nearest neighbors in the feature space, while regression predicts the average value of its `k` nearest neighbors. It is a distance-based algorithm where feature scaling is crucial for accurate results.

metadata.title: Decision Tree Learning
metadata.definition: A supervised machine learning method that constructs a tree-like model of decisions and their possible consequences. Each internal node represents a test on an attribute, each branch represents an outcome of the test, and each leaf node represents a class label (for classification) or a numerical value (for regression). Decision trees are highly interpretable and can handle both numerical and categorical data.

metadata.title: ID3 Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm used for building decision trees, developed by Ross Quinlan. ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3) constructs a decision tree by iteratively choosing the attribute that best splits the dataset based on information gain, then recursively building subtrees for each outcome until all examples in a subset belong to the same class or no more attributes are available. It is primarily used for classification tasks with categorical features and does not handle numerical attributes directly.

metadata.title: CART Algorithm
metadata.definition: An acronym for Classification and Regression Trees, developed by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, and Stone. CART is a versatile algorithm that can build both classification and regression trees. It recursively partitions the data by choosing the split that maximizes impurity reduction (e.g., Gini impurity for classification, mean squared error for regression) until a stopping criterion is met. Unlike ID3, CART handles both categorical and numerical features and produces binary splits.

metadata.title: Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM)
metadata.definition: A powerful ensemble machine learning technique that builds a strong predictive model from an ensemble of weak prediction models, typically decision trees. GBM works by sequentially adding new models that correct the errors made by previous models, with each new model trained to predict the residual errors (gradients) of the combined ensemble. It minimizes a differentiable loss function using a gradient descent approach, often yielding high accuracy.

metadata.title: XGBoost
metadata.definition: An optimized distributed gradient boosting library designed to be highly efficient, flexible, and portable. It implements machine learning algorithms under the Gradient Boosting framework, offering parallel tree boosting and various enhancements over traditional GBMs, such as regularization (L1 and L2), handling missing values, and tree pruning. XGBoost is widely recognized for its speed, scalability, and superior performance in competitive machine learning, making it a go-to choice for tabular data.

metadata.title: LightGBM
metadata.definition: LightGBM (Light Gradient Boosting Machine) is an open-source gradient boosting framework that uses tree-based learning algorithms. It is designed for high speed and efficiency, achieving faster training times and lower memory usage than other boosting algorithms, particularly on large datasets, by using techniques like Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB).

metadata.title: CatBoost
metadata.definition: CatBoost is a gradient boosting algorithm that excels at automatically and effectively handling categorical features without requiring extensive preprocessing. It employs oblivious decision trees and a novel scheme for calculating leaf values to combat prediction shift caused by target leakage, often achieving high accuracy with robust performance.

metadata.title: Stacking
metadata.definition: Stacking (Stacked Generalization) is an ensemble learning technique where multiple diverse base models (first-level learners) are trained on the training data, and their predictions are then used as input to a meta-model (second-level learner). The meta-model learns to combine the strengths of these base models, making the final prediction to improve overall predictive performance.

metadata.title: DBSCAN
metadata.definition: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) is a density-based clustering algorithm that groups together points that are closely packed together, marking as outliers points that lie alone in low-density regions. It can discover clusters of arbitrary shape and does not require pre-specifying the number of clusters, instead relying on two parameters: epsilon (radius) and min_samples (minimum number of points).

metadata.title: Hierarchical Clustering
metadata.definition: Hierarchical Clustering is a type of clustering algorithm that builds a hierarchy of clusters, represented as a dendrogram. It can be agglomerative (bottom-up), starting with individual data points and iteratively merging them into larger clusters, or divisive (top-down), starting with one large cluster and recursively splitting it into smaller ones. This method provides a visual understanding of the relationships between data points at different levels of granularity.

metadata.title: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm
metadata.definition: The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative algorithm used to find maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimates of parameters in statistical models, particularly when the model depends on unobserved latent variables. It alternates between two steps: the E-step (Expectation), which computes the expected values of the latent variables, and the M-step (Maximization), which updates the model parameters to maximize the likelihood given these expected values.

metadata.title: Anomaly Detection
metadata.definition: Anomaly Detection is the process of identifying data points, events, or observations that deviate significantly from the majority of the data, often indicating unusual behavior, errors, or rare events. These deviations, or anomalies, can be indicative of critical incidents like fraud, system failures, security breaches, or medical problems, and are also known as outliers or novelties.

metadata.title: Outlier Detection
metadata.definition: Outlier Detection is a specific branch of anomaly detection focusing on identifying individual data points that are significantly different from the rest of the dataset and typically represent extreme values. While often used interchangeably with anomaly detection, outlier detection usually refers to isolated data points that are far removed from the data's central tendency or clusters, whereas anomaly detection can also encompass broader unusual patterns or events.

metadata.title: One-Class SVM
metadata.definition: One-Class SVM (Support Vector Machine) is an unsupervised learning algorithm primarily used for anomaly detection when only 'normal' data is available for training. It aims to learn a decision boundary that encapsulates the majority of the normal data points in a high-dimensional feature space, effectively identifying any data points that fall outside this learned region as outliers or anomalies.

metadata.title: Isolation Forest
metadata.definition: Isolation Forest is an ensemble machine learning algorithm for anomaly detection that works by explicitly isolating anomalies rather than profiling normal data points. It builds an ensemble of isolation trees (similar to decision trees), where anomalies, being fewer and having different characteristics, require fewer splits to be isolated in the tree structure compared to normal data points. This makes it efficient and effective for high-dimensional data.

metadata.title: Accuracy (Classification Metric)
metadata.definition: Accuracy is a fundamental classification metric that measures the proportion of correctly classified instances (both true positives and true negatives) out of the total number of instances in the dataset. While intuitive, it can be misleading for imbalanced datasets where one class significantly outnumbers the others, as a model can achieve high accuracy by simply predicting the majority class.

metadata.title: Precision (Classification Metric)
metadata.definition: Precision is a classification metric that measures the proportion of true positive predictions among all positive predictions made by the model. It answers the question: 'Of all instances predicted as positive, how many were actually positive?' High precision indicates a low false positive rate, meaning the model is good at avoiding incorrect positive classifications.

metadata.title: Recall (Classification Metric)
metadata.definition: Recall (also known as Sensitivity or True Positive Rate) is a classification metric that measures the proportion of true positive predictions among all actual positive instances in the dataset. It answers the question: 'Of all actual positive instances, how many were correctly identified?' High recall indicates a low false negative rate, meaning the model is good at finding most of the positive cases.

metadata.title: F1 Score
metadata.definition: The F1 Score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single metric that balances both concerns. It is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets where a simple accuracy score might be misleading, as it penalizes models that have large numbers of either false positives or false negatives, making it a robust measure for evaluating binary classifiers.

metadata.title: AUC Score
metadata.definition: The AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) Score is a performance metric for binary classification models that measures the ability of a classifier to distinguish between classes across all possible classification thresholds. It represents the probability that the classifier will rank a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance, with a score of 1.0 indicating a perfect classifier and 0.5 indicating performance no better than random guessing.

metadata.title: Precision-Recall Curve
metadata.definition: A Precision-Recall Curve is a plot that illustrates the trade-off between precision and recall for different classification thresholds of a binary classifier. It is particularly informative and preferred over the ROC curve for highly imbalanced datasets where the positive class is rare, as it focuses on the performance of the model on the positive class without being influenced by the number of true negatives.

metadata.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
metadata.definition: Mean Squared Error (MSE) is a common regression loss function and evaluation metric that measures the average of the squares of the errors, where an error is the difference between the actual observed value and the predicted value. By squaring the errors, MSE penalizes larger errors more significantly than smaller ones, making it sensitive to outliers.

metadata.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
metadata.definition: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) is a regression evaluation metric calculated as the square root of the Mean Squared Error (MSE). This transformation makes the error metric interpretable in the same units as the target variable, which is often more intuitive. RMSE gives a relatively high weight to large errors, making it particularly useful when significant errors are especially undesirable.

metadata.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
metadata.definition: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is a regression loss function and evaluation metric that measures the average of the absolute differences between the actual observed values and the predicted values. Unlike MSE, MAE treats all errors equally, regardless of their magnitude, making it more robust to outliers as it does not square the errors.

metadata.title: R-squared
metadata.definition: R-squared, also known as the coefficient of determination, is a regression evaluation metric that represents the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variables by the model. It ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates that the model explains all the variability of the response data around its mean, providing a measure of the goodness of fit.

metadata.title: Silhouette Score
metadata.definition: The Silhouette Score measures how similar an object is to its own cluster (cohesion) compared to other clusters (separation). It ranges from -1 to +1, where a high value indicates good clustering, 0 indicates overlapping clusters, and negative values suggest that data points might be assigned to the wrong cluster.

metadata.title: Davies-Bouldin Index
metadata.definition: The Davies-Bouldin Index is a metric for evaluating clustering algorithms, where a lower value indicates better clustering. It is defined as the average similarity measure of each cluster with its most similar cluster, prioritizing clusters that are compact and well-separated.

metadata.title: Adjusted Rand Index
metadata.definition: The Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) is a measure of similarity between two data clusterings, correcting for chance agreement. It is a 'corrected for chance' version of the Rand Index, ensuring that random labeling yields an ARI close to 0, while perfect match is 1.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Graphical Model
metadata.definition: A Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) is a framework that uses graphs to represent the conditional dependencies between random variables, allowing for efficient representation and inference of complex joint probability distributions. Nodes in the graph represent variables, and edges represent dependencies.

metadata.title: Bayesian Network
metadata.definition: A Bayesian Network is a type of Probabilistic Graphical Model that represents a set of random variables and their conditional dependencies via a directed acyclic graph (DAG). It allows for calculating the probability of certain outcomes by encoding conditional probability distributions at each node.

metadata.title: Markov Random Field
metadata.definition: A Markov Random Field (MRF), also known as an undirected graphical model, represents a joint probability distribution over a set of variables where dependencies are shown by an undirected graph. It implies that each variable is conditionally independent of all other variables given its neighbors.

metadata.title: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
metadata.definition: A Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a statistical Markov model in which the system being modeled is assumed to be a Markov process with unobserved (hidden) states. It provides a framework to model systems where we observe a sequence of outputs, but not the underlying states that produced them.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra for ML
metadata.definition: Linear Algebra for Machine Learning involves the study of vectors, matrices, and linear transformations, which are fundamental tools for representing data, understanding algorithms, and performing computations in ML. It provides the mathematical language for concepts like dimensionality reduction, eigen-decomposition, and matrix operations.

metadata.title: Calculus for ML
metadata.definition: Calculus for Machine Learning encompasses differential calculus and optimization techniques essential for training models and minimizing error functions. Concepts like derivatives, gradients, and partial derivatives are crucial for understanding how model parameters are updated during learning algorithms like gradient descent.

metadata.title: Probability Theory for ML
metadata.definition: Probability Theory for Machine Learning provides the mathematical framework for dealing with uncertainty and making predictions based on data. It underpins many ML algorithms, enabling them to model random events, quantify uncertainty, and make decisions under incomplete information.

metadata.title: Information Theory for ML
metadata.definition: Information Theory for Machine Learning quantifies information, entropy, and mutual information, providing tools to measure the uncertainty in data and the relationship between variables. It's fundamental for understanding concepts like decision trees, feature selection, and model complexity.

metadata.title: Generative Model
metadata.definition: A Generative Model learns the joint probability distribution P(X, Y) of the input features X and the target variable Y, or just P(X) for unsupervised tasks. It can generate new samples that resemble the training data and can also be used for classification by estimating P(X|Y)P(Y).

metadata.title: Discriminative Model
metadata.definition: A Discriminative Model directly learns the conditional probability distribution P(Y|X) of the target variable Y given the input features X, or a direct mapping from inputs to outputs. It focuses on finding the decision boundary between classes without modeling the underlying distribution of the data.

metadata.title: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)
metadata.definition: An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the structure and function of biological neural networks, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized in layers. ANNs learn to recognize patterns and make predictions by adjusting the weights of connections between neurons during training.

metadata.title: Perceptron
metadata.definition: The Perceptron is the simplest form of an artificial neural network, a linear binary classifier that takes multiple binary inputs and produces a single binary output. It learns a decision boundary by adjusting weights and a bias to correctly classify inputs based on a threshold function.

metadata.title: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)
metadata.definition: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is a type of feedforward artificial neural network composed of at least three layers: an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Unlike a single perceptron, MLPs can learn non-linear relationships by incorporating non-linear activation functions in their hidden layers, enabling them to solve complex problems like the XOR problem.

metadata.title: Activation Function
metadata.definition: An Activation Function in an artificial neural network determines whether a neuron should be activated ('fired') and to what extent, based on its weighted input sum. It introduces non-linearity into the network, allowing it to learn and model complex, non-linear relationships in data.

metadata.title: ReLU Activation Function
metadata.definition: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a popular activation function defined as f(x) = max(0, x). It outputs the input directly if it is positive, otherwise, it outputs zero. ReLU introduces non-linearity while mitigating the vanishing gradient problem, making neural networks faster to train.

metadata.title: Sigmoid Activation Function
metadata.definition: The Sigmoid Activation Function, defined as f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^-x), squashes any input value into an output between 0 and 1. It is often used in the output layer of binary classification models as it can be interpreted as a probability.

metadata.title: Tanh Activation Function
metadata.definition: The Tanh (hyperbolic tangent) Activation Function is a non-linear function that squashes input values to an output range between -1 and 1, centered at 0. It is similar to the sigmoid function but generally performs better in hidden layers as its zero-centered output helps in propagating gradients more effectively.

metadata.title: Softmax Activation Function
metadata.definition: The Softmax activation function normalizes a vector of arbitrary real values into a probability distribution, where each value is between 0 and 1, and the sum of all values is 1. It is commonly used as the last layer in a neural network for multi-class classification tasks.

metadata.title: Loss Function
metadata.definition: A loss function, also known as a cost function, quantifies the error or discrepancy between the predicted output of a model and the true target values. The goal of a machine learning algorithm is to minimize this loss function during training, guiding the model to make more accurate predictions.

metadata.title: Mean Squared Error Loss
metadata.definition: Mean Squared Error (MSE) is a common loss function used in regression tasks that calculates the average of the squared differences between predicted and actual values. It penalizes larger errors more significantly than smaller ones due to the squaring operation, making it sensitive to outliers.

metadata.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
metadata.definition: Cross-Entropy Loss is a widely used loss function for classification problems, especially when the model outputs probabilities for multiple classes. It measures the dissimilarity between the true probability distribution (often one-hot encoded) and the predicted probability distribution.

metadata.title: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss
metadata.definition: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss is a specific form of cross-entropy loss used for binary classification problems, where there are only two possible output classes. It quantifies the difference between the predicted probability of the positive class and the actual binary label (0 or 1).

metadata.title: Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss
metadata.definition: Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss is a specific form of cross-entropy loss used for multi-class classification problems where each instance belongs to exactly one class. It is applied when the true labels are one-hot encoded and the model outputs a probability distribution over the classes via a Softmax activation.

metadata.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
metadata.definition: Stochastic Gradient Descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize an objective function by updating model parameters based on the gradient calculated from a single randomly chosen training example at each step. This makes it much faster for large datasets compared to Batch Gradient Descent, though updates can be noisy.

metadata.title: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent is an optimization algorithm that updates model parameters using the average gradient computed over a small, randomly selected subset (mini-batch) of the training data at each iteration. It strikes a balance between the computational efficiency of SGD and the stability of Batch Gradient Descent, and is widely used in deep learning.

metadata.title: Batch Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: Batch Gradient Descent is an optimization algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to the model parameters using the *entire* training dataset before performing a single parameter update. While it guarantees convergence to the global minimum for convex functions, it can be computationally expensive and slow for very large datasets.

metadata.title: Learning Rate
metadata.definition: The learning rate is a hyperparameter in optimization algorithms that determines the step size at each iteration while moving towards the minimum of a loss function. A carefully chosen learning rate is crucial for efficient convergence; too high, and the model might overshoot the minimum; too low, and training will be very slow.

metadata.title: Learning Rate Schedule
metadata.definition: A learning rate schedule is a strategy for dynamically adjusting the learning rate during the training of a neural network, rather than keeping it constant. Its purpose is to improve model convergence and performance, often by starting with a higher learning rate and gradually decreasing it as training progresses to fine-tune the weights.

metadata.title: Momentum Optimizer
metadata.definition: The Momentum optimizer is an extension of Gradient Descent that accelerates convergence by adding a fraction of the update vector from the previous time step to the current update. This helps to smooth out oscillations in the gradient descent path, escape shallow local minima, and allows the optimizer to 'roll' over plateaus.

metadata.title: Adagrad Optimizer
metadata.definition: Adagrad (Adaptive Gradient Algorithm) is an adaptive learning rate optimizer that adjusts the learning rate for each parameter individually based on the historical sum of squared gradients for that parameter. It assigns larger updates to parameters with sparse gradients and smaller updates to parameters with frequent gradients.

metadata.title: RMSprop Optimizer
metadata.definition: RMSprop (Root Mean Square Propagation) is an adaptive learning rate optimizer that addresses Adagrad's tendency to monotonically decrease the learning rate too aggressively. It achieves this by using a moving average of squared gradients instead of the sum, allowing the learning rate to adapt based on recent gradients.

metadata.title: Adam Optimizer
metadata.definition: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) is an adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm that combines the best aspects of Adagrad and RMSprop. It calculates adaptive learning rates for each parameter by keeping track of exponentially decaying averages of past gradients (momentum) and past squared gradients (RMSprop).

metadata.title: AdamW Optimizer
metadata.definition: AdamW is a variant of the Adam optimizer that decouples weight decay from the L2 regularization term in the loss function. This separation improves generalization performance, especially in deep learning models, by applying weight decay directly to the weights rather than incorporating it into the adaptive gradient updates, which can interact poorly.

metadata.title: Backpropagation Algorithm
metadata.definition: Backpropagation is a fundamental algorithm used to train artificial neural networks by efficiently calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to all the weights in the network. It works by propagating the error backwards from the output layer through the network's layers, using the chain rule of calculus.

metadata.title: Computational Graph
metadata.definition: A computational graph is an abstract representation of mathematical operations as a directed acyclic graph, where nodes represent operations (e.g., addition, multiplication) or variables (e.g., inputs, weights), and edges represent the flow of data. It serves as the backbone for automatic differentiation and is crucial for implementing backpropagation efficiently.

metadata.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
metadata.definition: The vanishing gradient problem occurs during the training of deep neural networks when gradients become extremely small as they are backpropagated through many layers, especially with activation functions like sigmoid or tanh. This causes the updates to the weights in earlier layers to become negligible, hindering effective learning.

metadata.title: Exploding Gradient Problem
metadata.definition: The exploding gradient problem occurs during the training of deep neural networks when gradients accumulate to be very large, leading to unstable network training. This results in extremely large weight updates that cause the model's loss to diverge (become `NaN` or infinite), making the model unable to learn effectively.

metadata.title: Weight Initialization
metadata.definition: The process of setting the initial values for the weights (parameters) of a neural network before training begins. Proper initialization is crucial to prevent issues like vanishing or exploding gradients and to speed up convergence during training.

metadata.title: Xavier Initialization
metadata.definition: A weight initialization technique designed to keep the variance of activations consistent across layers, preventing signals from exploding or vanishing. It samples weights from a distribution with a specific variance dependent on the number of input and output units of the layer.

metadata.title: He Initialization
metadata.definition: A weight initialization strategy specifically designed for neural networks that use ReLU or its variants (e.g., Leaky ReLU) as activation functions. It scales the weights by a factor that takes into account only the number of input units, aiming to maintain the variance of activations.

metadata.title: Dropout Regularization
metadata.definition: A regularization technique used in neural networks to prevent overfitting by randomly setting a fraction of neurons to zero (i.e., 'dropping out' units) during each training iteration. This forces the network to learn more robust features that are not dependent on specific neurons.

metadata.title: Batch Normalization
metadata.definition: A technique to normalize the inputs of each layer in a neural network, usually applied between the linear transformation and the activation function. It rescales and re-centers the activations to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one for each mini-batch, mitigating internal covariate shift and accelerating training.

metadata.title: Layer Normalization
metadata.definition: A normalization technique that normalizes the inputs across all features for a single training example within a layer, rather than across the batch for a single feature like Batch Normalization. It is particularly useful in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers, where batch sizes can vary or sequences are long.

metadata.title: Weight Decay
metadata.definition: A regularization technique, also known as L2 regularization, that adds a penalty to the loss function proportional to the square of the magnitude of the weights. This encourages the network to learn smaller weights, reducing the complexity of the model and preventing overfitting.

metadata.title: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
metadata.definition: A class of deep neural networks specifically designed for processing structured grid-like data, such as images. CNNs employ specialized layers like convolutional layers and pooling layers to automatically and adaptively learn spatial hierarchies of features.

metadata.title: Convolutional Layer
metadata.definition: The core building block of a CNN, which applies a set of learnable filters (kernels) to the input data, performing a convolution operation. This operation extracts features by detecting patterns such as edges, textures, or shapes in different regions of the input.

metadata.title: Pooling Layer
metadata.definition: A layer in a CNN that reduces the spatial dimensions (width and height) of the input volume, typically after a convolutional layer, while retaining the most important information. This helps to reduce the number of parameters and computational cost, and to make the network more robust to small shifts and distortions (translational invariance).

metadata.title: Max Pooling
metadata.definition: A type of pooling operation that selects the maximum value from a cluster of neurons in the previous layer's feature map. This aggressively downsamples the input, highlighting the most prominent feature within each receptive field and contributing to translational invariance.

metadata.title: Average Pooling
metadata.definition: A type of pooling operation that calculates the average value for each cluster of neurons in the previous layer's feature map. This operation provides a smoothed, lower-resolution representation of the features and can be useful for preserving more general information or in specific network architectures.

metadata.title: Stride (CNN)
metadata.definition: The step size or number of pixels by which the kernel (filter) moves across the input image or feature map during a convolutional or pooling operation. A stride greater than one reduces the spatial dimensions of the output volume.

metadata.title: Padding (CNN)
metadata.definition: The process of adding extra pixels, typically zeros, around the border of the input image or feature map before a convolutional or pooling operation. Padding is used to control the spatial dimensions of the output, preventing the loss of information at the edges and allowing the output size to match the input size (e.g., 'same' padding).

metadata.title: Kernel (CNN)
metadata.definition: Also known as a filter, the kernel is a small matrix of learnable weights that slides over the input data during a convolutional operation. Each kernel is designed to detect a specific feature or pattern within the input, such as edges, corners, or textures.

metadata.title: Receptive Field
metadata.definition: The area in the input image or feature map that a particular neuron in a deeper layer of a CNN is 'seeing' or influenced by. As layers stack, the receptive field grows, allowing neurons in deeper layers to integrate information from larger regions of the original input.

metadata.title: Residual Connection
metadata.definition: A shortcut connection in a neural network that bypasses one or more layers, directly adding the input of the skipped layers to their output. This mechanism helps alleviate the vanishing gradient problem in very deep networks and facilitates training by allowing the network to learn residual functions instead of entirely new mappings.

metadata.title: Skip Connection
metadata.definition: A general term referring to any connection in a neural network that feeds the output of one layer as input to a later layer, skipping intermediate layers. These connections help mitigate vanishing gradients, improve information flow, and allow for feature reuse across different depths of the network.

metadata.title: VGG Network
metadata.definition: A pioneering convolutional neural network architecture known for its simplicity and depth, primarily consisting of stacks of small 3x3 convolutional layers followed by max-pooling layers. VGG demonstrated that increasing network depth, with small filters, significantly improves performance in large-scale image recognition tasks.

metadata.title: ResNet
metadata.definition: Short for Residual Network, a groundbreaking deep convolutional neural network architecture that introduced residual connections (or skip connections) to address the degradation problem in very deep networks. By enabling blocks of layers to learn residual mappings, ResNet allows for the training of networks with hundreds or even thousands of layers.

metadata.title: Inception Network
metadata.definition: A type of convolutional neural network (CNN) that uses "inception modules" to allow the network to choose among multiple convolutional filter sizes and pooling operations at each layer, effectively performing multiple transformations in parallel and concatenating their results. This design helps in optimizing computational resources and increasing network depth and width efficiently.

metadata.title: DenseNet
metadata.definition: A convolutional neural network architecture where each layer is directly connected to every other layer in a feed-forward fashion within a dense block, allowing feature maps from all preceding layers to be used as inputs to subsequent layers. This connectivity pattern enhances feature reuse, reduces the number of parameters, and mitigates the vanishing gradient problem.

metadata.title: U-Net
metadata.definition: A convolutional neural network architecture primarily used for image segmentation tasks, characterized by its U-shaped symmetric encoder-decoder structure with skip connections between corresponding layers in the downsampling path (encoder) and upsampling path (decoder). These skip connections allow the decoder to recover fine-grained spatial information lost during downsampling, leading to precise segmentation.

metadata.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture
metadata.definition: A general neural network framework composed of two main components: an encoder that transforms an input sequence into a fixed-size context vector (or thought vector), and a decoder that generates an output sequence from this context vector. The encoder typically captures the essential features and semantic information of the input, while the decoder uses this representation to produce the desired output.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
metadata.definition: A type of neural network designed to process sequential data, where connections between nodes form a directed graph along a temporal sequence. Unlike feedforward networks, RNNs have an internal memory that allows them to use information from previous inputs in the sequence to influence the current output, making them suitable for tasks involving time series or natural language.

metadata.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
metadata.definition: A specialized type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) designed to overcome the vanishing gradient problem and better capture long-range dependencies in sequential data. LSTMs achieve this through a sophisticated internal structure called a 'cell' which includes three gates (input, forget, and output) that regulate the flow of information, allowing the network to selectively remember or forget past information.

metadata.title: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)
metadata.definition: A type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that, similar to LSTMs, addresses the vanishing gradient problem and captures long-range dependencies, but with a simpler architecture. GRUs consolidate the input and forget gates into a single "update gate" and combine the cell state and hidden state, resulting in fewer parameters and often faster training while maintaining comparable performance to LSTMs on many tasks.

metadata.title: Sequence-to-Sequence Model
metadata.definition: A general neural network architecture that maps an input sequence to an output sequence of potentially different lengths, typically implemented using an Encoder-Decoder framework. The encoder processes the input sequence into a context vector, and the decoder then generates the output sequence one element at a time, often employing recurrent neural networks or Transformer blocks.

metadata.title: Self-Attention Mechanism
metadata.definition: A mechanism that allows a neural network to weigh the importance of different parts of an input sequence relative to each other when processing a specific element, by computing attention scores between all elements in the sequence. It enables the model to capture long-range dependencies and contextual relationships within a single sequence without relying on recurrent connections, improving sequence modeling capabilities.

metadata.title: Transformer Architecture
metadata.definition: A neural network architecture introduced in 2017, entirely relying on attention mechanisms, particularly Self-Attention and Multi-Head Attention, instead of recurrent or convolutional layers for processing sequential data. Its parallelizable nature and ability to capture long-range dependencies effectively have made it the dominant architecture for natural language processing and increasingly for computer vision tasks.

metadata.title: Encoder (Transformer)
metadata.definition: In the Transformer architecture, the encoder is responsible for processing the input sequence and transforming it into a continuous representation that captures its contextual meaning. It consists of a stack of identical layers, each containing a Multi-Head Self-Attention mechanism and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization.

metadata.title: Decoder (Transformer)
metadata.definition: In the Transformer architecture, the decoder is responsible for generating the output sequence based on the contextual representation produced by the encoder and the previously generated decoder outputs. It consists of a stack of identical layers, each containing a masked Multi-Head Self-Attention mechanism (to prevent looking at future tokens), a Multi-Head Attention mechanism over the encoder's output, and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network, also with residual connections and layer normalization.

metadata.title: Positional Encoding
metadata.definition: A technique used in Transformer models to inject information about the relative or absolute position of tokens in a sequence, as the self-attention mechanism itself is permutation-invariant and lacks inherent knowledge of order. Positional encodings are typically added to the input embeddings before they are fed into the encoder and decoder stacks, allowing the model to learn from the sequence order.

metadata.title: Multi-Head Attention
metadata.definition: An extension of the self-attention mechanism used in Transformer models, where attention is performed multiple times in parallel with different learned linear projections (heads) of the query, key, and value matrices. The outputs from these independent attention heads are then concatenated and linearly transformed, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

metadata.title: BERT Model
metadata.definition: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) is a powerful pre-trained language model that employs a Transformer encoder to learn deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context. Unlike previous unidirectional models, BERT can understand the context of a word based on all its surroundings, making it highly effective for various downstream NLP tasks.

metadata.title: GPT Model
metadata.definition: Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) is a series of large language models that use a Transformer decoder architecture to generate human-like text by predicting the next token in a sequence, based on a vast amount of pre-trained unlabeled text data. GPT models are characterized by their strong generative capabilities and ability to perform various zero-shot or few-shot NLP tasks without extensive fine-tuning.

metadata.title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
metadata.definition: A neural network architecture that applies the Transformer model, originally designed for natural language processing, directly to image classification tasks. ViT treats images as sequences of fixed-size patches, which are then linearly embedded, augmented with positional encodings, and fed into a standard Transformer encoder, demonstrating strong performance competitive with state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks.

metadata.title: Diffusion Model
