It consists of multiple layers of sorted linked lists, where each layer acts as an 'express lane' for the layer below it, allowing traversal to skip multiple elements with high probability.

metadata.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
metadata.definition: A data structure that maintains a collection of disjoint (non-overlapping) sets and supports two primary operations: `find` (determining which set an element belongs to) and `union` (merging two sets). It is often used to keep track of connected components in a graph or to detect cycles.

metadata.title: Union-Find Algorithm (DSU)
metadata.definition: The specific set of operations and optimizations (like path compression for `find` and union by rank/size for `union`) used to implement a Disjoint Set Union data structure efficiently. These optimizations lead to nearly constant amortized time complexity for operations.

metadata.title: Graph Representation (Adjacency Matrix)
metadata.definition: A square matrix used to represent a finite graph, where `matrix[i][j]` indicates if there is an edge between vertex `i` and vertex `j`. For unweighted graphs, values are typically 0 or 1; for weighted graphs, values are edge weights or infinity for no edge.

metadata.title: Graph Representation (Adjacency List)
metadata.definition: An array or hash map where each index or key `i` stores a list (or set) of vertices adjacent to vertex `i`. This representation is generally preferred for sparse graphs as it uses less memory and allows for efficient traversal of a vertex's neighbors.

metadata.title: Graph Representation (Edge List)
metadata.definition: A simple representation where a graph is stored as a collection of tuples, each tuple representing an edge. For unweighted graphs, an edge is `(u, v)`; for weighted graphs, it's `(u, v, weight)`.

metadata.title: Topological Sort (DFS-based)
metadata.definition: An algorithm that uses Depth-First Search to produce a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge `(u, v)`, vertex `u` comes before `v` in the ordering. The order is obtained by adding vertices to the sorted list in reverse order of their finishing times in DFS.

metadata.title: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
metadata.definition: An algorithm for topological sorting that works by iteratively finding nodes with no incoming edges (in-degree 0), adding them to the sorted list, and then removing their outgoing edges. This process updates the in-degrees of subsequent nodes, continuing until all nodes are processed or a cycle is detected.

metadata.title: Strongly Connected Components (Tarjan's)
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm for finding the strongly connected components (SCCs) of a directed graph using a single Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal. It identifies SCCs by tracking discovery times and low-link values (the lowest discovery time reachable from a node, including itself, through a path of tree edges followed by at most one back-edge) in the recursion stack.

metadata.title: Strongly Connected Components (Kosaraju's)
metadata.definition: An algorithm to find strongly connected components (SCCs) in a directed graph using two passes of Depth-First Search. The first DFS pass processes the original graph to determine the finishing times of all vertices, and the second DFS pass is performed on the transpose of the graph (with all edges reversed) in decreasing order of finishing times.

metadata.title: Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
metadata.definition: A subgraph of a connected, edge-weighted undirected graph that connects all the vertices together, without any cycles and with the minimum possible total edge weight. MST algorithms like Prim's and Kruskal's find such a tree.

metadata.title: Shortest Path Algorithm (DAG)
metadata.definition: A specialized algorithm to find the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in O(V+E) time. It processes vertices in topological order, relaxing edges to update distances, and can handle negative edge weights, unlike Dijkstra's.

metadata.title: All-Pairs Shortest Path
metadata.definition: The problem of finding the shortest paths between all possible pairs of vertices in a graph. Common algorithms to solve this include the Floyd-Warshall algorithm (for general graphs with non-negative or negative-cycle-free weights) and running Dijkstra's algorithm from each vertex (for non-negative weights).

metadata.title: Transitive Closure (Graphs)
metadata.definition: A graph, or more often a boolean matrix, that represents reachability between all pairs of vertices in a given directed graph. For every pair `(u, v)`, it indicates if there is a path from `u` to `v` in the original graph, capturing all indirect connections.

metadata.title: Maximum Flow (Network Flow)
metadata.definition: The problem of finding the maximum possible amount of 'flow' that can be sent from a source vertex to a sink vertex in a flow network, where each edge has a specified capacity constraint that cannot be exceeded. This concept is fundamental to network optimization.

metadata.title: Minimum Cut (Network Flow)
metadata.definition: A partition of the vertices of a flow network into two sets, one containing the source and one containing the sink, such that the sum of capacities of edges going from the source set to the sink set is minimized. The celebrated Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem states that the value of the maximum flow through a network is equal to the capacity of a minimum cut.

metadata.title: Edmonds-Karp Algorithm
metadata.definition: An implementation of the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm for finding the maximum flow in a flow network. It uses Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find augmenting paths in the residual graph, specifically focusing on paths with the fewest edges, which guarantees polynomial time complexity, typically O(VE²).

metadata.title: Dinic's Algorithm
metadata.definition: A more efficient algorithm for computing the maximum flow in a flow network, improving upon Edmonds-Karp. It operates in phases, where each phase constructs a level graph using BFS and then finds a 'blocking flow' by performing multiple DFS traversals on this level graph, leading to a complexity of O(V²E) for general graphs and O(VE) for unit capacity networks.

metadata.title: Max Bipartite Matching
metadata.definition: The problem of finding a matching in a bipartite graph such that no two edges share a common vertex and the number of edges (i.e., paired vertices) in the matching is maximized. This can be solved using augmenting paths with DFS/BFS or by reducing it to a maximum flow problem.

metadata.title: Hungarian Algorithm (Assignment Problem)
metadata.definition: A combinatorial optimization algorithm that solves the assignment problem in polynomial time, specifically finding a perfect matching with the minimum total cost in a weighted bipartite graph. It operates by reducing the cost matrix until an optimal assignment can be found.

metadata.title: Eulerian Path/Circuit
metadata.definition: An Eulerian path is a path in a graph that visits every edge exactly once. An Eulerian circuit is an Eulerian path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Such paths or circuits exist if and only if the graph is connected and all (for a circuit) or all but two (for a path) vertices have even degrees.

metadata.title: Hamiltonian Path/Circuit
metadata.definition: A Hamiltonian Path in an undirected or directed graph is a path that visits each vertex exactly once. A Hamiltonian Circuit (or Cycle) is a Hamiltonian Path that starts and ends at the same vertex.

metadata.title: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP)
metadata.definition: The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) asks for the shortest possible route that visits a given set of 'cities' and returns to the origin city, visiting each city exactly once. It is a classic NP-hard optimization problem.

metadata.title: Chinese Postman Problem
metadata.definition: The Chinese Postman Problem (CPP), also known as the Route Inspection Problem, seeks the shortest closed walk or circuit that traverses every edge of a given graph at least once and returns to the starting vertex. It is solvable in polynomial time for undirected graphs.

metadata.title: Graph Coloring Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Graph Coloring Algorithm assigns colors to elements of a graph (usually vertices) such that no two adjacent elements share the same color. The goal is often to use the minimum number of colors, known as the chromatic number.

metadata.title: Clique Problem
metadata.definition: The Clique Problem is the computational task of finding a clique (a subgraph where every pair of distinct vertices is connected by an edge) within a given graph. The maximum clique problem seeks the clique with the largest number of vertices.

metadata.title: String Matching
metadata.definition: String Matching is the problem of finding all occurrences of a shorter string (the pattern) within a longer string (the text). It is a fundamental problem in computer science with various applications.

metadata.title: Naive String Matching
metadata.definition: Naive String Matching is a straightforward algorithm that searches for a pattern within a text by sliding the pattern one character at a time across the text and comparing characters at each possible alignment. It has a worst-case time complexity of O(M*N), where M is pattern length and N is text length.

metadata.title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) Algorithm
metadata.definition: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm is an efficient string matching algorithm that avoids re-checking characters that have already been matched. It achieves linear time complexity by pre-processing the pattern to construct a 'Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix' (LPS) array, which guides shifts in case of a mismatch.

metadata.title: Rabin-Karp Algorithm
metadata.definition: The Rabin-Karp algorithm is a string matching algorithm that uses hashing to efficiently find a pattern within a text. It employs a rolling hash function to quickly update the hash value of a window of text as it slides, reducing the number of direct character comparisons.

metadata.title: Z-Algorithm (String)
metadata.definition: The Z-Algorithm computes the Z-array for a given string, where Z[i] for each index 'i' is the length of the longest substring starting at 'i' that is also a prefix of the entire string. This array allows for efficient pattern matching and other string operations.

metadata.title: Manacher's Algorithm (Palindromes)
metadata.definition: Manacher's Algorithm is a linear-time algorithm for finding the longest palindromic substring within a given string. It cleverly utilizes previously computed palindrome information to avoid redundant comparisons, achieving optimal O(N) complexity.

metadata.title: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
metadata.definition: The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem involves finding the longest subsequence that is common to two given sequences. A subsequence does not require consecutive elements, only that they appear in the same relative order.

metadata.title: Longest Common Substring
metadata.definition: The Longest Common Substring problem is to find the longest string that is a contiguous substring of two or more given strings. Unlike subsequences, substrings must occupy consecutive positions within the original strings.

metadata.title: Edit Distance (Levenshtein Distance)
metadata.definition: Edit Distance, commonly referring to Levenshtein Distance, is the minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions, or substitutions) required to change one word or string into another. It quantifies the similarity between two strings.

metadata.title: Aho-Corasick Algorithm
metadata.definition: The Aho-Corasick algorithm is a dictionary-matching algorithm that finds all occurrences of a finite set of patterns (a dictionary) within a given text. It constructs a finite automaton from the patterns using a trie combined with 'failure links' to achieve linear-time search.

metadata.title: Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT)
metadata.definition: The Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT) is a reversible data transformation algorithm used in data compression. It reorders a block of characters into a form that has many identical consecutive characters, making it highly amenable to subsequent compression algorithms like move-to-front encoding and run-length encoding.

metadata.title: Convex Hull Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Convex Hull Algorithm computes the smallest convex polygon that encloses a given set of points in a plane. A convex polygon is one where for every two points within the polygon, the line segment connecting them is entirely contained within the polygon.

metadata.title: Graham Scan
metadata.definition: Graham Scan is a classic O(N log N) algorithm for computing the convex hull of a finite set of points in the plane. It works by sorting the points by angle around a pivot point and then processing them in order, using a stack to maintain candidate hull vertices and removing turns that are not counter-clockwise.

metadata.title: Jarvis March (Gift Wrapping)
metadata.definition: Jarvis March, also known as the Gift Wrapping algorithm, is a convex hull algorithm that finds the vertices of the convex hull in O(N*H) time, where N is the number of points and H is the number of vertices on the hull. It iteratively finds the 'next' vertex on the hull by picking the point that forms the smallest angle with the current hull edge.

metadata.title: Line Intersection Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Line Intersection Algorithm determines whether two given line segments (or lines) intersect, and if they do, calculates the coordinates of their intersection point. This involves solving a system of linear equations or using geometric properties like cross products.

metadata.title: Closest Pair of Points Algorithm
metadata.definition: This algorithm finds two points in a set of 'n' points that have the smallest Euclidean distance between them. It is typically solved using a divide-and-conquer approach, achieving an optimal time complexity of O(N log N).

metadata.title: Voronoi Diagram (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A Voronoi Diagram partitions a plane containing 'n' points (called sites) into 'n' convex polygons. Each polygon, called a Voronoi cell, consists of all points in the plane that are closer to its associated site than to any other site. Algorithms like Fortune's algorithm can construct it efficiently.

metadata.title: Delaunay Triangulation (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A Delaunay Triangulation of a set of points in a plane is a triangulation such that no point lies inside the circumcircle of any triangle. It maximizes the minimum angle of all triangles, tending to avoid 'sliver' triangles, and is the dual of the Voronoi diagram.

metadata.title: Point in Polygon Test
metadata.definition: This test determines whether a given point lies inside, outside, or exactly on the boundary of a polygon. Common algorithms include the ray casting (or winding number) algorithm, which counts intersections of a ray from the point with the polygon's edges.

metadata.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) (Euclidean)
metadata.definition: The Euclidean algorithm efficiently finds the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two non-negative integers. It is based on the principle that the GCD of two numbers also divides their difference, and can be computed recursively by taking remainders until one number becomes zero.

metadata.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
metadata.definition: An extension of the Euclidean algorithm that, in addition to computing the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers 'a' and 'b', also finds integers 'x' and 'y' such that `ax + by = GCD(a, b)`. These integers 'x' and 'y' are known as Bézout coefficients.

metadata.title: Modular Exponentiation (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: This algorithm efficiently computes the remainder of a large integer exponentiation, `(base^exponent) % modulus`. It works by repeatedly squaring the base and applying the modulus at each step, leveraging the binary representation of the exponent to perform calculations in logarithmic time.

metadata.title: Primality Testing (Naive)
metadata.definition: A straightforward method to determine if a given integer 'n' is a prime number by iteratively checking for divisibility by all integers from 2 up to the square root of 'n'. If any divisor is found, the number is composite; otherwise, it is prime.

metadata.title: Miller-Rabin Primality Test
metadata.definition: A probabilistic primality test that efficiently determines whether a large number is composite or probably prime. It is based on properties of modular arithmetic and Fermat's Little Theorem, providing a high degree of confidence with a very small probability of error for composite numbers.

metadata.title: Pollard's Rho Algorithm (Factoring)
metadata.definition: A probabilistic integer factorization algorithm designed to find small prime factors of a composite number relatively quickly. It uses a cycle-finding algorithm (Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm) to detect collisions in a sequence generated by a pseudo-random function modulo 'n', leveraging the birthday paradox.

metadata.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
metadata.definition: An ancient, highly efficient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a specified integer 'n'. It works by iteratively marking as composite (i.e., not prime) the multiples of each prime, starting with 2, until only prime numbers remain unmarked.

metadata.title: Modular Inverse Algorithm
metadata.definition: This algorithm computes the modular multiplicative inverse of an integer 'a' modulo 'm', which is an integer 'x' such that `(a * x) % m = 1`. It typically relies on the Extended Euclidean Algorithm or, if 'm' is prime, Fermat's Little Theorem.

metadata.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: The Chinese Remainder Theorem provides a unique solution to a system of linear congruences with distinct, pairwise coprime moduli. The associated algorithms construct an integer 'x' that satisfies all given congruences simultaneously.

metadata.title: RSA Algorithm (Basic Steps)
metadata.definition: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem widely used for secure data transmission, based on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. Its basic steps involve key generation (public and private keys), encryption using the public key, and decryption using the private key, all leveraging modular exponentiation.

metadata.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange (Basic Steps)
metadata.definition: Diffie-Hellman is a method of securely exchanging cryptographic keys over a public channel, allowing two parties to establish a shared secret key without any prior shared secret. It relies on the mathematical difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem in modular arithmetic.

metadata.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (Basic Concept)
metadata.definition: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) is an approach to public-key cryptography based on the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields. It offers equivalent security to non-ECC cryptography with smaller key sizes, leveraging the computational difficulty of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP).

metadata.title: Linear Programming (Simplex Method)
metadata.definition: The Simplex Method is an iterative algorithm for solving linear programming problems, which involve optimizing a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints. It systematically moves from one vertex of the feasible region to an adjacent one, always improving the objective function value until an optimal solution is reached.

metadata.title: Integer Linear Programming (Concept)
metadata.definition: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) is a type of linear programming where some or all of the decision variables are restricted to be integers. Unlike standard linear programming, which can be solved in polynomial time, ILP problems are generally NP-hard, making them significantly more complex to solve.

metadata.title: Gradient Descent Algorithm
metadata.definition: Gradient Descent is a first-order iterative optimization algorithm used for finding the local minimum of a differentiable function. It works by repeatedly taking steps proportional to the negative of the gradient of the function at the current point, effectively moving in the direction of steepest descent.

metadata.title: Genetic Algorithm (Concept)
metadata.definition: A Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a metaheuristic search algorithm inspired by the process of natural selection and evolution. It operates on a population of candidate solutions, applying genetic operators like mutation, crossover, and selection over generations to evolve progressively better solutions to optimization and search problems.

metadata.title: Ant Colony Optimization (Concept)
metadata.definition: Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a probabilistic metaheuristic technique for solving computational problems which can be reduced to finding good paths through graphs. It is inspired by the foraging behavior of real ants, where ants collectively find shortest paths between their colony and food sources by depositing pheromone trails. The algorithm simulates this process, with artificial ants constructing solutions based on heuristic information and pheromone levels, which are then updated to reflect the quality of the solutions.

metadata.title: Parallel Computing Model (PRAM)
metadata.definition: The Parallel Random Access Machine (PRAM) is a theoretical shared-memory model for parallel computation, where multiple processors can access a common global memory in unit time. It abstracts away communication costs and synchronization overheads, focusing on the inherent parallelism of an algorithm. PRAM models are categorized by how they handle concurrent read/write operations to the same memory location (e.g., EREW, CREW, CRCW).

metadata.title: Work-Depth Model
metadata.definition: The Work-Depth model is a theoretical framework for analyzing the efficiency of parallel algorithms, independent of the number of available processors. It characterizes an algorithm by two main metrics: 'work' (the total number of operations performed by all processors) and 'depth' (the length of the longest chain of dependencies, also known as span or critical path length). This model helps determine the maximum speedup achievable and the minimum possible execution time on an infinite number of processors.

metadata.title: MapReduce Paradigm
metadata.definition: MapReduce is a programming model and an associated distributed framework for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster of computers. It simplifies distributed data processing by breaking down tasks into two main phases: a 'Map' phase, which processes input key-value pairs independently to generate intermediate key-value pairs, and a 'Reduce' phase, which aggregates these intermediate values based on their keys to produce the final output.

metadata.title: Distributed Consensus (Paxos Concept)
metadata.definition: Paxos is a family of protocols for solving the distributed consensus problem, enabling a set of processes to agree on a single value, even if some processes fail or messages are lost. It guarantees safety (all agreed-upon values are valid and consistent) and liveness (eventually, a value will be agreed upon) in an asynchronous network with crash failures, making it fundamental for building fault-tolerant distributed systems.

metadata.title: Distributed Consensus (Raft Concept)
metadata.definition: Raft is a distributed consensus algorithm designed for understandability and proven to be equivalent to Paxos in fault tolerance and performance. It achieves consensus by electing a single strong leader who is responsible for managing a replicated log, ensuring that all state changes are consistently applied across all servers in a cluster. The protocol simplifies the problem into three subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety.

metadata.title: Load Balancing Algorithm
metadata.definition: A load balancing algorithm distributes computing workloads across multiple resources, such as servers, network links, or CPUs, to optimize resource utilization, maximize throughput, minimize response time, and prevent any single resource from becoming overloaded. Its primary goal is to improve the overall performance, scalability, and reliability of a system by efficiently sharing the computational demand.

metadata.title: Parallel Sorting (Odd-Even Transposition)
metadata.definition: Odd-Even Transposition Sort is a simple parallel sorting algorithm particularly well-suited for a linear array of processors. It works in alternating phases: 'odd' phases where odd-indexed elements compare and swap with their right neighbors, and 'even' phases where even-indexed elements compare and swap with their right neighbors. This process repeats `N` times for an array of `N` elements, ensuring that the array is sorted.

metadata.title: Las Vegas Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Las Vegas algorithm is a randomized algorithm that always produces the correct output (or finds a correct solution), but its running time is probabilistic and may vary on different executions. While it is guaranteed to produce a correct result upon termination, there is no deterministic upper bound on its execution time, and it might occasionally take an extremely long time or fail to terminate within practical limits.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Monte Carlo algorithm is a randomized algorithm that has a deterministic running time, but its output may be incorrect with a certain (usually small and controllable) probability. These algorithms are useful when a correct answer is too expensive to compute deterministically, and an approximate or possibly incorrect answer within a fixed time budget is acceptable. They typically offer either a 'yes-biased' (false positives) or 'no-biased' (false negatives) error probability.

metadata.title: Randomized Quick Sort
metadata.definition: Randomized Quick Sort is a variant of the Quick Sort algorithm where the pivot element is chosen randomly from the array elements at each step. This randomization helps to ensure that the algorithm's worst-case time complexity of O(n^2), which typically occurs with consistently bad pivot choices, becomes extremely unlikely. The expected time complexity of Randomized Quick Sort remains O(n log n) for any input distribution, making it robust in practice.

metadata.title: Randomized Primality Test (Miller-Rabin)
metadata.definition: The Miller-Rabin primality test is a probabilistic (Monte Carlo) algorithm used to efficiently determine if a given large number is prime. It works by testing a number against several randomly chosen 'witnesses' for properties that all prime numbers satisfy. If the number fails any test, it is definitively composite; if it passes all tests, it is declared 'probably prime' with a high probability, which increases with the number of witnesses used.

metadata.title: Min-Cut Algorithm (Karger's)
metadata.definition: Karger's algorithm is a randomized algorithm for finding a minimum cut in an undirected graph. It repeatedly selects a random edge and contracts its two endpoints into a single new vertex, preserving multiedges. This process continues until only two vertices remain, at which point the edges between these two super-vertices form a cut. By repeating the algorithm multiple times, one can find the minimum cut with a high probability.

metadata.title: Approximation Ratio
metadata.definition: The approximation ratio (or approximation factor) is a performance metric for approximation algorithms that quantifies how close the algorithm's solution is to the optimal solution for an optimization problem. For a minimization problem, it's defined as the ratio of the algorithm's solution value to the optimal solution value (always ≥ 1). For a maximization problem, it's the ratio of the optimal value to the algorithm's solution value (also always ≥ 1).

metadata.title: Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS)
metadata.definition: A Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) is a family of approximation algorithms for an optimization problem that can achieve an approximation ratio arbitrarily close to optimal. For any desired constant `ε > 0`, there exists an algorithm within the scheme that produces a solution with an approximation ratio of `(1+ε)` for minimization problems or `(1-ε)` for maximization problems. The running time of a PTAS is polynomial in the input size `n`, but may be exponential in `1/ε`.

metadata.title: Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS)
metadata.definition: A Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) is a more powerful type of approximation scheme than a PTAS. For an FPTAS, not only is its running time polynomial in the input size `n`, but it is also polynomial in `1/ε`, where `ε` is the error parameter determining the approximation ratio. This means an FPTAS is practical even when a very high degree of accuracy (small `ε`) is required, as its exponential dependence on `1/ε` is removed.

metadata.title: Vertex Cover Approximation
metadata.definition: The Vertex Cover problem is NP-hard, requiring finding the smallest set of vertices in a graph such that every edge has at least one endpoint in the set. A simple and widely known 2-approximation algorithm for Vertex Cover works by repeatedly picking an arbitrary edge, adding both of its endpoints to the vertex cover set, and then removing all edges incident to these two vertices, continuing until no edges remain. This greedy strategy guarantees that the size of the found vertex cover is at most twice the size of the minimum vertex cover.

metadata.title: Set Cover Approximation
metadata.definition: The Set Cover problem is NP-hard, involving finding the minimum number of sets from a given collection whose union contains all elements of a universal set. A standard greedy approximation algorithm for Set Cover repeatedly selects the set that covers the maximum number of currently uncovered elements until all elements are covered. This algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of `ln(max_set_size) + 1` (where `max_set_size` is the maximum number of elements in any set), which is also denoted as `H(max_set_size)` where `H` is the harmonic number.

metadata.title: TSP Approximation (Triangle Inequality)
metadata.definition: For the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), which is NP-hard, when the edge weights satisfy the triangle inequality (direct path is always shortest or equal to indirect paths), there exist effective approximation algorithms. A well-known 2-approximation algorithm involves first computing a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of the graph, then performing a depth-first traversal of the MST, and finally constructing a tour by visiting vertices in the order they are first encountered in the DFS. This tour's length is guaranteed to be at most twice the length of the optimal TSP tour.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem Approximation
metadata.definition: The Knapsack Problem is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem where the goal is to choose a subset of items, each with a weight and a value, to maximize the total value while not exceeding a given weight capacity. While the 0/1 Knapsack problem is NP-hard, it admits a Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS). This FPTAS can produce a solution whose total value is within a `(1-ε)` factor of the optimal value, with a running time that is polynomial in both the number of items (`n`) and `1/ε`.

metadata.title: Turing Machine (Deterministic)
metadata.definition: A deterministic Turing Machine (DTM) is a mathematical model of computation consisting of a finite state control, an infinite tape divided into cells, and a read/write head. At each step, based on its current state and the symbol under the head, it deterministically writes a symbol, moves the head, and transitions to a new state.

metadata.title: Turing Machine (Non-Deterministic)
metadata.definition: A non-deterministic Turing Machine (NTM) is a variant of the Turing Machine where, for a given state and tape symbol, there can be multiple possible next actions (write, move, new state). An NTM accepts an input if at least one sequence of choices leads to an accepting state.

metadata.title: Complexity Class P
metadata.definition: The complexity class P (Polynomial time) consists of all decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time, meaning the running time is bounded by O(n^k) for some constant k, where n is the input size.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NP
metadata.definition: The complexity class NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial time) comprises decision problems for which a 'yes' instance's solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. Equivalently, problems in NP can be solved by a non-deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NP-Complete
metadata.definition: A problem is NP-Complete if it is in NP and is also NP-Hard. This means it is among the 'hardest' problems in NP, as any other problem in NP can be polynomially reduced to it, implying that an efficient solution for one NP-Complete problem would lead to efficient solutions for all problems in NP.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NP-Hard
metadata.definition: A problem is NP-Hard if every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time. This implies that NP-Hard problems are at least as computationally difficult as any problem in NP, though they themselves are not necessarily restricted to being decision problems or belonging to NP.

metadata.title: Polynomial-Time Reduction
metadata.definition: A polynomial-time reduction is a transformation from an instance of problem A to an instance of problem B such that A has a 'yes' answer if and only if B has a 'yes' answer, and the transformation process itself can be computed in polynomial time. It demonstrates that problem A is no harder than problem B, denoted A ≤p B.

metadata.title: P vs NP Problem
metadata.definition: The P vs NP problem is a major unsolved question in theoretical computer science asking whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified (NP) can also be quickly solved (P). Formally, it asks if the complexity classes P and NP are equivalent (P = NP) or if P is a proper subset of NP (P ⊂ NP).

metadata.title: Space Complexity (General)
metadata.definition: Space complexity measures the amount of auxiliary memory or working storage required by an algorithm to solve a computational problem, as a function of the input size. It typically quantifies the memory used beyond the space needed to store the input itself.

metadata.title: Complexity Class L (Logarithmic Space)
metadata.definition: The complexity class L (Logarithmic Space) consists of all decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine using an amount of auxiliary space logarithmic with respect to the input size, where the input tape is read-only. Formally, space usage is O(log n).

metadata.title: Complexity Class NL (Non-Deterministic Logarithmic Space)
metadata.definition: The complexity class NL (Non-deterministic Logarithmic Space) comprises all decision problems solvable by a non-deterministic Turing machine using a logarithmic amount of auxiliary space, with a read-only input tape. A key result, Immerman-Szelepcsényi Theorem, shows NL = co-NL.

metadata.title: Complexity Class PSPACE
metadata.definition: The complexity class PSPACE (Polynomial Space) encompasses all decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine using a polynomial amount of space. It is known that P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE and NL ⊆ PSPACE.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NPSPACE
metadata.definition: The complexity class NPSPACE (Non-deterministic Polynomial Space) includes all decision problems solvable by a non-deterministic Turing machine using a polynomial amount of space. A fundamental result, Savitch's Theorem, proves that PSPACE = NPSPACE, meaning non-determinism does not increase the power of polynomial-space computation.

metadata.title: Complexity Class EXP
metadata.definition: The complexity class EXP (Exponential Time) consists of all decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in exponential time, specifically O(2^(poly(n))) where poly(n) is a polynomial function of the input size n. It is known that P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP.

metadata.title: Hierarchy Theorem (Time)
metadata.definition: The Time Hierarchy Theorem states that for any 'well-behaved' (constructible) function f(n), there exist decision problems solvable in time O(f(n) log f(n)) that cannot be solved in time O(f(n)). This formally proves that providing more time strictly increases the class of problems that can be solved.

metadata.title: Hierarchy Theorem (Space)
metadata.definition: The Space Hierarchy Theorem states that for any 'well-behaved' (constructible) function f(n), there exist decision problems solvable in space O(f(n) log f(n)) that cannot be solved in space O(f(n)). This formally proves that providing more space strictly increases the class of problems that can be solved.

metadata.title: Interactive Proof System (Concept)
metadata.definition: An interactive proof system is a computational model involving two parties: a computationally powerful but untrusted Prover (P) and a polynomial-time Verifier (V). The Prover attempts to convince the Verifier of the truth of a statement through a series of messages, with the Verifier accepting true statements with high probability and rejecting false ones with high probability.

metadata.title: Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCP)
metadata.definition: A Probabilistically Checkable Proof (PCP) is a type of interactive proof where a Verifier, using randomization, checks a proof of a mathematical statement by querying only a small, constant number of bits from the proof. The PCP Theorem states that every language in NP has a probabilistically checkable proof that can be checked in polynomial time using a logarithmic number of random bits and querying only a constant number of bits.

metadata.title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability (FPT)
metadata.definition: A problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if it can be solved by an algorithm whose running time is f(k) * poly(n), where n is the input size, k is a parameter of the input, f is an arbitrary computable function, and poly is a polynomial function. This means the exponential growth in runtime is confined to the parameter k, making the problem tractable for small k, even if it is NP-hard in general.

metadata.title: Parameterized Complexity
metadata.definition: Parameterized Complexity is a framework for analyzing the computational difficulty of problems by considering their input size 'n' and one or more additional 'parameters' 'k' that describe structural properties of the input. It seeks to classify problems as fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if they admit algorithms with running times f(k) * poly(n), allowing for efficient solutions when the parameter k is small, even if the problem is NP-hard in general.

metadata.title: Undecidability
metadata.definition: Undecidability refers to the property of a decision problem for which no algorithm can be constructed that always produces a correct 'yes' or 'no' answer in a finite amount of time, regardless of the input. Such problems are inherently impossible to solve algorithmically.

metadata.title: Halting Problem
metadata.definition: The Halting Problem is a famous undecidable decision problem asking whether, given a description of an arbitrary computer program and an arbitrary input, one can determine if the program will finish running or continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can solve the Halting Problem for all possible program-input pairs.

metadata.title: Reduction (Computability)
metadata.definition: In computability and complexity theory, a reduction is an algorithm that transforms instances of one problem (Problem A) into instances of another problem (Problem B). If Problem A can be reduced to Problem B, then solving Problem B can be used to solve Problem A, implying that Problem B is 'at least as hard' as Problem A.

metadata.title: Online Algorithms (General Concept)
metadata.definition: Online algorithms are algorithms that process their input piece-by-piece in a serial fashion, without having the entire input available at the start. They must make decisions locally at each step, based only on the information processed so far, without knowledge of future input.

metadata.title: Competitive Analysis (Online Algorithms)
metadata.definition: Competitive analysis is a method for evaluating the performance of online algorithms by comparing their output to that of an optimal offline algorithm, which has full knowledge of the entire input in advance. The competitive ratio is defined as the worst-case ratio of the online algorithm's cost to the optimal offline algorithm's cost.

metadata.title: External Memory Algorithm
metadata.definition: External memory algorithms (or out-of-core algorithms) are designed to process data that is too large to fit into a computer's main memory (RAM). These algorithms optimize for minimizing accesses to slower external storage devices, such as hard drives or SSDs, often by exploiting principles like locality and sequential access.

metadata.title: Streaming Algorithm
metadata.definition: Streaming algorithms are a class of online algorithms designed to process massive amounts of data sequentially, typically making only one or a few passes over the data. They operate under strict memory constraints, using significantly less memory than the total size of the input stream to compute properties or statistics.

metadata.title: Data Stream Model
metadata.definition: The Data Stream Model is a computational model where input arrives as a continuous stream of items, and an algorithm must process this data using significantly less memory than the total stream size. Algorithms in this model typically make a single pass over the data and produce an approximate answer due to memory limitations.

metadata.title: Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
metadata.definition: Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) is a randomized technique used for efficiently finding approximate nearest neighbors in high-dimensional spaces. It works by hashing similar items to the same 'buckets' with high probability, while dissimilar items are hashed to different buckets with high probability, thereby speeding up similarity searches.

metadata.title: Bloom Filter (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is a member of a set. It can yield false positives (reporting an element is in the set when it's not) but never false negatives (never failing to report an element that is in the set), and offers constant time insertion and query operations.

metadata.title: Count-Min Sketch
metadata.definition: The Count-Min Sketch is a probabilistic data structure used to estimate the frequencies of elements in a data stream. It uses multiple hash functions and a 2D array of counters to provide an estimate for the count of any item, with bounded error and small memory footprint.

metadata.title: Convex Optimization (Algorithms)
metadata.definition: Convex optimization is a subfield of mathematical optimization that deals with minimizing convex functions over convex sets. Algorithms in this field guarantee finding a global optimum efficiently, making them fundamental to various applications in machine learning, engineering, and operations research.

metadata.title: Quantum Algorithm (Basic Concept)
metadata.definition: A quantum algorithm is an algorithm that runs on a realistic model of quantum computation, typically a quantum computer. These algorithms exploit quantum-mechanical phenomena like superposition, entanglement, and interference to solve certain computational problems significantly faster than any known classical algorithm.

metadata.title: Shor's Algorithm (Factoring)
metadata.definition: Shor's algorithm is a quantum algorithm for integer factorization that can find the prime factors of a large number significantly faster than any known classical algorithm. It leverages the quantum Fourier transform to efficiently find the period of a modular exponential function, which is critical for factorization.

metadata.title: Grover's Algorithm (Search)
metadata.definition: Grover's algorithm is a quantum algorithm that offers a quadratic speedup for searching an unstructured database or solving problems that can be phrased as finding an 'item' among N possibilities. It achieves this by using quantum superposition and interference to amplify the amplitude of the desired state.

metadata.title: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP)
metadata.definition: GRASP is a metaheuristic algorithm for combinatorial optimization problems, often used for NP-hard problems. It iteratively constructs a solution in two phases: a greedy randomized construction phase that builds a feasible solution, followed by a local search phase that improves the solution until a local optimum is found.

metadata.title: Pathfinding Algorithm (General)
metadata.definition: Pathfinding algorithms are designed to find a path between two points (nodes) in a graph or grid, typically optimizing for a certain cost, such as shortest distance, least time, or lowest resource consumption. These algorithms are fundamental in areas like navigation, robotics, and game AI.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Game Theory (Basic Concepts)
metadata.definition: Algorithmic Game Theory is an interdisciplinary field that combines concepts from algorithm design and game theory to analyze and design algorithms in strategic environments. It studies how self-interested agents interact and how their strategic behavior impacts the performance and design of algorithms.

metadata.title: Mechanism Design (Algorithmic Aspects)
metadata.definition: Mechanism Design, within algorithmic game theory, focuses on designing the 'rules of the game' (mechanisms) to achieve a desired outcome, even when participants act selfishly. It involves creating algorithms for things like auctions or resource allocation that incentivize agents to reveal their true preferences.

metadata.title: Adversarial Machine Learning (Algorithmic Aspects)
metadata.definition: Adversarial Machine Learning is a field that studies the vulnerabilities of machine learning models to malicious inputs (adversarial examples) and develops robust algorithms to defend against such attacks. It explores methods for both generating and detecting adversarial attacks, focusing on the algorithmic techniques behind them.

metadata.title: Q-learning (Algorithmic Aspects)
metadata.definition: A model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that learns an optimal action-selection policy for a given finite Markov Decision Process by estimating the expected maximum future rewards for actions taken in specific states. It uses a Q-table to store and iteratively update Q-values, which represent the quality of taking a particular action in a particular state.

metadata.title: Kernel Trick (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A method used in machine learning to implicitly map data into a higher-dimensional feature space without explicitly calculating the coordinates of the data in that space. It achieves this by using a kernel function that computes the inner product between the images of two data points in the higher-dimensional space, enabling algorithms to learn complex non-linear decision boundaries efficiently.

metadata.title: Support Vector Machine (SVM - Algorithmic Aspects)
metadata.definition: A supervised machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression that constructs an optimal hyperplane to separate data points into different classes. It maximizes the margin between the hyperplane and the closest data points, known as support vectors, and can handle non-linear separation through the use of the Kernel Trick.

metadata.title: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm to compute the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and its inverse, reducing the computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N log N). It works by recursively breaking down the DFT of a sequence into smaller DFTs, exploiting symmetries.

metadata.title: Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform (FWHT)
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm similar to FFT but operating on the Walsh-Hadamard basis, transforming a sequence of 2^n numbers into another sequence in O(N log N) time. It is particularly useful for performing convolutions in boolean algebra and for analysis of signals with binary components.

metadata.title: Matrix Multiplication Algorithm (Strassen's)
metadata.definition: A divide-and-conquer algorithm for matrix multiplication that is asymptotically faster than the standard algorithm. It recursively splits matrices into smaller sub-matrices and performs 7 multiplications instead of 8 for each block, reducing the computational complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^log2(7)), approximately O(N^2.807).

metadata.title: Coppersmith-Winograd Algorithm
metadata.definition: Currently the asymptotically fastest known algorithm for matrix multiplication, achieving a complexity of O(N^2.3728596). While it offers a theoretical improvement over Strassen's algorithm, its extremely large constant factor makes it impractical for real-world matrix sizes.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Data Structures (General)
metadata.definition: Data structures that leverage randomization and hashing to achieve superior space or time complexity compared to their deterministic counterparts, at the cost of accepting a small, controlled probability of error (e.g., false positives or approximate answers). They are often employed when exactness is not strictly necessary or when resources are highly constrained.

metadata.title: Geometric Hashing
metadata.definition: An indexing technique primarily used in computer vision and computational geometry for efficient object or pattern recognition under geometric transformations such as rotation, translation, and scaling. It works by creating a hash table of invariant geometric features extracted from an object's reference frame, allowing for rapid retrieval during the recognition phase.

metadata.title: Branch Prediction (CPU Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A CPU algorithm designed to improve pipeline efficiency by predicting the outcome of conditional branches (e.g., if-statements, loops) before they are executed. By speculatively fetching and executing instructions along the predicted path, it minimizes costly pipeline stalls that would otherwise occur when waiting for branch conditions to resolve.

metadata.title: Cache-Oblivious Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms designed to perform well on a hierarchical memory system without needing to know the specific parameters (like cache size or block size) of any level of the memory hierarchy. They achieve this by exhibiting good locality of reference inherently, typically through a recursive, divide-and-conquer strategy that ensures efficient cache utilization across various memory levels.

metadata.title: Memoization
metadata.definition: An optimization technique where the results of expensive function calls are stored (cached) and returned when the same inputs occur again, thereby avoiding redundant computations. It is commonly applied in recursive functions and top-down dynamic programming to solve problems with overlapping subproblems.

metadata.title: Tabulation (Dynamic Programming)
metadata.definition: A bottom-up dynamic programming technique where solutions to subproblems are computed iteratively and stored, typically in a multi-dimensional array or table. It explicitly fills the table from the smallest subproblems up to the final solution, rather than relying on recursion and memoization.

metadata.title: Fairness in Algorithms
metadata.definition: The field of study and practice focused on designing and evaluating algorithms to ensure equitable outcomes and prevent discriminatory biases against certain groups, particularly in automated decision-making processes. It involves identifying sources of bias in data and models, defining various mathematical notions of fairness, and developing techniques to mitigate bias.

metadata.title: Privacy-Preserving Algorithms (Differential Privacy Concept)
metadata.definition: Algorithms engineered to analyze datasets and extract valuable insights while rigorously safeguarding the privacy of individual data subjects. Differential Privacy provides a strong mathematical guarantee that an individual's presence or absence from a dataset does not significantly alter the output of the analysis, thus protecting their sensitive information.

metadata.title: Blockchain Consensus Algorithms (Proof of Work Concept)
metadata.definition: Algorithms used in distributed blockchain networks to achieve agreement among participants on the shared state of the ledger, preventing issues like double-spending and ensuring transaction validity. Proof of Work (PoW) is a prominent type of consensus algorithm where participants (miners) expend significant computational effort to solve a cryptographic puzzle, thereby earning the right to propose and validate new blocks, securing the network.

metadata.title: Homomorphic Encryption (Algorithmic Concept)
metadata.definition: A form of encryption that permits computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without prior decryption, yielding an encrypted result that, when decrypted, is identical to the result of performing the same operations on the unencrypted data. This capability enables secure data processing in untrusted environments, such as cloud servers, while maintaining data privacy.

metadata.title: Quantum Annealing (Algorithmic Concept)
metadata.definition: A metaheuristic optimization algorithm that leverages quantum mechanical phenomena like quantum tunneling and superposition to find the global minimum of a function over a set of candidate solutions. It is particularly well-suited for solving complex optimization problems by slowly evolving a quantum system to its lowest energy state.

metadata.title: Variable Declaration
metadata.definition: The process of defining a variable's name and its data type before it's used, which also allocates a specific amount of memory to store its value. This establishes the variable's scope and type constraints.

metadata.title: Integer Data Type
metadata.definition: A fundamental data type used to store whole numbers (positive, negative, or zero) without any fractional part. It is typically used for counting or representing discrete quantities.

metadata.title: Floating Point Data Type
metadata.definition: A data type used to store numbers with fractional parts, often representing real numbers with a decimal point. They are typically used for calculations requiring precision beyond whole numbers.

metadata.title: Boolean Data Type
metadata.definition: A data type that can only hold one of two possible values: `true` or `false`, representing logical states. It is fundamental for control flow and decision-making within programs.

metadata.title: Character Data Type
metadata.definition: A data type used to store a single character, such as a letter, number, or symbol, typically enclosed in single quotes. It represents individual textual units.

metadata.title: String Data Type
metadata.definition: A data type used to store a sequence of characters, commonly representing text. In many programming languages, strings are considered immutable arrays of characters.

metadata.title: Type Casting
metadata.definition: The process of explicitly converting a value from one data type to another. This can be either a widening conversion (safe, e.g., int to double) or a narrowing conversion (potentially lossy, e.g., double to int).

metadata.title: Arithmetic Operator
metadata.definition: Symbols used to perform mathematical calculations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo on numeric values. They produce a numeric result.

metadata.title: Comparison Operator
metadata.definition: Symbols used to compare two values, resulting in a boolean (`true` or `false`) outcome based on their relationship. Common comparisons include equality, inequality, greater than, and less than.

metadata.title: Logical Operator
metadata.definition: Symbols used to combine or negate boolean expressions, producing a single boolean result (`true` or `false`). The primary logical operators are AND, OR, and NOT.

metadata.title: Assignment Operator
metadata.definition: A symbol used to assign a value to a variable. The most common is the equals sign (`=`), but compound assignment operators also exist (e.g., `+=`, `-=`) for shorthand operations.

metadata.title: Bitwise Operator
metadata.definition: Operators that perform operations directly on the individual bits (binary digits) of integer data types. They are used for low-level manipulation, such as setting, clearing, or flipping specific bits, and for efficient data packing.

metadata.title: Conditional Statement
metadata.definition: A programming construct that executes different blocks of code based on whether a specified boolean condition evaluates to true or false. The most common form is the `if-else` statement, enabling decision-making in programs.

metadata.title: Switch Statement
metadata.definition: A control flow statement that allows a variable or expression to be checked against multiple possible values (cases) and execute different code blocks based on a match. It provides an alternative to long `if-else if` chains for cleaner code.

metadata.title: For Loop
metadata.definition: A control flow statement that repeatedly executes a block of code a specific number of times. It typically consists of an initialization, a condition, and an iteration step, making it ideal for definite iterations.

metadata.title: While Loop
metadata.definition: A control flow statement that repeatedly executes a block of code as long as a specified boolean condition remains true. The condition is evaluated before each iteration, meaning the loop might not execute at all if the condition is initially false.

metadata.title: Do-While Loop
metadata.definition: A control flow statement that repeatedly executes a block of code at least once, and then continues as long as a specified boolean condition remains true. The condition is evaluated after each iteration, guaranteeing at least one execution.

metadata.title: Function Definition
metadata.definition: The complete block of code that specifies the behavior of a function, including its name, parameters, return type, and the statements it executes. It outlines what the function does and how it can be called.

metadata.title: Function Parameter
metadata.definition: A variable listed inside the parentheses of a function definition, used to receive values (arguments) passed into the function when it is called. Parameters act as local variables within the function's scope, allowing for flexible and reusable code.

metadata.title: Return Value
metadata.definition: The data that a function sends back to the part of the program that called it, after it has completed its execution. This value is specified by the function's return type and often represents the result of its computation.

metadata.title: Local Variable Scope
metadata.definition: The region of a program where a local variable is accessible, typically confined to the block, function, or method in which it is declared. Once the execution leaves that region, the variable is destroyed and its memory released.

metadata.title: Global Variable Scope
metadata.definition: The region of a program where a global variable is accessible throughout its entire execution, meaning it can be read and modified from any part of the code after its declaration. Global variables persist for the lifetime of the program.

metadata.title: Recursion
metadata.definition: A programming technique where a function calls itself, either directly or indirectly, to solve a problem by breaking it down into smaller, similar subproblems. It relies on a base case to terminate the sequence of calls and prevent infinite loops.

metadata.title: Base Case (Recursion)
metadata.definition: The non-recursive condition within a recursive function that defines when the function should stop calling itself and instead return a direct result. It is crucial for terminating recursion and preventing infinite loops.

metadata.title: Call Stack
metadata.definition: A stack data structure that stores information about the active subroutines (functions/methods) of a computer program. When a function is called, a new stack frame is pushed onto the stack; when it returns, its frame is popped off.

metadata.title: Memory Address (Pointer)
metadata.definition: A memory address is a unique identifier for a specific location in computer memory where data is stored. A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address, enabling indirect access to the data located at that address.

metadata.title: Reference (Programming)
metadata.definition: A mechanism that provides an alias or an alternative name for an existing variable or object, allowing indirect access to its data. Unlike pointers, references typically cannot be null or reassigned to point to a different object after initialization in many languages.

metadata.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: The process of allocating memory during program execution (runtime) rather than at compile time, allowing programs to manage memory resources more flexibly based on actual needs. This memory is typically allocated from the heap.

metadata.title: Heap Memory Management
metadata.definition: The process of managing a region of memory, known as the heap, where dynamically allocated data resides. Programmers or runtime environments are responsible for requesting memory blocks from the heap and releasing them when no longer needed to prevent memory leaks.

metadata.title: Stack Memory Management
metadata.definition: The process of managing a region of memory, known as the stack, which is primarily used for storing local variables, function parameters, and return addresses. Memory is automatically allocated when a function is called and deallocated when it returns, following a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: An automatic memory management technique that aims to reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program, thereby preventing memory leaks. It identifies and frees unused memory without explicit programmer intervention.

metadata.title: Manual Memory Management
metadata.definition: A programming approach where the developer explicitly handles the allocation and deallocation of memory resources. This requires careful tracking of memory usage to prevent both memory leaks (unfreed memory) and dangling pointers (accessing freed memory).

metadata.title: Error Code
metadata.definition: A numerical or symbolic value returned by a function or system call to indicate the success or failure of an operation, often providing specific information about the type of error encountered. Error codes require the caller to explicitly check and handle them.

metadata.title: Assertion (Programming)
metadata.definition: A declarative statement placed in a program to assert that a certain condition must be true at a specific point during execution. If the condition evaluates to false, the program typically terminates with an error, indicating a critical bug or unexpected state.

metadata.title: Standard Input
metadata.definition: A predefined data stream, typically originating from the keyboard or a file, that a program can read data from. It is one of the three standard I/O streams automatically available to most programs, represented by `stdin`.

metadata.title: Standard Output
metadata.definition: A predefined data stream, typically directed to the console or a file, where a program writes its normal output. It is one of the three standard I/O streams automatically available to most programs, represented by `stdout`.

metadata.title: File Input/Output
metadata.definition: The process of reading data from and writing data to files stored on a persistent storage device, such as a hard drive. It allows programs to store and retrieve information beyond their immediate runtime execution.

metadata.title: Command Line Argument
metadata.definition: Values supplied to a program when it is executed from the command line, allowing users to configure its behavior or provide initial data without requiring interactive input. These arguments are typically parsed by the program's main function.

metadata.title: Object (OOP)
metadata.definition: An instance of a class, representing a real-world entity or concept, that encapsulates data (attributes/properties) and behavior (methods/functions) into a single, self-contained unit. Objects interact with each other by sending messages or invoking methods.

metadata.title: Class (OOP)
metadata.definition: A blueprint or template for creating objects, defining their common structure (attributes/properties) and behavior (methods/functions). A class specifies the properties and actions that all objects of its type will possess.

metadata.title: Constructor (OOP)
metadata.definition: A special method in a class that is automatically called when an object of that class is created. Its primary purpose is to initialize the object's state (its fields or properties) and set up any necessary resources.

metadata.title: Destructor (OOP)
metadata.definition: A special method in a class that is automatically called when an object is about to be destroyed or deallocated from memory. Its main role is to perform cleanup tasks, such as releasing unmanaged resources like file handles or network connections.

metadata.title: Encapsulation (OOP)
metadata.definition: The bundling of data (attributes) and methods (functions) that operate on the data into a single unit (class), along with restricting direct access to some of an object's components. It hides the internal state and requires all interaction to occur via the object's public interface, promoting data integrity.

metadata.title: Inheritance (OOP)
metadata.definition: A mechanism where a new class (subclass or derived class) is created from an existing class (superclass or base class), allowing the new class to reuse, extend, or modify the attributes and behaviors of the existing class. It models an "is-a" relationship between classes, promoting code reusability and establishing a hierarchy.

metadata.title: Polymorphism (OOP)
metadata.definition: The ability of an object to take on many forms, enabling objects of different classes to be treated as objects of a common type. It primarily manifests as method overriding (runtime polymorphism) and method overloading (compile-time polymorphism), allowing a single interface to represent different underlying forms.

metadata.title: Abstraction (OOP)
metadata.definition: The process of simplifying complex reality by modeling classes based on the essential properties and behaviors required for a specific context, while hiding unnecessary details from the user. It focuses on "what" an object does rather than "how" it does it, reducing complexity and improving maintainability.

metadata.title: Interface (Programming)
metadata.definition: A contract that defines a set of methods (and sometimes properties/events) that a class must implement, without providing any implementation details. It specifies what an object can do, enabling polymorphism, enforcing common behavior, and allowing for loose coupling between components.

metadata.title: Abstract Class
metadata.definition: A class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain abstract methods (methods declared without an implementation) along with concrete methods and fields. It serves as a base class for other classes, providing a common interface and possibly some default behavior, while forcing subclasses to implement the abstract parts.

metadata.title: Method Overloading
metadata.definition: A feature that allows a class to have multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters). The compiler determines which specific method to call based on the arguments provided at compile time, demonstrating compile-time polymorphism.

metadata.title: Static Method
metadata.definition: A method that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. It can be called directly on the class name without creating an object, and it cannot access instance-specific data (non-static fields or methods) because it doesn't operate on a particular object.

metadata.title: Static Field
metadata.definition: A field (variable) that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. There is only one copy of a static field, shared by all instances of the class, and it can be accessed directly using the class name, making it suitable for representing class-wide data.

metadata.title: Functional Programming Paradigm
metadata.definition: A programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions and emphasizes immutability, pure functions, and higher-order functions. It seeks to avoid changing state and mutable data, leading to more predictable, testable, and concurrent-friendly code.

metadata.title: Pure Function
metadata.definition: A function that adheres to two main properties: given the same inputs, it will always return the same output (deterministic), and it produces no observable side effects. It relies only on its input parameters for computation and does not modify any external state or perform I/O that affects anything outside its scope.

metadata.title: Immutability (Programming)
metadata.definition: The principle that once an object or data structure is created, its internal state cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify an immutable object will instead return a new object with the desired changes, leaving the original object untouched. This enhances predictability, thread safety, and simplifies reasoning about program state.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Function
metadata.definition: A function that either takes one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function as its result, or both. They are fundamental to functional programming paradigms, enabling powerful abstractions, composition, and code reusability by treating functions as first-class citizens.

metadata.title: Lambda Expression
metadata.definition: A concise way to define an anonymous function (a function without a name) directly at the place where it is used. They are often used for short, one-time operations, particularly as arguments to higher-order functions or for creating closures, simplifying code by avoiding verbose function declarations.

metadata.title: First-Class Function
metadata.definition: A programming language concept where functions are treated as first-class citizens, meaning they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, returned from other functions, and stored in data structures, just like any other data type (e.g., numbers or strings). This enables flexible and powerful programming patterns like higher-order functions.

metadata.title: Side Effect (Programming)
metadata.definition: Any observable change to the system's state or behavior that occurs outside the local scope of a function, beyond returning a value. Common side effects include modifying a global variable, writing to a file, performing I/O operations, or mutating an object passed as an argument, making code harder to reason about and test.

metadata.title: Closure (Programming)
metadata.definition: A function that "remembers" its lexical environment (the scope in which it was declared) even after that environment has finished executing. This allows the function to access and manipulate variables from its outer scope, even when called from a different, unrelated scope, effectively 'closing over' those variables.

metadata.title: Decorator (Programming)
metadata.definition: A design pattern or language construct that allows behavior to be added to an existing object or function dynamically without modifying its structure. It typically involves wrapping a function or object with another function or object that provides additional functionality before or after the original call, enhancing it non-invasively.

metadata.title: Generics (Programming)
metadata.definition: Generics is a feature that allows writing code that can work with different data types without being rewritten for each type, promoting type safety and code reuse. It enables classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on types that are specified as parameters when the class, interface, or method is instantiated.

metadata.title: Static Type System
metadata.definition: A static type system is one where the types of variables, parameters, and expressions are checked at compile-time, before the program is run. This helps catch type-related errors early, improving reliability and often performance by reducing runtime type checks.

metadata.title: Dynamic Type System
metadata.definition: A dynamic type system is one where the types of variables are checked at runtime, rather than at compile-time. Variables hold values, and the type is associated with the value itself, allowing a variable to potentially hold values of different types over its lifetime.

metadata.title: Null Pointer Exception
metadata.definition: A Null Pointer Exception (NPE) is a runtime error that occurs when a program attempts to use a reference variable that currently points to no object (is null) as if it were pointing to an actual object. This typically happens when trying to access a member or invoke a method on a null reference.

metadata.title: Array Index Out of Bounds Exception
metadata.definition: An Array Index Out of Bounds Exception is a runtime error that occurs when a program attempts to access an array element using an index that is outside the valid range of indices for that array. Valid indices typically range from 0 to `length - 1` for an array of `length` elements.

metadata.title: Anonymous Function
metadata.definition: An anonymous function is a function that is not bound to an identifier (name). It is typically defined inline where it is used, often passed as an argument to another function, assigned to a variable, or returned as a value.

metadata.title: Dynamic Array
metadata.definition: A dynamic array is a data structure that behaves like an array but can automatically grow or shrink in size as elements are added or removed. Unlike a static array, it doesn't require a fixed size at initialization, offering more flexibility at the cost of potential reallocations.

metadata.title: Deque (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A Deque (Double-Ended Queue) is a linear data structure that supports adding and removing elements from both its front and rear ends. This allows it to efficiently function as both a queue (FIFO) and a stack (LIFO).

metadata.title: Hash Function
metadata.definition: A hash function is a mathematical function that takes an input (or 'key') of arbitrary size and returns a fixed-size output (or 'hash value' or 'hash code'), typically a smaller integer. Its primary purpose is to map keys to indices in a hash table or to quickly verify data integrity.

metadata.title: Chaining (Collision Resolution)
metadata.definition: Chaining is a collision resolution technique used in hash tables where each slot (or 'bucket') in the hash table array points to a linked list of all key-value pairs that hash to that same index. When a collision occurs, the new item is simply added to the linked list at the corresponding bucket.

metadata.title: Open Addressing (Collision Resolution)
metadata.definition: Open addressing is a collision resolution technique for hash tables where all elements are stored directly within the hash table array itself, rather than in separate data structures. If a collision occurs at a calculated index, the system probes for another open slot in the table using a predefined sequence until an empty slot is found.

metadata.title: Trie (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A Trie, also known as a prefix tree, is a tree-like data structure used to store a dynamic set or associative array where keys are typically strings. It efficiently retrieves keys by traversing the tree based on the characters of the key, making it highly suitable for tasks like autocomplete and spell checking.

metadata.title: Min-Heap
metadata.definition: A min-heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the min-heap property: for any given node `N`, the value of `N` is less than or equal to the value of its children. This property ensures that the smallest element is always at the root of the heap.

metadata.title: Max-Heap
metadata.definition: A max-heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the max-heap property: for any given node `N`, the value of `N` is greater than or equal to the value of its children. This property ensures that the largest element is always at the root of the heap.

metadata.title: Priority Queue
metadata.definition: A priority queue is an abstract data type similar to a regular queue or stack, but where each element has a 'priority' associated with it. Elements are dequeued based on their priority, typically with the highest (or lowest) priority element served first, rather than strict FIFO or LIFO order.

metadata.title: Graph (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of a finite set of vertices (or nodes) and a set of edges connecting pairs of these vertices. It is used to model pairwise relationships between objects, representing networks and connections.

metadata.title: Disjoint Set Union
metadata.definition: Disjoint Set Union (DSU), also known as Union-Find, is a data structure that maintains a collection of disjoint (non-overlapping) sets and supports two primary operations: finding the representative of the set an element belongs to, and uniting (merging) two sets into one. It is highly optimized for these operations.

metadata.title: Set (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A set is an abstract data type that stores a collection of unique elements, with no particular order. It typically supports operations like adding an element, removing an element, checking for membership, and performing mathematical set operations such as union, intersection, and difference.

metadata.title: Map (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A map, also known as an associative array or dictionary, is an abstract data type that stores a collection of key-value pairs, where each key is unique and maps to exactly one value. It allows for efficient retrieval, insertion, and deletion of values based on their associated keys.

metadata.title: Worst-Case Complexity Analysis
