metadata.title: Halting Problem
metadata.definition: The Halting Problem is a famous undecidable decision problem asking whether, given a description of an arbitrary computer program and an arbitrary input, one can determine if the program will finish running or continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can solve the Halting Problem for all possible program-input pairs.

metadata.title: Reduction (Computability)
metadata.definition: In computability and complexity theory, a reduction is an algorithm that transforms instances of one problem (Problem A) into instances of another problem (Problem B). If Problem A can be reduced to Problem B, then solving Problem B can be used to solve Problem A, implying that Problem B is 'at least as hard' as Problem A.

metadata.title: Online Algorithms (General Concept)
metadata.definition: Online algorithms are algorithms that process their input piece-by-piece in a serial fashion, without having the entire input available at the start. They must make decisions locally at each step, based only on the information processed so far, without knowledge of future input.

metadata.title: Competitive Analysis (Online Algorithms)
metadata.definition: Competitive analysis is a method for evaluating the performance of online algorithms by comparing their output to that of an optimal offline algorithm, which has full knowledge of the entire input in advance. The competitive ratio is defined as the worst-case ratio of the online algorithm's cost to the optimal offline algorithm's cost.

metadata.title: External Memory Algorithm
metadata.definition: External memory algorithms (or out-of-core algorithms) are designed to process data that is too large to fit into a computer's main memory (RAM). These algorithms optimize for minimizing accesses to slower external storage devices, such as hard drives or SSDs, often by exploiting principles like locality and sequential access.

metadata.definition: Streaming algorithms are a class of online algorithms designed to process massive amounts of data sequentially, typically making only one or a few passes over the data. Definition: A mechanism where a new class (subclass or derived class) is created from an existing class (superclass or base class), allowing the new class to reuse, extend, or modify the attributes and behaviors of the existing class. It models an "is-a" relationship between classes, promoting code reusability and establishing a hierarchy.

metadata.title: Polymorphism (OOP)
metadata.definition: The ability of an object to take on many forms, enabling objects of different classes to be treated as objects of a common type. It primarily manifests as method overriding (runtime polymorphism) and method overloading (compile-time polymorphism), allowing a single interface to represent different underlying forms.

metadata.title: Abstraction (OOP)

It focuses on "what" an object does rather than "how" it does it, reducing complexity and improving maintainability.

metadata.title: Static Method
metadata.definition: A method that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. It can be called directly on the class name without creating an object, and it cannot access instance-specific data (non-static fields or methods) because it doesn't operate on a particular object.

metadata.title: Pure Function
metadata.definition: A function that adheres to two main properties: given the same inputs, it will always return the same output (deterministic), and it produces no observable side effects. It relies only on its input parameters for computation and does not modify any external state or perform I/O that affects anything outside its scope.

metadata.title: Immutability (Programming)
metadata.definition: The principle that once an object or data structure is created, its internal state cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify an immutable object will instead return a new object with the desired changes, leaving the original object untouched. This enhances predictability, thread safety, and simplifies reasoning about program state.

metadata.title: Side Effect (Programming)
metadata.definition: Any observable change to the system's state or behavior that occurs outside the local scope of a function, beyond returning a value. Common side effects include modifying a global variable, writing to a file, performing I/O operations, or mutating an object passed as an argument, making code harder to reason about and test.

metadata.title: Closure (Programming)
metadata.definition: A function that "remembers" its lexical environment (the scope in which it was declared) even after that environment has finished executing. This allows the function to access and manipulate variables from its outer scope, even when called from a different, unrelated scope, effectively 'closing over' those variables.

It typically supports operations like adding an element, removing an element, checking for membership, and performing mathematical set operations such as union, intersection, and difference.

metadata.title: Map (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A map, also known as an associative array or dictionary, is an abstract data type that stores a collection of key-value pairs, where each key is unique and maps to exactly one value. It allows for efficient retrieval, insertion, and deletion of values based on their associated keys.

metadata.title: Worst-Case Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Worst-case complexity analysis is a method used to determine the maximum amount of resources (time or space) an algorithm will use for any input of a given size. It provides an upper bound on the algorithm's performance, guaranteeing that the algorithm will not take longer or use more memory than this bound, regardless of the specific input arrangement.

metadata.title: Bubble Sort Algorithm
metadata.definition: Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The pass through the list is repeated until no swaps are needed, indicating the list is sorted.

metadata.title: Selection Sort Algorithm

metadata.definition: Merge Sort is an efficient, comparison-based, divide and conquer sorting algorithm. metadata.title: Quick Sort Algorithm
metadata.definition: Quick Sort is an efficient, in-place, comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a divide and conquer strategy. metadata.title: Context-Free Grammar (CFG)
metadata.definition: A formal grammar in which every production rule is of the form V → w, where V is a single non-terminal symbol and w is a string of terminals and/or non-terminals. CFGs are fundamental for defining the syntax of programming languages and are recognized by pushdown automata.

metadata.title: Pushdown Automaton
metadata.definition: A type of automaton that extends a finite automaton with a stack, enabling it to recognize context-free languages. It can push and pop symbols from the stack, allowing it to remember an unbounded amount of information about the input seen so far, making it suitable for parsing nested structures.

metadata.title: NP Complexity Class

metadata.title: NP-Completeness
metadata.definition: A property of decision problems that are both in NP and are NP-hard. This means they are among the 'hardest' problems in NP; if any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then all problems in NP can be solved in polynomial time (implying P=NP).

metadata.title: NP-Hardness
metadata.definition: A property of problems that are at least as hard as any problem in NP. A problem H is NP-hard if every problem L in NP can be reduced to H in polynomial time, meaning H is at least as computationally challenging as all NP problems. NP-hard problems do not necessarily have to be in NP themselves.

It supports two atomic operations, `wait` (or `P` or `acquire`) and `signal` (or `V` or `release`), to manage a counter that represents available resources.

metadata.title: Monitor (Synchronization)
metadata.definition: A high-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared data and the procedures that operate on that data, ensuring only one process or thread can be active within the monitor at any given time. It simplifies concurrent programming by automatically handling mutual exclusion and providing condition variables for more complex synchronization.

metadata.title: Deadlock (OS)
metadata.definition: A situation in a multi-process or multi-thread system where two or more processes are permanently blocked because each is waiting for the other to release a resource. Deadlocks occur when four conditions are simultaneously met: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

metadata.title: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A strategy for preventing deadlocks by dynamically analyzing resource-allocation requests to ensure that the system always remains in a 'safe state.' The Banker's Algorithm, a prominent example, checks if granting a resource request would lead to an unsafe state where a deadlock could eventually occur, and only grants the request if the state remains safe.

metadata.title: Deadlock Detection
metadata.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks by allowing the system to enter a deadlocked state, then periodically running an algorithm to identify deadlocked processes and resolve the situation. Once detected, the system typically recovers by preempting resources or terminating one or more processes involved in the deadlock.

metadata.title: CPU Scheduling
metadata.definition: The process of determining which process or thread will execute on the CPU next, and for how long, from the set of ready-to-run processes. Its primary goal is to maximize CPU utilization, throughput, and minimize turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.

metadata.title: First-Come, First-Served Scheduling
metadata.definition: A non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm where processes are executed strictly in the order they arrive in the ready queue. It is simple to implement but can lead to long waiting times if a long process arrives before several short ones, a phenomenon known as the convoy effect.

metadata.title: Shortest Job Next Scheduling
metadata.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the smallest estimated execution time to be executed next. It aims to minimize the average waiting time and average turnaround time for a given set of processes but requires accurate prediction of future CPU burst times.

metadata.title: Priority Scheduling
metadata.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm where each process is assigned a priority, and the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority. It can be preemptive (where a high-priority process can interrupt a low-priority one) or non-preemptive, but it commonly suffers from the potential issue of starvation for low-priority processes.

metadata.title: Round Robin Scheduling

metadata.title: Shared Memory (IPC)
metadata.definition: An IPC mechanism where multiple processes can access the same region of physical memory. This allows for very fast data exchange as processes don't need to copy data through the kernel, but requires careful synchronization to prevent race conditions.

Each layer performs specific tasks and communicates with the layers directly above and below it, facilitating interoperability and modular design.

metadata.title: Isolation (ACID)

metadata.title: Locking (Database)
metadata.definition: A concurrency control mechanism where a database object (like a row, table, or page) is marked as 'in-use' by a transaction, preventing other transactions from accessing or modifying it until the lock is released. Locks can be shared (allowing multiple reads) or exclusive (allowing only one write or read).

metadata.title: Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY Principle)
metadata.definition: A software development principle stating that every piece of knowledge or logic should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. Its goal is to reduce redundancy and improve maintainability by avoiding duplicate code.

metadata.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
metadata.definition: A SOLID principle stating that a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change. This means each class should be responsible for a single part of the functionality, leading to better organization and easier modification.

metadata.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

metadata.definition: A SOLID principle stating that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Instead of one large, 'fat' interface, it is better to have many smaller, role-specific interfaces, promoting clearer contracts and reducing unintended coupling.

metadata.title: Git Commit
metadata.definition: A snapshot of the changes made to the repository's files at a specific point in time, along with a message describing those changes. Each commit forms a distinct point in the project's history, allowing you to revert or compare versions.

This operation is unary and is primarily used for clarity, to resolve ambiguity in queries involving multiple instances of the same relation (self-joins), or to make relations union-compatible for set operations.

metadata.title: Division Operation (Relational Algebra)
metadata.definition: The Division operation (R ÷ S) in relational algebra is a powerful operation used to find tuples in one relation (R) that are associated with *all* tuples in another relation (S). It is defined for relations R(A, B) and S(B) where A and B are sets of attributes; the result is a relation containing attributes A, with tuples (a) such that for all tuples (b) in S, the tuple (a, b) exists in R.

metadata.title: Functional Dependency
metadata.definition: A Functional Dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation, typically expressed as X → Y. It states that if two tuples have the same values for attributes in set X, then they must also have the same values for attributes in set Y; essentially, X uniquely determines Y.

metadata.title: Trivial Functional Dependency
metadata.definition: A Trivial Functional Dependency (TFD) is a functional dependency X → Y where Y is a subset of X (Y ⊆ X). These dependencies are always true and provide no additional information about the relationships between attributes, as the values for Y are inherently determined by X if Y is part of X.

metadata.title: ROLLBACK Statement
metadata.definition: The ROLLBACK statement is a Transaction Control Language (TCL) command that undoes all changes performed during the current transaction since its beginning or since the last SAVEPOINT, restoring the database to a previous consistent state. This ensures the 'A' (Atomicity) in ACID properties, preventing partial updates from being permanently saved.

metadata.title: SAVEPOINT Statement

metadata.title: RAID 0
metadata.definition: RAID 0 (Striping) is a RAID level that stripes data across multiple disks, distributing data blocks sequentially. It provides improved performance by allowing simultaneous read/write operations but offers no data redundancy or fault tolerance; the failure of any single disk results in complete data loss.

metadata.title: RAID 1
metadata.definition: RAID 1 (Mirroring) is a RAID level that mirrors data identically across two or more disks, creating an exact copy of the data on each drive. It offers excellent fault tolerance and read performance, as data can be read from any disk, but at the cost of storage capacity (50% efficiency for two disks).

metadata.title: RAID 5
metadata.definition: RAID 5 (Striping with Parity) is a RAID level that stripes data at a block level across a minimum of three disks and distributes parity information among all disks in the array. It provides a good balance of performance, storage capacity (N-1 disks worth), and fault tolerance, as the array can withstand the failure of any single disk without data loss.

It is typically accessed via APIs over HTTP and designed for massive scalability and cost-effectiveness with unstructured data.

It evaluates various possible execution strategies, considering factors like join orders, index usage, and access paths, to minimize resource consumption (e.g., I/O, CPU time).

Transactions must adhere to the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) to ensure data integrity and reliability.

metadata.title: Lost Update Problem
metadata.definition: The Lost Update Problem is a concurrency anomaly where an update made by one transaction is overwritten and effectively disappears due to another concurrent transaction updating the same data item. This leads to data inconsistency, as one of the updates is permanently lost.

metadata.definition: The Dirty Read Problem, also known as reading uncommitted data, occurs when one transaction reads data that has been modified by another transaction but not yet committed. If the second transaction later rolls back, the data read by the first transaction becomes invalid or 'dirty', leading to incorrect conclusions.

metadata.definition: The Non-Repeatable Read Problem is a concurrency anomaly where a transaction reads the same data item twice during its execution and observes different values. metadata.title: Phantom Read Problem

This happens because another *committed* transaction inserted or deleted rows that satisfy the query's `WHERE` clause between the two reads.

metadata.title: Conflict Serializability
metadata.definition: Conflict serializability is a property of a schedule of concurrent transactions where its effect is equivalent to some serial schedule (where transactions execute one after another in some order) by preserving the order of all conflicting operations. Conflicting operations involve at least one write operation and refer to the same data item (e.g., read-write, write-read, write-write).

metadata.title: View Serializability
metadata.definition: View serializability is a property of a schedule of concurrent transactions where its effect is equivalent to some serial schedule. It ensures that for every transaction in the schedule, it reads the same initial values, sees the same sequence of updates, and produces the same final write values as it would in some serial execution, making it a weaker condition than conflict serializability.

metadata.title: Strict Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
metadata.definition: A concurrency control protocol that requires transactions to acquire all locks before releasing any, and holds all exclusive (write) locks until after the transaction commits or aborts, ensuring both serializability and strict recoverability. This prevents cascading rollbacks and guarantees that only committed changes are visible.

metadata.title: Timestamp Ordering Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: A concurrency control protocol that assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and orders operations based on these timestamps to ensure serializability. Transactions are allowed to proceed only if their operations maintain the timestamp order of conflicting operations, potentially aborting transactions that violate this order.

metadata.definition: A concurrency control method that maintains multiple versions of data items, allowing read operations to access older, consistent versions without blocking write operations, and write operations to create new versions. This minimizes read-write conflicts, improves concurrency, and often enables snapshot isolation.

metadata.definition: A concurrency control approach that assumes conflicts between concurrent transactions are highly likely, and therefore prevents conflicts by acquiring locks on data items before operations are performed. This strategy prioritizes data consistency and integrity by blocking transactions until locks are released.

metadata.title: Serializable Isolation Level

metadata.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
metadata.definition: A standard technique for ensuring atomicity and durability in database systems, where all changes to the database are first recorded in a persistent log file before being applied to the actual data files. This ensures that in case of a crash, changes can be recovered (redo) or undone (undo) based on the log, maintaining data integrity.

metadata.title: Checkpoint (Database)
metadata.definition: A mechanism in database recovery that periodically flushes all dirty (modified) data pages from memory to disk and records the current state in the transaction log. Checkpoints reduce the amount of work required during recovery by limiting the portion of the log that needs to be scanned for redo and undo operations after a system crash.

metadata.title: Shadow Paging

All updates are applied to new physical pages, and only upon commit is the shadow page directory atomically swapped to become the current directory, ensuring atomicity and durability without explicit undo/redo logging.

metadata.title: Duck Typing
metadata.definition: Duck typing is a style of dynamic typing where the suitability of an object for a particular use is determined by the presence of certain methods or properties, rather than by its explicit type or class inheritance. The idiom is 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, then it must be a duck.'

metadata.title: Type Compatibility
metadata.definition: Type compatibility refers to the rules that determine whether a value of one data type can be used where a value of another data type is expected without causing a type error. This often involves subtyping, implicit conversions, or explicit casting.

metadata.title: Type Conversion
metadata.definition: Type conversion is the process of changing a value from one data type to another. This can occur either implicitly (type coercion) by the compiler or runtime, or explicitly (type casting) through programmer instruction.

metadata.title: Generics (Parametric Polymorphism)
metadata.definition: Generics, also known as parametric polymorphism, is a feature that allows code to be written to work with types that are specified as parameters, rather than fixed types. This enables the creation of reusable code components that maintain type safety across different data types.

metadata.title: Covariance (Type Theory)
metadata.definition: Covariance in type theory means that if `A` is a subtype of `B`, then a generic type `G<A>` is considered a subtype of `G<B>`. This relationship typically applies to 'producer' contexts, such as return types, where values are only read from the generic type.

metadata.definition: Contravariance in type theory means that if `A` is a subtype of `B`, then a generic type `G<B>` is considered a subtype of `G<A>`. This 'reverse' relationship typically applies to 'consumer' contexts, such as parameter types, where values are only written into the generic type.

metadata.title: Algebraic Data Type (ADT)
metadata.definition: An Algebraic Data Type (ADT) is a composite data type built from other types, typically representing either a sum of types (tagged unions/enums) or a product of types (records/structs). ADTs provide a structured way to define complex data structures using fundamental type constructors.

metadata.title: Sum Type
metadata.definition: A sum type is an Algebraic Data Type that represents a value which can be one of several different types, but only one at any given time. It is often referred to as a tagged union, discriminated union, or variant type, and typically involves pattern matching for handling its different cases.

metadata.title: Tail Call Optimization
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization technique where a tail call is transformed into a simple jump, preventing the allocation of a new stack frame for the called function. This optimization saves memory by reusing the current stack frame, effectively turning tail recursion into efficient iteration and avoiding stack overflows.

metadata.title: Mark-Sweep Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: A two-phase garbage collection algorithm. In the 'mark' phase, the collector traverses the object graph starting from root references to identify all reachable (live) objects. In the 'sweep' phase, it then iterates through the entire heap, reclaiming memory from all unmarked (unreachable) objects and making it available for future allocations.

metadata.title: Copying Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm that divides the heap into two or more regions, typically called 'from-space' and 'to-space'. During collection, it copies all live objects from the 'from-space' to the 'to-space', compacting them contiguously, and then the entire 'from-space' is discarded. This method naturally prevents fragmentation.

metadata.title: Generational Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: An optimization strategy for garbage collection based on the 'weak generational hypothesis', which states that most objects die young, and old objects are likely to stay alive longer. The heap is divided into different generations (e.g., young, old), with young generations collected more frequently using faster algorithms, while older generations are collected less often using more robust but slower algorithms.

metadata.title: Reference Counting Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: A garbage collection technique where each object maintains a count of references pointing to it. When the reference count drops to zero, the object is considered unreachable and its memory is automatically reclaimed. This method is relatively simple but cannot collect cyclic data structures unless augmented with other techniques.

metadata.title: Green Thread
metadata.definition: A type of thread managed entirely by the user-level runtime system or library, rather than by the operating system kernel. Fibers allow explicit control over scheduling and context switching, enabling very fine-grained and efficient task switching without kernel involvement, making them suitable for high-performance I/O operations.

metadata.title: Starvation (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A condition in concurrent programming where a particular process or thread repeatedly loses the race for a shared resource or CPU time, indefinitely preventing it from making progress. This can happen due to unfair scheduling policies, persistent contention, or biased resource allocation, effectively blocking the starved entity from ever executing.

metadata.title: Orthogonality (Language Design)

metadata.title: Simplicity (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Simplicity, as a language design principle, advocates for a small number of basic constructs and features, with minimal exceptions, special cases, or redundant ways to achieve the same task. A simple language is generally easier to learn, understand, implement, and maintain, reducing the cognitive load on developers.

metadata.title: Safety (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Safety in programming language design refers to the degree to which a language prevents invalid operations or unintended program behaviors, thereby contributing to program correctness and integrity. This often involves robust mechanisms for type checking, memory management, and error handling to reduce the likelihood of bugs and security vulnerabilities.

metadata.title: Turing Completeness
metadata.definition: Turing completeness is a property of a computational system (such as a programming language or an abstract machine) indicating that it can simulate any arbitrary Turing machine. A Turing-complete system is theoretically capable of performing any computation that a computer can perform, given enough time and memory.

metadata.title: Type Theory
metadata.definition: Type theory is a branch of mathematical logic, computer science, and philosophy that studies formal systems involving types, particularly as they apply to programming languages. It provides a rigorous framework for designing, analyzing, and proving properties about type systems, ensuring program correctness, safety, and consistent behavior.

metadata.title: Programming Language Specification
metadata.definition: A programming language specification is a formal or informal document that precisely defines the syntax, semantics, and often the standard library of a programming language. It serves as the definitive reference for language implementers (e.g., compiler or interpreter writers) and users, ensuring consistency across different implementations and understanding of language behavior.

metadata.title: Dependent Type
metadata.definition: A dependent type is a type whose definition depends on a value, meaning that types can embed information known only at runtime or derived from program logic. This allows for incredibly expressive and precise type systems, enabling the compiler or type checker to prove complex properties about programs, extending well beyond traditional static typing.

metadata.title: Linear Type
metadata.definition: A linear type is a feature in a type system that ensures a resource or value typed as 'linear' is used exactly once: it must be consumed and neither discarded nor duplicated. This property is primarily used to manage unique resources safely, prevent unwanted side effects from uncontrolled aliasing, and enable more precise control over memory or I/O operations.

metadata.title: Gradual Typing
metadata.definition: Gradual typing is a type system that allows a programming language to support both static and dynamic typing within the same codebase, enabling a smooth transition between flexible prototyping and robust, type-checked code. It typically allows dynamically typed code to interact with statically typed code through runtime type checks at their boundaries.

metadata.title: Isomorphism (Type Theory)
metadata.definition: In type theory, two types A and B are isomorphic if there exist two functions, f: A → B and g: B → A, such that composing them in either direction yields the identity function (g(f(x)) = x and f(g(y)) = y). This signifies that the types are structurally equivalent and can be converted into each other without any loss of information.

metadata.title: Dependency Management
metadata.definition: Dependency management is the process of identifying, acquiring, configuring, and updating external libraries, frameworks, or modules (dependencies) that a software project relies on. It ensures that all necessary components are available in the correct versions for the project to build, run, and function correctly.

metadata.title: Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL)
metadata.definition: A REPL is an interactive programming environment that repeatedly reads a single user input, evaluates it, prints the result, and then loops to await the next input. It provides immediate feedback, making it a valuable tool for experimentation, learning, debugging, and rapid prototyping.

metadata.title: Debugger
metadata.definition: A debugger is a software tool used to test and debug target programs by monitoring their execution, allowing developers to set breakpoints, step through code line by line, inspect variable values, and examine memory states. It is essential for identifying and resolving logical errors (bugs) within an application.

metadata.title: Profiler (Programming)
metadata.definition: A profiler is a software tool that analyzes the performance characteristics of a program, measuring resource usage such as execution time, memory consumption, CPU cycles, and function call frequencies. Its primary goal is to help developers identify performance bottlenecks and areas for optimization within an application.

metadata.title: Static Analysis Tool
metadata.definition: A static analysis tool examines source code or compiled code without executing it, to detect potential bugs, security vulnerabilities, and deviations from coding standards. It helps improve code quality, reliability, and security early in the development lifecycle by identifying issues before runtime.
